summary: The Mathematics of 3D Printing Slicing: STL Geometry, Ray-Casting & Toolpaths is an open-access engineering monograph and interactive instructional module published by the Prep4Uni.Online OER Initiative . This work provides an analytical, undergraduate/postgraduate-level treatment of the computational geometry foundations required to translate three-dimensional surface meshes into layer-by-layer machine toolpaths. Aligned with international accreditation standards—specifically the Washington Accord (WA1–WA5) and EUR-ACE First/Second Cycle frameworks—this publication establishes the mathematical proofs, vector algorithms, and point-in-polygon logic governing modern additive manufacturing slicing software. Core Mathematical & Computational Themes: STL Topology & Facet Representation: Analysis of unstructured triangulated surface meshes, outward unit normal vectors (\(\mathbf{n}\)), vertex coordinate systems, and planar boundary extraction. Parametric Facet-Plane Intersection: Step-by-step vector linear interpolation for deriving the intersection segment \(S_k\) formed by cutting planes at \(z = z_k\), addressing non-manifold edges, vertex touching, and numerical epsilon shifts. Jordan Curve Theorem & Parity Logic: Formal implementation of the 2D Ray-Casting algorithm and Even-Odd Parity test for robust interior, exterior, and internal void classification across arbitrary closed slices. Toolpath Trajectory Generation: Comparative kinematics and geometry between continuous concentric perimeter offset loops and 45° zigzag parallel hatch raster patterns. Formative Assessment Suite: A three-tier verification suite comprising 8 foundational concepts, 7 real-world slicer failure debugging scenarios, and 6 step-by-step quantitative engineering worked examples. Note: The full interactive web edition—featuring client-side HTML5 simulation canvas engines, dynamic parameter sliders, and real-time slice projection mathematics—is accessible at: https://prep4uni.online/stem/physical-technologies/industrial-and-manufacturing-technologies/additive-manufacturing-3d-printing/mathematics-of-slicing/
title: The Mathematics of 3D Printing Slicing: STL Geometry, Ray-Casting & Toolpaths

summary: This replication package contains the experimental artifacts, anonymized empirical benchmark dataset (N = 5,000 paired student-opportunity records), statistical verification scripts, database definitions, and microservices source code for the research paper: "Hybrid Vector-Temporal Matching for Student Freelance Placement: An Empirical Study of Database-Level Vector Offloading" Targeted for Information and Software Technology (IST, Elsevier). Package Contents: data/: Anonymized benchmark dataset (students_data_tesis_final.csv) featuring 168-hour weekly availability matrices and raw ablation output. benchmarks/: Automated Python scripts for Stratified 5-fold cross-validation ablation (C1 to C4), Wilcoxon Signed-Rank hypothesis testing, Cliff's Delta effect size calculation, and bootstrap confidence intervals. database/: PostgreSQL 16 schema and stored procedure definitions for HNSW Approximate Nearest Neighbor vector search (pgvector) and dynamic schedule intersection. turborepo-src/: Clean source code of the decoupled microservices monorepo (API Gateway, Matching Service, ML Engine, and shared Protocol Buffers). System Requirements: Python 3.10+ with NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, Scikit-Learn, and NLTK. Node.js v20+ / pnpm v9+ and Docker Engine for microservice orchestration.
title: Replication Package: Hybrid Vector-Temporal Matching for Student Freelance Placement

summary: We have presented a mathematically closed, comprehensive foundation for the C861 discrete spectral benchmark. By establishing the exact rank-two projector geometry, resolving Dirichlet sum cancellations, providing constructive proofs for linear B-spline KAN operator reproduction, and formalizing the Lyapunov convergence of Dense Associative Memory on spherical manifolds, this framework eliminates ambiguities in evaluating learned physical operators. Furthermore, the spectral interlacing analysis of the CN → PN structural homotopy equips the scientific machine learning community with a tool to distinguish authentic topological sensitivity from numerical discretization artifacts.
title: Exact Discrete Spectral Invariants as a Falsification Baseline for Learned Operator

summary: Level-2 (restricted) archive, version 1.0.1, of the replication package of the article Auditing successor selection in software repository mining: Evidence from filtering AI-attributed commits (H. Jeong, Hanyang University ERICA; manuscript under review). Changes in 1.0.1: two files with the per-identity counts of the exploratory published-measure analysis (file-based churn, cohort B; Supplementary Section S13 of the article) were added, re-keyed like the other cohort-B files; every file of version 1.0.0 is unchanged. The files are per-unit derived counts of the 3,687 cohort-A accounts and the cohort-B identities, with random identifiers (marker dates reduced to the month; no account names, e-mail addresses, repository names, commit SHAs or commit times). Access is restricted because cohort-B rows keep the positions of their repositories in the public sampling order, which the registered repository-cluster bootstrap needs. Changes in 1.0.3: an exploratory analysis applies the fixed-anchor audit to a published file-based churn measure in cohort B ( jss_v2/exploratory_v37/ : the dated plan of 2026-10-17, whose SHA-256 is recorded in both deviation logs, the program w2_file_churn.py and its tests; aggregate results in jss_v2/results/v37/ ). The supplement (version 3.7) adds Section S13 with Tables S58 to S60 and names the exploratory convention for the anchor's own block the anchor-retained convention; the figure programs label that convention accordingly and write 800-dpi RGB TIFF files, with unchanged figure data. reproduce.py runs the new tests, checks the hash of the second dated plan and, with --level2 , recomputes the new aggregate from version 1.0.1 of the Level-2 archive. The registered code and every aggregate result of version 1.0.2 are unchanged, so the SHA-256 values registered in OSF hyf36 and 7jasg still match. Contents: the audit tool (Python, standard library only) with its 47 automated tests and a synthetic example; the registered analysis programs, whose SHA-256 values match those registered in OSF hyf36 (cohort A) and OSF 7jasg (cohort B); the exploratory programs with the dated plans of 2026-10-08 and 2026-10-17 and the record-level conformance checker; aggregate results for every table and figure; the deviation logs of both registrations; the 22-study literature evidence matrix; the cohort-B sampling frame and collection programs; and the generators of the supplement and the figures. Run python3 reproduce.py (Python 3.10 or later, numpy, matplotlib and git). It checks the registered hashes, runs the tests and the synthetic example, and regenerates the supplement tables and the figure data from the aggregate results. With --level2 <folder> it also recomputes, from the restricted per-unit files of the Level-2 archive (version 1.0.1: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23430270), every registered aggregate and every exploratory aggregate that does not require the source commit logs, and compares every regenerated file with the shipped result. summary: Reproducibility package for the manuscript Coordinated Optimization of Microgrid Power Purchase and Energy Storage under Information-Temporal Constraints (Junjie Chen, Yu Liu, Ziyan Wang), submitted to Transactions on Energy Systems and Engineering Applications . The archive contains: (i) the solver and forecasting source code, including the entries that re-solve the whole evaluation period from the raw data files, export the per-slot quantities and re-check the evaluation period independently of the solver; (ii) the four case data files as released with the 2026 China Undergraduate Mathematical Contest in Modeling, Problem C; (iii) the daily result tables for the four information structures; and (iv) the verification outputs, comprising the pointwise physical verification over 192,384 strategy intervals, the independent cost back-calculation, the future-data and same-slot perturbation archives, and the strictly executable re-executions with their acceptance checks. Reproduction: unpack the archive and run the commands listed in README.txt from the archive root. Every script locates the archive root from its own position and uses no absolute path. A single structure takes about 15-20 minutes on one desktop core. Evaluation-period costs under the strictly executable protocol: 23.2305 million CNY (structure B, frozen day-ahead plan), 20.0279 (C, rolling adjustment), 24.5852 (D-B) and 20.5285 (D-C). The idealized-reference values reported alongside in the manuscript are 22.4599, 19.3188, 23.8493 and 19.8623 million CNY.

summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23432006 . The paper (arXiv 2610.21914) is a pre-registered study of 465 merged agent-authored pull requests from 246 repositories (Sections 3.2-3.5). A frozen pipeline of four review agents and one fix agent ran every PR with three LLMs, and one mixed model per LLM tests CodeHealth against log total tokens (Sections 3.6-3.9). Each CodeHealth point goes with 3.5% to 6.1% lower token cost (Section 4.2, Table 8), but adding the size of the scored files absorbs the coefficient (Section 4.6.4, Table 15). I liked the handling of the pre-registration: the disclosure that review sessions started before filing, the amendment with a full re-collection of the 67 affected PRs (Section 3.12), and the file-size refit that weakens your own headline. I read it as a practitioner who runs coding agents every day. In my company the software development is done by AI agents, so maybe my practical side is useful here. Four comments. 1. On heavy tails (Sections 3.9, 4.2) - you note that one pilot PR was about 45% of a tier's mean token total, while in the main collection no PR exceeded 8.2% of a tier's token sum. In my measurement of 722 agent sessions (150,902 model calls, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22759216), about 3% of sessions gave 80% of the modeled cost. Sessions longer than 200 calls (8% of sessions) gave more than 90% of the money. So in my data the average is driven by a thin tail. What share of each LLM's tokens comes from the top 10% of PRs, and does the CodeHealth slope hold without them? 2. On cache and price (Section 3.8, Table 4, Section 6.3) - the outcome is input plus output tokens, with cached input recorded separately. In the same 722 sessions, more than 85% of the modeled cost was work with context (cache reads and cache writes). In a separate run of 168 sessions, 94.4% of billed tokens were re-reading context already sent (contextburn, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22712985). That is a share of tokens, not of the bill, because cached reads are the cheapest tokens. So a raw token total and a bill can rank PRs differently. Could you refit H1 with cached input priced at each provider's cache-read rate? 3. On paging long files (Sections 3.6, 5.2, 3.13) - the paper links the extra iterations to the 500-line limit per read call. In my guides I write that quality drops as the agent's context fills, and that heavy reading should go to a subagent so the main conversation stays clean. Since tool results are appended to the message history (Section 3.6), paging the median unhealthy-tier file of 2,146 lines puts every page into history that is re-sent on every later call. From the session records, can you count file-read calls and repeat reads of the same file per tier? That would test the paging explanation directly. 4. On the cost of what (Sections 5.5, 5.6, 6.3) - the study does not assess whether comments are correct or fixes are good. In my guides I write that every task needs its own check the agent can run. Without it, "looks done" is the only signal the agent has. I also use a second, fresh agent whose job is to refute the first one, because AI sounds equally sure when it is right and when it is wrong. For the 27-PR replication subsample (Section 3.11), you could run the repository tests after the fix and have a fresh agent try to refute each comment. Tokens per surviving finding would be a cheap first step toward Section 5.6. Thank you for a clear and useful paper. Competing interests Yes: the text cites the author's own technical reports (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22759216, 10.5281/zenodo.22712985); no connection to the article's authors. Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) The author declares that they used generative AI to come up with new ideas for their review.
title: PREreview of "CodeHealth Predicts the Token Cost of Agentic Code Review: A Pre-Registered Study of 465 Agent-Authored Pull Requests"

A frozen pipeline of four review agents and one fix agent ran every PR with three LLMs, and one mixed model per LLM tests CodeHealth against log total tokens (Sections 3.6-3.9). Each CodeHealth point goes with 3.5% to 6.1% lower token cost (Section 4.2, Table 8), but adding the size of the scored files absorbs the coefficient (Section 4.6.4, Table 15). I liked the handling of the pre-registration: the disclosure that review sessions started before filing, the amendment with a full re-collection of the 67 affected PRs (Section 3.12), and the file-size refit that weakens your own headline. I read it as a practitioner who runs coding agents every day. In my company the software development is done by AI agents, so maybe my practical side is useful here. Four comments. 1. On heavy tails (Sections 3.9, 4.2) - you note that one pilot PR was about 45% of a tier's mean token total, while in the main collection no PR exceeded 8.2% of a tier's token sum. In my measurement of 722 agent sessions (150,902 model calls, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22759216), about 3% of sessions gave 80% of the modeled cost. Sessions longer than 200 calls (8% of sessions) gave more than 90% of the money. So in my data the average is driven by a thin tail. What share of each LLM's tokens comes from the top 10% of PRs, and does the CodeHealth slope hold without them? 2. On cache and price (Section 3.8, Table 4, Section 6.3) - the outcome is input plus output tokens, with cached input recorded separately. In the same 722 sessions, more than 85% of the modeled cost was work with context (cache reads and cache writes). In a separate run of 168 sessions, 94.4% of billed tokens were re-reading context already sent (contextburn, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22712985). That is a share of tokens, not of the bill, because cached reads are the cheapest tokens. So a raw token total and a bill can rank PRs differently. Could you refit H1 with cached input priced at each provider's cache-read rate? 3. On paging long files (Sections 3.6, 5.2, 3.13) - the paper links the extra iterations to the 500-line limit per read call. In my guides I write that quality drops as the agent's context fills, and that heavy reading should go to a subagent so the main conversation stays clean. Since tool results are appended to the message history (Section 3.6), paging the median unhealthy-tier file of 2,146 lines puts every page into history that is re-sent on every later call. From the session records, can you count file-read calls and repeat reads of the same file per tier? That would test the paging explanation directly. 4. On the cost of what (Sections 5.5, 5.6, 6.3) - the study does not assess whether comments are correct or fixes are good. In my guides I write that every task needs its own check the agent can run. Without it, "looks done" is the only signal the agent has. I also use a second, fresh agent whose job is to refute the first one, because AI sounds equally sure when it is right and when it is wrong. For the 27-PR replication subsample (Section 3.11), you could run the repository tests after the fix and have a fresh agent try to refute each comment. Tokens per surviving finding would be a cheap first step toward Section 5.6. Thank you for a clear and useful paper. Competing interests Yes: the text cites the author's own technical reports (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22759216, 10.5281/zenodo.22712985); no connection to the article's authors. Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) The author declares that they used generative AI to come up with new ideas for their review.

summary: Python code that reproduces all results, figures and supporting tables of Dixit, AchutaRao and Sandeep, "Future Warming Shortens the Memory of the Pacific Decadal Oscillation and Erodes a Source of Near-Term Predictability" (submitted to Earth's Future). The analysis uses eleven CMIP6 models (piControl, historical, SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, SSP5-8.5), the CESM2 and MIROC6 large ensembles and ERSSTv5, regridded to the 2-degree ERSSTv5 grid. "bash run_all.sh" runs the full analysis. The folder results/ contains the outputs used in the paper, from which most figures can be redrawn without the model data. See README.md for requirements, input data layout and the mapping of scripts to sections, figures and tables.
title: Code and results for "Future Warming Shortens the Memory of the Pacific Decadal Oscillation and Erodes a Source of Near-Term Predictability"

summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a Structured PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23431625 . Does the introduction explain the objective of the research presented in the preprint? Yes The introduction clearly explains the research objectives. It states that the study aims to replicate the quantitative analysis of Krause, Krause, and Bränfors (2018), assess the reproducibility of their findings, and examine potential limitations concerning statistical power and model specification. Are the methods well-suited for this research? Somewhat appropriate The replication approach is suitable for the research, as the authors reproduce the original Cox proportional hazards models and robustness tests. However, the methodological assessment has some gaps. In particular, the power analysis reports values of 0.44 and 0.99 without providing the formula, software procedure, or sufficient calculation details to allow readers to reproduce the estimates. The choice of 42 events in Table 6 also needs clarification, given that Table 5 reports 54 events overall. Additionally, the differences between the original and reproduced sample sizes remain unexplained. These issues weaken the transparency and reproducibility of the analysis. Are the conclusions supported by the data? Somewhat supported The main conclusion is that the original findings can be reproduced, which is supported by the reported results. The authors also reasonably identify the small number of female-signatory agreements and the limitations of drawing causal conclusions from the observed association. However, the claim that the analysis has low statistical power relies on a calculation for which the formula and detailed procedure are not provided (Table 6). The differences between the original and reproduced sample sizes also remain unexplained. These limitations make some aspects of the interpretation less conclusive than they could be. Are the data presentations, including visualizations, well-suited to represent the data? summary: Background: Long-segment intramedullary cervical cord lesions can present a diagnostic challenge, particularly when imaging findings raise suspicion of an intramedullary neoplasm. Differentiating a syrinx from an intramedullary tumor is important for operative planning, as the surgical strategy may differ substantially. Case presentation: A 43-year-old female presented with a six-month history of progressive cervical pain with radicular symptoms, vertigo, left upper-limb sensory disturbance, and impaired left-hand grip. Neurological examination revealed preserved motor power of 5/5 in all four limbs, normal reflexes, and reduced functional grip in the left hand. MRI of the cervical spine demonstrated a long-segment expansile intramedullary lesion extending from the cervicomedullary junction to C7, without contrast enhancement. The radiological report also described Chiari malformation and syringomyelia. Given the diagnostic uncertainty and progressive symptoms, we performed urgent surgical exploration within two days of admission. We performed a C3–C7 laminoplasty to provide multilevel posterior access while preserving the laminar elements without instrumented fixation. Following durotomy and midline myelotomy, a syrinx was identified, with no obvious intramedullary tumor. Syringotomy and drainage were performed, and adjacent spinal cord tissue was obtained for biopsy. Graft duraplasty and reconstruction of the elevated laminae were completed. The patient had an uncomplicated postoperative course, with relief of pain and vertigo and resolution of sensory symptoms. She was discharged with intact motor power and improved but residual left-hand grip weakness. Follow-up MRI demonstrated cord decompression and drainage of the syrinx. Conclusion: This case illustrates the diagnostic uncertainty that may arise when a long-segment non-enhancing intramedullary cervical lesion is suspected to represent a tumor. Intraoperative findings guided the surgical procedure toward syringotomy and drainage, with tissue sampling to investigate a possible underlying neoplasm. Multilevel laminoplasty provided posterior access while allowing reconstruction of the cervical laminar elements. Histopathological confirmation and longer-term follow-up remain necessary.

summary: This paper interprets black holes as information relay stations under global unitarity and fast scrambling. It connects holographic encoding, entanglement, Hayden–Preskill recovery, and Page-curve behaviour into a framework describing how infalling information is recorded and redistributed into radiation correlations. The central contribution is the separation of record and relay functions. Recording occurs on the scrambling timescale, while substantial recovery of information deposited before the Page time occurs near the Page transition. Unitary qubit models with up to fourteen black-hole qubits examine these connections using a mutual-information recovery proxy, revealing the role of early radiation and an approximately logistic recovery transition. Two model-specific predictions are proposed: gravitational-wave echoes spaced approximately by the scrambling time, conditional on a reflecting surface at a Planck-scale distance above the horizon; and a recovery transition whose rate remains of order one as system size increases, testable in quantum simulators. The contribution is a functional synthesis supported by model calculations. Keywords: black hole information paradox, holography, unitarity, Hayden–Preskill protocol, Page curve, information relay station, scrambling time, gravitational-wave echoes.
title: Black Holes as Information Relay Stations: A Six-Principle Synthesis from Holography to Unitarity

summary: EHR2Trace converts local hospital EHR extracts (delimited text and spreadsheets) into OMOP CDM 5.4 and MEDS. The two targets are derived independently from a single canonical layer rather than one from the other, every published row carries a link back to the source rows it came from, and fifty-five checks encode the properties a conversion must satisfy before it can be used as training data, including the leakage failures that are invisible to schema validation. Where the data does not answer a question, the converter blocks and says so instead of substituting a default. Companion paper: EHR2Trace: Auditable EHR Data Infrastructure for Patient World Models and Clinical Agents (arXiv:2609.38193).
title: EHR2Trace: a deterministic converter from local EHR exports to OMOP CDM 5.4 and MEDS, with row-level lineage

summary: Welcome to WARP WARP (WDL Analysis Research Pipelines) repository is a collection of cloud-optimized pipelines for processing biological data from the Broad Institute Data Sciences Platform and collaborators. The contents of this repository are open source and released under the BSD 3-Clause license . Table of Contents WARP Overview Navigating WARP Using WARP WARP Versioning and Releasing Testing in WARP Feedback Acknowledgements WARP Overview WARP pipelines provide robust, standardized data analysis for the Broad Institute Genomics Platform and large consortia like the Human Cell Atlas and the BRAIN Initiative. You can count on WARP for rigorously scientifically validated, high scale, reproducible and open source pipelines. Our pipelines are written as "workflows" using the Workflow Description Language (WDL) and they process a broad spectrum of "omic" and array-related datasets (see the overview table below). | Pipeline Category | Data Types | | --- | --- | | Germline Variant Discovery | Genomes, Exomes | | Genotyping Arrays | Variant discovery, Chip validation, Joint array analysis | | Single-cell/nuclei Transcriptomics | Droplet based (10x Genomics), Smartseq2 | | Single-cell Epigenomics | Single nuclei ATAC-seq, Single nuclei MethylC-seq | | Joint Genotyping | Genomes, Exomes | | Somatic Alignment (beta) | Exomes | Try our pipelines in Terra , a platform for collaborative cloud analysis! Learn how in the Using WARP section. Navigating WARP All versioned and released pipelines are in one of the three pipelines subdirectories: broad (pipelines for the Broad Institute's Genomics Platform), cemba (pipelines for the BRAIN Initiative) or skylab (pipelines for the Human Cell Atlas Project). Each pipeline directory hosts a main workflow WDL that includes a pipeline version number and a corresponding changelog file. Workflows may call additional WDLs, referred to as tasks, that are located in the tasks directory. Pipelines that are in progress or have not yet been validated are in the beta-pipelines folder. Using WARP There are three ways to use WARP pipelines: 1. Download the workflow and run on a WDL-compatible execution engine WDL workflows run on multiple systems, including Cromwell , miniWDL , and dxWDL (see the openwdl documentation ). To run a pipeline's latest release, first navigate to WARP Releases , search for your pipeline's tag, and download the pipeline's assets (the WDL workflow, the JSON, and the ZIP with accompanying dependencies; see Optimus example below). You can also access a pipeline's release page by selecting the pipeline version number at the top of the pipeline's README. After downloading the pipeline's assets, launch the workflow following your execution engine's instructions. 2. Run the pipeline in Terra Several WARP pipelines are available in public workspaces on the Terra cloud platform. These workspaces include both the WDL workflow and downsampled data so that you can test the pipeline at low-cost. If you are new to Terra, you can get started by registering with your Google account and visiting Terra Support . After registration, search for WARP-related workspaces with the "warp-pipelines" tag. To test the pipeline, clone (make a copy of) the workspace following the instructions in this Terra Support guide . 3. Run or export the pipeline from Dockstore Dockstore is a GA4GH compliant open platform for sharing Docker-based tools like WDL workflows. You can find WARP pipelines in Dockstore and run them on the Dockstore platform or export them to other platforms (including Terra). To view all available pipelines, just search "warp" in the Dockstore search and browse the workflow list. See Dockstore documentation for details on launching the workflow. summary: EHR2Trace converts local hospital EHR extracts (delimited text and spreadsheets) into OMOP CDM 5.4 and MEDS. The two targets are derived independently from a single canonical layer rather than one from the other, every published row carries a link back to the source rows it came from, and fifty-five checks encode the properties a conversion must satisfy before it can be used as training data, including the leakage failures that are invisible to schema validation. Where the data does not answer a question, the converter blocks and says so instead of substituting a default. Companion paper: EHR2Trace: Auditable EHR Data Infrastructure for Patient World Models and Clinical Agents (arXiv:2609.38193).
title: EHR2Trace: a deterministic converter from local EHR exports to OMOP CDM 5.4 and MEDS, with row-level lineage

summary: Welcome to WARP WARP (WDL Analysis Research Pipelines) repository is a collection of cloud-optimized pipelines for processing biological data from the Broad Institute Data Sciences Platform and collaborators. You can count on WARP for rigorously scientifically validated, high scale, reproducible and open source pipelines. Learn how in the Using WARP section. Navigating WARP All versioned and released pipelines are in one of the three pipelines subdirectories: broad (pipelines for the Broad Institute's Genomics Platform), cemba (pipelines for the BRAIN Initiative) or skylab (pipelines for the Human Cell Atlas Project). Each pipeline directory hosts a main workflow WDL that includes a pipeline version number and a corresponding changelog file. Workflows may call additional WDLs, referred to as tasks, that are located in the tasks directory. Pipelines that are in progress or have not yet been validated are in the beta-pipelines folder. Using WARP There are three ways to use WARP pipelines: 1. Download the workflow and run on a WDL-compatible execution engine WDL workflows run on multiple systems, including Cromwell , miniWDL , and dxWDL (see the openwdl documentation ). To run a pipeline's latest release, first navigate to WARP Releases , search for your pipeline's tag, and download the pipeline's assets (the WDL workflow, the JSON, and the ZIP with accompanying dependencies; see Optimus example below). You can also access a pipeline's release page by selecting the pipeline version number at the top of the pipeline's README. After downloading the pipeline's assets, launch the workflow following your execution engine's instructions. 2. Run the pipeline in Terra Several WARP pipelines are available in public workspaces on the Terra cloud platform. These workspaces include both the WDL workflow and downsampled data so that you can test the pipeline at low-cost. If you are new to Terra, you can get started by registering with your Google account and visiting Terra Support . After registration, search for WARP-related workspaces with the "warp-pipelines" tag. To test the pipeline, clone (make a copy of) the workspace following the instructions in this Terra Support guide . 3. Run or export the pipeline from Dockstore Dockstore is a GA4GH compliant open platform for sharing Docker-based tools like WDL workflows. You can find WARP pipelines in Dockstore and run them on the Dockstore platform or export them to other platforms (including Terra). To view all available pipelines, just search "warp" in the Dockstore search and browse the workflow list. See Dockstore documentation for details on launching the workflow. summary: Експертна методика визначає стадії та операції дослідження, однак сама їх послідовність іще не пояснює, за яких умов результатом однієї операції можна скористатися в наступній. У судовій гірничотехнічній експертизі найбільш відповідальними є переходи від відомостей, що їх містять матеріали, до реконструкції механізму події, від реконструкції – до оцінювання причинного значення обставин, а від установленої дії або бездіяльності – до її технічного співвіднесення з функціями конкретної особи. Мета роботи полягає у формуванні критеріїв, за якими придатність проміжного результату перевіряють до його застосування в наступній операції, та у з’ясуванні зв’язку між фактичною основою – сукупністю достатніх, узгоджених і простежуваних відомостей – і допустимими межами підсумкової відповіді експерта. Дослідження поєднало структурне моделювання, формально-логічний аналіз експертного міркування, зіставлення з положеннями судової експертології та теоретико-методичне узагальнення професійного досвіду у сфері судової гірничотехнічної експертизи. Застосування моделі проілюстровано на двох знеособлених типізованих ситуаціях із завершеної експертної практики 2015–2023 років, що відображають різний стан фактичної основи. Обґрунтовано поняття критерію контрольованого переходу й сім функціональних контрольних точок: відповідності питання компетенції експерта; достатності матеріалів; узгодженості та простежуваності відомостей; можливості реконструкції механізму; причинного значення обставин; суб’єктно-функціонального співвіднесення; синтезу й оцінювання результатів. Для фіксації методичного рішення запропоновано статуси контрольованого переходу: Т+ – дозволений перехід, Т± – обмежено дозволений перехід, Т– – недозволений перехід. Практичними результатами є модель проходження контрольної точки, матриця методичних рішень і структура робочої карти, придатні для використання як методичний модуль судової гірничотехнічної експертизи. Застосування критеріїв контрольованого переходу пов’язує стан фактичної основи з допустимим напрямом подальшого аналізу й запобігає формулюванню відповіді поза обумовленими межами.
title: Критерії контрольованого переходу між операціями судово-експертного дослідження як засіб забезпечення обґрунтованості висновку в судовій гірничотехнічній експертизі

У судовій гірничотехнічній експертизі найбільш відповідальними є переходи від відомостей, що їх містять матеріали, до реконструкції механізму події, від реконструкції – до оцінювання причинного значення обставин, а від установленої дії або бездіяльності – до її технічного співвіднесення з функціями конкретної особи. Мета роботи полягає у формуванні критеріїв, за якими придатність проміжного результату перевіряють до його застосування в наступній операції, та у з’ясуванні зв’язку між фактичною основою – сукупністю достатніх, узгоджених і простежуваних відомостей – і допустимими межами підсумкової відповіді експерта. Дослідження поєднало структурне моделювання, формально-логічний аналіз експертного міркування, зіставлення з положеннями судової експертології та теоретико-методичне узагальнення професійного досвіду у сфері судової гірничотехнічної експертизи. Застосування моделі проілюстровано на двох знеособлених типізованих ситуаціях із завершеної експертної практики 2015–2023 років, що відображають різний стан фактичної основи. Обґрунтовано поняття критерію контрольованого переходу й сім функціональних контрольних точок: відповідності питання компетенції експерта; достатності матеріалів; узгодженості та простежуваності відомостей; можливості реконструкції механізму; причинного значення обставин; суб’єктно-функціонального співвіднесення; синтезу й оцінювання результатів. Для фіксації методичного рішення запропоновано статуси контрольованого переходу: Т+ – дозволений перехід, Т± – обмежено дозволений перехід, Т– – недозволений перехід. Практичними результатами є модель проходження контрольної точки, матриця методичних рішень і структура робочої карти, придатні для використання як методичний модуль судової гірничотехнічної експертизи. Застосування критеріїв контрольованого переходу пов’язує стан фактичної основи з допустимим напрямом подальшого аналізу й запобігає формулюванню відповіді поза обумовленими межами.

summary: Scripts, dated analysis plans, run logs, and deal-level estimates for a study of 38,991 completed acquisitions by listed or delisted acquirers across 37 countries, rumored between 2007 and 2025. Version 2.1 accompanies a manuscript under double anonymized peer review; author identification is withheld during the review. It changes no script, log, plan, or data file of version 2.0: it updates the title of the manuscript and renumbers the exhibits in the index (NUMBERS.md) to those of the manuscript as submitted (Tables 1 to 6; Online Appendix S1 to S22). Licensed return series and deal and firm data cannot be redistributed and are documented rather than included (LICENSE_AND_DATA.md). Start with README.md.
title: Replication package: Do acquisitions change systematic risk? Evidence on beta from 38,991 deals in 37 countries over 19 years

summary: Added Headline comparator configuration (Palomar follow-up item 5): a configuration naming the paper's main results, declared by lean-pkg formalization NAME --headline-config PATH ( --write records it), the registry field headline_config ( lean-pkg update NAME --headline-config PATH , '' clears) or the convention comparator.headline.json . Palomar's six keys only. formalization.yaml status.main_results then lists its theorems only, while the receipt and the gate keep binding the full comparison. Subset rule against the gate-bound comparator receipt validated at HEAD: every name covered (the --coverage rule) by a receipted configuration with the same Challenge and Solution modules, every definition hole signed in lean-pkg-signoff.json by such a configuration (the headline's own entry first; a main configuration's sign-off covers the same hole in the same modules); else refused, naming them. No receipt validating at HEAD: not applied, a warning, the old behaviour. palomar check runs the configuration checks on it and adds comparator.headline_uncovered (error) / comparator.headline_unjudged (warn), JSON headline ; palomar prepare bundles it under configs/ and README.txt names it for the main-results entry (Palomar: one configuration per submission). formalization --json gains headline . docs/comparator.md#headline-configuration-the-papers-main-results comparator host-check --routes [--json] : host and cluster planning before sbatch (field report #5). Per route ( judge : lake comparator in bwrap ; prepare : comparator-receipt --prepare ; transfer : build here, check the copied oleans with --verify-oleans , judge on a host that passes judge ), supported yes/no with the exact reason and the recommended command lines; executables resolved like type -P (the receipt slurm --template tool list read from the template), locale (a set locale that is not installed warns: the stderr warning a strict receipt refuses), ulimit -n and /proc/sys/fs/file-nr with the LEAN_NUM_THREADS=3 advice when tight, CPU affinity count and the cgroup v1/v2 memory limit. Additive JSON keys ( routes_schema host-routes/1 ); read-only, no network; never an unsandboxed route. comparator-receipt keeps earlier attempts. Before a run replaces an earlier run's stage files (it reruns the setup, or reruns the comparison after an earlier comparison, estimate or failure), it copies them to comparator-stages/attempts/NNN/ : stages.json , the stage logs, the olean manifest, the partial report and the per-unit files. The copy gets an attempt.json (schema comparator-attempt/1 : n , reason , commit , started_at , finished_at , failed_stage , verdict , olean_manifest_sha256 , and the sha256 of each kept file) and is made read-only. Before this, a rerun overwrote stages.json and cleared the logs of the failed run. Numbers are zero-padded and never reused ( attempts/NEXT survives a deleted attempt). lean-pkg never deletes an attempt or reads one back: resume, the slot cache and setup reuse read the current stage files, --from-prepared or --evidence-dir pointing into an attempt is refused, and receipts bind the current run only. A reused --prepare setup carries over without an attempt. stages.json gains started_at . comparator-receipt --attempts [DIR] [--json] lists the attempts read-only (exit 1 when a kept file changed or went missing). Nothing prunes attempts automatically; docs/comparator.md (Attempts) shows how to prune by hand. palomar port-modules NAME [--dry-run | --write] [--agent A] : the mechanical port of a package's tracked .lean files to Lean's module system, which Palomar requires. A dry run by default: from git objects at HEAD, a per-file report and a unified diff ( module first, after ordinary comments; import X to public import X , meta import to public meta import , never public import all ; the body in public section ... end , with no end when a scope stays open). Module-headed files are skipped, so a second run is a no-op; prelude files are refused with a reason

summary: Abstract : Background: The production of high-quality planting material during the nursery stage is essential for establishing productive, competitive, and sustainable oil palm plantations. Genetic material and container type may influence seedling development. Objective: To evaluate the growth of seedlings of two oil palm varieties, Deli × Compacta and Compacta × Ghana (Elaeis guineensis Jacq.), produced using two container types. Methods: The experiment was conducted in Macuspana, Tabasco, Mexico. Seedling growth was evaluated in two varieties, Deli × Compacta and Compacta × Ghana, using tube containers and plastic bags. A randomized complete block design was established with four treatments and four replications, with 100 seedlings per replication (400 seedlings per treatment; 1,600 seedlings in total). Plant height, number of leaves, and stipe diameter were measured every 15 days over 180 days. The same agronomic management was applied to all treatments. Descriptive statistics, analysis of variance (ANOVA), and Tukey’s multiple comparison test. Results: Significant differences among treatments were detected for the evaluated growth variables. For plant height, T3 (Compacta × Ghana in tube containers; CxGt) showed the greatest value at 180 days, reaching 68.37 ± 0.61 cm. For number of leaves, T1 (Deli × Compacta in tube containers; DxCt) and T3 (Compacta × Ghana in tube containers; CxGt) recorded 12.95 ± 0.11 and 12.38 ± 0.10 leaves, respectively, at 180 days. For stipe diameter, T1 and T2 showed the highest values at 180 days, with 2.21 ± 0.03 and 2.19 ± 0.03 cm, respectively, whereas T4 recorded 1.95 ± 0.02 cm. summary: Background: Hyperlipidemia is a major risk factor for atherosclerosis and cardiovascular diseases. Evaluating drug utilization patterns provides critical insights into clinical practice and rational medicine use. Aim: To analyze the drug utilization patterns, clinical characteristics, and treatment outcomes among patients with hyperlipidemia in a hospital setting. Methodology: A retrospective observational study was conducted involving 150 hyperlipidemic patients receiving lipid-lowering pharmacotherapy at Visva Medical Centre and Hospital. Demographic data, prescribed treatment regimens, baseline, and post-treatment lipid profiles (Total Cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and Triglycerides) were collected and analyzed. Statistical significance was assessed using p-values. Results: Among the 150 participants, males constituted 53.33% (n=80) and females 46.67% (n=70). The majority of patients belonged to the 41–50 age group (n=42) and were classified as overweight based on BMI (n=65). Statin monotherapy was the predominant treatment choice. Atorvastatin was the most frequently prescribed agent (38.00%, n=57), followed by Rosuvastatin (26.67%, n=40), and Fenofibrate (20.00%, n=30). Combination therapy was prescribed in 15.34% (n=23) of patients. Post-treatment evaluation demonstrated statistically significant improvements across all lipid parameters (p < 0.001). Rosuvastatin monotherapy achieved the lowest current mean LDL level (114.35 mg/dL), Atorvastatin showed the highest mean HDL level (50.70 mg/dL), and Fenofibrate + Atorvastatin combination achieved the lowest triglyceride levels (161.60 mg/dL). Conclusion: Atorvastatin was the most commonly utilized lipid-lowering drug. All prescribed monotherapies and combination regimens resulted in statistically significant improvements in lipid profiles, demonstrating effective therapeutic outcomes in routine clinical practice.

summary: Agentic frameworks, software libraries that coordinate large language model calls, tool use, memory, and multi step reasoning into autonomous or semi autonomous workflows, have moved from research prototypes to production infrastructure within a span of roughly two years. Four frameworks have emerged as leading options for enterprise adoption: LangGraph, a graph based orchestration library built around explicit state machines, CrewAI, a role based framework that models agents as a crew of collaborating specialists, Strands Agents, a model driven software development kit that emphasizes minimal orchestration code, and watsonx Orchestrate, a managed enterprise platform built around prepackaged skills and governance tooling. Despite rapid adoption, there has been little independent, head to head measurement of how these frameworks compare on the dimensions that matter most to enterprise adopters: end to end latency, latency under concurrent load, cost per task, reliability and error recovery, and enterprise readiness characteristics such as security, observability, and governance. This article presents an empirical benchmark of all four frameworks against a common task suite spanning six task categories and three complexity tiers. We report latency percentiles, a stage level latency breakdown, concurrency scaling behavior, cost per task, task success rates, and a structured enterprise readiness score. We further document each framework's orchestration topology, developer experience characteristics, and security and governance posture, and we translate the results into a practical decision framework for selecting among the four frameworks under different enterprise constraints. All benchmark figures in this article are illustrative, reflecting a representative test harness and reference workload rather than any single vendor's published numbers, and are intended to demonstrate a repeatable evaluation method rather than a definitive ranking.
title: LANGGRAPH, CREWAI, STRANDS, OR WATSONX ORCHESTRATE? AN EMPIRICAL BENCHMARK OF AGENTIC FRAMEWORKS FOR ENTERPRISE READINESS AND LATENCY

Four frameworks have emerged as leading options for enterprise adoption: LangGraph, a graph based orchestration library built around explicit state machines, CrewAI, a role based framework that models agents as a crew of collaborating specialists, Strands Agents, a model driven software development kit that emphasizes minimal orchestration code, and watsonx Orchestrate, a managed enterprise platform built around prepackaged skills and governance tooling. Despite rapid adoption, there has been little independent, head to head measurement of how these frameworks compare on the dimensions that matter most to enterprise adopters: end to end latency, latency under concurrent load, cost per task, reliability and error recovery, and enterprise readiness characteristics such as security, observability, and governance. This article presents an empirical benchmark of all four frameworks against a common task suite spanning six task categories and three complexity tiers. We report latency percentiles, a stage level latency breakdown, concurrency scaling behavior, cost per task, task success rates, and a structured enterprise readiness score. We further document each framework's orchestration topology, developer experience characteristics, and security and governance posture, and we translate the results into a practical decision framework for selecting among the four frameworks under different enterprise constraints. All benchmark figures in this article are illustrative, reflecting a representative test harness and reference workload rather than any single vendor's published numbers, and are intended to demonstrate a repeatable evaluation method rather than a definitive ranking.

summary: This repository provides the Python implementation of a self-supervised hybrid deep learning framework for lung CT image classification. The pipeline includes CT image preprocessing, SimCLR-based self-supervised learning, VGG16 and Swin Transformer feature extraction, attention-based feature fusion, PCA-based dimensionality reduction, and classification using XGBoost, Random Forest, and MLP. The repository also includes dataset preparation scripts, baseline comparisons, ablation experiments, evaluation metrics, explainable AI methods, configuration files, and implementation documentation. The framework is designed for binary classification of benign and malignant lung nodules using LIDC-IDRI and IQ-OTH/NCCD CT datasets.
tags: Lung Cancer, CT Images, SimCLR, VGG16, Swin Transformer, XGBoost, Deep Learning

summary: Reproducibility package for the manuscript Coordinated Optimization of Microgrid Power Purchase and Energy Storage under Information-Temporal Constraints (Junjie Chen, Yu Liu, Ziyan Wang), submitted to Transactions on Energy Systems and Engineering Applications . The archive contains: (i) the solver and forecasting source code, including the entries that re-solve the whole evaluation period from the raw data files, export the per-slot quantities and re-check the evaluation period independently of the solver; (ii) the four case data files as released with the 2026 China Undergraduate Mathematical Contest in Modeling, Problem C; (iii) the daily result tables for the four information structures; and (iv) the verification outputs, comprising the pointwise physical verification over 192,384 strategy intervals, the independent cost back-calculation, the future-data and same-slot perturbation archives, and the strictly executable re-executions with their acceptance checks. Reproduction: unpack the archive and run the commands listed in README.txt from the archive root. Every script locates the archive root from its own position and uses no absolute path. A single structure takes about 15-20 minutes on one desktop core. Evaluation-period costs under the strictly executable protocol: 23.2305 million CNY (structure B, frozen day-ahead plan), 20.0279 (C, rolling adjustment), 24.5852 (D-B) and 20.5285 (D-C). The idealized-reference values reported alongside in the manuscript are 22.4599, 19.3188, 23.8493 and 19.8623 million CNY.
title: Reproducibility package for "Coordinated Optimization of Microgrid Power Purchase and Energy Storage under Information-Temporal Constraints"

summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23432006 . The paper (arXiv 2610.21914) is a pre-registered study of 465 merged agent-authored pull requests from 246 repositories (Sections 3.2-3.5). A frozen pipeline of four review agents and one fix agent ran every PR with three LLMs, and one mixed model per LLM tests CodeHealth against log total tokens (Sections 3.6-3.9). Each CodeHealth point goes with 3.5% to 6.1% lower token cost (Section 4.2, Table 8), but adding the size of the scored files absorbs the coefficient (Section 4.6.4, Table 15). I liked the handling of the pre-registration: the disclosure that review sessions started before filing, the amendment with a full re-collection of the 67 affected PRs (Section 3.12), and the file-size refit that weakens your own headline. I read it as a practitioner who runs coding agents every day. In my company the software development is done by AI agents, so maybe my practical side is useful here. Four comments. 1. On heavy tails (Sections 3.9, 4.2) - you note that one pilot PR was about 45% of a tier's mean token total, while in the main collection no PR exceeded 8.2% of a tier's token sum. In my measurement of 722 agent sessions (150,902 model calls, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22759216), about 3% of sessions gave 80% of the modeled cost. Sessions longer than 200 calls (8% of sessions) gave more than 90% of the money. So in my data the average is driven by a thin tail. What share of each LLM's tokens comes from the top 10% of PRs, and does the CodeHealth slope hold without them? 2. On cache and price (Section 3.8, Table 4, Section 6.3) - the outcome is input plus output tokens, with cached input recorded separately. In the same 722 sessions, more than 85% of the modeled cost was work with context (cache reads and cache writes). In a separate run of 168 sessions, 94.4% of billed tokens were re-reading context already sent (contextburn, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22712985). That is a share of tokens, not of the bill, because cached reads are the cheapest tokens. So a raw token total and a bill can rank PRs differently. Could you refit H1 with cached input priced at each provider's cache-read rate? 3. On paging long files (Sections 3.6, 5.2, 3.13) - the paper links the extra iterations to the 500-line limit per read call. In my guides I write that quality drops as the agent's context fills, and that heavy reading should go to a subagent so the main conversation stays clean. Since tool results are appended to the message history (Section 3.6), paging the median unhealthy-tier file of 2,146 lines puts every page into history that is re-sent on every later call. From the session records, can you count file-read calls and repeat reads of the same file per tier? That would test the paging explanation directly. 4. On the cost of what (Sections 5.5, 5.6, 6.3) - the study does not assess whether comments are correct or fixes are good. In my guides I write that every task needs its own check the agent can run. Without it, "looks done" is the only signal the agent has. I also use a second, fresh agent whose job is to refute the first one, because AI sounds equally sure when it is right and when it is wrong. For the 27-PR replication subsample (Section 3.11), you could run the repository tests after the fix and have a fresh agent try to refute each comment. Tokens per surviving finding would be a cheap first step toward Section 5.6. Thank you for a clear and useful paper. Competing interests Yes: the text cites the author's own technical reports (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22759216, 10.5281/zenodo.22712985); no connection to the article's authors. Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) The author declares that they used generative AI to come up with new ideas for their review.
title: PREreview of "CodeHealth Predicts the Token Cost of Agentic Code Review: A Pre-Registered Study of 465 Agent-Authored Pull Requests"

summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a Structured PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23431625 . Does the introduction explain the objective of the research presented in the preprint? Yes The introduction clearly explains the research objectives. It states that the study aims to replicate the quantitative analysis of Krause, Krause, and Bränfors (2018), assess the reproducibility of their findings, and examine potential limitations concerning statistical power and model specification. Are the methods well-suited for this research? Somewhat appropriate The replication approach is suitable for the research, as the authors reproduce the original Cox proportional hazards models and robustness tests. However, the methodological assessment has some gaps. In particular, the power analysis reports values of 0.44 and 0.99 without providing the formula, software procedure, or sufficient calculation details to allow readers to reproduce the estimates. The choice of 42 events in Table 6 also needs clarification, given that Table 5 reports 54 events overall. Additionally, the differences between the original and reproduced sample sizes remain unexplained. These issues weaken the transparency and reproducibility of the analysis. Are the conclusions supported by the data? Somewhat supported The main conclusion is that the original findings can be reproduced, which is supported by the reported results. The authors also reasonably identify the small number of female-signatory agreements and the limitations of drawing causal conclusions from the observed association. However, the claim that the analysis has low statistical power relies on a calculation for which the formula and detailed procedure are not provided (Table 6). The differences between the original and reproduced sample sizes also remain unexplained. These limitations make some aspects of the interpretation less conclusive than they could be. Are the data presentations, including visualizations, well-suited to represent the data? Somewhat appropriate and clear The survival analysis and regression tables are suitable for presenting the findings. However, some numerical inconsistencies in the descriptive statistics and differences in sample sizes across the original and reproduced models need clarification to ensure the results are presented accurately. For instance, Table 3 presents: three major statistical flaws: 1: Conflict Intensity row, where Female Signatories = 1: has SD of 1.2 while the Max is 0.45, which is statistically incorrect. Similarly, (2) Democracy row where Female Signatories = 1, has Mean 0.92 < Min 1. And lastly, on page 5, UN peacekeeping is written as a binary number, however, in Table 3, the binary UN Peacekeeping has Max > 1. All these minor inconsistencies require clarification. How clearly do the authors discuss, explain, and interpret their findings and potential next steps for the research? Very clearly The authors explain their findings, acknowledge the limitations of the small number of agreements with female signatories, and discuss the implications for causal interpretation. They also identify the need for further research, although the power analysis and differences in sample sizes could be explained more transparently. Is the preprint likely to advance academic knowledge? Somewhat likely If the author clarified the sample-size discrepancies and documented the power analysis more transparently, then it would substantially contribute to the reproducibility of an influential finding, as it already highlights the reproducibility of the findings and highlights the limitations in statistical power and causal interpretation. Would it benefit from language editing? No The languages is clear and no major errors could be found hinderig the understanding of the resarch. However some minor issues could be corrected, such as, constant capitalisation of the first letter in column names. Would you
title: Structured PREreview of "Female Signatories and Peace Durability: Replicating Krause, Krause, and Bränfors (2018)"

summary: EHR2Trace converts local hospital EHR extracts (delimited text and spreadsheets) into OMOP CDM 5.4 and MEDS. The two targets are derived independently from a single canonical layer rather than one from the other, every published row carries a link back to the source rows it came from, and fifty-five checks encode the properties a conversion must satisfy before it can be used as training data, including the leakage failures that are invisible to schema validation. Where the data does not answer a question, the converter blocks and says so instead of substituting a default. Companion paper: EHR2Trace: Auditable EHR Data Infrastructure for Patient World Models and Clinical Agents (arXiv:2609.38193).
title: EHR2Trace: a deterministic converter from local EHR exports to OMOP CDM 5.4 and MEDS, with row-level lineage

summary: Added Headline comparator configuration (Palomar follow-up item 5): a configuration naming the paper's main results, declared by lean-pkg formalization NAME --headline-config PATH ( --write records it), the registry field headline_config ( lean-pkg update NAME --headline-config PATH , '' clears) or the convention comparator.headline.json . Palomar's six keys only. formalization.yaml status.main_results then lists its theorems only, while the receipt and the gate keep binding the full comparison. Subset rule against the gate-bound comparator receipt validated at HEAD: every name covered (the --coverage rule) by a receipted configuration with the same Challenge and Solution modules, every definition hole signed in lean-pkg-signoff.json by such a configuration (the headline's own entry first; a main configuration's sign-off covers the same hole in the same modules); else refused, naming them. No receipt validating at HEAD: not applied, a warning, the old behaviour. palomar check runs the configuration checks on it and adds comparator.headline_uncovered (error) / comparator.headline_unjudged (warn), JSON headline ; palomar prepare bundles it under configs/ and README.txt names it for the main-results entry (Palomar: one configuration per submission). formalization --json gains headline . docs/comparator.md#headline-configuration-the-papers-main-results comparator host-check --routes [--json] : host and cluster planning before sbatch (field report #5). Per route ( judge : lake comparator in bwrap ; prepare : comparator-receipt --prepare ; transfer : build here, check the copied oleans with --verify-oleans , judge on a host that passes judge ), supported yes/no with the exact reason and the recommended command lines; executables resolved like type -P (the receipt slurm --template tool list read from the template), locale (a set locale that is not installed warns: the stderr warning a strict receipt refuses), ulimit -n and /proc/sys/fs/file-nr with the LEAN_NUM_THREADS=3 advice when tight, CPU affinity count and the cgroup v1/v2 memory limit. Additive JSON keys ( routes_schema host-routes/1 ); read-only, no network; never an unsandboxed route. comparator-receipt keeps earlier attempts. Before a run replaces an earlier run's stage files (it reruns the setup, or reruns the comparison after an earlier comparison, estimate or failure), it copies them to comparator-stages/attempts/NNN/ : stages.json , the stage logs, the olean manifest, the partial report and the per-unit files. The copy gets an attempt.json (schema comparator-attempt/1 : n , reason , commit , started_at , finished_at , failed_stage , verdict , olean_manifest_sha256 , and the sha256 of each kept file) and is made read-only. Before this, a rerun overwrote stages.json and cleared the logs of the failed run. Numbers are zero-padded and never reused ( attempts/NEXT survives a deleted attempt). lean-pkg never deletes an attempt or reads one back: resume, the slot cache and setup reuse read the current stage files, --from-prepared or --evidence-dir pointing into an attempt is refused, and receipts bind the current run only. A reused --prepare setup carries over without an attempt. stages.json gains started_at . comparator-receipt --attempts [DIR] [--json] lists the attempts read-only (exit 1 when a kept file changed or went missing). Nothing prunes attempts automatically; docs/comparator.md (Attempts) shows how to prune by hand. palomar port-modules NAME [--dry-run | --write] [--agent A] : the mechanical port of a package's tracked .lean files to Lean's module system, which Palomar requires. A dry run by default: from git objects at HEAD, a per-file report and a unified diff ( module first, after ordinary comments; import X to public import X , meta import to public meta import , never public import all ; the body in public section ... end , with no end when a scope stays open). Module-headed files are skipped, so a second run is a no-op; prelude files are refused with a reason
title: lean-pkg: a registry and trust gate for Lean 4 formalization packages

summary: Chlorine-based disinfectants are standard for environmental-surface disinfection in healthcare facilities, yet their reaction with organic residues generates disinfection by-products (DBPs) whose occurrence, levels, and occupational relevance on hospital surfaces remain uncharacterized. Key gaps are the lack of a validated method and baseline data, the unresolved origin of surface N-nitrosamines, and the unknown influence of chlorine, temperature, humidity, and pre-cleaning on the surface DBP signal. We developed an isotope-dilution wipe-sampling, solid-phase extraction, and ultra-performance liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS) method for eight priority DBPs, applied it to 125 wipe samples from five departments across three campuses of a tertiary hospital in Wenzhou, and complemented field work with stainless-steel coupon experiments. Validation gave r ≥ 0.999, detection limits of 0.8–3.8 pg/cm², and recoveries of 78.4%–96.8%; field detection and quantification frequencies were 87.2% (95% CI 80.2–92.0%) and 69.6% (95% CI 61.1–77.0%), with operating rooms showing the highest total load (Kruskal–Wallis H(4) = 27.86, P < 0.001) though no pairwise contrast survived Bonferroni correction. In coupon experiments the net signal rose with chlorine and temperature but not humidity, with an unexplained chlorine-dependent increment (≈55% at 2000 mg/L) reflecting analytical signal behavior rather than verified formation chemistry, and pre-cleaning reduced haloacetic acids and chlorophenols by 35–55% but N-nitrosamines by only 3–9%. These results provide the first isotope-dilution baseline of DBP loads on healthcare surfaces, a reproducible monitoring method, and occurrence data for revising disinfection and occupational-hygiene standards, and they identify precursor-controlled formation experiments, biological monitoring, and direct testing of medical rubber as next steps.

title: Determination of Chlorination Disinfection By-products on Healthcare Environmental Surfaces by Ultra-Performance Liquid Chromatography–Tandem Mass Spectrometry

summary: Python code that reproduces all results, figures and supporting tables of Dixit, AchutaRao and Sandeep, "Future Warming Shortens the Memory of the Pacific Decadal Oscillation and Erodes a Source of Near-Term Predictability" (submitted to Earth's Future). The analysis uses eleven CMIP6 models (piControl, historical, SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, SSP5-8.5), the CESM2 and MIROC6 large ensembles and ERSSTv5, regridded to the 2-degree ERSSTv5 grid. "bash run_all.sh" runs the full analysis. The folder results/ contains the outputs used in the paper, from which most figures can be redrawn without the model data. See README.md for requirements, input data layout and the mapping of scripts to sections, figures and tables.

summary: EHR2Trace converts local hospital EHR extracts (delimited text and spreadsheets) into OMOP CDM 5.4 and MEDS. The two targets are derived independently from a single canonical layer rather than one from the other, every published row carries a link back to the source rows it came from, and fifty-five checks encode the properties a conversion must satisfy before it can be used as training data, including the leakage failures that are invisible to schema validation. Where the data does not answer a question, the converter blocks and says so instead of substituting a default. Companion paper: EHR2Trace: Auditable EHR Data Infrastructure for Patient World Models and Clinical Agents (arXiv:2609.38193).
title: EHR2Trace: a deterministic converter from local EHR exports to OMOP CDM 5.4 and MEDS, with row-level lineage

summary: Agentic frameworks, software libraries that coordinate large language model calls, tool use, memory, and multi step reasoning into autonomous or semi autonomous workflows, have moved from research prototypes to production infrastructure within a span of roughly two years. Four frameworks have emerged as leading options for enterprise adoption: LangGraph, a graph based orchestration library built around explicit state machines, CrewAI, a role based framework that models agents as a crew of collaborating specialists, Strands Agents, a model driven software development kit that emphasizes minimal orchestration code, and watsonx Orchestrate, a managed enterprise platform built around prepackaged skills and governance tooling. Despite rapid adoption, there has been little independent, head to head measurement of how these frameworks compare on the dimensions that matter most to enterprise adopters: end to end latency, latency under concurrent load, cost per task, reliability and error recovery, and enterprise readiness characteristics such as security, observability, and governance. This article presents an empirical benchmark of all four frameworks against a common task suite spanning six task categories and three complexity tiers. We report latency percentiles, a stage level latency breakdown, concurrency scaling behavior, cost per task, task success rates, and a structured enterprise readiness score. We further document each framework's orchestration topology, developer experience characteristics, and security and governance posture, and we translate the results into a practical decision framework for selecting among the four frameworks under different enterprise constraints. All benchmark figures in this article are illustrative, reflecting a representative test harness and reference workload rather than any single vendor's published numbers, and are intended to demonstrate a repeatable evaluation method rather than a definitive ranking.
title: LANGGRAPH, CREWAI, STRANDS, OR WATSONX ORCHESTRATE? AN EMPIRICAL BENCHMARK OF AGENTIC FRAMEWORKS FOR ENTERPRISE READINESS AND LATENCY

summary: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can participate in producing educational research data as well as analysing them. This dual role creates opportunities for studying intellectual activity while complicating the relationship between observation and intervention. This conceptual article connects two research routes: analysis of existing narrative documents and study of trajectories produced through human–AI interaction. A selective historical genealogy links scientific photography, personal documents, concept mapping and verbal protocols to contemporary hybrid intelligence and learning analytics. Observable cognition denotes recorded manifestations of intellectual activity, interpreted under explicit conditions. Multiscale narrative analysis connects events, episodes, trajectories and corpora through within-case interpretation, cross-case comparison and return to original evidence. The central proposal is to preserve a revisable link between each cross-case claim, its supporting episodes, the provenance of contributions and evidence that could challenge the interpretation. The framework extends from conversational generative interaction to increasingly agentic configurations, in which greater trace granularity also increases the need to attribute operations to the human participant, the system, or distributed activity between them. The framework specifies data units, audit procedures and four propositions for empirical evaluation. A fictional educational design episode illustrates how the same revision can support competing explanations. The proposed tests separate the informational value of process records from claims about learning gains, and assess whether assisted analysis preserves consequential context at an acceptable cost. The framework integrates established methods into an assessable research design; its feasibility and comparative advantage remain to be demonstrated. -------- Preprint v1.0. This version has not undergone peer review.
title: From tacit knowledge to observable cognition: A framework for tracing interaction with AI and analysing educational narratives across scales

summary: Data Type: CSV, Experiment  Organized by: Research group of Shenzhen Research Institute, University of International Business and Economics, and a principal researcher from the University of Sassari, Italy  Approval ID: UIBE-4635876 The dataset contains 876 linked scene records representing 73 participants, each contributing responses to 12 virtual tourism presentations. Six destination settings are represented: a heritage courtyard, coastal promenade, forest trail, museum gallery, mountain lookout and historic street. Each setting has a LiDAR and a photogrammetric version, yielding 438 records per reconstruction condition. Each row identifies a participant, destination and reconstruction condition. The source CSV contains participant age and VR familiarity, presentation order, exposure duration, experiential ratings and technical descriptors. Experiential variables include psychological immersion, presence, perceived spatial coherence, emotional valence, arousal and workload. Technical variables include geometric error, texture ratings, frame rate, motion summaries and the interval between modality sessions. Neural features comprise 1,200 EEG values organised across 30 channels and 40 frequency bins spanning 1–40 Hz, together with 12 fMRI regional summaries. The regional labels cover bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal, precentral, postcentral, inferior parietal and superior parietal regions, plus ventromedial prefrontal cortex and precuneus. These values use arbitrary units and do not represent raw electrical waveforms or anatomically extracted BOLD measurements. The analysis CSV aggregates EEG frequency values into five bands: delta, theta, alpha, beta and gamma. This produces 150 EEG features per record. Combining these with the 12 regional summaries produces 162 neural predictors. Mean immersion combines the two session ratings; values of at least 4.5 define the high immersion category. The analysis file also contains participant validation fold assignments, held-out predictions and classifier scores. All records from a participant share the same validation fold. Prediction and score columns are analytical outputs and must be excluded from model inputs. Mean immersion is 4.59 for LiDAR and 3.95 for photogrammetry. Verified primary balanced accuracy is 81.97% for EEG, 79.66% for fMRI and 79.01% for the combined model.
title: Decoding Immersive VR Tourism: Reconstruction Quality and Neural Indicators of Immersion

summary: R scripts and aggregate tables that reproduce every number, table and figure in the article What a national health information system measures: a cross-sectional analysis of respiratory syncytial virus records in Bulgaria, 2022–2026 (Folia Medica, manuscript 215603) and its supplementary files. The package contains the reconstruction ledger of the Ministry of Health release of Bulgarian National Health Information System (NHIS) records for ICD-10 J21.0, J12.1, J20.5 and B97.4; exclusion and validation counts; the 110 distinct laboratory result values (109 text strings and the empty text field of numeric results) with their assigned RSV class and the rule that fired; a script that rebuilds the hospitalisation episodes from the released worksheet; annual population denominators at national and district level (National Statistical Institute table 206/649, population on 31 December 2022–2025); the aggregate model input (year × age × sex cases and person-years, with and without Sliven); model output and diagnostics; and the article figures. Aggregate data only. No record-level rows, identifiers or dates of birth are included; the record-level extract can be requested from the Bulgarian Ministry of Health under the Access to Public Information Act. See README.md for the file map, data sources, disclosure control and how to re-run the pipeline. Tables and figures: CC BY 4.0; R scripts: MIT licence.

The package contains the reconstruction ledger of the Ministry of Health release of Bulgarian National Health Information System (NHIS) records for ICD-10 J21.0, J12.1, J20.5 and B97.4; exclusion and validation counts; the 110 distinct laboratory result values (109 text strings and the empty text field of numeric results) with their assigned RSV class and the rule that fired; a script that rebuilds the hospitalisation episodes from the released worksheet; annual population denominators at national and district level (National Statistical Institute table 206/649, population on 31 December 2022–2025); the aggregate model input (year × age × sex cases and person-years, with and without Sliven); model output and diagnostics; and the article figures. Aggregate data only. No record-level rows, identifiers or dates of birth are included; the record-level extract can be requested from the Bulgarian Ministry of Health under the Access to Public Information Act. See README.md for the file map, data sources, disclosure control and how to re-run the pipeline. Tables and figures: CC BY 4.0; R scripts: MIT licence.

summary: Source data, live Excel calculations, source-reference key and reproducible analysis code supporting Yield advantages and resource-reporting gaps in plant factories with artificial lighting. A meta-analysis . The curated workbook contains 784 plant-factory treatment records from 154 sources, with eligibility flags selecting 689 analyzed records from 125 sources. All 14 worksheets are visible and 10,566 Excel formulas are retained. A Word table links 160 study numbers to Zotero references, including six additional comparison articles. CSV exports, the 538-source screening ledger, original automated extraction (1,504 records), Python and R code, and an editable Figure 1 PowerPoint are included. The corrected workbook is authoritative; raw automated extraction records are retained for provenance and may contain errors. Published experimental associations do not establish an optimal commercial configuration. Follow README.md for file scope, software requirements and reproduction commands. Compiled data and documentation: CC BY 4.0. Software: MIT (license included in the code archive). Natural Earth map data: public domain. The cited original publications retain their own rights.
