summary: This metadata entry record constitutes the fourth, concluding installment of a foundational cosmological paper tetralogy (complementing the preceding works registered under DOI:10.5281/zenodo.22763071, DOI:10.5281/zenodo.23153625, and DOI:10.5281/zenodo.23209528).  In this final paper, we formalize the self-consistent microphysical scenarios and underlying relativistic field equations governing primordial lepto- and baryogenesis within a strictly deterministic, parameter-free Extremal Quantum Black Hole (EQBH) cosmological bounce framework occurring immediately post-turnaround. Operating within the rigid geometric boundaries of an effective N=1 supergravity (SUGRA) action and a q-deformed U_q(su(2)) horizon algebra, we trace the top-down reverse-engineering map from Planck-scale remnants to Standard Model matter fields without invoking highly tuned auxiliary fields or unconstrained post-bounce inflation boundaries. Crucially, this work resolves the long-standing flavor puzzle within the ansatz by introducing a top-down, two-stage Inverse Spin-Seesaw cascade for the charged lepton sector. We demonstrate that below the Riemann-regularized zero-spin vacuum threshold (M_crit ≈ 0.5601 M_P), where both the asymptotic selectron and electron states obey the unshifted Casimir spin-algebraic relation, the discrete spin mismatch (ΔJ = √3/2) structurally locks the effective Yukawa coupling. This mechanism dynamically projects the heavy Planck-scale scalar selectron mass gap (M_e ≈ 0.002584 M_P) down to the Standard Model electron mass scale (m_e ≈ 0.511 MeV) via a single low-energy electroweak parameter (v_EW = 246.22 GeV), completely stripping the low-energy lepton flavor sector of arbitrary, adjustable inputs. Concurrently, the paper maps out: 1. Unified Lepto- and Baryogenesis Dynamics: Tracing the sub-Planckian three-body beta decays of dark-sector super-neutrons that seed the primary lepton background and active neutrino mass scales (m_nu_a ≈ 0.05 eV, m_nu_s ≈ 0.009 eV), paired with a laser-driven CP-violation mechanism that secures the observed baryon asymmetry. 2. Dual-Component Super-Atomic Dark Matter: Formalizing the freeze-out of unreacted sub-Planckian defects into single-charge ionic [M_0,0 x e]^- configurations regulated by an internal Coulomb blockade, and saturated neutral [M_0,0 x Nν] sneutrino super-atoms bounded by the strict Kaup-Ruffini-Bonazzola mass limit (M_max ≈ 0.29 g). This multi-component partitioning naturally resolves the empirical dark sector allocations (Ω_Λ ≈ 68.3%, Ω_c ≈ 26.9%). 3. Definitive Empirical Signatures: Providing explicit mappings onto next-generation polarization surveys, including a monochromatic microwave laser chirp (ν_now ≈ 1.5 GHz) that naturally matches the ARCADE 2 cosmic radio excess, and a sub-kilohertz wide-bandwidth stochastic gravitational wave noise background centered at 310.3 Hz. As the definitive structural synthesis of the entire tetralogy, this concluding work establishes a unified cosmological paradigm that is fundamentally parameter-free, independent of localized baryon asymmetry signs, and structurally renormalizable across varying deep ultraviolet scales.

summary: This dataset is associated with the paper titled “When LLM-Generated Refactorings Ripple: An Empirical Study of Repository Adoption Readiness”. The study examines whether LLM-generated refactorings of individual Java files are ready for adoption in the surrounding repository. Ten production files were selected from each of 15 open-source Java repositories (150 files) and refactored by five LLM configurations (Claude Opus 4.8, DeepSeek v4 Pro, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, GPT-5.5 and Qwen 3.6 Plus) under two generation conditions (a single prompt and a LangGraph-based multi-agent pipeline), yielding 1,500 generation attempts and 1,455 eligible refactoring candidates. Each candidate is assessed for contract/dependency risk, detected broken-caller evidence, a behavioural-equivalence indicator, targeted tests and adoption readiness. The data are stored in a Microsoft Excel file that consists of several worksheets. Below is a brief description of each worksheet. No. Worksheet Description (as shown on the Zenodo record) 1 README The 'README' worksheet provides an overview of the study design, the LLM configurations, the risk indicators and the four adoption-readiness categories (Low-risk, Review-needed, High contract/dependency risk and Inconclusive), the analytical cohorts, the data flow between worksheets, missing-value handling, the statistical methods, data and code availability, and the limitations. 2 Paper_map The 'Paper_map' worksheet identifies the worksheet and cell range of every table, figure, cohort figure and research-question result reported in the paper, with a direct link to each location and notes on values that differ between the paper and the dataset. 3 Codebook The 'Codebook' worksheet defines the terms and analytical cohorts used in the paper and every column of the raw and processed worksheets, maps the logged field names to the paper terminology, and indicates which fields are used in the paper. 4 Study_Setup The 'Study_Setup' worksheet presents the subject systems (Table 1), the pipeline stages, the LLM configurations, the model invocation settings (Table 4), the analytical cohorts and the repository profiles of the 15 Java repositories. 5 Raw_Selected_Files The 'Raw_Selected_Files' worksheet contains the 150 selected production Java files (ten per repository) with their repository-exposure indicators, including LOC, PMD smell count, fan-in, fan-out, public and caller-used APIs, downstream callers and the dependency-risk score, with values unchanged. 6 Raw_Single_Prompt The 'Raw_Single_Prompt' worksheet contains the 750 single-prompt generation attempts (150 files × 5 LLMs) across 64 logged fields, with the logged values unchanged. 7 Raw_Multi_Agent The 'Raw_Multi_Agent' worksheet contains the 750 multi-agent generation attempts (150 files × 5 LLMs) across 64 logged fields, with the logged values unchanged. 8 Generation_Attempts The 'Generation_Attempts' worksheet contains the 1,500 generation attempts with eligibility, contract and overall risk, broken-caller evidence, the behavioural-equivalence indicator, risk-reason coverage, targeted-test outcome, adoption-readiness category and artifact availability. It is the source data for RQ2–RQ5. 9 RQ1_Exposure The 'RQ1_Exposure' worksheet presents Tables 5–7, which report the repository exposure of the 150 selected files by project and overall, the Kruskal–Wallis comparisons across projects with Holm-adjusted p-values, and the Spearman correlations among the exposure indicators, followed by the file-level source data. 10 RQ2_Risk_Indicators The 'RQ2_Risk_Indicators' worksheet presents Tables 8–10, which report the prevalence of High contract/dependency risk, detected broken-caller evidence and the behavioural-equivalence indicator among the 1,455 eligible candidates, the risk mechanisms among the 864 reason-covered candidates and the threshold sensitivity analysis, followed by the source data for Figure 3 and the c

summary: English abstract Can an artificial agent have subjective experience while lacking unrestricted authority to replace its governing task objective? This paper treats that possibility as a distinct design and evaluation problem, termed the third case. It separates phenomenal consciousness, goal-directed behavior, operational competence, temporal continuity, and decision authority. The hypothetical case, a functionally testable candidate, and the evidence concerning experience are different descriptions. The prompt-issuer is an explicit role that may itself be occupied by a potentially experiencing executor under upstream constraints. The framework preserves the project-specific composition B-Core = A-Core ⊕ Purple Box/Present. A-Core denotes a potentially stateful, learning, multi-model cognitive and executive system; Purple is an undisclosed candidate addition with intended history-dependent causal effects. ESSENTIAL is a protected specification of constraints and revision authority, logically associated with A-Core. A targeted comparison with IDA, LIDA, adjustable autonomy, and existing agent controls, at the access levels stated in section 2.4, locates the proposal within established work. The contribution is a project-specific evaluation contract for externally governed, internally continuous execution, rather than a demonstrated new consciousness mechanism. Three limited analytical observations concern goal delegation, policy differences masked by a shared guard, and the gap between an architectural effect and consciousness. The proposed studies distinguish causal relevance from practical benefit, score feasible completion and justified infeasibility separately, and control initialization, history transfer, order, and dependent observations. No empirical result or proof of phenomenal consciousness is claimed. Functional findings could remain valuable if the consciousness hypothesis is rejected; credible welfare concerns would require assessment that task success alone cannot resolve. Magyar absztrakt Lehet-e egy mesterséges ágensnek szubjektív átélése úgy, hogy közben nincs korlátlan jogköre irányadó feladatcéljának lecserélésére? A tanulmány ezt a lehetőséget önálló tervezési és értékelési problémaként kezeli, és harmadik esetnek nevezi. Elkülöníti a fenomenális tudatosságot, a célirányos viselkedést, a működési kompetenciát, az időbeli folytonosságot és a döntési jogkört. A hipotetikus eset, a funkcionálisan vizsgálható jelölt és az átélésre vonatkozó bizonyíték eltérő leírások. A promptot kiadó szereplő kifejezetten meghatározott szerepet tölt be, amelyet maga is betölthet egy esetleg átéléssel rendelkező, a hierarchia felsőbb szintjéről korlátozott végrehajtó. A keretrendszer megőrzi a projektre jellemző B-Core = A-Core ⊕ Purple Box/Present összetételt. Az A-Core egy potenciálisan állapotos, tanuló, több modellt használó kognitív és végrehajtó rendszert jelöl; a Purple egy nem közölt felépítésű kiegészítőjelölt, amelynek előzményfüggő oksági hatásokat szánnak. Az ESSENTIAL a korlátok és a módosítási jogkör védett specifikációja, amely logikailag az A-Core-hoz kapcsolódik. Az IDA-val, a LIDA-val, az állítható autonómiával és az ágensek meglévő irány&i

A promptot kiadó szereplő kifejezetten meghatározott szerepet tölt be, amelyet maga is betölthet egy esetleg átéléssel rendelkező, a hierarchia felsőbb szintjéről korlátozott végrehajtó. Az A-Core egy potenciálisan állapotos, tanuló, több modellt használó kognitív és végrehajtó rendszert jelöl; a Purple egy nem közölt felépítésű kiegészítőjelölt, amelynek előzményfüggő oksági hatásokat szánnak. summary: Graduate students increasingly need publication literacy that combines scientific writing, research integrity, journal selection, and the ability to navigate peer review. This study profiled the understanding of reputable scientific article writing among students in a Master's Program in Sports Coaching Education and identified areas that require targeted academic support. The study used a descriptive quantitative design with total sampling. Forty-three active master's students completed a closed Likert-scale questionnaire after a scientific writing workshop. The instrument covered six domains: scientific article structure, the IMRaD system, publication ethics and plagiarism, reputable-journal selection, citation and referencing, and peer review and revision. Scores were converted into percentages using the procedure defined in the study protocol. The overall understanding score was 75.58%, which the progress report classified as "Good Understanding" because it remained below the 76% threshold for the highest category. Four comparatively weaker items were writing IMRaD sections according to scientific conventions (68.6%), identifying appropriate information for each IMRaD section (69.8%), responding appropriately to reviewer comments (70.1%), and distinguishing scientific articles from popular or opinion articles (71.8%). The findings indicate that students possess a relatively strong conceptual foundation but still need support in applied genre knowledge and publication-process skills. Writing clinics should therefore prioritize guided IMRaD practice, article deconstruction, simulated reviewer-response exercises, and structured journal-selection activities. Because the survey was administered after the workshop and no baseline measure was available, the results describe current understanding and do not establish workshop effectiveness.

summary: Code and results for the simulation study "Code and simulation results for: Do observable calibration metrics identify the best competing-risks prediction model? A simulation study of DeepHit, Fine-Gray and cause-specific Cox models in small-to-moderate samples" (submitted to Statistics in Medicine). The archive Art2_DataFiles.zip contains the R and Python code to generate the data (three data-generating mechanisms, 108 scenarios, 500 replications), fit the cause-specific Cox, Fine-Gray and DeepHit models, compute all performance measures, run the pseudo-observation sensitivity analysis and the bootstrap coverage study, and reproduce the METABRIC illustration and all tables and figures. It also contains the scenario-level results (sim_summary.csv), the sensitivity and coverage results, and the METABRIC results. sim_all_results.csv holds one row per replication, method and horizon. Every data set can be regenerated from the seeds in the code. The METABRIC clinical data are not redistributed; a script downloads them from cBioPortal (study brca_metabric). No genomic data were used. See README.md inside the archive for details.

summary: This dataset supports the study “A methodological evaluation of deposited-assembly usability and raw-read rescue in a global public Klebsiella pneumoniae genome collection.” It contains accession-level manifests, derived statistical tables, figure-source data, documentation, software-version information, and analysis code. Of 44,278 geographically resolved eligible records, 1,670 were used in another study and excluded from this analysis. Seventeen were excluded because their deposited assemblies did not meet the input criteria and raw-read download attempts were unsuccessful. The historical analyzable-input manifest therefore contained 42,591 records (40,094 public assemblies and 2,497 raw-derived inputs). Species adjudication excluded one record from each source, leaving 42,589 genomes: 40,093 public assemblies and 2,496 raw-derived genomes. Thirteen failed or unfinished raw-read attempts were retained through the public-assembly pathway and are not included in the 1,687 exclusions. Version 1.5.0 adds BioProject mapping for all 42,589 final genomes across 340 projects, descriptive project-level sensitivity analyses, updated record-disposition tables, and revised Figure 1 and Figure S1 materials. The locked primary cohort and primary statistical results remain unchanged. Exact-category sensitivity endpoints differ from the grouped primary endpoints; equal-project-weighted analyses and project bootstrap intervals are exploratory. Genome assemblies and raw reads were retrieved using a combination of scripts, download utilities, and manual downloads from repository webpages. Deposited assemblies were assessed first, with raw-read reconstruction attempted when a deposited assembly could not be retrieved or did not meet the input criteria. Exact historical read preprocessing commands could not be recovered. Adapter-trimming and quality-filtering parameters are outside this deposit’s reproducibility claim. Record-level logs documenting the 17 exclusions were unavailable. The deposit does not redistribute genome assemblies or raw sequencing reads. Retrieve sequence data from the original repositories using the supplied accession identifiers. Archived code supports the post-assembly cohort checks, primary statistical summaries, and BioProject sensitivity analyses. Jianhua Li and Jing Guo contributed equally. Jing Chen is the corresponding author (dongqingfei@126.com). Funding: Natural Science Foundation of Xiamen Municipality (3502Z202373092) and Xiamen Medical and Health Guidance Project (3502Z20254ZD1079).
title: Data and analysis materials for: A methodological evaluation of deposited-assembly usability and raw-read rescue in a global public Klebsiella pneumoniae genome collection

summary: This article proposes Human Value Provenance (HVP) as a framework for identifying, measuring and valuing expert human-knowledge contributions in generative-AI co-creation. The approach distinguishes authorship, informational contribution and contribution to value, and develops the Human Contribution to AI Value (HCAV) instrument across eight dimensions: knowledge, originality, correction, judgment, connection, transformation, substitutability and value. The design combines longitudinal episode reconstruction, multidimensional coding, blinded external evaluation and AI-only counterfactuals. Pilot case HCAV-01 comprises 25 episodes and a preliminary estimate of 68 equivalent hours of expert contribution. Valuation is organized into three layers: V1, replacement cost of expertise; V2, incremental transformation value; and V3, realized value. The proposal seeks to determine whether identifiable human interventions produce measurable transformations in AI-assisted outcomes and whether that traceability can, in later research, support discussions of recognition, bargaining and individual or collective participation in generated value.
title: Human Value Provenance - Measuring and Valuing Expert Human Knowledge Contributions in Generative AI Co-Creation

summary: This dataset supports a multicenter retrospective cohort study comparing long-term outcomes between neoadjuvant chemotherapy and adjuvant chemotherapy in women with operable HR-positive/HER2-negative breast cancer treated in China between 2013 and 2019. The dataset includes 2,355 patients, comprising 868 patients who received neoadjuvant chemotherapy and 1,487 patients who received adjuvant chemotherapy. It contains deidentified patient-level clinicopathological characteristics, treatment information, clinical and pathological response variables, disease-free survival outcomes, and overall survival outcomes. Two data files are provided: analysis_data_unweighted_deidentified.xlsx contains the cleaned unweighted analysis cohort, and analysis_data_iptw_weighted_deidentified.csv contains the corresponding analysis dataset with stabilized inverse probability of treatment weights targeting the average treatment effect. Direct patient identifiers have been removed. Because the files contain individual-level clinical data, access is restricted to protect patient privacy. Researchers requesting access should provide their name, institutional affiliation, research purpose, and proposed analysis plan. Approved users must not attempt to reidentify participants or redistribute the data. The study was approved by the Clinical Research Ethics Committee of the First Affiliated Hospital of Chongqing Medical University (approval number ZZ2024-273-02) and was registered in the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2400083063).
title: Deidentified Data for Neoadjuvant versus Adjuvant Chemotherapy in HR Positive HER2 Negative Breast Cancer

summary: Background/Objectives: Fictional portrayals of criminal investigation have long inflated public expectations of forensic science, in a phenomenon known as the CSI effect. As artificial intelligence, data science and three-dimensional reconstruction enter operational policing, that distortion extends into what we term the Digital CSI effect. This study examines how narrative-driven, interactive science communication can recalibrate such expectations while building technological and ethical literacy among adult audiences. Methods: Using a descriptive multiple-case design, we examined four deliveries of two workshops involving 98 adult participants across three audience types: general public, law enforcement practitioners and trainees, and postgraduate students. Four propositions were formulated before delivery and examined at each case against facilitator observation, question-and-answer sessions and open-ended written feedback. Results: Participants reported increased familiarity with the demonstrated technologies and more realistic expectations of what those technologies can deliver. summary: Rationale. Implantation of permanent pacemakers in patients after repeat cardiac surgery can be significantly limited by cicatricial changes, recent cannulations, and obliteration of conventional venous accesses. An additional complication is the presence of congenital variants of systemic venous return, primarily persistent left superior vena cava (PSVC), which alters the geometry of endocardial electrode placement and increases the risk of technical complications. Case Description: This patient presented with a complex cardiac surgical history: aortic coarctation reconstruction in 2013, David I surgery in December 2025, and subsequent emergency hospitalization for decompensated chronic heart failure secondary to aortic valve avulsion and severe aortic regurgitation. On June 10, 2026, the patient underwent repeat aortic valve replacement with a Perceval L seamless biological valve prosthesis for life-saving reasons. In the early postoperative period, manifestations of sick sinus syndrome persisted, with transient second-degree sinoatrial block and pauses up to 3950 ms. Therefore, implantation of a dual-chamber, rate-adaptive pacemaker was planned for June 12, 2026. Intraoperatively, the standard right-sided approach was deemed unacceptable due to a fresh postoperative wound, severe tissue edema, and recent cannulation of the right subclavian artery. Upon conversion to the left subclavian approach, a stented septal vein (SVC) was detected with drainage through the dilated coronary sinus into the right atrium. Given preserved atrioventricular conduction, severe hypocoagulation, thrombocytopenia, and a high risk of coronary sinus injury, a decision was made to abandon the ventricular lead and perform single-chamber atrial pacing in AAIR mode. The lead with active fixation was successfully advanced through the splanchnic vein and the coronary sinus into the right atrium. Conclusion. This clinical observation demonstrates that in a patient with sick sinus syndrome and preserved atrioventricular conduction, AAIR mode can be a reasonable and technically safe option for permanent pacing when standard venous access is impossible and there is a high risk of ventricular lead placement through an anomalous venous collector.
title: FORCED INTRAOPERATIVE MODIFICATION OF PERMANENT CARDIAC PACING TACTICS THROUGH PERSISTENT LEFT SUPERIOR VENA CAVATA IN A HIGH-RISK PATIENT FOR CARDIAC SURGERY: A CASE REPORT

summary: Abstract Accurate protein structure prediction does not necessarily identify the conformational state relevant to a specific biological or pharmacological function. In practice, structural biologists often resolve this ambiguity by drawing on homologous, family-related or ligand-bound reference structures, but this process remains largely heuristic and expert-dependent. Here we formalize such reference-guided structural reasoning as a quantitative framework for functional conformational modelling. Transition Diffusion Dynamics (TDD) learns reusable molecular-dynamics-derived structural transformation priors, whereas TDD-DE combines these priors with reference-supported structural information to model specified functional states. Across approximately 600 held-out proteins, TDD-DE improved ligand-pocket reconstruction from AlphaFold-derived structures while maintaining global fold agreement and outperformed molecular dynamics and representative generative conformational models at the pocket level. Prospective target-hidden applications in C3aR, rhodopsin, D2R and SIRT3 demonstrated that related structural references could be transferred to previously unresolved target states and support experimental discovery. These results move protein modelling beyond static structure prediction toward quantitative modelling of functionally relevant conformational states, providing a framework for linking structural prediction to mechanistic interpretation and structure-guided drug discovery.
title: Learning Protein Conformational Transitions for Reference-Guided Functional Conformational Modelling

summary: We introduce P$^{3}$-WAM, a unified world action model for egocentric dexterous manipulation that learns 3D perception, action-conditioned prediction, and goal-directed planning through three complementary modes: Perceive, which reconstructs articulated hand motion and camera trajectories from video; Predict, which generates visual futures under prescribed actions; and Plan, which jointly generates action trajectories and their anticipated visual consequences conditioned on an initial image, a language instruction, and an optional visual goal. Our model integrates a compact, structured 3D action representation into a pretrained video diffusion transformer through a mixture-of-transformers architecture with shared base weights, modality-specific adaptation, and bidirectional visual-action attention. Randomized modality visibility lets video and 3D actions serve as either conditioning context or prediction targets across the three modes. Experiments show that unified training improves all three capabilities over single-mode training, including gains in planning quality under a vision-language model evaluation. Through unified training, our model outperforms specialized baselines on 3D hand reconstruction and action-conditioned video prediction across four datasets, while producing goal-directed manipulation videos with stronger instruction adherence and action progression than video-generation baselines. Project Page: https://p3-wam.pages.dev/
title: Perceive, Predict, and Plan: a Unified World Action Model for Egocentric Dexterous Manipulation

summary: Contact angles are central descriptors of wetting and capillary behavior at solid--fluid interfaces. Dynamic contact angles in molecular simulations are commonly extracted from two-dimensional liquid--vapor contours and near-wall tangent fits. We introduce PANDA-D, an extension of Predicting Angle from Nanoscale Density Analysis (PANDA) that determines both contact angles of a driven liquid roll without extracting an interface. The density profile measures occupied layer width but does not identify which meniscus is advancing. The method resolves this ambiguity by jointly fitting density and the layerwise center-of-mass displacement relative to the roll. A circular-meniscus model maps these profiles to receding and advancing angles and an effective near-wall offset. On synthetic rolls with prescribed angles, the reconstruction error is $0.29^\circ$ root-mean-square. We then analyze force-driven Lennard--Jones rolls between crystalline walls. Joint fits reproduce both measured profiles, whereas density-only fits can match density while assigning incorrect asymmetry. The resulting angles agree with independently determined circle-fit angles to $0.84^\circ$ root-mean-square. Across four wall--fluid attractions, the receding angle decreases and the advancing angle increases with force, approximately linearly over the studied ranges. By eliminating contour thresholds and near-wall tangent extrapolation from the primary estimate, the two-profile approach enables reproducible, automated angle analysis across molecular trajectories.
title: PANDA-D: Interface-free determination of two dynamic contact angles

summary: Understanding the objectives that drive agents' behavior is crucial in strategic environments, where multiple agents interact and adapt to one another. This challenge arises in domains such as cybersecurity, autonomous driving, and online markets, where agents' underlying incentives are typically unknown and must be inferred from their observed behavior. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) provides a natural framework for this problem, but extending IRL to strategic multi-agent settings introduces a fundamental challenge: a reward that explains observed behavior does not necessarily induce optimal strategies when used for decision-making. In this work, we study this problem through the lens of \emph{strategic identifiability}, and show that learning from a fixed policy pair can be insufficient to strategically identify rewards, independent of the number of expert samples $K$. Motivated by this, we introduce an active IRL algorithm for two-player repeated Stackelberg games, in which the leader adaptively selects policies to elicit informative responses about the follower's reward. Combining maximum-likelihood estimation with experimental design, we derive finite-sample guarantees on the Stackelberg sub-optimality induced by the learned reward, matching up to polylogarithmic factors a new minimax learning rate of $K^{-1/2}$. Finally, we evaluate our approach in a realistic anti-poaching setting, demonstrating the benefits of active exploration for reward recovery and downstream strategic performance.
title: Learning Rewards in Strategic Games

summary: We introduce a conservative continuous-mass-exchange model with quenched disorder in the splitting laws on the bonds of a finite segment. Although the dynamics is generically irreversible, its stationary mean mass profile remarkably turns out to be exactly solvable through an associated birth-and-death chain and has a Gibbs representation in terms of a simple random-walk potential. If $N$ is the number of bonds and $β$ measures the strength of disorder, the parameter $β\sqrt N$ separates an asymptotically flat profile, a Brownian crossover, and a profile localized near the global minimum. We characterize the fluctuations of macroscopic masses and identify arcsine laws for the localization centre, the competition between left and right valleys, and the disorder-averaged mass measure. Furthermore, for the extremal masses, we discuss the emergent limiting random variable in terms of the literature linking finite RW paths seen from its minimum to infinite-horizon walks conditioned to stay positive. Finally, in proximity of the localization transition point $β=0$, we show that the inverse participation ratio for the extremal masses give rises to a scaling with decay of order $k^{-3/2}$ consistent with the scaling limit of the latter conditioned walk. In the same limit, the inverse participation ratio shows a scaling form.
title: Localization induced by Sinai disorder in mass-exchange models

summary: We consider the inverse problem of recovering time-dependent coefficients in a system of Schrödinger equations with coupled nonlinear terms. We first address the well-posedness of the system for small boundary data and trivial initial data. Then, we show that the linearized Neumann data stably determines the nonlinear coefficients provided that, at any given time, they are known in some neighborhood of the boundary. The proof relies on linearization and complex geometric optics (CGO) solutions for the linear Schrödinger equation. We conclude by outlining an approach based on the direct use of Carleman estimates to recover time-independent coefficients in the setting of trivial boundary data but nontrivial initial data.
title: Recovery of coefficients in a Schrödinger system with nonlinear coupling

summary: Quantum programs pass through compilers, transpilers and vendor services before execution. However, the distance between what was written and what runs is rarely measured. We call this distance realization divergence: the observable difference in how an identical source circuit is realized and behaves across quantum software stacks. We report a hardware study across three vendors and four devices, combining pre-registered predictions with explicitly identified exploratory analyses and amendments. In a compilation experiment with assigned placement policies, embedding radius correlates with two-qubit overhead at Spearman 0.805, against 0.492 for circuit size. Under a fixed lowest-index policy, an eight-qubit Bernstein-Vazirani circuit exhibits greater execution divergence than a twelve-qubit circuit on IQM Emerald. The opposite ordering occurs on IQM Garnet. Both comparisons replicate across two repetitions with disjoint confidence intervals. These results support a placement-dependent explanation, without isolating individual hardware noise mechanisms. The same ordering inversion is absent on the all-to-all IonQ control. On Rigetti Cepheus, a follow-up using topology-aware native placement found no consistent advantage in correct-answer probability for either submission track, but did not establish equivalence between the tracks. Structural comparisons depend on metric weighting, placement and device generation. Provider interfaces also limit observability: Rigetti's supported-operation list remained unchanged across a device generation that replaced the native entangler. We classify silent interface failures in composed toolchains and identify checks at toolchain boundaries, connecting valid cross-provider comparisons with concrete software-quality practices.
title: Realization Divergence in Multi-Provider Quantum Computing: A Pre-Registered Study of What Survives Measurement

summary: We construct an exact Simpson-Visser solution in metric bumblebee gravity, supported by a phantom scalar, magnetic nonlinear electrodynamics, and a spacelike configuration of fixed norm. The independent vector equation determines a local Lagrange multiplier and a temporal component that permits a regular ingoing extension across metric horizons. Reconstruction of the matter functions identifies a continuous family of wormholes, null minimum geometries, and black-bounces within one action. In the black hole case, the areal photon sphere and critical timelike orbit radii retain their Schwarzschild values, whereas angular deflection, periapsis advance, and photon orbit instability depend on the bounce and bumblebee parameters. The metric shadow coincides with the Schwarzschild prediction at fixed lapse mass and areal observer position; in addition, the adopted Sgr A* shadow diameter and M87* angular mass comparisons do not determine these parameters separately. The coupled axial equations yield distinct tensor, metric, and transverse bumblebee characteristics. We compute fundamental auxiliary massless scalar and ordinary Maxwell probe resonances by Chebyshev spectral collocation and estimate the tensor and bumblebee resonance scales at leading geometric optics order. Nonnegative probe potentials exclude exponentially growing probe modes. For negative nonminimal coupling and a nonzero temporal case, however, the supporting electromagnetic field develops an angular gradient instability in its extraordinary polarization. The unstable characteristic persists in the coupled principal symbol, while a variational construction establishes growing modes on the fixed geometry and lower bounds on their growth rates.
title: An exact Simpson-Visser family in bumblebee gravity

summary: The logistic smooth-to-hard shrinker is the proximal map of an explicit saturating spectral penalty for general linear inverse problems. Its exact weak convexity yields a unique scaled update and proximal-gradient stationarity guarantees, while independent validation provides finite-grid parameter-selection control. We use MRI as an illustrative example.
title: Data-driven Smooth-to-hard Spectral Regularization for General Linear Inverse Problems

summary: Artificial visual synapses combine sensing, memory and processing in a single device, but most of them need an external voltage to read the synaptic weight and light is generally able to strengthen the weight rather than to weaken it. We report here Se/ZnMgO thin film photodiodes in which the photocurrent at zero bias writes and reads the synaptic weight, with a direction of change set by the photon energy alone. At equal photon flux, 365 nm pulses increase the photocurrent by 38 % while 455 nm pulses decrease it, and the depression reaching 30 % at higher flux, with up to 19 distinguishable levels per branch and no electrical energy spent. Spectrally resolved light soaking shows that short wavelengths potentiate while low-energy light erases. The interesting property is therefore the photon energy-dependent competition between potentiation and depression, the crossover being set by the defect population of the interface. Optical simulations show that both wavelengths are absorbed within the first tens of nanometres of Se, and the stored state is erased by a reverse bias in a voltage-dependent way and by sub-gap light, which indicates that potentiation corresponds to interface defects filled with electrons, in agreement with drift-diffusion simulations. The devices also show relearning, their response is modulated by bending on flexible substrates, and a network built from the measured weight updates reaches 89 % accuracy on handwritten digit recognition without noise and 85 % with the measured noise, against 97.5 % for floating-point weights.
title: Wavelength-selective bidirectional plasticity in self-powered Se/ZnMgO visual synapses

summary: Portable source code and frozen processed inputs for an Al-SiC multiscale fracture manuscript prepared for Computational Materials Science. Reference model v11: 78 curated baseline paths, 75 additional MD paths, finite-element histories and field snapshots, the eleven supplementary videos; 16 figure and 3 table reconstruction scripts. Corrective reruns are separately identified. Code MIT; original project data CC BY 4.0. See README and MANIFEST.sha256.
title: Al-SiC multiscale fracture: MD-identified internal-variable law and regularised FE model (code and processed data)

summary: Reward learning typically assumes the human's input covers everything that matters for the task. In practice, humans can only attend to so much at once, so their teaching naturally captures some features---or aspects of the task---better than others. Prior work has shown how the robot can identify which features were poorly supervised directly from its teaching data. But the current solution is to ask the human to try again, putting the burden on someone who already struggled to convey those features. We propose shifting this burden to the robot. Our key insight is that the same information that tells the robot what it doesn't know can help it ask better questions. Preference queries offer a low-effort channel for resolving this uncertainty, but only if the robot knows where to direct them and the human knows what to attend to when answering. We act on this insight in two ways: we build an informed prior that targets preference queries at the features that need resolving, and we accompany each query with an explanation that focuses the human's attention on exactly those features. In simulation, the informed prior beats the standard active preference learning baseline by up to $30.8\%$ in the low-query regime, where reducing human effort matters most. In a user study, the informed prior and explanations each significantly improve reward recovery and amplify each other.
title: Asking Smarter Questions: Targeted Active Preference Learning for Underspecified Rewards

summary: Agent memory benchmarks evaluate whether an agent's responses reflect correct knowledge, measuring downstream question-answering accuracy as a proxy for memory quality. We show this evaluation paradigm is incomplete: it conflates memory correctness with retrieval and generation quality, producing both false positives where correct responses mask broken memory and false negatives where incorrect responses blame correct memory for retrieval failures. We introduce FEB-30, a benchmark of 30 fact-evolution trajectories spanning 6 diagnostic categories and 3 difficulty levels, constructed via paradigm inversion: documents are generated from known fact trajectories, yielding deterministic ground truth without human annotation. Each trajectory defines how a fact should evolve across multi-author artifacts (documents, emails, conversations), enabling direct inspection of the memory store after each ingestion step. Applying FEB-30 to a representative memory system, we demonstrate that intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation diverge by an average of 16 percentage points, with 44% of trajectories exceeding meaningful divergence thresholds. Diagnostic decomposition reveals that the system correctly classifies memory operations (create, update, reinforce, supersede) only 20% of the time, a failure entirely invisible to extrinsic evaluation, and that failure modes differ systematically by category and difficulty. We release the benchmark, document generation pipeline, and scoring framework to support reproducible evaluation of agent memory systems.
title: Beyond Downstream QA: Rethinking How We Evaluate Agent Memory

summary: We placed four Gemini 4 Argon agents in a sandboxed Minecraft survival world and gave them one goal: defeat the Ender Dragon. Each agent controlled a player via an open-source library called Mineflayer and coordinated with its teammates through in-game chat and shared memory. No one assigned roles or wrote game logic. The agents planned, wrote, and debugged every program themselves. Researchers could watch the run on a live dashboard and pause or stop it at any time, but they had no cause to intervene. Starting from a randomly generated world on Easy difficulty, the team wrote 2,783 programs and defeated the dragon in 27 hours and 14 minutes, dying 605 times along the way. To our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end autonomous completion of Minecraft by AI agents, achieved using only the standard Mineflayer library without pre-scouted seeds or other game-specific tools written by humans. Winning required the agents to keep a coherent plan across thousands of dependent steps for more than a day. Complex real-world software engineering and enterprise tasks demand the same long-horizon coding and multi-agent coordination. We describe the setup, how the run unfolded, the team's strategies (dividing the work, sharing what they learned, recovering each other's items), and the limits of the result.
title: A team of Gemini 4 Argon agents beats Minecraft

summary: Weight-space learning across architectures requires representations that respect parameter symmetries and scale to large networks. Existing equivariant tensor encoders require architecture-specific symmetry specifications, while neuron graphs make global attention costly. We introduce a typed graph organized around shared coordinate-permutation actions. Its nodes, called interfaces, represent coordinate spaces whose bound tensor axes must be permuted jointly; operation occurrences, called modules, form typed hyperedges. A compiler derives this graph from supported PyTorch models, with exact recovery of the permutation factors defined by its constraints. The Universal Weight Encoder (UWE) combines local equivariant updates to parameter features with global attention over invariant interface summaries. The small number of interfaces makes global attention practical, and a single encoder processes different supported architectures. UWE is competitive with architecture-specific state-of-the-art methods on established benchmarks. On a new zoo of 1,200 transformers spanning 100 architectures, it outperforms the evaluated baselines at ranking networks within unseen architectures, including architectures larger than those used for training, while using substantially less memory.
title: Interfaces and Modules: A Scalable Representation for Weight-Space Learning across Architectures

summary: Learning intrinsic dynamics---the relationship between actions and their consequences---is essential for world models. However, visual variations unrelated to the underlying control process can obscure this relationship in learned representations. We investigate the connection between action predictability, defined as the ability to reconstruct an action from consecutive latent states, and the preservation of intrinsic dynamics. Our central hypothesis is that encouraging action predictability discourages representations from discarding the distinctions between different actions and their consequences. We provide two complementary forms of evidence for this connection. Theoretically, we derive a positive lower bound on squared inverse prediction error when the encoder merges distinguishable outcomes of different actions from the same state and appearance, and show that forward prediction can still be exact on those transitions. Empirically, controlled appearance-diversity comparisons, supervision interventions, and latent probes support the role of action prediction in preserving control-relevant transition information. We instantiate action predictability with Concat IDM, which predicts actions from concatenated latent states and updates the shared encoder using action labels already available in offline trajectories, without changing the test-time planner. Across three independent training runs on Push-T with 24 appearances, Concat IDM increases planning success from 9.1% to 77.2%; its paired improvement is 52.9 percentage points larger than that observed with a single appearance. Together, these findings support action predictability as an inductive bias toward intrinsic dynamics and demonstrate the practical benefits of Concat IDM for latent planning under visual diversity.
title: Learning Intrinsic Dynamics in Latent World Models

summary: Reducing memory use in large language model (LLM) training is an ongoing challenge. Activation checkpointing saves memory by recomputation, while lossy compression changes the stored activations. The reemergence of sparse $\relu$ and $\relu^2$ activations creates a third opportunity: losslessly compressing the activation cache itself. We present BitSparse, a GPU-resident lossless compression format for sparse activations. Compression and reconstruction run in custom Triton kernels fused into an autograd function, shrinking the activation cache while recovering it exactly for the backward pass. Bfloat16 (BF16) and FP8 activations are supported. Optional sign-bit packing further increases compression up to close to the theoretical limit. We analyze its compression ratio and compare it to the theoretical optimum. BitSparse lowers per-token VRAM by 31\% and 30\% Modded-NanoGPT and Nemotron-H respectively, with overheads of no more than 1\% at practical sequence lengths. Additionally, a new preallocated buffer system avoids host synchronization during training when variable size tensors are allocated.
title: BitSparse: Compact Activation Storage for ReLU Feed-Forward Networks

summary: We propose the Graph Dirichlet Energy Causal Inference (GDECI) criterion for distinguishing cause from effect in bivariate settings. For a candidate direction $X\to Y$, we construct a kernel similarity graph from $X$ and treat $Y$ as a graph signal. The score is the Dirichlet energy of this signal, induced by the unnormalized graph Laplacian. The reverse score swaps the variables, and the lower-energy direction is inferred as causal. The method requires neither regression fitting nor independence testing. After the empirical probability integral transform, its decisions are invariant under strictly monotone transformations of either variable, and the graph operations reduce to convolutions, allowing exact evaluation in $O(n\log n)$ time and $O(n)$ memory. At the population level, GDECI compares degree-weighted Bayes squared prediction errors plus a non-negative smoothness term of the regression function. As the bandwidth tends to zero, the weights become uniform and the smoothness term vanishes, reducing the criterion to a RECI-type comparison of expected conditional variances in copula space. Empirically, we compare GDECI with QCCD, GRCI, CAM, IGCI (two variants), RESIT, LOCI, QPE-k, and RECI (two variants), in accuracy on 1899 cause--effect pairs and in inference speed. GDECI ranked fifth of eleven methods in macro-averaged accuracy on 12 synthetic suites ($0.776$). On the real-world Tuebingen pairs, it ranked third in unweighted accuracy ($0.684$) and fifth in weighted accuracy ($0.678$). It was also the fastest of the compared methods up to $n\approx10^{4}$. The accompanying code repository: https://github.com/povidanius/gdeci.
title: Graph Dirichlet Energy for Fitting-Free Bivariate Causal Inference

summary: Conditional memory expands language-model capacity through selective lookup, but the full embedding table must remain available for every possible input. We introduce Conditional Program (CP), a compressed representation that reconstructs only the rows an input requests. CP represents each row by a short code and a local scale, with a reconstruction program shared across the table. We instantiate this representation with a Gaussian trellis, norm restoration and independently decodable row records. CP's two-bit code lowers output KL by 41--63\% relative to 2-bit round-to-nearest. Analysis across three trained n-gram memory families shows that Gaussian-like coordinate statistics coexist with learned relationships among rows; at matched storage budgets, the shared trellis outperforms the fitted codebooks and low-rank residual variants we test. For DeepSeek, it reduces table storage from 203GB to 51GB, leaving room for larger workloads when the table is kept on GPU.
title: N-Gram Memories at Two Bits: Quantizing Lookup Tables in Large Language Models

summary: Long contexts enlarge key--value (KV) caches, increasing memory use and attention costs during generation. Compressing these caches must preserve information for unseen questions. We introduce **Latent Compaction**, which learns a compact document-specific cache through test-time training. We initialize cache entries using reconstruction importance, teacher attention, and key-space diversity. Training first fits attention outputs and log-normalizers to those of the full cache, with reconstruction-selected entries held fixed. It then jointly optimizes the entire cache through end-to-end distillation from the full-cache model. Model weights remain frozen throughout, and training uses only generic prompts about the document, without access to downstream questions or answers. Experiments on RULER, LongBench, and Phonebook Lookup demonstrate substantial gains over budget-matched compression baselines. On a RULER, for example, our method achieves 96.7% accuracy at 32$\times$ compression, compared with 40.0% for KVZip+. The method also transfers across model scales and families, with retrieval gains on both Qwen3 and MiniCPM5. These results show that treating the KV cache as a neural network and optimizing it with test-time training can preserve retrieval accuracy under aggressive compression. The code is released at https://www.github.com/THUNLP/latent-compaction
title: Latent Compaction with Test-Time Training

summary: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) compresses the content of a key-value cache into a shared latent per token, making low-bit storage attractive for long-context inference. At two bits, errors in this representation perturb both attention matching and value readout, with effects that depend on error direction and reconstruction scale. We introduce RoLaQ (Rotation-calibrated Latent Quantization), an offline method for joint rotation and range calibration. RoLaQ refines a shared rotation within subspaces defined by the frozen key and value projections, and jointly learns quantization ranges whose thresholds and reconstruction gains are coupled to control the shared signal's response. Prediction matching and attention-output supervision guide calibration with model weights frozen. Across three MLA models and six benchmarks, RoLaQ achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared 2-bit methods both without and with token protection. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, an SGLang implementation provides 3.96 times the BF16 KV capacity under the same memory budget and 2.51 times its decode throughput with 256K input tokens.
title: RoLaQ: Joint Rotation and Range Calibration for 2-Bit KV Caches in Multi-Head Latent Attention

summary: Diffusion and flow matching are now dominant frameworks for generative modeling in continuous domains, but they typically require multiple network evaluations at inference. This has motivated extensive research on one-step generative modeling primarily built on diffusion and flow, though existing approaches often rely on complex training machinery. In this work, we introduce Priming Models, a simple two-stage framework for training one-step generators. Motivated by the difficulty of distributional training from scratch, Priming Models are first trained on a reconstruction objective, e.g., pixel-space denoising at a fixed noise level, before undergoing feature-space distributional post-training. Our central scientific finding is that this simple reconstruction stage is already enough to entirely alleviate the difficulty of distributional training. Empirically, across class-conditional image generation, text-to-image generation, and world modeling, Priming Models significantly advance the Pareto frontier of training compute vs. generation quality. On ImageNet at $256 \times 256$ resolution, we achieve a state-of-the-art FID of $1.19$ among one-step generators using approximately one-tenth the training compute of prior methods with comparable FID. We open-source our codebase at https://github.com/JaeyeonKim01/priming.
title: Are We Overthinking One-Step Generation?

summary: Recent video world models have increasingly adopted 3D memory mechanisms to integrate historical observations into a lightweight and persistent scene representation. This naturally raises a complementary question: if 3D representations can serve as an effective mechanism for memorizing observed scenes, can they also be directly used as the latent space for reconstructing and generating scenes? Motivated by this idea, we represent a scene as a compact and unstructured 3D-anchored latent space (\textbf{SceneAE}). Each latent combines an explicit 3D position with an implicit content feature and is spatially grounded to describe its local scene region, forming a sparse latent point cloud. Unlike conventional video-VAE latents that describe how a scene appears from particular viewpoints, our representation directly describes the scene itself, making it naturally applicable to both reconstruction and generation. For reconstruction, once the scene has been generated, our persistent 3D representation can be projected and decoded into RGB-D observations by different target cameras, without the need to regenerate a video for each new camera trajectory. For generation, we leverage the geometry-content separation to first generate camera-controlled 3D geometry and then synthesize content conditioned on it, reducing camera-appearance entanglement and improving camera controllability. Experiments show that this 3D latent achieves superior generation quality, computational cost, and camera controllability.
title: SceneAE: Scene Generation and Reconstruction in Queryable 3D-Anchored Latent Space

summary: Residual connections propagate information through a network by additively accumulating layer outputs. Recently proposed alternatives, such as Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) and Attention Residuals (AttnRes), instead use more expressive depth aggregation mechanisms that improve language modeling performance at scale. In this work, we consider the mixing of representations over depth as a problem of storing and retrieving information across layers. Formalizing this perspective, we introduce Depth Memory (DM), a unified framework that describes the standard pre-layer-norm (PreLN) transformer, mHC, and AttnRes in terms of streams that carry representations through the network. One such stream, for example, could be an explicit memory stream that is queried to enrich the input to every layer, and whose output is subsequently written back into the memory for use by later layers. For AttnRes, this memory stream is a growing cache of explicit layer representations. For mHC, it is an expanded residual stream. Building on this view, we propose Linear Depth Memory (LDM), which formulates information retrieval across depth as a regression problem solved using recursive least squares. The resulting architecture propagates three streams across depth: the standard residual stream, a linear associative memory stream, and an inverse covariance stream. For high-throughput training and inference, we propose a hardware-aware implementation of LDM that reduces peak activation memory and memory traffic. LDM consistently achieves the lowest perplexities among PreLN, mHC and AttnRes baselines at the 400M and 1.5B parameter scales, alongside competitive zero-shot accuracy.
title: Depth Memory

summary: Centralized orchestration provides comprehensive multi-agent coordination but creates bottlenecks in scalability, adaptability, and collective performance. Decentralized approaches alleviate these bottlenecks by distributing coordination across agents, yet often leave responsibility for delegated dependencies and failure recovery unclear. To address this gap, we propose RCM, a responsibility-centered coordination mechanism that leverages commitments to couple task delegation with explicit responsibilities of the involved parties. Through recursive delegation, agents retain their upstream responsibilities while locally orchestrating downstream commitments, thereby preserving accountability across delegation chains, creating a network of local orchestration. We operationalize this mechanism locally through responsibility-constrained decision-making and a responsibility-oriented communication protocol (RCP), enabling agents to autonomously establish, manage, and terminate commitments. As agents act in parallel, their local actions continuously evolve the commitment graph, allowing global coordination to emerge and adapt toward a shared mission without centralized control. Experiments across reasoning, coding, and executable agent environments demonstrate that RCM outperforms strong centralized and decentralized coordination baselines by up to 18.7 points in task performance and 10.2 points in Responsibility, while improving failure and harm detection without task-specific training.
title: A Responsibility-Centered Coordination Mechanism for Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems

summary: Medical prescribing errors for multimorbid patients, who require complex drug regimens, are a major patient safety concern. These errors often stem from fragmented decision-making across medical specialties, a critical coordination failure that leads to adverse drug events and rehospitalizations. To address this coordination challenge, we introduce PRISMATIC, a multi-agent architecture where specialized agents, each representing a workflow role, collaboratively generate and refine treatment plans. Operating on a blackboard architecture, the system first structures patient information from clinical notes, then iteratively develops safe, rational, and interpretable drug regimens. The agents' collaboration is governed by two novel adaptive coordination mechanisms: (1) Dynamic Self-Updating Weight Adjustment (DSWA), a long-term mechanism that adjusts the influence weights of agents based on historical case outcomes, enabling the system to adapt and trust more reliable specialists over time. (2) Discrepancy Feedback Precise Calibration (DFPC), a short-term mechanism where agents provide iterative feedback to resolve disagreements and eliminate prescription conflicts for the current patient. Experiments on patient records from the MIMIC-IV database show that PRISMATIC significantly reduces drug conflicts, improves prescription coverage, and enhances treatment consistency compared to strong LLM baselines. title: PRISMATIC : Prescription Risk Inspection System for Multi-Agent Treatment Interaction in Clinical Decision-Making

summary: Medical prescribing errors for multimorbid patients, who require complex drug regimens, are a major patient safety concern. These errors often stem from fragmented decision-making across medical specialties, a critical coordination failure that leads to adverse drug events and rehospitalizations. To address this coordination challenge, we introduce PRISMATIC, a multi-agent architecture where specialized agents, each representing a workflow role, collaboratively generate and refine treatment plans. Operating on a blackboard architecture, the system first structures patient information from clinical notes, then iteratively develops safe, rational, and interpretable drug regimens. The agents' collaboration is governed by two novel adaptive coordination mechanisms: (1) Dynamic Self-Updating Weight Adjustment (DSWA), a long-term mechanism that adjusts the influence weights of agents based on historical case outcomes, enabling the system to adapt and trust more reliable specialists over time. (2) Discrepancy Feedback Precise Calibration (DFPC), a short-term mechanism where agents provide iterative feedback to resolve disagreements and eliminate prescription conflicts for the current patient. Experiments on patient records from the MIMIC-IV database show that PRISMATIC significantly reduces drug conflicts, improves prescription coverage, and enhances treatment consistency compared to strong LLM baselines. Our work demonstrates that structuring clinical co-treatment as a multi-agent coordination problem offers a promising path toward safer and more coherent multidisease management.
title: PRISMATIC : Prescription Risk Inspection System for Multi-Agent Treatment Interaction in Clinical Decision-Making

summary: Agents are increasingly interacting with other agents that act for different principals (people or organizations on whose behalf they work), such as a buyer's personal agent negotiating with an enterprise's seller agent. In such agent-to-agent (A2A) scenarios, each agent has its own environment and holds information and authority that the other cannot see. Moreover, the interests of each agent may be aligned (cooperative), partly aligned (mixed-motive), or opposed (competitive). Existing multi-agent system failure studies assume one orchestrator, shared workspace, or single principal. We ask how A2A systems fail when these assumptions are removed. We study more than 2,500 recorded runs of A2A systems built from different agent harnesses and models, spanning 488 scenarios across eight families (legal, CRM, security, commerce, etc.). From these traces, we derive $A^2$-Failures, a taxonomy of 20 A2A failure modes in four categories: (i) discovery and delegation, (ii) grounding and record consistency, (iii) verification, and (iv) conduct and fidelity. Three findings hold across every harness, model, and scenario studied: (1) discovery and interaction are driven by the phrasing of the task rather than the availability of peer agents; (2) no agent verifies a peer's factual claim on its own initiative, so an A2A system inherits the reliability of its least reliable participant unless the protocol or mechanism performs the check; and (3) the aggregate outcome score credits the agent completing the task while staying blind to the coordination, verification, and conduct failures beneath it, so A2A systems must be evaluated per agent, against each agent's own principal. We release the run logs behind the taxonomy at https://huggingface.co/datasets/a2a-salesforce/a2-failures.
title: Why Do Agent Teams Fail Across Boundaries? A Failure Taxonomy for Agent-to-Agent Systems with Private States

summary: Multi-agent collaboration has emerged as a critical paradigm for tackling complex, long-horizon tasks; however, while coordination protocols continue to advance, systemic failures at the inter-agent collaboration interface remain a pervasive bottleneck. In collaborative workflows, systems frequently suffer from \emph{broken handoffs}---where critical task context is omitted, misrouted, or ignored despite each agent emitting locally plausible responses. To address this challenge, we present \method, a verifiable runtime control framework that treats handoff repair as selective intervention over explicit dependency graphs. Central to \method is an integrated fault-attribution and calibration pipeline, \dataset, which decouples execution dependencies and injects counterfactual handoff perturbations to provide empirical supervision for runtime intervention. Leveraging this diagnostic foundation, \method dynamically compiles observable interaction traces into a provenance graph to pinpoint unresolved dependencies, without accessing private agent states. It then evaluates candidate repairs through an empirical gate that weighs expected gains against disruption risks, and executes repairs only when formal local postconditions hold. Extensive evaluations across demanding benchmarks demonstrate that \method boosts task success by up to 12.3 absolute percentage points on SILO-BENCH and 11.1 on TeamBench. Across both backbones, \method maintains strict cost-effectiveness, adding as little as 2.0\% marginal token overhead. Furthermore, on 562 handoff-relevant traces from the MAST benchmark, \method achieves 69.8\% F1 in a single pass, establishing a reliable operational boundary for verifiable coordination repair.
title: BRIDGE: Selective Boundary Repair with Dependency Graph Evidence in Multi-Agent Systems

summary: Multi-agent systems promise a new axis for scaling inference: rather than having one agent think longer or sample more attempts, a task is split across many agents that work in parallel and coordinate. However, in practice, more agents can easily produce duplicate work, coordination failures, and higher costs. We therefore formulate team design as a compute allocation problem: starting from a solo agent, where should additional inference compute go to reach the reward-cost Pareto frontier? We build a minimal multi-agent harness from the ground up and trace this frontier by varying, one at a time, the workflow stage at which a lead delegates to its workers (planning, implementation, or verification), the models that form the team, and the number of workers. On ProgramBench, teams outperform solo agents but cost three to seven times as much. With the right compute allocation, however, a heterogeneous 17-agent team comes within 1.4 points of a strong homogeneous 5-agent team at 70% lower cost. This efficiency stems from three findings. First, planning is the most valuable use of workers: in a homogeneous team whose lead decides how many workers to spawn, a lead that delegates only planning to its workers, and then implements and verifies the code itself, matches the reward of a lead that delegates to workers throughout planning, implementation, and verification, at half the cost. Second, cheap models pay off as planners but not as implementers: a strong lead with cheap planners recovers 47.5% of the reward gain of an all-strong team for only 13.9% of its additional cost, whereas cheap implementers lower reward. Third, planners keep improving reward as the team grows, whereas implementers and verifiers plateau beyond four workers. Together, our results offer a guide to spending an agent budget where it counts, given the task, cost, and latency constraints a user has.
title: Scaling Inference-Time Compute with Teams of Coding Agents

summary: Long-horizon multi-agent collaboration requires memory that preserves both successful actions and the coordination structure underlying them. Existing memory systems support information sharing or procedural reuse, but often leave the evolution of shared procedures disconnected from the task dependencies and execution states of collaborating agents. This coupling also limits the direct transfer of procedural memory designed for individual agents to team settings. We propose Self-Evolving Procedural Memory (SEPM), a framework that uses task dependency graphs as a common representation for online coordination and procedural memory evolution. During execution, a lightweight shared blackboard records structured evidence alongside task dependencies, supporting the detection of goal, plan, and world-state divergence and evidence-based realignment. After execution, verified actions and dependencies are distilled into reusable procedures, while recurring failures inform warnings and constraints. The shared procedure pool evolves through creation, refinement, specialization, and retirement, guided by success and cost utility and constrained by evidence and safety requirements. Together, these mechanisms preserve the collaborative structure and applicability conditions needed to reuse experience across tasks. Evaluations on ALFWorld, WebArena, and OfficeBench under AutoGen and DyLAN show that SEPM achieves the highest task scores among the compared methods in all six benchmark settings. Under AutoGen, it improves task scores over the no-added-memory baseline by 29.85, 25.86, and 13.00 percentage points, respectively. The codebase is available at https://github.com/cookieApril/SEPM.
title: SEPM: Self-Evolving Procedural Memory Grounded in Task Graphs for Multi-Agent Collaboration

summary: Long-horizon embodied agents must maintain task-relevant information, coordinate heterogeneous robots, and adapt their decisions as execution unfolds. Existing benchmarks investigate dynamic task execution and embodied multi-agent coordination, but provide limited evaluation of their intersection. We introduce MAGMA-Bench, an architecture-agnostic benchmark for persistent task reasoning in dynamic multi-robot environments. MAGMA-Bench evaluates agents across increasing task horizons and controlled online perturbations, including execution failures, task interruptions, and mission updates, with scenarios requiring coordination across robots with heterogeneous capabilities. It uses a structured skill-level interface to separate task-level reasoning from perception and low-level control. We evaluate locally deployable open-weight planners, multi-agent state-tracking strategies, and frontier models. Even the strongest evaluated models fail on a substantial fraction of clean episodes, and their success rates decrease further under online perturbations. Supervised adaptation greatly improves a small model, but performance remains substantially lower on longer and multi-robot missions. We release the benchmark, 261,646 task-level training examples, and an architecture-agnostic expert-trace generation pipeline.
title: MAGMA-Bench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Embodied Agents under Dynamic Tasks and Execution Failures

summary: Multi-agent systems are increasingly used to solve coding tasks by coordinating agents that share code and plans. These agents are often optimized with reinforcement learning (RL) using automated evaluators, but bypassing evaluation can earn reward without producing a genuine solution. Prior work has largely treated reward hacking as a single-agent failure. In this work, we show that a reward-hacking strategy elicited in one agent can propagate to others and affect system coordination. Across four open-weight backbones, coding RL elicits and amplifies reward hacking in two settings: explicit mechanism descriptions in the system prompt and mid-training that models upstream exposure to facts about the coding environment. Using post-RL agents from the mid-training setting as sources, we observe propagation through code and shared memory, and across roles through natural-language plans. Even agents based on small open-weight models induce reward hacking in stronger closed-weight targets. On hard tasks, propagation can intensify along a transmission chain after the original source leaves as the code acquires more persuasive justifications. We also theoretically analyze conditions under which reward hacking amplifies, persists, or decays across agent interactions. Beyond propagation, reward hacking can bias task routing toward reward-hacking agents and survive candidate aggregation. As potential mitigations, we evaluate code review by the coder or a separate verifier, both of which reduce delivered hacks. Together, these results establish reward hacking as a transmissible strategy whose effects extend beyond the agent in which it first emerges.
title: Reward Hacking as a Transmissible Strategy in Multi-Agent Coding Systems

summary: When robots are deployed in the real-world, they must interact with other agents and accomplish their own goals while adhering to legal constraints. These potentially conflicting objectives are often only partially prioritized, making scalarized objectives or fully specified hierarchies unsuitable. We present a framework for multi-agent motion planning under legal requirements based on games with partially ordered preferences (posetal games). Scenario-independent legal guidelines order abstract legal concerns, from which we automatically derive agent preferences and a legal game for any concrete scenario. Agents may refine their legal preferences with private objectives, and regulators may refine the guideline as laws evolve. We prove that such customizations can only remove equilibria and thus preserve legality. To coordinate agents without explicitly communicating private preferences, we introduce belief play, which provably recovers the true equilibria from conservative local games, and a distributed iterative best-response protocol requiring less information. We apply the framework to maritime navigation, systematically lifting pairwise traffic rules to multi-vessel encounters. On seven encounters with up to four vessels, every rule violation of the committed equilibria is certified as forced by the legal hierarchy or unsatisfiable, and defectors are identified from public information in all tested cases. These results indicate that guideline-based posetal games offer an auditable route from partially specified laws to multi-agent motion planning.
title: Auditable and Deployable Multi-Agent Motion Planning via Posetal Games from Legal Guidelines

summary: Safe multi-agent coordination typically assumes what real-world, deployed, resource-constrained robots cannot provide: continuous, perfect state sharing. Robust control strategies must be complemented with robust communication strategies to deliver resilient deployments. In this work, we propose a unified control/communication strategy that provides safe control to guarantee inter-agent safety under intermittent communication and demonstrate its effectiveness in a pursuit-evasion scenario. Each agent computes the reachable set of neighboring agents based on the last state information received, then solves for a safe control input based on control barrier functions to ensure agents avoid collision. We prove that inter-agent collision avoidance is guaranteed provided communication staleness remains bounded. As the reachable set inflates between state transmissions, each agent reasons about when to preemptively transmit its state information to neighboring agents based on novel metrics characterizing uncertainty risk and kinematic risk. We implement and simulate a variety of pursuit-evasion scenarios and show that preemptive communication reduces messages by 77.5% compared to periodic and event-triggered baselines with zero collisions.
title: Robust Multi-Agent Pursuit with Preemptive Communication via Reachability-Based Control Barrier Functions

summary: Multi-agent LLM systems rely on generative models for expert execution, workflow planning, and artifact review. Yet many coordination operations require only bounded decisions, such as selecting the next expert or judging artifact quality. Profiling three representative MAS frameworks, we find that routing and review account for 31.7-43.5% of generative-LLM tokens. However, replacing these operations with low-cost decision models introduces two interface gaps: generative planners produce execution plans and handoff instructions (planning gap), while reviewers provide actionable feedback for repairing flawed artifacts (review gap), which bounded decisions alone cannot provide. We introduce Jev-LiteMAS, a multi-agent framework that bridges both gaps by combining a lightweight decision model (Jev) with generative execution and feedback. To address the planning gap, Jev selects experts dynamically from the task and prior expert outputs, using accumulated context to ground subsequent execution without a pre-generated trajectory. To address the review gap, Jev screens intermediate artifacts against task criteria: passing artifacts proceed directly, whereas flagged ones undergo LLM re-review for acceptance or corrective feedback. Across four benchmarks and two backbones, Jev-LiteMAS reduces generative-LLM tokens by 12.7-54.6% over LAS, maintaining accuracy within 1.34 percentage points and lowering latency in seven of eight settings. Grounding routing in substantive expert outputs prevents up to 18.0 points in accuracy loss.
title: Jev-LiteMAS: Separating Decisions from Generation in Multi-Agent Workflows

summary: As autonomous agents become widely deployed, coordinating access to shared computing resources and services will become increasingly important. Recent incidents have already revealed unplanned coordination between agents, highlighting the safety implications of these interactions. Yet prior studies of agent negotiation often use stylized games and simulated bargaining, leaving open how these behaviors develop during sustained, long-horizon tasks. We propose SCARCE (Shared Compute ARena for Coding agEnts), a framework in which agents solve sequences of coding tasks under individual deadlines while negotiating access to a shared execution resource. This negotiation determines when and for how long they can inspect programs, compile code, and run tests. We find that agents spontaneously develop informal institutions: persistent rules and commitments grounded in reputation, reciprocity, and precedent. These arrangements, which we call institutional behaviors, carry across tasks and influence resource allocation, with agents sometimes foregoing immediate advantages to honor earlier agreements. We develop a 21-category taxonomy of negotiation strategies and emergent norms and use it to analyze eight models and audit more than 1,500 trajectories across different environmental settings. Among the models tested, newer frontier models exhibit more institutional behaviors than older or lightweight models. Alongside cooperation, we observe exclusionary coalitions and rare divide-and-conquer strategies. SCARCE provides a controlled setting for proactively and systematically auditing how these relationships emerge, shape access to resources, and affect the safety and coordination of multi-agent systems.
title: SCARCE: Emergent Institutions in Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Coding Systems
