summary: Fisher information metric tensors for the 41 held-out SONICOM test subjects, as used in “Evaluating Spatial Discriminability Preservation in HRTF Upsampling Using Fisher Information” (D. Bassett). Code and reproduction instructions: https://github.com/domfrbassett/fisher-rao-hrtf-upsampling What the tensors are At each of the 793 directions of the SONICOM grid, the 2×2 tensor g = JᵀΣ⁻¹J describes how well the auditory cues separate that direction from its neighbours. J is the spatial Jacobian of the cues: Barumerli monaural PGE features, ILD and MaxIACCe-transformed ITD, each fitted with real spherical harmonics. Σ holds the cue noise (σ_mon = 1.25 dB, σ_ILD = 1 dB, σ_ITD = 0.569). All fields are low-pass filtered at 16 kHz before the cues are extracted. The tensor is expressed in a local tangent basis u₁ = a × r, u₂ = r × u₁, where a = z, or y when |r_z| > 0.9, and its units are d′² per rad². Contents metric_tensors.zip has one folder per subject, metric_tensors/subject_####/ , containing 25 files per subject (1,025 in total): reference_metric_tensor.mat : the dense measured HRTF. <METHOD>_N###_metric_tensor.mat : one file per reconstruction. There are six methods: SUpDEq_SH , SUpDEq_MCA , SUpDEq_NN_MCA_6dB (SUpDEq-Natural-MCA in the paper), SUpDEq_Bary_MCA_6dB , RANF and FSP_AE . Each is reconstructed from N = 100, 19, 5 and 3 retained directions. The 164 natural-neighbour and barycentric files at N = 5 and 3 have status “ not_applicable ”. The interpolation is undefined for those masks, so these files carry no tensors. Variables in each file: metricTensor : the tensors at SH order 6 [2×2×793]. familyGram : per-cue-family Gram matrices JᵀJ before noise weighting, at SH orders 4, 6 and 8 [2×2×793×3 families×3 orders]. They let you recompute the tensors with other noise values or SH orders. In reconstruction files only: crossFamilyGram : the unsymmetrised cross terms J_refᵀ J_recon, same layout as familyGram . airmByDirection : the pointwise AIRM discrepancy from the reference. Metadata: coordinates (Cartesian and azimuth/elevation in degrees), cue band, noise values (reference files only), status (“ completed ” or “ not_applicable ”) and, for not-applicable files, a message giving the reason. SHA256SUMS.txt lists a checksum for every file. Format and use The files are MATLAB v7.3 (HDF5), so MATLAB, h5py or any HDF5 reader can open them. Note that h5py reverses MATLAB’s axis order. scripts/fisher_lib.py in the repository reads them and recomputes tensors, AIRM and thresholds from the Gram matrices. To rerun the analysis scripts, unzip into results/evaluation/ so the subject folders sit in results/evaluation/metric_tensors/ . Provenance Produced with run_evaluation("tensors") from the repository above. The values are numerically identical to the tensor files behind results/evaluation/full_evaluation_summary.csv ; this run additionally stores the cross terms. The tensors are derived from the SONICOM HRTF Dataset (Engel et al., J. Audio Eng. Soc. 71(5), 2023, doi:10.17743/jaes.2022.0066). The SONICOM HRTFs are released under the MIT licence. This work develops research begun for the author’s B.Sc. dissertation at Birmingham City University.
title: Fisher information metric tensors for 'Evaluating Spatial Discriminability Preservation in HRTF Upsampling Using Fisher Information'

summary: Code, pre-registrations, generated model text and result files for the manuscript “How Much Text Reveals a Watermark? A Detection Law for Keyless Auditing of Language-Model Watermarks” (submitted to IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security). The archive holds the five pre-registered experiments of the paper: P54 (synthetic text, Unigram watermark), P54b (real text from Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct with fixed-list and context-keyed watermarks and a SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct reference), P54c (repeated queries with the key derived from the whole prompt), P54d/P54e (repeated queries with the key from the last h tokens, passive counting of watermarks that are unbiased over keys including SynthID-Text, and additional real-text analyses) and P54f (the word-counting audit repeated on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct). Each experiment folder contains the pre-registration with its SHA-256 lock file written before the run (Turkish original and English translation), the analysis and generation scripts, the generated text, the result files and a result note. The folder manuscript_numbers contains the script that produces every number, table and figure of the manuscript from the result files, so that no number in the paper is typed by hand. README.md describes the layout, how to verify the lock files and how to reproduce the numbers and the experiments; SHA256SUMS.txt lists the checksum of every file. Code: MIT licence. Text, pre-registrations and generated model outputs: CC BY 4.0. The generated texts are outputs of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct under their respective licences.
title: How Much Text Reveals a Watermark? A Detection Law for Keyless Auditing of Language-Model Watermarks — code, pre-registrations, generated text and results

summary: We investigate the rigidity of smooth stationary solutions to the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations in ℝⁿ with singularities along a linear subspace Σ ≅ ℝᵏ. Assuming the scale-invariant transverse bound ‖u(x)‖ ≤ C‖x′‖⁻¹, where x′ ∈ ℝᵐ represents the transverse coordinates and m = n − k is the codimension of the singularity, we prove that u ≡ 0 provided m ≥ 4 and 1 ≤ k < m. This result generalizes the recent theorem of Gui, Liu, Wang, and Xie (2026), which corresponds to the case k = 1 and n ≥ 5. Our proof relies on a quantitative local regularity theorem showing that the transverse bound implies the removability of the singularity along Σ. The argument combines weak extension across the subspace, approximate Green functions for the adjoint drift operator, a one-sided bound for the total head pressure, and a localized Frehse–Růžička weighted estimate followed by a finite Stokes–Morrey bootstrap. Furthermore, we establish the sharpness of the codimension threshold m ≥ 4 by constructing non-trivial counterexamples for m = 1, m = 2, and m = 3 via trivial extensions of Jeffery–Hamel and Landau solutions, together with a new explicit family of non-trivial solutions in the borderline case m = 1. Finally, we discuss the technical obstruction preventing the immediate removal of the condition k < m and propose a conditional rigidity result under additional integrability assumptions.
title: RIGIDITY OF STATIONARY NAVIER–STOKES SOLUTIONS WITH TRANSVERSE BOUNDS NEAR HIGHER-CODIMENSIONAL SINGULAR SUBSPACES

summary: Abnormal  uterine  bleeding  (AUB)  is  a  symptom  rather  than  a  single disease, and diagnostic failure may follow when the bleeding phenotype is  mistaken for an etiological diagnosis. The International Federation of Gynecology  Obstetrics (FIGO) PALM–COEIN system provides a common vocabulary for  structural  and  nonstructural  causes,  but  its  practical  diagno stic  value  depends  on  examination  strategy,  phenotype  documentation,  access  to  investigations,  and  competing  risks.  Objective:  To  critically  evaluate  the  role  of  PALM–COEIN  in  triage, etiological work-up, longitudinal care, and real-world evidence generation,  with particular attention to digital decision support and feasibility in Uzbekistan

summary: Recent advances in deep learning have significantly improved underwater acoustic vessel recognition. However, existing publicly available datasets are typically limited in scale, hindering large-scale representation learning and downstream task evaluation. To address this limitation, we introduce ONCship, a large-scale underwater acoustic dataset comprising 4521 hours of curated recordings from Ocean Networks Canada (ONC) hydrophones and Automatic Identification System (AIS) data. We evaluate the proposed dataset across three tasks: self-supervised representation learning, vessel-type classification, and MMSI-Level Vessel Classification. Experiments on DeepShip and ShipsEar demonstrate the effectiveness of ONCship for acoustic representation learning, with joint pre-training on ONCship and AudioSet achieving a classification accuracy of 62.45% on DeepShip through linear probing. Furthermore, incorporating ONCship as auxiliary training data improves downstream vessel-type classification performance. Beyond conventional vessel-type classification, we further investigate MMSI-Level Vessel Classification, treating each vessel as a distinct identity. Experimental results show that models fine-tuned with different loss functions achieve Top-1 accuracies exceeding 53% and Top-5 accuracies approaching 69%, demonstrating the feasibility of distinguishing individual vessels through MMSI-Level Vessel Classification. Overall, ONCship provides a valuable resource for underwater acoustic representation learning and vessel recognition, while its rich vessel-level metadata enables further exploration of MMSI-Level Vessel Classification.
title: ONCship: A Large-Scale Underwater Acoustic Corpus for Ship Recognition

summary: Pareto Support Proofs is the computational companion to “Sparse exact certificates for weighted-sum unsupportedness in finite multi-objective optimisation”. This R1 distribution, OPTL-R1-20261017, contains the corrected engine 0.6.2, the preserved standalone checker 0.6.1 and reproduction layer AC3-candidate.1. The new controlled run is AC3_REPAIRED_20261017_01. Historical engine 0.6.1, R1_01 results and their provenance remain separately preserved. The companion provides exact certificate generation, generator-independent checking, JSON schemas, instances, certificates, raw observations, source manifests, figure sources and editable ODG files. Negative certificates are checked by exact arithmetic on recorded feasible decisions. Positive objects distinguish full P1 verification from the explicitly retained trusted-oracle P2 boundary. The retained study contains 225 objects: 190 correctness, 27 scaling and eight timing-case objects. Of these, 213 are fully verified at P1 and 12 positive binary-linear objects remain conditional P2. Separately implemented checks reproduce the 190 classifications and the arithmetic of all 102 negative objects. The 225 mathematical certificate payloads match the historical R1_01 payloads. All 225 historical trace files are preserved byte-for-byte; new provenance identifies the corrected run. The historical R1_01 timing batch has eight cases, 240 measurements and 24 warmups. The corrected shortest-path timing batch has three cases, 90 measurements and nine warmups. They are reported separately, including the supportable three-objective case in which checking has the higher median. The historical runner-hash gap remains disclosed. These records do not constitute formal software verification or independent human review. Source code is licensed under BSD-3-Clause. Data, instances, certificates, results, figures and prose documentation are licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0). The component boundaries and retained historical licences are documented inside the companion. AI-assisted preparation and validation are disclosed in the associated manuscript and supporting documentation; Antonio Clim remains responsible for the content. The four deposited files are ESM_1_Pareto_Support_Proofs_R1.zip, Fig1_Editable_Sources_R1.zip, PUBLIC_RELEASE_CONTEXT.md and SHA256SUMS.txt. They match the four named assets of the corresponding GitHub release. The ESM file is the journal's Online Resource 1; automatic GitHub source-code archives are different files. summary: This repository contains the data and computational materials supporting the study Age-Structured Epidemic Insurance Valuation with Hospitalisation and Contact Heterogeneity . The study considers an age-structured SVIHRD epidemic environment coupled with a multistate insurance valuation model. The archive contains the demographic, contact, clinical, vaccination and contractual inputs used in the numerical study; the aggregated age-contact matrix; stored uncertainty-analysis draws; machine-readable numerical outputs; and Python code used to reproduce the principal tables, sensitivity calculations, robustness experiments, duration-dependent hospital-benefit calculations, Shapley accounting decomposition, and derivative-validation results. The numerical study is a synthetic modelling experiment and does not contain individual-level patient, policyholder, or confidential insurer data. The monetary values reported in the accompanying manuscript are conditional model outputs for the specified illustrative insurance portfolio and parameter assumptions. The archive includes a README, data dictionary, provenance information, reproducibility notes, version information, and SHA-256 checksums. The principal numerical outputs were regenerated from a clean working directory and checked against the deposited reference results.

summary: Version 3 is an organisational change only: the four subsections of the verification section are reordered so that the two Krook levels, the amplitude equation and the Vlasov solver, precede the two with diffusion and drag, the amplitude equation with diffusion and drag and the Vlasov solver with the Fokker–Planck operator. No text, number, figure or table is changed from version 2, and the description below is version 2’s. Version 2 of this paper adds a related-work section placing the work against the analytic quasi-steady theory of Lestz and Duarte (2021), the regime maps of Zhang et al. (2026) and the steady-or-chirping criterion of Duarte et al. (2017, 2018); places the near-marginal comparison against Lestz and Duarte's two validity constraints and withdraws version 1's reading of the 24 percent gap, which is now a candidate explanation and not an established one; relabels the drag ratio of the ITER-like slice as the collisional ratio of Lilley et al. and places the turbulence-corrected ITER ratio, an order of magnitude smaller, between the two steady slices tested; states the comparison with the cold-background regime map at the point where the reduced model fails; narrows three statements of version 1 to what was tested; and adds the experiments version 1 left open, a reverse ramp pair at the first operating point and the edge and a benchmark pair at a second operating point. An erratum corrects a sentence of version 1's Limits section that had the two near-threshold amplitudes reversed: the held level of the full- f solver is 24 percent above the cubic equation's steady state, not the other way round. The paper builds and verifies a two-level reduced model of a fast-ion-driven mode, the Berk–Breizman bump-on-tail problem, as a plant whose purpose is to locate and characterise the regime in which the mode saturates to a steady state, the regime a fusion power plant must stay in. Level 0 is the near-threshold cubic amplitude equation with Krook, diffusive and drag collisions; Level 1 is a full- f one-dimensional Vlasov solver with a Krook operator; Level 2 adds drag and diffusion acting on the departure from the initial distribution. Each level was verified against the literature before its results were used: the amplitude equation reproduces the critical Krook rate 4.4 and the critical diffusion rate 2.05; the Vlasov solver reproduces the linear growth rate and frequency to 0.01 percent, conserves energy to second order, and reproduces the Berk–Breizman saturation law within 4 percent across the steady region and the diffusive saturation formula within 4 to 7 percent away from marginal stability. For the warm distribution used, the external damping on the field is only 87 percent effective as an amplitude damping, so marginal stability lies at a damping of 1.15 times the collisionless drive rather than 1.0; with that correction the full- f solver agrees with the cubic equation on the steady side of the bifurcation near threshold, and saturates 24 percent above it at a finite distance from marginal stability, in the direction and of the size that other simulations have reported against the same theory. The steady region is mapped in the damping–collision plane: with Krook collisions the oscillating region is a tongue at collision rates below 0.3 to 0.4 of the drive, closed above it; with diffusion equal to the drive, with or without drag at 0.7 of diffusion, every damping from 0.1 to 0.9 of the drive is steady, one point still rising at the end of its run; with drag at 1.2 of diffusion no steady point was found, and at the strongest drives the reduced model leaves its validity where a cold-background resonant model saturates steadily. The edge of the steady region along the collision axis lies between diffusion rates of 0.4 and 0.5 of the drive at a damping of 0.5 of the drive, converged on two velocity grids, and within the same bracket at a damping of 0.3, where every steady level is 1.41
title: A reduced bump-on-tail plant for the steady operating region of a fast-ion-driven mode: amplitude equation, full-f Vlasov solver with Fokker-Planck collisions, regime map and a detection benchmark

summary: This document contains supplemental material of the paper " Global Minima of the Thomson Problem in a Disk: A Molecular Dynamics Approach with Fixed Border Charges ", where the Thomson problem in a disk has been studied. Here we report the lowest minima for the configurations with N = 54 , 60 , 61 , 65 , 66 , 82 , 83 , 85 , 88 , 89 , 90 , 91 , 92 , 97 , 99 , 100 , 101 , 102 , 103 , 104 , 105 , 111 , 113 , 117 , 119 , 133 , 137 , 141 , 149 , 150 , 151 , 153 , 155 , 187 , 286 , and 318 confined particles, obtained by the Quenched Molecular Dynamics (QMD) method. The energy of these configurations is lower than that of the configurations reported by Amore and Zarate ([ Phys. Rev. E. 108 , 055302 (2023) ]; see the supplemental material in Ref. [ 10.5281/zenodo.8301044 ]). For systems with N = 92 , 100 , 102 , 113 , and 133 particles, in contrast to the asymmetric Voronoi diagrams obtained by previous optimization algorithms, our solutions exhibit a clear D1 (axial) symmetry of defects. For a system with N = 286 particles, in contrast to the asymmetric Voronoi diagrams obtained by previous optimization algorithms, our solution exhibits a clear C2  (central inversion) symmetry of defects. However, for a system with N = 150  particles, the lower energy configuration results in a reduction in the symmetry of the defects. Voronoi diagrams are displayed for the 26 configurations that exhibit structural or orientational changes in the defect pattern compared to Ref. [ 10.5281/zenodo.8301044 ], whereas for the remaining 10 systems (with N = 61 , 83 , 85 , 89 , 90 , 91 ,  97 , 99 , 119 , and 137 particles) QMD method refines the equilibrium coordinates and lowers the energy within the same Voronoi topology.
title: Global Minima of the Thomson Problem in a Disk: A Molecular Dynamics Approach with Fixed Border Charges. Supplemental Material

summary: Subclonal reconstruction results produced with CliPP 1.4 for three datasets: 5,424 tumors from TCGA, 2,008 whole-genome tumors from PCAWG, and CliPPSim4k, a cohort of 4,000 simulated tumors with known ground truth. Wenyi Wang is the corresponding author. README.md describes each archive's layout and the columns of every file.

summary: We study the fine phase-space spectral asymptotics of a model class of infinite-order pseudodifferential operators whose symbols grow like exp(c|ξ|^2), c > 0. The leading Weyl law for such operators is known, but the complete logarithmic structure of the heat trace, the singularity structure of the associated zeta function, and the correct notion of a renormalized determinant require a more delicate analysis. We prove that, in dimension four, the reduced heat trace admits the complete asymptotic expansion τ(t) = A L^2 + B L log L + C L + D (log L)^2 + E log L + F + O(1/L), where L = log(1/t), and all coefficients A, B, C, D, E, F are computed explicitly. Consequently, the model zeta function has the structure ζ(s) = α_2 s^(-2) + α_1 (log s)/s + β_1 s^(-1) + γ_2 (log s)^2 + γ_1 log s + ζ_0 + O(s log s) as s → 0^+, with all displayed coefficients determined explicitly. Because the remainder generally produces terms of the form s log s in the renormalized zeta function, the classical derivative ζ'_ren(0) is not automatically finite. We therefore introduce a finite-part renormalized determinant, defined through the constant term in the derivative expansion, and prove its existence under the full asymptotic hierarchy of the heat trace. We also show that in odd dimensions the zeta function possesses algebraic branch points rather than poles, and we explain why the classical zeta determinant construction must be modified. Finally, we recover the growth exponent α from the counting function in the model a(ξ) ∼ exp(c|ξ|^α), and we compare the results with the theories of Pilipović–Prangoski–Vindas, Gilkey–Grubb, Kontsevich–Vishik, and Nicola–Rodino.
title: Fine Structure of Spectral Asymptotics for Infinite-Order Pseudodifferential Operators with Second-Order Exponential Growth

summary: Suzuki proved that the Riemann hypothesis (RH) is equivalent to the nonnegativity of an explicit continuous function Ψ, the negative of the screw function of the Riemann zeta function. We show that this continuum of sign conditions reduces exactly to one inequality per interval between consecutive prime powers: the minimum of Ψ on the interval, its checkpoint margin, is nonnegative. The reduction rests on the exact curvature formula A″(log x) = (x³ − x − 1)/(√x · (x² − 1)) for the smooth archimedean part A of Ψ. This curvature changes sign only at x = ρ, the plastic constant (ρ³ = ρ + 1, ρ ≈ 1.3247), which lies below the first prime power 2. As the prime-power part of Ψ is affine between consecutive prime powers, Ψ is strictly convex on each such interval, with a unique minimizer. Each margin equals a weighted logarithmic von Mangoldt moment minus a restricted convex conjugate of A and admits a Bregman-divergence formula and two-sided curvature bounds, so finite ranges can be verified without a sampling mesh. We certify all 5,762,859 intervals through q = 10⁸ with directed-rounding MPFR arithmetic and prove Ψ(t) > 0 for 0 < t ≤ log 10⁸. With an independent ball-arithmetic enclosure, the certificate shows that the minimum of Ψ on [log 2, log 10⁸], 0.02149858082368106858…, is unique and lies in the interval beginning at q = 34,186,367. Unconditionally, no positive constant bounds the margins from below on any tail, and under RH their infimum is zero; finite positive margins therefore cannot be extrapolated. The infinite family of checkpoint inequalities remains open.

The reduction rests on the exact curvature formula A″(log x) = (x³ − x − 1)/(√x · (x² − 1)) for the smooth archimedean part A of Ψ. This curvature changes sign only at x = ρ, the plastic constant (ρ³ = ρ + 1, ρ ≈ 1.3247), which lies below the first prime power 2. As the prime-power part of Ψ is affine between consecutive prime powers, Ψ is strictly convex on each such interval, with a unique minimizer. Each margin equals a weighted logarithmic von Mangoldt moment minus a restricted convex conjugate of A and admits a Bregman-divergence formula and two-sided curvature bounds, so finite ranges can be verified without a sampling mesh. We certify all 5,762,859 intervals through q = 10⁸ with directed-rounding MPFR arithmetic and prove Ψ(t) > 0 for 0 < t ≤ log 10⁸. With an independent ball-arithmetic enclosure, the certificate shows that the minimum of Ψ on [log 2, log 10⁸], 0.02149858082368106858…, is unique and lies in the interval beginning at q = 34,186,367. Unconditionally, no positive constant bounds the margins from below on any tail, and under RH their infimum is zero; finite positive margins therefore cannot be extrapolated. The infinite family of checkpoint inequalities remains open.

title: Prime-Power Checkpoints for the Riemann Zeta Screw Function: Exact Interval Minima, Convex Duality and a Certificate through 10⁸ — Part 1

summary: Background. Antireflux fundoplication failure — recurrent reflux, dysphagia, gas-bloat syndrome, secondary to a herniated, slipped, too-tight, disrupted, or twisted valve — remains common, and its endoscopic diagnosis lacks a common, standardized reporting language. Aim. To narratively review existing endoscopic instruments for postoperative antireflux valve assessment, the evidence on their interobserver reliability, and to position an original instrument — the Endoscopic Fundoplication Score (SEF) — within this landscape. Methods. Narrative review, with a targeted search in PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar (last search: 24 September 2026) using the terms “fundoplication,” “endoscopic grading,” “gastroesophageal valve,” “Hill classification,” “antireflux surgery outcome,” “interobserver reliability,” “wrap integrity,” and “hiatal hernia recurrence,” covering literature published between 1996 and 2026 in English or with an English abstract, supplemented by reference-list screening of identified articles. Results. Three major endoscopic instruments were identified — the Hill classification (1996), the Jobe system (2004), and the American Foregut Society (AFS) nomenclature (2025) — alongside a descriptive, non-scored taxonomy of failure types (herniated, slipped, tight, disrupted, twisted). The interobserver reliability studies [1,2] identified in this review for the postoperative setting report low agreement, and a retrospective comparison of endoscopy reports [3] documented major discrepancies between external endoscopists and operating surgeons. The AFS classification of esophagogastric junction integrity achieved substantial agreement on static images (κ=0.65) but only fair agreement under dynamic conditions (κ=0.371), and the postoperative AFS nomenclature has not yet been tested for interobserver reliability. The SEF score, an 11-item composite instrument (0–16 points) applied to a cohort of 178 patients, correlated in preliminary single-centre data with the Hill classification, Los Angeles (LA) esophagitis grade, and the Visick patient-satisfaction score (own data, manuscript submitted for publication), offering a numeric, quantifiable alternative to existing categorical systems. The SEF threshold of ≤10 points, defined in the same cohort, is exploratory. Conclusions. The field of postoperative endoscopic antireflux valve assessment remains fragmented, without an interobserver-reliable consensus standard. The SEF score partially addresses this gap through a numeric structure, with experience-based weights and an exploratory threshold, but requires formal interobserver reliability testing and multicenter validation against the surgical gold standard.

summary: First tagged release of vmtools, R helpers for cardiovascular epidemiology. Includes: PREVENT (total CVD, ASCVD, heart failure) and Pooled Cohort Equations risk scores; HOMA-IR, HOMA-β, QUICKI, Matsuda and Avignon insulin indices; GLI-2012 predicted FEV1 and FVC (ages 25–95); Human Metabolome Database lookups; and utilities. Validated against the Goff 2013 PCE worked example, the PREVENT reference values in the preventr test suite, and the official GLI-2012 lookup tables (within 0.5%). Fixes since earlier versions predict_FVC : corrected a sign error affecting predicted FVC in women calcPREVENT.HF : added the missing age factor to the BMI interaction term predict_FEV1 / predict_FVC : explicit Caucasian option; "other" now uses GLI Other/mixed coefficients calcAvignon.SI , mqsave and HMDB_ID_from_name now work as documented Install: remotes::install_github("vlmurthylab/vmtools@v0.1.0")
title: vmtools: handy tools for cardiovascular epidemiology

summary: Input structures, calculation scripts, and results for the article "Benchmarking Universal Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials for Temperature-Dependent Elasticity of Binary and High-Entropy Refractory Carbides" (arXiv:2610.11878). elastic.zip (9 files, one per model) – the 153 elastic-constant calculations, 17 per model (five binary carbides and six SQS of each high-entropy carbide). sqs_generation.zip – the 12 special quasirandom structures used, with their ICET search records. speed_tests.zip – MD throughput and GPU-memory benchmarks on an RTX 4090 and an H100.

summary: Replication package for the article "Keeping Galway, losing the West Briton" (manuscript in preparation). It contains the executed Kaggle notebook; the sentence-level and paragraph-level segment files of James Joyce's "The Dead", as given to the model Turkish-Gemma-9b-v0.1 (commit 1bbe9f19a26a70dc4d0c709e1a816e6a9378a7f5); the raw and cleaned model outputs for both conditions (1,027 sentences, 455 paragraphs); the Python scripts that code 89 culture-specific items (499 occurrences) and produce Supplementary Data S1 and S2; and the supplementary files themselves. README.md lists the files, gives the provenance of the run and explains how to rerun the scripts.

summary: Version 0.5.0 archives the current analysis repository for Organisms associated with siphonophores revealed by short-read whole-genome sequencing . It is the first GitHub release after enabling Zenodo integration. This snapshot includes: The Snakemake workflow, configurations, methods guides, and generated rule graphs for analyses of 205 siphonophore specimens from three published studies. Publication figures and supporting tables for bacterial, archaeal, viral, and eukaryotic associates, including genome relationships, predicted functions, host distributions, and screening outcomes. Curated specimen metadata with separate analysis identifiers, museum vouchers, BioSample accessions, collecting-event and tissue-sample identifiers, collection context, tissue information, source provenance, and study-specific review tables. The current manuscript-facing summaries of Kraken2/Bracken, sylph, and phyloFlash evidence, including overlap with assembly-supported discoveries. The release preserves commit cd65400dc3fcac2b31991949e62b20ed361861cc . Creating the release does not alter analysis inputs or rerun sequence analyses. Metadata review remains in progress; missing values and evidence are retained explicitly. The archive contains tracked code, settings, selected source records, figures, and supporting tables. Large sequencing files, reference databases, and most sequence-analysis outputs are stored separately; see the README and workflow guides for accessions, input requirements, and reproduction instructions. The manuscript is maintained in a separate repository. Validation: the full repository test suite passed ( 64 passed ), and all 16 tracked workflow graphs reproduced exactly with the pinned Snakemake and Graphviz environment. No sequence-analysis jobs were executed.
title: caseywdunn/siph-associates: 0.5.0

summary: NANOROBOT-ENHANCED DIGITAL TWINS OF BRAIN STATE AT THE LIMIT A multiscale, uncertainty-aware research atlas on microrobotic observations, neural inverse problems, active model discrimination and the limits of computational brain twins. This research monograph asks whether additional microscale observations or strictly bounded reversible experiments can distinguish competing neural-state models that explain conventional measurements equally well. The twin is explicitly defined as a versioned scientific belief, not a digital person, a mind reader or a clinically validated instrument. Its objective is not maximum model complexity but improved identifiability, calibrated prediction under new conditions and faithful retention of failed hypotheses. The work develops five layers: multiscale neural and microenvironment state representation; posterior equivalence and prior sensitivity; non-clinical safe experimental design; frozen-version forking, rollback and reference ancestry; and blind prospective validation against classical state-space systems and independently specified alternatives. Its research architecture includes 30 distinct mathematical derivation plates linked to later chapters, 82 chapters with five independently paginated research sections apiece, 200 detailed Research Gates and 33 revisable Phoenix Answer Embryos. A DOI evidence ledger identifies existing support for brain modeling, latent neural dynamics, experiment design and preclinical microrobot tracking while preventing those sources from being mistaken for evidence of the proposed integrated system. Key research questions include: Can two equally accurate virtual brains be separated by a small, permissible observation? How can the effect of a measurement itself be separated from neural change? When does a prior dominate the inferred brain state? Can the model predict unseen function rather than reconstruct a training signal? Can another laboratory reproduce a rejected twin and safely return to an earlier version? SCIENTIFIC STATUS AND LIMITATIONS This is a forward-looking, non-clinical research synthesis and experimental hypothesis architecture. It provides no personal medical advice, patient-specific interpretations or instruction to deliver neural interventions. Existing murine microrobot tracking and virtual-brain modeling studies do not establish autonomous neural nanorobot readout, human safety, privacy-sensitive mind inference or therapeutic efficacy. Proposed formulas, experiments, research gates and answer embryos are not newly validated biological laws or executed experiments. The work keeps independent safety vetoes, privacy, external reproducibility and explicit model retirement as first-class constraints. Research questions remain open to refutation, correction and reconstruction by future human and AI researchers.

summary: Added lean-pkg-extract plan checks the licenses of adopted (vendored) files. A new manifest key adopted declares files taken from another project ( paths , upstream , upstream_commit , upstream_license_file , license , optional license_file and provenance ); the plan lists them under adopted[] and warns when the upstream license is not carried into the target (naming the files, the upstream license file and the commit, and the scoped LICENSES/LicenseRef-<Upstream>-<SPDX>.txt to copy it to), when the license or provenance file is excluded or missing, when the provenance list misses a file, and when a LICENSES/ file name is not a REUSE license id. Without a declaration it warns when the nearest LICENSE / COPYING above an included file is left behind. These are warnings ( warnings[] , totals.warnings , N warning(s) in the verdict): the verdict and the exit code do not change, and only a malformed adopted entry is refused. docs/extract.md, "Licenses of adopted files", documents the scoped, REUSE-compatible pattern (field report). lean-pkg new NAME --kind paper|library , paper by default (the 1.0 command tree). --kind paper writes a coverage.yaml of kind: paper that is incomplete on purpose: manuscript.version: unposted and FILL-ME markers for the title, the summary and the rows, which coverage check (and so page ) refuses until the author names the paper; the printed next steps and the README name formalization anchor NAME --arxiv <id>v<N> ... --write to bind the posted version. No manuscript is invented. --kind library is the previous scaffold. help start no longer marks new --kind as coming. --json gains kind , author , author_source , coverage_complete and warnings[] . lean-pkg new writes REUSE.toml (every file, including the receipts and logs the workflow adds later, under the chosen license and the author's copyright) and LICENSES/<SPDX>.txt , so reuse lint , which publish --dry-run runs, passes on a fresh package. lean-pkg new warns when the CITATION.cff author ( --author , else git config user.name ) has no space and so looks like a handle, and prints which source it used. lean-pkg formalization kept [--repo DIR] [--file REL] [--at REV] [--against REV2] [--json] : the canonical kept view of formalization.yaml (every key formalization render derives removed, formalization.DERIVED_PATHS and the renderer's acknowledgements lines) and the SHA-256 of its canonical JSON bytes, so a package's own release-input audit can pin what a person wrote without tripping over a derived-key refresh after a new receipt. --against REV2 lists the changed kept keys (the evidence-only rule's changed_kept_keys ) and exits 1 when any changed. Read-only, no registry; JSON schema formalization-kept/1 . The recipe (YAML 1.1 safe schema with timestamps kept as strings, JSON sort_keys , separators , : , UTF-8, no trailing newline) is documented in docs/formalization.md, "The kept view", precisely enough to reproduce without lean-pkg; a test pins it byte for byte and against jq -cjS (field request). comparator-receipt --seal-sacct RECEIPT [--sacct-file F] [--user NAME] [--json] : after a Slurm job finished, corroborate a comparator receipt's Slurm claim with the job's sacct record (main line COMPLETED , exit 0:0 , a zoned Start..End containing the receipt's generated_at , the sealing account and the receipt's node where known) and seal it: the normalized record (no user or node names) as .lean-receipts/<c12>-comparator-sacct.txt and an additive slurm_sacct block with its SHA-256 in the receipt. Reuses receipt slurm 's sacct parser, which now also reads Start , End , User and NodeList when a header names them. See docs/comparator.md, "Seal the Slurm claim with sacct". Docs: a first worked-example tutorial, docs/tutorial-pi-lambda.md: Dynkin's π-λ theorem and the uniqueness of probability measures, from the textbook statement to a verified page on one workstation ( lean-pkg new , the Challeng

summary: This replication package accompanies the paper "An Exploratory Evaluation of Targeted Label Poisoning in a Client-Local Feature Federated Ensemble for Chest X-Ray Classification." It contains code and saved experimental results for an exploratory study of Pneumonia-to-Normal label poisoning in four-class chest X-ray classification. The study uses 20,795 images from three public sources, with 20,557 perceptual groups kept intact across experimental partitions. The package covers 212 completed training jobs, including main and component comparisons, classifier-head sensitivity, image-model references, candidate probability banks, and earlier-poisoning experiments. The main comparisons and image-model references use ten deterministic seeds. The classifier-head and GRU-structure study uses three seeds. Included materials comprise dataset manifests and image checksums, perceptual-group metadata, split assignments, seeds and configurations, held-out predictions, candidate probabilities, numerical summaries, result figures, analysis and verification scripts, and scientific execution-source snapshots. Additional fixed-model analyses examine validation availability, validation-label contamination, and artifact retention. The README and reproducibility guide explain verification, reanalysis, environment requirements, and dataset reconstruction. Dataset images and model checkpoints are not included. Obtain the source images separately under their applicable access and use terms: COVID-19 Radiography Database: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/tawsifurrahman/covid19-radiography-database COVID19, Pneumonia, Normal Chest X-ray Images: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/sachinkumar413/covid-pneumonia-normal-chest-xray-images Tuberculosis Chest X-ray Dataset: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/tawsifurrahman/tuberculosis-tb-chest-xray-dataset The included metadata identify the exact study images for reconstruction from the original source bytes. Saved results can be checked without source images or retraining. The attack direction was selected exploratorily, perceptual grouping does not establish patient independence, and source-held-out generalization was not evaluated. Reuse rights are described in LICENSE_STATUS.txt. This work was supported by the Deanship of Scientific Research (DSR) at King Abdulaziz University, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, under grant No. IPP: 455-611-2026.

summary: Version 3.0 is the final data and analysis package supporting the manuscript “Registration, Outcome Changes, and Results Dissemination in Dental Erosion Research: A ClinicalTrials.gov Meta-Research Study.” It preserves the ClinicalTrials.gov search, screening, extraction, registration, results-dissemination, and publication-matching materials based on the fixed October 14, 2026 data-freeze date (D0), and adds the completed historical-registry analysis. The historical-registry extension was added after completion of the initial D0 analysis. Its protocol addendum and coding rules were finalized on October 15, 2026 before study-specific historical-registry extraction and coding. The completed extension reviewed 200 ClinicalTrials.gov record-history versions across 42 interventional studies and identified 25 actual outcome-state transitions. Seven of 42 studies had at least one substantive primary-outcome change and two had a Major change. Historical registry–publication primary-outcome agreement was assessed for the 21 Definite publication matches. Final agreement was Complete in 15/21, Partial in 3/21, and No clear in 3/21 using both the historical baseline and the D0 registry record; no masked historical discrepancy was identified. Historical transition severity and historical registry–publication agreement were independently assessed by two reviewers before consensus. Differences were resolved through discussion and consensus, and final classifications were rechecked against the relevant ClinicalTrials.gov record histories and publication sources. Version 3.0 also includes the completed blinded independent Reviewer-2 worksheet, raw ClinicalTrials.gov record-history captures, final consensus/QC datasets, and SHA-256 checksums.

summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have demonstrated strong capabilities in solving complex problems across diverse domains. Recently, the dynamic orchestration of agent systems has become an important research direction. However, existing methods suffer from limited composition, misaligned dependencies, and inflexible scale, restricting their ability to adapt to reasoning requirements during execution. To address these limitations, we reframe MAS design as a partially observable Markov decision process, in which both the composition and scale of the MAS are dynamically determined. We propose DHCG, a novel framework that coordinates three modules (Planner, Worker, and Generator) to progressively construct a dynamic hierarchical collaboration graph from scratch based on the query and evolving execution feedback. At each step, guided by feedback, the Planner generates a set of distinct and complementary roles tailored to the current reasoning needs and selectively routes relevant information to each role. It can also finalize the hierarchical collaboration graph early or progressively expand it when additional reasoning is required. We further introduce action-aware preference optimization to train the Planner to make more effective decisions when constructing hierarchical collaboration graphs. We systematically evaluate DHCG across code generation, mathematical reasoning, and domain-specific reasoning benchmarks. DHCG achieves state-of-the-art average performance among the compared methods, improving over the single-agent baseline by 13.06 points and outperforming both static and dynamic MAS baselines by 2.77-8.02 points. Additional experiments further demonstrate its generalization across different Planner backbones and unseen Worker models.
title: DHCG: Dynamic Construction of Hierarchical Collaboration Graphs for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Reasoning

summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) powered by large language models have shown strong performance across code generation, mathematical reasoning, and question answering. However, existing methods for automating MAS design mostly operate at the task level, producing a single fixed workflow per benchmark that is applied uniformly to all queries. This assumption fails under realistic conditions. Query difficulty varies widely within a task, and real-world workloads mix heterogeneous task types. We introduce OOPMAS, a training-free framework that generates both the agent set and the coordination workflow at the granularity of individual queries. Agents are represented as object-oriented class definitions with dedicated roles, tools, and persistent state, and workflows are expressed as executable main functions over these agent objects. A dynamic skill library accumulates structured lessons from execution feedback across optimization rounds, enabling in-context improvement without any gradient updates or fine-tuning. On a mixed-task benchmark of queries spanning code, math, and QA, OOPMAS achieves 89.6% accuracy, outperforming the strongest baseline by 18.1 percentage points. A model-swap study across four LLM backbones shows consistent scaling, reaching 92.4% with the strongest model.
title: OOPMAS: Object-Oriented Multi-Agent Systems for Query-Level Workflow Generation

summary: This record provides the public reproducibility materials associated with the study The Unequal Cultural City: Functional Differentiation and Spatial Inequality in London’s Cultural Infrastructure . The repository contains analytical code, public-safe derived neighbourhood data, spatial weights, source provenance, methodological protocols, confirmatory and robustness outputs, joint spatial re-estimation results, and supplementary materials for 4,994 Greater London 2021 LSOAs and a 2022 common-vintage cultural-infrastructure dataset. The study measures proximity-weighted availability of recorded cultural infrastructure and distinguishes Production from Encounter/Presentation functions. The two functions strongly overlap spatially. Their most consistently detected direct difference concerns metropolitan centrality: both decline with distance from London’s Central Activities Zone, with a steeper Encounter gradient. The differential deprivation association is model- and construct-sensitive, while the density difference remains unresolved. Cultural sustainability is treated as a bounded implication of the observed infrastructure configuration rather than as a directly measured sustainability outcome. The repository excludes raw site-level address/UPRN data and copyrighted source documents. Exact source provenance, reconstruction instructions, checksums, component-specific rights information, and reproducibility metadata are included.
title: Data, Code and Reproducibility Materials for "The Unequal Cultural City: Functional Differentiation and Spatial Inequality in London's Cultural Infrastructure"

summary: The existential theory of the reals asks whether polynomial constraints with integer coefficients have a real solution. We give a proof placing this problem in the counting hierarchy. The first argument is intended to expose the essential steps: a coercive minimum reduces feasibility to a finite critical algebra; residue formulas give its multiplication traces; and a short collection of derivative signs selects a real root. Exact formal power series and univariate resultants complete the calculation. This proof permits singular critical fibers and does not require a multivariate resultant algorithm. A separate analysis lowers the bound to \(\ETR\subseteq\BPP^{\Clevel3}\subseteq\Clevel4\). It uses a common formal homotopy, ordered labels for real roots, and randomized integer-sign reconstruction. For each fixed \(w\), sentences with \(w\) alternating real quantifier blocks lie in \(\Clevel{9w+17}\). We then treat exact semidefinite feasibility, \(\PosSLP\), square-root sum, geometric real counting, Euler characteristic, and complex feasibility in separate applications. The corresponding bounds include \(\BPP^{\Clevel2}\) for general SDP, \(\BPP^{\PP}\cap\Pclass^{\NP^{\PP}}\) for \(\PosSLP\) and square-root sum, and \(\FP^{\Clevel4}\) for total geometric real counting. Longer arithmetic proofs, conditional certificate routes, and limitations of other approaches are collected in the supplementary sections.
title: ETH in CH

A separate analysis lowers the bound to \(\ETR\subseteq\BPP^{\Clevel3}\subseteq\Clevel4\). It uses a common formal homotopy, ordered labels for real roots, and randomized integer-sign reconstruction. For each fixed \(w\), sentences with \(w\) alternating real quantifier blocks lie in \(\Clevel{9w+17}\). We then treat exact semidefinite feasibility, \(\PosSLP\), square-root sum, geometric real counting, Euler characteristic, and complex feasibility in separate applications. The corresponding bounds include \(\BPP^{\Clevel2}\) for general SDP, \(\BPP^{\PP}\cap\Pclass^{\NP^{\PP}}\) for \(\PosSLP\) and square-root sum, and \(\FP^{\Clevel4}\) for total geometric real counting. Longer arithmetic proofs, conditional certificate routes, and limitations of other approaches are collected in the supplementary sections.
title: ETH in CH

summary: This repository contains five human-labeled benchmark datasets developed for the study 'Automating literature screening and knowledge synthesis with large language models' . The datasets support evaluation of automated methods for literature screening, structured information extraction in knowledge synthesis, and scientific data discovery. The repository includes: Literature screening — machine learning in concrete materials science: 440 publications, including 272 labeled relevant and 168 labeled irrelevant. literature_screening_human_labels_ml_in_concrete.csv Literature screening — nanopore transport using molecular dynamics simulations: 205 publications, including 40 labeled relevant and 165 labeled irrelevant. literature_screening_human_labels_nanopore_transport.csv Literature screening — lithium extraction using NASICON-type materials: 200 publications, including 15 labeled relevant and 185 labeled irrelevant. literature_screening_human_labels_lithium_extraction.csv Knowledge synthesis — machine learning in concrete materials science: human labels for 50 full-text publications across five structured information fields: machine learning task, algorithm, binder system, prediction target, and input feature. knowledge_synthesis_extraction_human_labels_ml_in_concrete.csv Data discovery — silicate glass density: 200 publications, including 89 labeled as containing the target data and 111 labeled as not containing the target data. Supporting evidence for glass composition and density is also provided. data_discovery_human_labels_silicate_glass_density.csv The literature screening benchmark datasets provide DOI, publication year, title, abstract, and human relevance label. A label of  TRUE indicates that a publication was judged relevant according to the corresponding inclusion and exclusion criteria, whereas FALSE indicates that it was judged not relevant. The data discovery dataset uses the same binary labeling convention to indicate whether a publication contains the specified silicate glass density data. For the knowledge synthesis dataset, human annotations were assigned to five structured information fields using predefined controlled vocabularies. Details of benchmark construction, inclusion and exclusion criteria, annotation procedures, and inter-annotator agreement are provided in the Supplementary Information of the associated study.   Citation If you use these datasets, please cite both the associated publication and this repository: Li, Z., He, Q., Chen, W., Yang, K., & Gong, K. summary: Replication package for "Pricing Permanence: Settlement Charges and Refugee Sorting." The paper studies the United Kingdom's proposed settlement charge of about £10,000 per adult asylum-support recipient, collected from earnings above a threshold. It uses a six-destination Roy model of refugee destination choice with logit tastes. The package contains the derived data, the full calibration and estimation pipeline (minimum-distance estimation of the taste scale on Sweden's 2013 permanence expansion and Danish benefit reforms), all counterfactual and robustness scripts, the stored result files, and a verifier that checks every number reported in the manuscript and its Online Supplement against those result files. Start with REPLICATION_README.md; bash run_all.sh verify reproduces the checks. Third-party source data are documented with their access dates and licenses in the data catalog; files that cannot be redistributed are listed with download instructions.
tags: refugee policy, self-selection, settlement, skill portability, income-contingent loans.

summary: This research-software note introduces InstiAct v0.4.6, an independent Python framework for representing institutional admissibility and institutional state transitions in computational models. The note develops the modeling proposition that institutional structures can be represented as an explicit, inspectable, and experimentally variable state that filters candidate actions and can itself change through institutional events. It defines the boundary between institutional admissibility and physical feasibility, operational constraints, behavioral choice, learning, and optimization; documents the executable semantics of rights, hard constraints, defeasible norms, contracts, amendments, remedies, and transactions; and describes the interface for coupling InstiAct to agent-based models. DAMMAGE is treated as an explicit intellectual antecedent for executable rights-and-obligations environments, while InstiAct is positioned conservatively as an independent research implementation rather than a port, reconstruction, or claim of implementation equivalence. The note documents the v0.4.6 software release and supports reproducible computational experiments on institutional dynamics and changing action spaces.
title: InstiAct: An Executable Institutional Layer for Agent-Based and Computational Modeling — From Agreement Structures to Dynamic Action Spaces

summary: OpenAI’s October 2026 mathematics release raises a question about scholarly infrastructure: how can researchers make work public promptly while supporting scrutiny, durable citation and practical reuse? This article applies an earlier framework for research-archive release architecture to the GitHub release, arXiv’s moderation and submission limits, and Zenodo’s deposit and versioning arrangements. It distinguishes the authority to permit initial publication from the work of assessing a result. A repository’s limited evaluation capacity warrants attention, but does not by itself establish an appropriate limit on scientific production. Immediate release also creates responsibilities for producers, including clear verification status, usable exposition, stable references and support for subsequent understanding. A documented transfer difficulty and a reproducible inventory of 10,023 preprints files connect these institutional questions to practical access; repository-relative paths reach 271 characters, although the cause of the reported failure remains unresolved. The article proposes combining prompt public release with archived snapshots, explicit correction histories and independently organized scrutiny. GitHub and Zenodo can perform complementary roles, while persistent identifiers help readers locate the particular research object being discussed.
title: Making AI Research Public: Immediate Release, Scholarly Scrutiny and Durable Citation

summary: This volume develops the epistemological and research-practical foundations required for Generative Relational Economics. It examines how relational realities become accessible through evidence, manifestation, representation, interpretation, judgment, and historically situated inquiry, while maintaining a distinction between what is observed or represented and the relational structures inferred from those manifestations. The epistemological analysis addresses evidential mediation, uncertainty, salience, interpretation, representation, model dependence, inverse inference, and historical re-epistemization. Knowledge is treated as a relational achievement whose validity depends upon the interaction among objects of inquiry, observers, methods, institutions, records, and interpretive contexts. The volume then develops research as praxis. Historical, interpretive, qualitative, quantitative, empirical, formal, and computational approaches are treated as partially irreducible modes of epistemic access rather than as components of a universal methodological hierarchy. Their relations may involve complementarity, tension, mutual correction, and revision. The final portion develops a methodology of relational inquiry concerned with entities, relations, processes, events, states, properties, boundaries, memberships, networks, and historically evolving relational structures. Particular attention is given to the identification of relational objects, comparison across contexts, temporal reconstruction, representation, evidence, and the limits of relational attribution. The result is an epistemological and methodological architecture for studying relational economic systems without reducing them either to isolated entities or to a single privileged mode of representation.
title: Generative Relational Economics, Volume II: Epistemology, Research Praxis, and Relational Inquiry

summary: This repository contains processed data, Python scripts, computational results, molecular structures, figures, and quality-control reports supporting the associated manuscript. The study integrates molecular identity verification, experimental solubility harmonization, temperature-model comparison, solvent safety, health and environmental evidence, and residue–bioactive associations. The molecular library includes 17 bioactive compounds and 10 solvents associated with five agro-food residue matrices. The current curated database contains 911 records. The three-model temperature benchmark uses an earlier, explicitly identified input version comprising 251 eligible measurements across 41 systems. Separate analyses document quercetin exclusion sensitivity, reference-temperature coverage, solvent-ranking sensitivity, and the exclusion of 12 chlorogenic-acid mixture records from principal composition-based comparisons. The README identifies input versions, analysis boundaries, and the software environment. Historical results are retained in versioned directories. Complete package execution has not been independently verified. Publisher articles and downloaded article XML files are not included. The calculations describe equilibrium solubility and conditional solvent-capacity scenarios; they do not establish matrix-specific extraction yields or validated functional products. Experimental source publications are identified through DOI and provenance fields.
title: Data and Code for "From Agro-Food Waste to Functional Ingredients: A Computational Framework for Green Solvent Selection and Bioactive Compound Recovery"

summary: Doucette’s paper asks what a single scalar time series can establish about the distinction between thin and thick chaos. Standard methods—delay reconstruction and estimated Lyapunov exponents—show local instability but not transport between coherent sets. The paper proves that transport statistics defined by set membership, such as residence times and switching counts, survive injective delay embedding. However, if the observable is symmetric under a system symmetry, symmetry-related sets become indistinguishable, and their reconstructed images coincide. A two-state reduction gives switching rates and the second eigenvalue of the transition matrix, with a test of whether the reduced Markov description is valid. A record containing no switches can certify thinness only weakly: under a Poisson assumption, it bounds the switching rate and supports claims only over horizons much shorter than the record itself. Data from the thin side of a crisis cannot determine where the crisis occurs, because the crisis depends on a basin boundary the attractor does not visit; a measurable gap can help only if its critical value is supplied from a model or calibration. The Chua circuit is the test case. Immediately on either side of the merging crisis, the Lyapunov exponent is similar, but switching between scrolls is absent below the crisis. The transfer-matrix protocol recovers the scrolls when residence times exceed roughly six loop periods, but fails for faster switching or for a symmetric observable. A thin-side gap forecast the crisis to within about 0.002 when the critical gap came from the model, and was uninformative otherwise. The paper also tests noise, drift, and stationarity. Limitations include simulated data, one thin-regime system, partition dependence, a Poisson assumption, and biased Lyapunov estimates. The conclusion is that a single series can show chaos and sometimes transport between coherent sets, but only with a suitable observable, slow exchange, and careful attention to what data cannot decide.
title: Thin or Thick from a Single Time Series: What Can Be Measured, What Can Be Forecast, and What Cannot

summary: Doucette’s paper asks what a single scalar time series can establish about the distinction between thin and thick chaos. Standard methods—delay reconstruction and estimated Lyapunov exponents—show local instability but not transport between coherent sets. The paper proves that transport statistics defined by set membership, such as residence times and switching counts, survive injective delay embedding. However, if the observable is symmetric under a system symmetry, symmetry-related sets become indistinguishable, and their reconstructed images coincide. A two-state reduction gives switching rates and the second eigenvalue of the transition matrix, with a test of whether the reduced Markov description is valid. A record containing no switches can certify thinness only weakly: under a Poisson assumption, it bounds the switching rate and supports claims only over horizons much shorter than the record itself. Data from the thin side of a crisis cannot determine where the crisis occurs, because the crisis depends on a basin boundary the attractor does not visit; a measurable gap can help only if its critical value is supplied from a model or calibration. The Chua circuit is the test case. Immediately on either side of the merging crisis, the Lyapunov exponent is similar, but switching between scrolls is absent below the crisis. The transfer-matrix protocol recovers the scrolls when residence times exceed roughly six loop periods, but fails for faster switching or for a symmetric observable. A thin-side gap forecast the crisis to within about 0.002 when the critical gap came from the model, and was uninformative otherwise. The paper also tests noise, drift, and stationarity. Limitations include simulated data, one thin-regime system, partition dependence, a Poisson assumption, and biased Lyapunov estimates. The conclusion is that a single series can show chaos and sometimes transport between coherent sets, but only with a suitable observable, slow exchange, and careful attention to what data cannot decide.

The ceiling is documented and the library logs a warning, but the call still returns a number rather than raising, so a pipeline that does not read its logs silently reads a relabelled 90th percentile. For practice, the error metric has to match the loss the decision carries and the evaluation horizon has to match the replenishment cycle. summary: What's new Interface (optional, pip install "eprdating[gui]" ) Interactive interface for Jupyter and Google Colab: equivalent dose, sediment gamma spectrometry and age in three tabs, with downloads of results and settings. Intensity window centred on a g value or on a field in G or mT; Compare methods gives De with the four intensity methods. Weights of the dose-response fit: measured errors, 1/I² or equal. Spectra Reader for Freiberg Instruments MS5000 spectra (ESRStudio .xml , .csv export, or a folder of runs). Double integral with the derivative baseline fitted outside the window: about 40 % less scatter. empirical_template : line-shape template from the strongest spectra of a series. Optional protocol for enamel fragments measured at several angles: merged spectrum, angular profile, X-ray calibration (the isotropic correction is not included). Dose rate Optional alpha escape at the enamel surfaces ( ToothSample(alpha_escape=True) ): brings unstripped ROSY reference ages to within 0.5–2.5 %. Validation Public dose series of the Calio P4 enamel (Hakim et al. 2025, Nature; CC-BY 4.0) included and tested: SSE De 2259–2286 Gy vs published 2267 ± 99 Gy, once the 8000 and 15 000 Gy labels of the archive are exchanged. summary: Replication archive for the agent-based model reported in: Artıktay, G. G. (2026). Synthetic Abundance, Scarce Attention, and Platform Governance: An Agent-Based Model of AI-Generated Music in Streaming Markets (manuscript under review). The model studies how a platform-mediated streaming market converts AI-generated uploads into listening, payment, and revenue under alternative governance regimes (provenance detection with error, recommender demotion or exclusion, monetization and popularity recycling of bot streams, royalty thresholds, licensing splits, and listener-facing labels), with a particular interest in the gap disclosed by Deezer in 2026 between the upload share of fully AI-generated tracks (44%, then above 50%) and their stream share (1 to 3%). Version 1.2.1. No model code changed and every deposited output of version 1.2.0 is unchanged. This version completes the replication material of the revised design: the scripts behind the paired welfare comparisons (python/paired_welfare_v2.py), the twelve-month-window entry-shock trajectory (python/shock_window_v2.py) and the manuscript figures (python/figures_v2.py), their outputs, a codebook for outputs_v2/ (outputs_v2/README.md), the ODD protocol of the revised design (docs/ODD_protocol_v1.2.md), a fix to python/sensitivity_structure_v2.py (it now creates its output folder and accepts an output directory argument), and updated documentation. The whole pipeline was rerun from this archive on a second machine (Linux, Python 3.13, NumPy 2.5, SciPy 1.18, SALib 1.6) and every output file was identical to the deposited one. Contents: Python model (python/abm_music.py), scenario definitions (python/scenarios_v2.py), pipeline (python/run_pipeline_v2.py), Sobol and Latin-hypercube sensitivity analysis (python/sobol_v2.py), structural test (python/sensitivity_structure_v2.py), verification tests, the NetLogo replication of the version 1.1.0 design, every output file behind the manuscript's tables and figures (outputs_v2/), and documentation (README.md, CHANGELOG.md, docs/). Licence: CC BY 4.0.

summary: Achieving global coordination without a central controller or dense global communication is a defining challenge for both biological collectives and engineered swarms. We introduce and analyze a minimal model in which self-propelled agents in a bounded domain periodically reorient their motions toward the centroid of a small, randomly chosen subset of their peers, with no direct sensing of any individual neighbor's position or heading. We show that this sparse, non-local sampling rule reliably drives an initially disordered population to a globally aligned, nematic state, and that shrinking the sampled subset -- down to the minimum of two agents -- accelerates ordering rather than impeding it: the resulting estimation noise, filtered through a geometric turning rule, is itself the engine of symmetry breaking. We derive an analytical criterion, in quantitative agreement with simulation, that predicts when this ordering succeeds as a function of the sampling size and sampling frequency. We confirm the mechanism experimentally in a swarm of up to fifteen differential-drive robots. These results identify sparse random sampling as an information-efficient route to collective coordination, with implications for understanding animal collectives and for designing communication-limited robotic swarms.
title: Trend formation with sparse global sampling

summary: We develop a regularized finite element method for the fractional conductivity equation, recovering the conductivity on an exterior observation region from noisy Dirichlet-to-Neumann measurements and using this reconstruction to determine the interior conductivity. Mesh-localized inputs and mass-lumped Tikhonov regularization discretize the exterior determination principle of Covi--Railo--Zimmermann (2026, Calc. Var. PDE). We prove exterior \(L^2\)- and \(L^\infty\)-convergence with error estimates, including the logarithmic correction at the critical Hölder exponent. The exterior reconstruction enables the Liouville reduction to the Calderón problem for the fractional Schrödinger equation. Separated measurements recover the interior potential, after which overlapping measurements determine the exterior potential tail. Together with the recovered exterior conductivity, the tail supplies the exterior Cauchy data for a Tikhonov-regularized finite element least-squares continuation. We prove \(H^s\)-convergence of the transformed conductivity and \(L^2\)-convergence of the interior conductivity, together with logarithmic state-bias and conductivity error estimates for full observation spaces. The admissible reconstructions remain uniformly positive and bounded. We present one- and two-dimensional numerical experiments illustrating the accuracy of the exterior and interior reconstructions and their sensitivity to measurement noise and discretization.
title: A finite element exterior-to-interior reconstruction in the fractional conductivity inverse problem

summary: Much knowledge work produces new deliverables from files a workspace already holds, and LLM agents are beginning to take such work over. Through direct corpus interaction, an agent can search and read any of those files from a terminal with no indexing, and producing a deliverable from many of them in this way is what we call direct workspace interaction (DWI). Reaching the files, however, is only half the task: nothing keeps track of what the task asks for, what has been read, and what was listed but never opened, all of which slip through the context window without leaving a trace, so an agent may extract a figure and still deliver a report without it. To address this, we present RunningTab, a framework that equips direct workspace interaction with an environment-side tab: a per-task record of what the task still owes, kept by the environment alongside the agent. Specifically, the agent adds its requirements, while the environment records every file read as an excerpt with its provenance and every listed but unopened file as a candidate; the agent can then see each requirement beside its best-matching excerpts and top unopened candidates, resolve it against matching content or set it aside with a reason, and, should it try to finish with requirements still open, receive them in a finish check. We validate RunningTab on three benchmarks with three LLMs, where it consistently outperforms plain DWI and baselines that keep the record in the model, while its tab usually holds the values a deliverable needs once seen.
title: RunningTab: Direct Workspace Interaction with Environment-Side Tabs

summary: This dataset contains processed numerical source data and representative model setup files supporting the main and supplementary figures in the manuscript “Ocean memory amplifies Antarctica’s sea-level contribution after climate overshoot”. The source-data archive includes 58 CSV tables covering Antarctic and basin-scale sea-level contributions, additional contributions relative to the LOW reference experiment, ocean-recovery diagnostics, surface and basal mass-balance diagnostics, and model sensitivity analyses. Supporting summaries and integration audits are also included. A README, data dictionary, file-level provenance, and SHA-256 checksums document the contents, units, conventions, and file integrity. Original filenames are preserved; figure numbering reflects development names, and tables supporting alternative figure layouts are included. A separate archive contains the unpartitioned Antarctic computational mesh, a representative HIGH m005 Elmer/Ice configuration (SIF), supporting Lua files, and Fortran source files. A README, file-level provenance, and SHA-256 checksums document this package. Mesh partitions and configurations for other experiments and ensemble members are excluded. Raw simulation outputs, forcing fields, and restart files are excluded. Forcing and restart files are too large to include; users should contact the corresponding author, Dr Chen Zhao ( chen.zhao@utas.edu.au ), for access. Additional supporting inputs and matching XIOS configuration files are required to rerun the model. Analysis and plotting scripts are not included in these two archives. The processed source-data tables are licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0). Model source files retain their existing copyright and licence notices.
title: Source data for "Ocean memory amplifies Antarctica's sea-level contribution after climate overshoot"

summary: We introduce a flexible mixture model for the joint source-frame component-mass distribution of compact binaries, inferred simultaneously with cosmology, together with a framework that identifies structures in the reconstructed density, quantifying their posterior stability, local prominence, and cosmological relevance. Applied to GWTC-5.0, the workflow clarifies several familiar and emergent structures. The $\sim35~M_\odot$ feature is classified as a clear near-equal-mass peak despite an ambiguous interpretation in the primary-mass projection. A weaker unequal-mass concentration near $(21,12)~M_\odot$ is recovered frequently but with lower prominence. A tentative joint transition near $60~M_\odot$ appears at mildly unequal masses, with a more robust manifestation in the primary-mass projection. For cosmology, the two-dimensional mass model constraint on $H_0$ is $33\%$ narrower than a model that flexibly reconstructs only the primary mass, and only $\sim~10\%$ wider than analyses based on strongly parameterized one-dimensional spectral structure. At the feature level, we show that the $\sim10~M_\odot$ and $\sim35~M_\odot$ concentrations depend on $H_0$ mainly through a common scale which captures the entire $\sim~(1+z)$ cosmological rescaling of both masses; the intermediate unequal-mass feature instead retains residual dependence in the orthogonal mass-ratio direction. More generally, we argue that population prominence, formal inclusion in an astrophysical feature catalogue, and cosmological relevance need not coincide. These results suggest that a genuinely two-dimensional view may be required to fully exploit spectral-siren information. Our workflow provides a reproducible way to detect population structure and identify which aspects of its geometry are associated with spectral-siren constraints. The feature finder is directly applicable to other population reconstructions.
title: A weakly modelled view of the joint compact-binary mass plane: population structure and spectral-siren cosmology

summary: We consider the inverse problem of recovering a potential $q$, depending on space and time, in the wave equation $(\Box_g+q)u=0$ on a Lorentzian manifold. We prove Lipschitz stability for a formally determined version of this problem under a \textit{null-cone foliation} assumption. As a consequence, we obtain uniqueness in the Lorentzian Calderón problem for $q$ under this assumption. Our approach is based on a modification of the Bukhgeim--Klibanov method using distorted plane waves.
title: Stability for a formally determined Lorentzian inverse problem

summary: Deploying a joint audio-video diffusion transformer for real-time, interactive generation normally requires two essential modifications: block-autoregressive attention, so frames can be emitted before the whole clip is finished, and few-step sampling, so each block is cheap. Conventionally, the streaming video literature obtains both capabilities from a chained pipeline. It first distills a bidirectional teacher into a causal student, then into a few-step one, or proceeds in reverse order. Each stage of such a chain fine-tunes the weights the previous one produced, so a later objective can undo an earlier capability. Following the idea of model merging, we show that on a packed audio-video backbone the two capabilities can be acquired in parallel. A causal adapter is trained against the frozen backbone, and an off-the-shelf few-step adapter provides the few-step capability. As the two edit different functional axes, we predict, and then verify, that their weight-update directions are near-orthogonal, without any explicit orthogonality constraint during training. Orthogonal updates should combine without interfering, so parallel composition is a direct sum. The two adapters are simply added at inference, with no joint training, yielding few-step, streaming audio-video whose image quality tracks the bidirectional teacher. Compared to the chained baselines, the composed model matches or beats them on most metrics, making parallel composition a practical approach. The resulting streaming system generates joint audio-video in real time, $\approx$26 fps at $480\times832$ without quantization, and sustains 30 s of continuous generation with stable image quality.
title: Real-Time Joint Audio-Video Generation by Parallel Adapter Composition

summary: We study the low-frequency scattering of gravitational and pseudoscalar waves off a non-rotating black hole in dynamical Chern-Simons (dCS) gravity, where the axial (odd-parity) gravitational sector is irreducibly coupled to the dynamical pseudoscalar while the polar sector remains general relativistic. Working to first order in the dimensionless coupling zeta = (ell_CS/M)^4 and using matched asymptotic expansions, we obtain an exact closed form for the graviton-to-pseudoscalar conversion probability, d_2 = 3(pi^2-9)^2/8, and a high-precision reconstruction, in a proven transcendental basis, of the graviton greybody (absorption) asymmetry, kappa_2 = (21/80) pi^4 + (27/8) pi^2 - 89833/1536, for the quadrupole (ell=2) channel. Both reduce to combinations of pi^4, pi^2, and rational numbers, with no ln2 or odd-zeta terms in the reconstructed basis; the transmission-phase sector, by contrast, contains an analytically derived zeta(3)-9/8 static integral, while its overall matching prefactor is identified numerically. The leading reflection-phase asymmetry vanishes, so that no polarization rotation is imprinted on the reflected wave at leading low-frequency order, while a subleading O(omegazeta) asymmetry remains in the transmitted phase. The normalized flux asymmetries are numerically consistent with a 1/(Momega)^2 falloff in the geometric-optics limit, where the leading remaining flux effect is conversion loss. The matched-asymptotic results are checked against direct two-channel integration, while the one-dimensional integral determining kappa_2 is evaluated to high precision within an analytically controlled transcendental basis. The results provide analytic targets linking dCS parity violation in absorption and mode conversion to the axial/polar quasinormal-mode splitting.
title: Analytic parity-violating greybody factors of a dynamical Chern-Simons black hole
