summary: Graduate students increasingly need publication literacy that combines scientific writing, research integrity, journal selection, and the ability to navigate peer review. This study profiled the understanding of reputable scientific article writing among students in a Master's Program in Sports Coaching Education and identified areas that require targeted academic support. The study used a descriptive quantitative design with total sampling. Forty-three active master's students completed a closed Likert-scale questionnaire after a scientific writing workshop. The instrument covered six domains: scientific article structure, the IMRaD system, publication ethics and plagiarism, reputable-journal selection, citation and referencing, and peer review and revision. Scores were converted into percentages using the procedure defined in the study protocol. The overall understanding score was 75.58%, which the progress report classified as "Good Understanding" because it remained below the 76% threshold for the highest category. Four comparatively weaker items were writing IMRaD sections according to scientific conventions (68.6%), identifying appropriate information for each IMRaD section (69.8%), responding appropriately to reviewer comments (70.1%), and distinguishing scientific articles from popular or opinion articles (71.8%). The findings indicate that students possess a relatively strong conceptual foundation but still need support in applied genre knowledge and publication-process skills. Writing clinics should therefore prioritize guided IMRaD practice, article deconstruction, simulated reviewer-response exercises, and structured journal-selection activities. Because the survey was administered after the workshop and no baseline measure was available, the results describe current understanding and do not establish workshop effectiveness.

summary: Code and results for the simulation study "Code and simulation results for: Do observable calibration metrics identify the best competing-risks prediction model? A simulation study of DeepHit, Fine-Gray and cause-specific Cox models in small-to-moderate samples" (submitted to Statistics in Medicine). The archive Art2_DataFiles.zip contains the R and Python code to generate the data (three data-generating mechanisms, 108 scenarios, 500 replications), fit the cause-specific Cox, Fine-Gray and DeepHit models, compute all performance measures, run the pseudo-observation sensitivity analysis and the bootstrap coverage study, and reproduce the METABRIC illustration and all tables and figures. It also contains the scenario-level results (sim_summary.csv), the sensitivity and coverage results, and the METABRIC results. sim_all_results.csv holds one row per replication, method and horizon. Every data set can be regenerated from the seeds in the code. The METABRIC clinical data are not redistributed; a script downloads them from cBioPortal (study brca_metabric). No genomic data were used. See README.md inside the archive for details.
title: Code and simulation results for: Do observable calibration metrics identify the best competing-risks prediction model? A simulation study of DeepHit, Fine-Gray and cause-specific Cox models in small-to-moderate samples

summary: The capabilities of an agent swarm depend on both its individual members and how they coordinate. Yet existing multi-agent systems often train agents within fixed orchestration structures, separating the learning of individual capabilities from the organization of collective behavior. We introduce market-based post-training (MPT), a framework for jointly learning action policies and self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms. Agents express their willingness to participate through bids, which determine who acts and how collective outcomes provide local training credit. Learning both action and bidding behavior allows individual capabilities and patterns of participation to adapt together without a central coordinating agent. We evaluate MPT on embodied crafting, robot navigation, and deep research. Results show gains over monolithic post-training and confirm that agent participation indeed evolves with learning. With the same post-trained action policies, learned self-orchestration outperforms alternative coordination strategies. Ablations show that both action and bidding benefit from learning, and that learned bids provide more effective action-training signals. Beyond the original training objectives, trained swarms adapt faster to related tasks and achieve better performance with larger populations at inference time. Larger populations also suffer smaller performance losses under agent dropout, demonstrating that learned self-orchestration supports reuse, scaling, and robustness in decentralized agent swarms. Code and trained models are available at https://github.com/Embodied-Minds-Lab/MPT.
title: Learning Self-Orchestration in Decentralized Agent Swarms

summary: Cooperative driving at mixed-traffic unsignalized intersections is challenged by imperfect vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication, human-driven vehicle (HV) intentions that cannot be directly communicated, and the potential incompatibility of independently generated crossing decisions. This paper proposes State-Intent-Aware Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Driving under Imperfect V2X (SIGN-MAPPO) to address these challenges through three coordinated mechanisms. Each decision-eligible connected and automated vehicle (CAV) first reconstructs a receiver-specific traffic graph from its ego state and the peer-state records available to it, from which a shared graph-attention policy generates a raw Stop/Go intention augmented with predicted HV-intent features. CAV intentions are then exchanged through timestamped vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) messages, and a local conflict-aware arbitration layer converts each CAV's intention into a safe executable action despite potentially inconsistent peer information. In the principal Simulation of Urban MObility (SUMO) evaluation, SIGN-MAPPO achieves a 97.53% completion rate, a 0.10% collision rate, and a mean intersection traversal time of 35.28 s. Ablation studies further confirm the complementary contributions of HV-intent prediction and CAV-intent exchange to this performance. The trained policy also remains robust under the evaluated communication-delay and packet-loss ranges, and cross-scenario tests show complete traffic clearance across the tested settings, though safety margins narrow under compound unpredictable HV behavior.
title: SIGN-MAPPO: State-Intent-Aware Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Driving under Imperfect V2X

summary: This paper studies parameter families of finite exponential sums in which two tie endpoints of a near-maximum level set approach at the critical rate δ_r ≍ qr^{-1/2}. The endpoint separation, half-bowl width, and competitor-kernel decay length then coincide. The cluster trio is rigid: its three exponents are determined by the level and endpoint positions, while coefficient ratios and other competitors require separate control. In a realized family, six rescaled kernels carry the interaction through one microscopic phase. Under explicit kernel-convergence hypotheses, the second-order term has a joint limit given by the excess sublevel length of a limiting profile, decomposed into a separated-endpoint sum and an interaction term. For an explicit four-term family, the hypotheses are verified with uniform explicit constants for every admissible phase lock. Two families have identical spectra and corresponding coefficient moduli at every radius but different critical limits. Along an unlocked calibration, phase dependence yields non-existence of the critical limit for specified parameters; certified intervals quantify the gap, and failure persists on an open parameter set. For a positive zero-lock family, upper and lower bounds describe the excluded shared arc. Full exclusion never occurs, and nonempty exclusion requires an additional parameter condition. The formal endpoint-anchored cap cannot be realized by a family satisfying the cluster hypotheses. High-precision numerical measurements on actual exponential sums compare with the profiles and exhibit phase dependence.
title: Critical-Scale Clustering and the Breakdown of Universality for Near-Maximum Phase Measures of Exponential Sums

summary: We consider the three-dimensional Prandtl boundary layer equations near a smooth structured solution (u_s, K u_s) with ∂z K ≡ 0. Under a monotone-or-degenerate profile assumption on u_s(·), we prove local well-posedness, continuous dependence, and a priori estimates in the critical Sobolev space X^s = H^s_γ(r) × H^s_γ(q) × H^s_γ(∇{x,y} q), where r = u − u_s and q = v − K u. Our proof does not assume smallness of the data, monotonicity of ∂_z u_s, or Gevrey regularity. We also establish a nonlinear norm-inflation result showing that the raw H^s topology on q alone is insufficient, and we identify the minimal tangential derivative of q required. Several stress tests, counterexamples, and open problems are discussed.
title: Sobolev Well-Posedness for Three-Dimensional Prandtl Boundary Layers Near Proportional Structures in a Critical Transverse Space

summary: Replication package for Legrenzi, Ciola and Bazzana, “Adaptation to climate-induced macrofinancial risks: top-down and bottom-up solutions”. The package contains the MATLAB implementation of a Stock-Flow-Consistent Agent-Based Integrated Assessment Model, the empirical calibration and the PSO/RWMH structural estimation routines, the input data on emissions and climate damages, the full simulation output (13 scenarios with 250 Monte Carlo simulations each), and the scripts that regenerate figures and tables in the paper. Running "master_replication.m" in the package root reproduces the complete set of exhibits. See "README.txt" for software requirements, folder structure and a file-by-file description.

summary: Post-Soviet states have spent three decades rebuilding the civic curriculum around national rather than supranational loyalties, yet claims that modernized patriotic education changes what students know and value seldom face controlled scrutiny. This study evaluates a convergent model that couples national heritage content with interactive methods, digital gamification, STEAM-linked projects, and the weekly Kelajak Soati (Future Hour) curriculum in Uzbek general secondary schools. A three-stage quasi-experiment (ascertaining, 2022-2023; formative, 2023-2024; summative, 2024-2025) enrolled 1,192 students in ten schools across Tashkent, Fergana, and Navoiy, allocated to experimental (n = 594) and control (n = 598) conditions. Groups were equivalent at baseline (M = 3.52 vs. 3.53 on a three-level scale scored 3-5; t = −0.12, p = .90; χ 2 (2) = 0.40, p = .82). At post-test the experimental group outperformed the control group (M = 3.92 vs. 3.52; Welch t(1184.4) = 10.46, p < .001, d = 0.61; χ 2 (2) = 141.78, Cramér’s V = .34), with non-overlapping 97% confidence intervals and an effectiveness ratio of 1.11. Change concentrated at the lower threshold: the share of experimental students at the Low level fell from 58.4% to 23.9% while the Medium level rose from 30.8% to 60.6%; the control distribution did not move. Effects replicated in every region (d = 0.56-0.65), and net-of-baseline gains were as large in the rural Fergana district as in Navoiy. The model reliably converts civic disengagement into baseline civic literacy; whether it fosters constructive rather than conformist attachment remains untested. Implications for national scale-up and its evaluation are discussed.
title: HERITAGE, TECHNOLOGY, AND CIVIC ATTACHMENT: A THREE-REGION QUASI-EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION OF CONVERGENT PATRIOTIC EDUCATION IN UZBEK SECONDARY SCHOOLS, 2022-2025

summary: This technical note documents a conditional mathematical correspondence between the static spatial kernel used in conventional electromagnetic potential theory and the fixed-source gravitational potential in Lisa Doumbouya’s Harmonic Physics programme. Under supplied three-dimensional Euclidean geometry, spherical symmetry and stated boundary conditions, the derivation gives the static Green function 1/(4πr). Applying the existing gravitational source normalization yields the potential −μ/r, whose radial derivative gives the inward acceleration −μ/r². The note distinguishes potential, field amplitude, intensity, acceleration and optical measurement conversion, keeping geometric normalization separate from the distance exponent. The optical phase-ruler results are reviewed alongside the GRACE-FO forward forecasts. Calibrated reconstruction using measured phase retained micrometre-scale agreement with processed microwave ranging, while some forward models produced much larger errors. These results do not establish exponential error growth or identify a unique physical cause. The correspondence uses established mathematics and remains conditional on the supplied geometry, source calibration and physical interpretation. It does not establish an electromagnetic mechanism of gravity or derive spatial geometry from foundational Phase. The note includes the analytical proof, assumptions, evidence boundaries and requirements for a subsequent physical test. No new experimental data are introduced.
title: Inverse Radius Kernel and Optical Phase Registration

These are proposed research instruments: they have not been validated, no independent coding study has been completed, and the CSV contains no data.

summary: This working paper develops a relational Phase interpretation of black holes within the Harmonic Physics research programme, using general relativity, exact Kerr geometry and semiclassical black-hole thermodynamics as its physical baseline. It examines how phase organisation, temporal reference, observer accessibility and information persistence might relate to black-hole closure. Within the proposed framework, a phase-cycle is a closed relational structure that supports recurrence. Measured succession requires distinguishable relations and persistent records, while geometry and causal history are treated as observer-level reconstructions. The temporal-anchor hypothesis concerns a deeper terminal condition at which the parent domain loses the internally usable references needed to resolve further clocks and geometry. This proposed condition is kept distinct from the regular event horizon, across which local evolution continues. Observation is described through a joint observation relation among admitted source organisation, a physical channel and an observer-capable organisation. Source state, coupling and registered record retain separate roles; changes in accessibility may alter registration while the source organisation persists. The paper consolidates three bounded mathematical findings: exact Kerr ingoing and outgoing endpoints can have opposite trapped and anti-trapped orientations with the same mass and spin parameters; spherical source/exterior matching leaves the transition law undetermined; and a leading slow-rotation calculation permits the same sign of angular momentum in closing and opening configurations. These results establish compatibility within the stated geometric constructions. A physical transition mechanism remains to be derived. Black-to-white-hole models provide external theoretical comparisons. Return to the original exterior and the opening of a daughter phase are treated as distinct hypotheses, each requiring an appropriate causal structure, state map and conservation accounting. The remaining requirements include an invariant parent-relative terminal criterion, a physical Phase-to-boundary map, transition dynamics, information and entropy accounting, and a stable nonperturbative rotating completion. The paper remains a developing theoretical interpretation supported by standard-geometry comparisons and bounded symbolic checks. It does not establish a physical black-to-white transition, information recovery through evaporation or a daughter universe. Version 2.3, dated 17 October 2026, updates observation and self-nesting terminology, clarifies geodesic incompleteness and fixed-angular-momentum assumptions, and refreshes the references. The existing displayed equations and reported test results are retained. keywords: Phase Theory; black holes; event horizons; geodesic incompleteness; relational time; phase contraction; information accessibility; singularity; white holes; quantum gravity.
title: Black Holes as Temporal Anchors

summary: SELF-CALIBRATING NANO-NEURAL INTERFACES AND REFERENCE LINEAGE AT THE LIMIT Built-In References × Drift Attribution × Independent Functional Requalification STARLI / Institute XXIII / Research Flagship 17 PUBLICATION DESCRIPTION When a long-running neural interface changes, is the cause the sensor, the surrounding tissue, or the decoder? An adaptive algorithm can restore predictive accuracy while obscuring the physical origin of its own correction. This book proposes a rigorous, falsifiable architecture for self-calibrating nano-neural interfaces that must retain the scientific history of every reference and every update. Its central axiom is that self-calibration does not imply self-certification: measurement claims, permission to change, electrode safety and functional benefit demand independent evidence. summary: Overview This repository contains the two processed datasets analyzed in "Influence of land cover and shade on the thermal environments of schoolyards in Los Angeles" by Levinson et al. (in preparation). The data come from the LAUSD Cool Schoolyards experiment, a field study of how schoolyard surfaces affect surface temperature, air temperature, radiant heat, and outdoor thermal comfort at Los Angeles Unified School District (LAUSD) elementary schools. The study compares four surface types: uncoated asphalt pavement, pavement with a high-reflectance coating (coated pavement), turf, and garden. The first file holds mobile measurements taken with an instrumented cart that was moved across each schoolyard. The second holds continuous measurements from three stationary weather stations placed over different surfaces. Study sites and measurement periods Each school is identified in the data by a two-letter code: HE : Harrison Elementary School, City Terrace, Los Angeles, CA BE : Braddock Drive Elementary School and Gifted Magnet, Culver City area, Los Angeles, CA SE : Saticoy Elementary School, North Hollywood, Los Angeles, CA Mobile cart measurements were made at HE on 2025-09-06, at BE on 2025-09-07, and at SE on 2025-09-14. The weather stations were deployed at BE from 2025-09-10 13:00 to 2025-10-10 09:00 and at HE from 2025-10-10 14:00 to 2025-11-02 00:00. File 1: Transect measurements Transect measurement stats at 1 min + coded transects + open-meteo weather + shade + LSH.csv An instrumented cart was moved along a route of numbered locations ("transect points") across each schoolyard. At each point it stopped for about one minute and recorded readings every second. Each row summarizes one stop, giving the mean, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum of every measured variable. The route was traversed repeatedly in forward and reverse directions. The file includes: Identifiers: school, measurement number, transect point, a tag of the form MMM_SS_PP (measurement number, school, point), transect number, and direction. Microclimate: air temperature, relative humidity, and wind speed and direction measured about 1.5 m above the ground. Radiation and surfaces: downward solar irradiance, ground albedo (the fraction of sunlight the ground reflects), ground surface temperature, sky temperature, and mean radiant temperature (MRT, a measure of the total radiant heat a person receives). Readings from 12 radiometers are also included: six measuring sunlight and six measuring longwave (thermal) radiation, facing up, down, forward, back, left, and right. Instrument orientation and position: radiometer tilt, roll, and zenith angles, plus GPS coordinates. Surface properties: surface description and classification of each point, along with measured solar reflectance and thermal emittance. Derived quantities: solar position, local solar hour, the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI, an index of how hot conditions feel to a person) and its heat-stress category, and a shade classification for each stop. In the Classification column, the labels "Warm pavement," "Cool pavement," "Grass," and "Nature area" correspond to uncoated pavement, coated pavement, turf, and garden, respectively. summary: Fisher information metric tensors for the 41 held-out SONICOM test subjects, as used in “Evaluating Spatial Discriminability Preservation in HRTF Upsampling Using Fisher Information” (D. Bassett). Code and reproduction instructions: https://github.com/domfrbassett/fisher-rao-hrtf-upsampling What the tensors are At each of the 793 directions of the SONICOM grid, the 2×2 tensor g = JᵀΣ⁻¹J describes how well the auditory cues separate that direction from its neighbours. J is the spatial Jacobian of the cues: Barumerli monaural PGE features, ILD and MaxIACCe-transformed ITD, each fitted with real spherical harmonics. Σ holds the cue noise (σ_mon = 1.25 dB, σ_ILD = 1 dB, σ_ITD = 0.569). All fields are low-pass filtered at 16 kHz before the cues are extracted. The tensor is expressed in a local tangent basis u₁ = a × r, u₂ = r × u₁, where a = z, or y when |r_z| > 0.9, and its units are d′² per rad². Contents metric_tensors.zip has one folder per subject, metric_tensors/subject_####/ , containing 25 files per subject (1,025 in total): reference_metric_tensor.mat : the dense measured HRTF. <METHOD>_N###_metric_tensor.mat : one file per reconstruction. There are six methods: SUpDEq_SH , SUpDEq_MCA , SUpDEq_NN_MCA_6dB (SUpDEq-Natural-MCA in the paper), SUpDEq_Bary_MCA_6dB , RANF and FSP_AE . Each is reconstructed from N = 100, 19, 5 and 3 retained directions. The 164 natural-neighbour and barycentric files at N = 5 and 3 have status “ not_applicable ”. The interpolation is undefined for those masks, so these files carry no tensors. Variables in each file: metricTensor : the tensors at SH order 6 [2×2×793]. familyGram : per-cue-family Gram matrices JᵀJ before noise weighting, at SH orders 4, 6 and 8 [2×2×793×3 families×3 orders]. They let you recompute the tensors with other noise values or SH orders. In reconstruction files only: crossFamilyGram : the unsymmetrised cross terms J_refᵀ J_recon, same layout as familyGram . airmByDirection : the pointwise AIRM discrepancy from the reference. Metadata: coordinates (Cartesian and azimuth/elevation in degrees), cue band, noise values (reference files only), status (“ completed ” or “ not_applicable ”) and, for not-applicable files, a message giving the reason. SHA256SUMS.txt lists a checksum for every file. Format and use The files are MATLAB v7.3 (HDF5), so MATLAB, h5py or any HDF5 reader can open them. Note that h5py reverses MATLAB’s axis order. scripts/fisher_lib.py in the repository reads them and recomputes tensors, AIRM and thresholds from the Gram matrices. To rerun the analysis scripts, unzip into results/evaluation/ so the subject folders sit in results/evaluation/metric_tensors/ . Provenance Produced with run_evaluation("tensors") from the repository above. The values are numerically identical to the tensor files behind results/evaluation/full_evaluation_summary.csv ; this run additionally stores the cross terms. The tensors are derived from the SONICOM HRTF Dataset (Engel et al., J. Audio Eng. Soc. 71(5), 2023, doi:10.17743/jaes.2022.0066). The SONICOM HRTFs are released under the MIT licence. This work develops research begun for the author’s B.Sc. dissertation at Birmingham City University.

summary: Code, trained networks and data for the paper “Physics-informed neural networks for maximizing quantum Fisher information in time-dependent many-body systems”. The archive Zenodo_deposit.zip is self-contained. It holds the training method (a counter-diabatic control expanded in Pauli strings, with a learned schedule, propagated with a fourth-order commutator-free Magnus integrator), the trained network and configuration of every reported run, Supplementary Data 1 (source data of every figure and table), Supplementary Data 2 (pulse files), and a script that regenerates the figures, tables and reported numbers and checks them against the deposited values. Instructions are in README.md inside the archive. Version 2.0.6 re-exports the figure PDFs of the archive; the code, trained networks and data are those of version 2.0.5. Version 2.0.5 corrects the description of the QFI floor and of the stored candidates in the README so that it matches the code, redraws Supplementary Fig. 1 with a key grouped by kind of control, and adds the panels of the time-resolved QFI to Supplementary Fig. 4; the trained networks and data are those of version 2.0.4. Version 2.0.4 completes the regeneration path of the Supplementary Information: python reproduce.py baselines covers every size computed in the paper (ideal control up to twelve qubits), python reproduce.py symmetry also reports the symmetry fractions and compares the Holm-corrected p-values and partial correlations, python reproduce.py verify --exact repeats the dense validation, python reproduce.py replay retrains a paper run against its stored history, and the three runs of the propagation-cadence calibration are included (983 runs). The README documents the selection rules and step control as implemented. Supplementary Data 1 no longer lists the unreported right-limit probe rows of exact_controls.csv ; the trained networks and all other data are unchanged. Download: the archive is stored in eleven parts. Rejoin them with cat Zenodo_deposit.zip.part-* > Zenodo_deposit.zip (on Windows, copy /b Zenodo_deposit.zip.part-aa + Zenodo_deposit.zip.part-ab + ... Zenodo_deposit.zip , listing the parts in order) and check the result with shasum -a 256 -c Zenodo_deposit.zip.sha256 . License: the code is released under the MIT License, and the data, trained networks, figures and tables under CC BY 4.0. Preprint of the first version of the manuscript: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18506
title: Physics-informed neural networks for maximizing quantum Fisher information in time-dependent many-body systems

summary: Code, pre-registrations, generated model text and result files for the manuscript “How Much Text Reveals a Watermark? A Detection Law for Keyless Auditing of Language-Model Watermarks” (submitted to IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security). The archive holds the five pre-registered experiments of the paper: P54 (synthetic text, Unigram watermark), P54b (real text from Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct with fixed-list and context-keyed watermarks and a SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct reference), P54c (repeated queries with the key derived from the whole prompt), P54d/P54e (repeated queries with the key from the last h tokens, passive counting of watermarks that are unbiased over keys including SynthID-Text, and additional real-text analyses) and P54f (the word-counting audit repeated on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct). Each experiment folder contains the pre-registration with its SHA-256 lock file written before the run (Turkish original and English translation), the analysis and generation scripts, the generated text, the result files and a result note. The folder manuscript_numbers contains the script that produces every number, table and figure of the manuscript from the result files, so that no number in the paper is typed by hand. README.md describes the layout, how to verify the lock files and how to reproduce the numbers and the experiments; SHA256SUMS.txt lists the checksum of every file. Code: MIT licence. Text, pre-registrations and generated model outputs: CC BY 4.0. The generated texts are outputs of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct under their respective licences.
title: How Much Text Reveals a Watermark? A Detection Law for Keyless Auditing of Language-Model Watermarks — code, pre-registrations, generated text and results

summary: We investigate the rigidity of smooth stationary solutions to the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations in ℝⁿ with singularities along a linear subspace Σ ≅ ℝᵏ. Assuming the scale-invariant transverse bound ‖u(x)‖ ≤ C‖x′‖⁻¹, where x′ ∈ ℝᵐ represents the transverse coordinates and m = n − k is the codimension of the singularity, we prove that u ≡ 0 provided m ≥ 4 and 1 ≤ k < m. This result generalizes the recent theorem of Gui, Liu, Wang, and Xie (2026), which corresponds to the case k = 1 and n ≥ 5. Our proof relies on a quantitative local regularity theorem showing that the transverse bound implies the removability of the singularity along Σ. The argument combines weak extension across the subspace, approximate Green functions for the adjoint drift operator, a one-sided bound for the total head pressure, and a localized Frehse–Růžička weighted estimate followed by a finite Stokes–Morrey bootstrap. Furthermore, we establish the sharpness of the codimension threshold m ≥ 4 by constructing non-trivial counterexamples for m = 1, m = 2, and m = 3 via trivial extensions of Jeffery–Hamel and Landau solutions, together with a new explicit family of non-trivial solutions in the borderline case m = 1. Finally, we discuss the technical obstruction preventing the immediate removal of the condition k < m and propose a conditional rigidity result under additional integrability assumptions.
title: RIGIDITY OF STATIONARY NAVIER–STOKES SOLUTIONS WITH TRANSVERSE BOUNDS NEAR HIGHER-CODIMENSIONAL SINGULAR SUBSPACES

summary: Abnormal  uterine  bleeding  (AUB)  is  a  symptom  rather  than  a  single disease, and diagnostic failure may follow when the bleeding phenotype is  mistaken for an etiological diagnosis. The International Federation of Gynecology  Obstetrics (FIGO) PALM–COEIN system provides a common vocabulary for  structural  and  nonstructural  causes,  but  its  practical  diagno stic  value  depends  on  examination  strategy,  phenotype  documentation,  access  to  investigations,  and  competing  risks.  Objective:  To  critically  evaluate  the  role  of  PALM–COEIN  in  triage, etiological work-up, longitudinal care, and real-world evidence generation,  with particular attention to digital decision support and feasibility in Uzbekistan

title: Diagnostic Significance of the FIGO PALM–COEIN Classification in the Evaluation of Abnormal Uterine Bleeding: An Integrative Critical Review

summary: QMBL: Open Problems is a record book of the state of the art in quantum many-body simulation for problems with no exact ground-state energy. Scientists and AI systems should use the shared results to build on each other's work more efficiently and advance frontier science. This snapshot holds the launch target list (targets/v1.json, 153 instances frozen from QMBL v0.4.0; 152 are open today, as one has since been solved exactly), the entry format and its checks, and the maintainer's re-measurement flow; the verifier is quantum-many-body-leaderboard/verifier.

summary: Underwater acoustic target detection and recognition are essential to marine surveillance and intelligent ocean sensing. Despite substantial advances in deep learning, existing systems typically produce binary detection decisions, categorical labels, or scalar confidence scores, offering limited insight into the physical evidence underlying their outputs. Large language models (LLMs) offer an opportunity to move underwater acoustic sensing toward interpretable, evidence-grounded understanding; however, generic audio encoders struggle to capture the distinctive physical characteristics of underwater acoustics, and physically annotated data are scarce. In this paper, the first of a two-part series, we propose a from-signals-to-evidence framework that integrates physics-aware acoustic encoding with a pretrained LLM, organized around a unified feature-evidence-decision chain with a shared reasoning core. An open input layer accommodates heterogeneous information-raw waveforms, time-frequency representations, environmental and geographic data, and textual physical priors-unifying detection and recognition within a common formulation. In Part I, we instantiate this framework for target recognition through an Underwater Acoustic Physics-aware Transformer (UPT), which tokenizes complementary acoustic representations and learns task-disentangled physical representations through four physics-oriented learning tasks. We develop a physics-parameterized data engine that provides traceable supervision at two levels of granularity and introduce an attribute-level evaluation protocol to assess the physical fidelity of generated descriptions. Experiments on simulated recordings of four vessels demonstrate accurate vessel recognition and reliable estimation of shaft frequency, blade-passing frequency, and machinery-related attributes.
title: From Signals to Evidence: Interpretable Underwater Acoustic Target Sensing with Large Language Models - Part I: Framework and Recognition

summary: Recent advances in deep learning have significantly improved underwater acoustic vessel recognition. However, existing publicly available datasets are typically limited in scale, hindering large-scale representation learning and downstream task evaluation. To address this limitation, we introduce ONCship, a large-scale underwater acoustic dataset comprising 4521 hours of curated recordings from Ocean Networks Canada (ONC) hydrophones and Automatic Identification System (AIS) data. We evaluate the proposed dataset across three tasks: self-supervised representation learning, vessel-type classification, and MMSI-Level Vessel Classification. Experiments on DeepShip and ShipsEar demonstrate the effectiveness of ONCship for acoustic representation learning, with joint pre-training on ONCship and AudioSet achieving a classification accuracy of 62.45% on DeepShip through linear probing. Furthermore, incorporating ONCship as auxiliary training data improves downstream vessel-type classification performance. Beyond conventional vessel-type classification, we further investigate MMSI-Level Vessel Classification, treating each vessel as a distinct identity. Experimental results show that models fine-tuned with different loss functions achieve Top-1 accuracies exceeding 53% and Top-5 accuracies approaching 69%, demonstrating the feasibility of distinguishing individual vessels through MMSI-Level Vessel Classification. Overall, ONCship provides a valuable resource for underwater acoustic representation learning and vessel recognition, while its rich vessel-level metadata enables further exploration of MMSI-Level Vessel Classification.

summary: Large audio-language models (LALMs) are fast becoming a general interface to sound, yet how far their broad pretraining carries into specialized domains remains largely open. Vessel monitoring, maritime safety, and ocean sensing all depend on recognizing underwater signals, but to our knowledge LALMs have not been systematically evaluated on them. Annotated recordings are costly to collect, and a faithful synthetic alternative has to bring together many interacting factors: the structure of detection pulses, communication waveforms, and ship-radiated noise, and the sound-speed profile, geometry, and multipath propagation through which each reaches the receiver. We address this by proposing \textbf{UA-Bench}, to our knowledge the first large-scale benchmark for evaluating LALMs on underwater acoustic signal recognition. It comprises 375,051 audio records that couple parameterized sources with modeled propagation, so that every record can be traced to the conditions that produced it. The records span these three signal families, and each carries a three-level label hierarchy (13 leaf classes), a templated multi-turn dialogue, and source and channel metadata. We evaluate on a balanced 2,600-record subset with a gated coarse-to-fine protocol that locates each error at source routing, fine-grained classification, or output format, and add a paired silent-audio control to test whether the waveform is actually used. Nine open LALMs, evaluated without task-specific adaptation, reach only 2.0\%--13.1\% leaf accuracy, against a random reference of 7.7\%. The waveform helps source routing far more than leaf recognition (for one model, +29.5 versus +2.3 points over silence), and just four models gain reliably at the leaf level, by at most 4.7 points. UA-Bench thus gives a reference point for these models, and its released training partition supports follow-up adaptation work.

summary: Adaptive modulation and coding (AMC) improves the spectral efficiency of underwater acoustic (UWA) links, but its feedback is inevitably stale: sound propagates slowly, and by the time channel state information (CSI) arrives, the fast time-varying multipath channel has moved on. Predictive link adaptation therefore needs more than a point forecast: it needs a distribution over each candidate action's consequences. We propose PRB-WM, a physics-regularized Beta world model for predictive per-subcarrier link adaptation on real time-varying UWA channels. A persistence-anchored stochastic latent-space dynamics model learns how the channel evolves; a counterfactual outcome head evaluates, for every candidate modulation and coding scheme (MCS), a Beta-binomial distribution of bit errors on shared imagined futures; and a chance-constrained receding-horizon model predictive controller maximizes expected spectral efficiency subject to a bounded probability of violating the bit error rate (BER) target. To the best of our knowledge, PRB-WM is the first world model for UWA communications. In closed-loop replay of six measured sea-trial links from the public UWA Channel Library against a 24-method pool spanning the full methodological spectrum, PRB-WM attains a mean goodput 87% above the strongest baseline, ranks first on all six time-varying links at the longest lookahead, and is the only method whose realized frame risk decreases systematically with lookahead, meeting the BER-violation contract where no baseline does. Ablations confirm that rollout sampling dispersion is essential to the chance constraint and that the physics anchor is necessary for trainability.

summary: The underwater sound speed distribution directly governs acoustic propagation paths, rendering it critically important for underwater acoustic communication and target localization. Conventional sound speed profile (SSP) prediction methods provide a good way to estimate the underwater sound speed distribution without on-site data measurement, thus breaking through the coverage area constraints of sonar observation equipment and making the model universal in most marine areas. However, underwater sound speed exhibits multi-scale variations, such as diurnal, quarterly, and intermittent fluctuations caused by ocean processes such as internal waves. This makes it difficult for the fixed structure models in existing methods to have good generalization ability for multi-scale sound speed distribution patterns. To tackle this problem, we proposed a lightweight hybrid basis-function empowered Kolmogorov-Arnold network (LHBF-KAN) model for multi-scale sound speed prediction. We aim to construct a multi-branch representation layer in which different basis functions respond to distinct temporal patterns, from slowly varying background trends to rapid fluctuations induced by dynamic ocean processes, allowing the model to naturally accommodate the inherently multi-scale evolution of sound speed at different depths. To prevent the multi-branch structure from increasing model size, a pruning strategy is further introduced to suppress branches with consistently low contribution during training, yielding a compact architecture, suitable for deployment on resource constrained underwater platforms.
title: Robust Prediction of Internal Wave-Affected Multi-Scale Sound Speed Distribution Using Lightweight Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with Hybrid Basis Functions

summary: Ultrasound (US)-based auricular vagus nerve stimulation (aVNS) is emerging as a versatile, noninvasive modality for neuromodulation - spanning clinical therapies (e.g., pain management, depression) and general well-being applications. However, most existing US-based aVNS systems remain bulky and require wet coupling media (e.g., ultrasound gel) to achieve both spatially localized stimulation and efficient acoustic transmission. We present a wearable US stimulation system combining a personalized, dry-coupled earpiece with a battery-powered, wireless US probe. The earpiece integrates a 2 MHz piezoelectric transducer fully encapsulated in Humimic material designed for anatomical fit and stable coupling without externally applied gel. Hydrophone measurements of the fully encapsulated earpiece in water give a peak rarefactional pressure of 0.24 MPa at 15 mm for a 15 V unipolar excitation. We further demonstrate in vivo feasibility through fully dry, in-ear 2 MHz pulse-echo acquisitions under realistic wearing conditions, confirming effective US transmission without the need for coupling gel. These results demonstrate the integration of a personalized dry acoustic interface with battery-powered stimulation electronics, providing a wearable platform for investigating US-based aVNS. Future studies will focus on functional outcomes, including heart rate variability and pupillary responses during stimulation.
title: Towards an Earpiece for Wearable and Dry Ultrasonic Vagus Nerve Stimulation

summary: Localizing an autonomous underwater vehicle without pre-deployed seabed transponders, or direct access to onboard vehicle sensors remains a core challenge. We present a receiver-passive 3-D localization and spatial mapping system utilizing a single floating surface buoy equipped with a hydrophone array and an inertial measurement unit (IMU). The central difficulty is that surface wave motion induces six-degree-of-freedom (6-DOF) perturbations that rotate the array between snapshots, degrading conventional subspace processing. We resolve this by introducing a fixed-point iterative MUltiple SIgnal Classification algorithm (FP-MUSIC) that uses IMU measurements to de-warp snapshot covariances prior to direction-of-arrival estimation. Furthermore, we employ a subspace-projected wideband matched filter to resolve beacon ranges and use power asymmetry for independent front-back identification. Evaluations across simulated sea states demonstrate that FP-MUSIC substantially reduces localization error relative to uncompensated methods and sustains robust 3-D tracking and vehicle orientation estimation under wave-induced motion. At moderate sea state, FP-MUSIC increases the 2-m beacon-separation accuracy from approximately 45% to 75%.
title: Wave-Robust Passive AUV Localization Using FP-MUSIC

System administration: Work with user accounts and groups. System security configuration (file permissions, timestamps, ACL, SELinux ). Service management (installation, configuration, ...) Block devices and partitioning, disk formats, and filesystems. RAID (hardware and software) and LVM2 NAS and SAN storage systems overview SAN storage systems: iSCSI Fibre Channel (FC) Disk I/O subsystems and optimizations. Disk I/O performance and monitoring  System analysis and optimizations (perf, strace, ltrace, dstat). Working with log files and services. Kernel dump/core dump. Computer networks: Copper vs Optical networks: Copper: cabling and standards. Fiberoptics: standards, cabling, FTTH specifics. Network interfaces (NIC) design and details, classic (copper) NICs (RJ-45), and SFP specifics. Networking concepts and protocols (topology, CSMA/CD, Bridging, OSI model): OSI 2 model and protocols: Bridges, ARP, and Flow control. STP, LACP, LLDP, OSI 2 network interfaces,.... OSI 3 model and protocols: IP, QoS, IP Fragmentation. TTL, MTU. NAT (DNAT, SNAT). Redundancy and VRRP, .... Transport layer: UDP  TCP: SYN, ACK, SACK.  TCP Window, Window scaling, congestion control.  PSH&URG, ... . Multipath TCP Network in Linux (configuration and details). Optimizing network interfaces and services for 10+Gbps (10/25/100Gbps) Common network commands:  traceroute, nslookup. netstat, nstat, ss, lsof. ip, ethtool. tcpdump. Network services and protocols: DHCP, Bootp, TFTP DNS: Protocol details Types of DNS requests DNS records: A, AAA, PTR, CNAME, DNAME, MX, NS, SOA, SPF, DKIM, DMARC, ... Telnet and SSH. NFS E-mail: SMTP, POP3, IMAP HTTP/HTTPS, Proxy NTP Syslog SNMP Work with the firewall: iptables ipset nftables eBPF Namespaces and isolation Virtualization and Linux containers: LXC  Podman Security: Enforcements Compliance (NIST, CIS, DISA STIG, ...) summary: Code and data of Chapter 3 of the doctoral thesis Mathematical models to describe tumoral behaviors under treatment regimens (Graduate Program in Biometrics, Institute of Biosciences, São Paulo State University, Botucatu, 2026). The deposit covers a three-population ordinary differential equation model of cutaneous melanoma under CAR T-cell therapy with tumor-associated macrophages: its equilibria and local asymptotic stability, the Hopf bifurcation driven by the pro-tumoral action of the macrophages, a variance-based global sensitivity analysis (eFAST), the Bayesian calibration against the immunocompetent B16 data of Jilani et al. (2024), the structural identifiability analysis with StructuralIdentifiability.jl, the profile-likelihood analysis of practical identifiability, the Fisher-information comparison of experimental designs, and the computational scenarios built on the calibrated model. Each folder has a README with its structure, and REPRODUCE.md gives the command that produces each figure and table of the chapter. The MCMC chains are deposited separately because of their size.
title: Melanoma under CAR T-cell therapy with TAM-mediated immunosuppression: model analysis, Bayesian calibration and identifiability (code and data)

summary: Pareto Support Proofs is the computational companion to “Sparse exact certificates for weighted-sum unsupportedness in finite multi-objective optimisation”. This R1 distribution, OPTL-R1-20261017, contains the corrected engine 0.6.2, the preserved standalone checker 0.6.1 and reproduction layer AC3-candidate.1. The new controlled run is AC3_REPAIRED_20261017_01. Historical engine 0.6.1, R1_01 results and their provenance remain separately preserved. The companion provides exact certificate generation, generator-independent checking, JSON schemas, instances, certificates, raw observations, source manifests, figure sources and editable ODG files. Negative certificates are checked by exact arithmetic on recorded feasible decisions. Positive objects distinguish full P1 verification from the explicitly retained trusted-oracle P2 boundary. The retained study contains 225 objects: 190 correctness, 27 scaling and eight timing-case objects. Of these, 213 are fully verified at P1 and 12 positive binary-linear objects remain conditional P2. Separately implemented checks reproduce the 190 classifications and the arithmetic of all 102 negative objects. The 225 mathematical certificate payloads match the historical R1_01 payloads. All 225 historical trace files are preserved byte-for-byte; new provenance identifies the corrected run. The historical R1_01 timing batch has eight cases, 240 measurements and 24 warmups. The corrected shortest-path timing batch has three cases, 90 measurements and nine warmups. They are reported separately, including the supportable three-objective case in which checking has the higher median. The historical runner-hash gap remains disclosed. These records do not constitute formal software verification or independent human review. Source code is licensed under BSD-3-Clause. Data, instances, certificates, results, figures and prose documentation are licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0). The component boundaries and retained historical licences are documented inside the companion. AI-assisted preparation and validation are disclosed in the associated manuscript and supporting documentation; Antonio Clim remains responsible for the content. The four deposited files are ESM_1_Pareto_Support_Proofs_R1.zip, Fig1_Editable_Sources_R1.zip, PUBLIC_RELEASE_CONTEXT.md and SHA256SUMS.txt. They match the four named assets of the corresponding GitHub release. The ESM file is the journal's Online Resource 1; automatic GitHub source-code archives are different files. summary: Version 3 is an organisational change only: the four subsections of the verification section are reordered so that the two Krook levels, the amplitude equation and the Vlasov solver, precede the two with diffusion and drag, the amplitude equation with diffusion and drag and the Vlasov solver with the Fokker–Planck operator. No text, number, figure or table is changed from version 2, and the description below is version 2’s. Version 2 of this paper adds a related-work section placing the work against the analytic quasi-steady theory of Lestz and Duarte (2021), the regime maps of Zhang et al. (2026) and the steady-or-chirping criterion of Duarte et al. (2017, 2018); places the near-marginal comparison against Lestz and Duarte's two validity constraints and withdraws version 1's reading of the 24 percent gap, which is now a candidate explanation and not an established one; relabels the drag ratio of the ITER-like slice as the collisional ratio of Lilley et al. and places the turbulence-corrected ITER ratio, an order of magnitude smaller, between the two steady slices tested; states the comparison with the cold-background regime map at the point where the reduced model fails; narrows three statements of version 1 to what was tested; and adds the experiments version 1 left open, a reverse ramp pair at the first operating point and the edge and a benchmark pair at a second operating point. An erratum corrects a sentence of version 1's Limits section that had the two near-threshold amplitudes reversed: the held level of the full- f solver is 24 percent above the cubic equation's steady state, not the other way round. The paper builds and verifies a two-level reduced model of a fast-ion-driven mode, the Berk–Breizman bump-on-tail problem, as a plant whose purpose is to locate and characterise the regime in which the mode saturates to a steady state, the regime a fusion power plant must stay in. Level 0 is the near-threshold cubic amplitude equation with Krook, diffusive and drag collisions; Level 1 is a full- f one-dimensional Vlasov solver with a Krook operator; Level 2 adds drag and diffusion acting on the departure from the initial distribution. Each level was verified against the literature before its results were used: the amplitude equation reproduces the critical Krook rate 4.4 and the critical diffusion rate 2.05; the Vlasov solver reproduces the linear growth rate and frequency to 0.01 percent, conserves energy to second order, and reproduces the Berk–Breizman saturation law within 4 percent across the steady region and the diffusive saturation formula within 4 to 7 percent away from marginal stability. For the warm distribution used, the external damping on the field is only 87 percent effective as an amplitude damping, so marginal stability lies at a damping of 1.15 times the collisionless drive rather than 1.0; with that correction the full- f solver agrees with the cubic equation on the steady side of the bifurcation near threshold, and saturates 24 percent above it at a finite distance from marginal stability, in the direction and of the size that other simulations have reported against the same theory. The steady region is mapped in the damping–collision plane: with Krook collisions the oscillating region is a tongue at collision rates below 0.3 to 0.4 of the drive, closed above it; with diffusion equal to the drive, with or without drag at 0.7 of diffusion, every damping from 0.1 to 0.9 of the drive is steady, one point still rising at the end of its run; with drag at 1.2 of diffusion no steady point was found, and at the strongest drives the reduced model leaves its validity where a cold-background resonant model saturates steadily. The edge of the steady region along the collision axis lies between diffusion rates of 0.4 and 0.5 of the drive at a damping of 0.5 of the drive, converged on two velocity grids, and within the same bracket at a damping of 0.3, where every steady level is 1.41
title: A reduced bump-on-tail plant for the steady operating region of a fast-ion-driven mode: amplitude equation, full-f Vlasov solver with Fokker-Planck collisions, regime map and a detection benchmark

summary: This document contains supplemental material of the paper " Global Minima of the Thomson Problem in a Disk: A Molecular Dynamics Approach with Fixed Border Charges ", where the Thomson problem in a disk has been studied. Here we report the lowest minima for the configurations with N = 54 , 60 , 61 , 65 , 66 , 82 , 83 , 85 , 88 , 89 , 90 , 91 , 92 , 97 , 99 , 100 , 101 , 102 , 103 , 104 , 105 , 111 , 113 , 117 , 119 , 133 , 137 , 141 , 149 , 150 , 151 , 153 , 155 , 187 , 286 , and 318 confined particles, obtained by the Quenched Molecular Dynamics (QMD) method. The energy of these configurations is lower than that of the configurations reported by Amore and Zarate ([ Phys. Rev. E. 108 , 055302 (2023) ]; see the supplemental material in Ref. [ 10.5281/zenodo.8301044 ]). For systems with N = 92 , 100 , 102 , 113 , and 133 particles, in contrast to the asymmetric Voronoi diagrams obtained by previous optimization algorithms, our solutions exhibit a clear D1 (axial) symmetry of defects. For a system with N = 286 particles, in contrast to the asymmetric Voronoi diagrams obtained by previous optimization algorithms, our solution exhibits a clear C2  (central inversion) symmetry of defects. However, for a system with N = 150  particles, the lower energy configuration results in a reduction in the symmetry of the defects. Voronoi diagrams are displayed for the 26 configurations that exhibit structural or orientational changes in the defect pattern compared to Ref. [ 10.5281/zenodo.8301044 ], whereas for the remaining 10 systems (with N = 61 , 83 , 85 , 89 , 90 , 91 ,  97 , 99 , 119 , and 137 particles) QMD method refines the equilibrium coordinates and lowers the energy within the same Voronoi topology.
title: Global Minima of the Thomson Problem in a Disk: A Molecular Dynamics Approach with Fixed Border Charges. Supplemental Material

summary: Subclonal reconstruction results produced with CliPP 1.4 for three datasets: 5,424 tumors from TCGA, 2,008 whole-genome tumors from PCAWG, and CliPPSim4k, a cohort of 4,000 simulated tumors with known ground truth. Wenyi Wang is the corresponding author. README.md describes each archive's layout and the columns of every file.

summary: We study the fine phase-space spectral asymptotics of a model class of infinite-order pseudodifferential operators whose symbols grow like exp(c|ξ|^2), c > 0. The leading Weyl law for such operators is known, but the complete logarithmic structure of the heat trace, the singularity structure of the associated zeta function, and the correct notion of a renormalized determinant require a more delicate analysis. We prove that, in dimension four, the reduced heat trace admits the complete asymptotic expansion τ(t) = A L^2 + B L log L + C L + D (log L)^2 + E log L + F + O(1/L), where L = log(1/t), and all coefficients A, B, C, D, E, F are computed explicitly. Consequently, the model zeta function has the structure ζ(s) = α_2 s^(-2) + α_1 (log s)/s + β_1 s^(-1) + γ_2 (log s)^2 + γ_1 log s + ζ_0 + O(s log s) as s → 0^+, with all displayed coefficients determined explicitly. Because the remainder generally produces terms of the form s log s in the renormalized zeta function, the classical derivative ζ'_ren(0) is not automatically finite. We therefore introduce a finite-part renormalized determinant, defined through the constant term in the derivative expansion, and prove its existence under the full asymptotic hierarchy of the heat trace. We also show that in odd dimensions the zeta function possesses algebraic branch points rather than poles, and we explain why the classical zeta determinant construction must be modified. Finally, we recover the growth exponent α from the counting function in the model a(ξ) ∼ exp(c|ξ|^α), and we compare the results with the theories of Pilipović–Prangoski–Vindas, Gilkey–Grubb, Kontsevich–Vishik, and Nicola–Rodino.
title: Fine Structure of Spectral Asymptotics for Infinite-Order Pseudodifferential Operators with Second-Order Exponential Growth

summary: Background. Antireflux fundoplication failure — recurrent reflux, dysphagia, gas-bloat syndrome, secondary to a herniated, slipped, too-tight, disrupted, or twisted valve — remains common, and its endoscopic diagnosis lacks a common, standardized reporting language. Aim. To narratively review existing endoscopic instruments for postoperative antireflux valve assessment, the evidence on their interobserver reliability, and to position an original instrument — the Endoscopic Fundoplication Score (SEF) — within this landscape. Methods. Narrative review, with a targeted search in PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar (last search: 24 September 2026) using the terms “fundoplication,” “endoscopic grading,” “gastroesophageal valve,” “Hill classification,” “antireflux surgery outcome,” “interobserver reliability,” “wrap integrity,” and “hiatal hernia recurrence,” covering literature published between 1996 and 2026 in English or with an English abstract, supplemented by reference-list screening of identified articles. Results. Three major endoscopic instruments were identified — the Hill classification (1996), the Jobe system (2004), and the American Foregut Society (AFS) nomenclature (2025) — alongside a descriptive, non-scored taxonomy of failure types (herniated, slipped, tight, disrupted, twisted). The interobserver reliability studies [1,2] identified in this review for the postoperative setting report low agreement, and a retrospective comparison of endoscopy reports [3] documented major discrepancies between external endoscopists and operating surgeons. The AFS classification of esophagogastric junction integrity achieved substantial agreement on static images (κ=0.65) but only fair agreement under dynamic conditions (κ=0.371), and the postoperative AFS nomenclature has not yet been tested for interobserver reliability. The SEF score, an 11-item composite instrument (0–16 points) applied to a cohort of 178 patients, correlated in preliminary single-centre data with the Hill classification, Los Angeles (LA) esophagitis grade, and the Visick patient-satisfaction score (own data, manuscript submitted for publication), offering a numeric, quantifiable alternative to existing categorical systems. The SEF threshold of ≤10 points, defined in the same cohort, is exploratory. Conclusions. The field of postoperative endoscopic antireflux valve assessment remains fragmented, without an interobserver-reliable consensus standard. The SEF score partially addresses this gap through a numeric structure, with experience-based weights and an exploratory threshold, but requires formal interobserver reliability testing and multicenter validation against the surgical gold standard.
title: ENDOSCOPIC EVALUATION OF THE ANTIREFLUX VALVE AFTER FUNDOPLICATION: SYNTHESIS OF THE EVIDENCE AND PROPOSAL OF A FUNCTIONAL ENDOSCOPIC SCORE

summary: First tagged release of vmtools, R helpers for cardiovascular epidemiology. Includes: PREVENT (total CVD, ASCVD, heart failure) and Pooled Cohort Equations risk scores; HOMA-IR, HOMA-β, QUICKI, Matsuda and Avignon insulin indices; GLI-2012 predicted FEV1 and FVC (ages 25–95); Human Metabolome Database lookups; and utilities. Validated against the Goff 2013 PCE worked example, the PREVENT reference values in the preventr test suite, and the official GLI-2012 lookup tables (within 0.5%). Fixes since earlier versions predict_FVC : corrected a sign error affecting predicted FVC in women calcPREVENT.HF : added the missing age factor to the BMI interaction term predict_FEV1 / predict_FVC : explicit Caucasian option; "other" now uses GLI Other/mixed coefficients calcAvignon.SI , mqsave and HMDB_ID_from_name now work as documented Install: remotes::install_github("vlmurthylab/vmtools@v0.1.0")
title: vmtools: handy tools for cardiovascular epidemiology

summary: NANOROBOT-ENHANCED DIGITAL TWINS OF BRAIN STATE AT THE LIMIT A multiscale, uncertainty-aware research atlas on microrobotic observations, neural inverse problems, active model discrimination and the limits of computational brain twins. This research monograph asks whether additional microscale observations or strictly bounded reversible experiments can distinguish competing neural-state models that explain conventional measurements equally well. The twin is explicitly defined as a versioned scientific belief, not a digital person, a mind reader or a clinically validated instrument. Its objective is not maximum model complexity but improved identifiability, calibrated prediction under new conditions and faithful retention of failed hypotheses. The work develops five layers: multiscale neural and microenvironment state representation; posterior equivalence and prior sensitivity; non-clinical safe experimental design; frozen-version forking, rollback and reference ancestry; and blind prospective validation against classical state-space systems and independently specified alternatives. Its research architecture includes 30 distinct mathematical derivation plates linked to later chapters, 82 chapters with five independently paginated research sections apiece, 200 detailed Research Gates and 33 revisable Phoenix Answer Embryos. A DOI evidence ledger identifies existing support for brain modeling, latent neural dynamics, experiment design and preclinical microrobot tracking while preventing those sources from being mistaken for evidence of the proposed integrated system. Key research questions include: Can two equally accurate virtual brains be separated by a small, permissible observation? How can the effect of a measurement itself be separated from neural change? When does a prior dominate the inferred brain state? Can the model predict unseen function rather than reconstruct a training signal? Can another laboratory reproduce a rejected twin and safely return to an earlier version? SCIENTIFIC STATUS AND LIMITATIONS This is a forward-looking, non-clinical research synthesis and experimental hypothesis architecture. summary: This replication package accompanies the paper "An Exploratory Evaluation of Targeted Label Poisoning in a Client-Local Feature Federated Ensemble for Chest X-Ray Classification." It contains code and saved experimental results for an exploratory study of Pneumonia-to-Normal label poisoning in four-class chest X-ray classification. The study uses 20,795 images from three public sources, with 20,557 perceptual groups kept intact across experimental partitions. The package covers 212 completed training jobs, including main and component comparisons, classifier-head sensitivity, image-model references, candidate probability banks, and earlier-poisoning experiments. The main comparisons and image-model references use ten deterministic seeds. The classifier-head and GRU-structure study uses three seeds. Included materials comprise dataset manifests and image checksums, perceptual-group metadata, split assignments, seeds and configurations, held-out predictions, candidate probabilities, numerical summaries, result figures, analysis and verification scripts, and scientific execution-source snapshots. Additional fixed-model analyses examine validation availability, validation-label contamination, and artifact retention. The README and reproducibility guide explain verification, reanalysis, environment requirements, and dataset reconstruction. Dataset images and model checkpoints are not included. Obtain the source images separately under their applicable access and use terms: COVID-19 Radiography Database: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/tawsifurrahman/covid19-radiography-database COVID19, Pneumonia, Normal Chest X-ray Images: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/sachinkumar413/covid-pneumonia-normal-chest-xray-images Tuberculosis Chest X-ray Dataset: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/tawsifurrahman/tuberculosis-tb-chest-xray-dataset The included metadata identify the exact study images for reconstruction from the original source bytes. Saved results can be checked without source images or retraining. The attack direction was selected exploratorily, perceptual grouping does not establish patient independence, and source-held-out generalization was not evaluated. Reuse rights are described in LICENSE_STATUS.txt. This work was supported by the Deanship of Scientific Research (DSR) at King Abdulaziz University, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, under grant No. IPP: 455-611-2026.

summary: Version 3.0 is the final data and analysis package supporting the manuscript “Registration, Outcome Changes, and Results Dissemination in Dental Erosion Research: A ClinicalTrials.gov Meta-Research Study.” It preserves the ClinicalTrials.gov search, screening, extraction, registration, results-dissemination, and publication-matching materials based on the fixed October 14, 2026 data-freeze date (D0), and adds the completed historical-registry analysis. The historical-registry extension was added after completion of the initial D0 analysis. Its protocol addendum and coding rules were finalized on October 15, 2026 before study-specific historical-registry extraction and coding. The completed extension reviewed 200 ClinicalTrials.gov record-history versions across 42 interventional studies and identified 25 actual outcome-state transitions. Seven of 42 studies had at least one substantive primary-outcome change and two had a Major change. Historical registry–publication primary-outcome agreement was assessed for the 21 Definite publication matches. Final agreement was Complete in 15/21, Partial in 3/21, and No clear in 3/21 using both the historical baseline and the D0 registry record; no masked historical discrepancy was identified. Historical transition severity and historical registry–publication agreement were independently assessed by two reviewers before consensus. Differences were resolved through discussion and consensus, and final classifications were rechecked against the relevant ClinicalTrials.gov record histories and publication sources. Version 3.0 also includes the completed blinded independent Reviewer-2 worksheet, raw ClinicalTrials.gov record-history captures, final consensus/QC datasets, and SHA-256 checksums.

The historical-registry extension was added after completion of the initial D0 analysis. Its protocol addendum and coding rules were finalized on October 15, 2026 before study-specific historical-registry extraction and coding. The completed extension reviewed 200 ClinicalTrials.gov record-history versions across 42 interventional studies and identified 25 actual outcome-state transitions. Seven of 42 studies had at least one substantive primary-outcome change and two had a Major change. Historical registry–publication primary-outcome agreement was assessed for the 21 Definite publication matches. Final agreement was Complete in 15/21, Partial in 3/21, and No clear in 3/21 using both the historical baseline and the D0 registry record; no masked historical discrepancy was identified. Historical transition severity and historical registry–publication agreement were independently assessed by two reviewers before consensus. Differences were resolved through discussion and consensus, and final classifications were rechecked against the relevant ClinicalTrials.gov record histories and publication sources. Version 3.0 also includes the completed blinded independent Reviewer-2 worksheet, raw ClinicalTrials.gov record-history captures, final consensus/QC datasets, and SHA-256 checksums.

summary: Large audio language models (LALMs) have made substantial progress in audio understanding. However, in high-throughput applications requiring frequent selection, judgment, and scoring, autoregressive text generation introduces additional computational overhead and response latency. To address this limitation, we introduce Qwen-Audio-Jev by augmenting Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR-Flash-Next with a dedicated Jev decision head. The model unifies selection, binary judgment, and scoring through three decision primitives: CHOICE, NOUL, and SCORE. Given audio, a natural-language question, and an explicit answer specification, it directly produces a task-conditioned probability distribution or a numerical score through typed decision readouts. Evaluation across 18 labeled configurations covers all three primitives: for CHOICE, Qwen-Audio-Jev achieves accuracies of 78.70% on MMAU-mini and 84.06% on MMSU; for NOUL, it achieves an equal error rate of 6.50% on the VoxCeleb1-O speaker verification benchmark; and for SCORE, the model achieves a normalized mean absolute error of 0.1062 on NISQA overall quality assessment, with Pearson and Spearman correlations of 0.8210 and 0.8074, respectively. Compared with the original Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR-Flash-Next, Qwen-Audio-Jev achieves an approximately 20x inference speedup. It demonstrates its potential for efficient, high-throughput audio decision-making in applications such as large-scale audio screening, speaker verification, and automated quality assessment.

summary: Neural instrument synthesizers can clone the timbre of a solo instrument, letting music producers make music with the sound they desire. However, an instrument of interest is often embedded in a fully produced, multi-instrument recording, beyond the reach of existing methods. Source separation before timbre cloning is an approach, but it may suffer from separation artifacts and is also likely a detour for the task. In this work, we propose Point-and-Play, a system that clones the timbre of a cued source directly from a polyphonic mixture and uses it to synthesize new pitches and velocities. To achieve this, we introduce a Cue-Gated Statistics Pooling (CGSP) module that extracts the timbre code of the cued instrument from adapted CLAP embeddings of the music mixture. This extracted timbre code is then used to condition a separately trained note synthesizer together with pitch and velocity inputs. Experiments show that our proposed system outperforms separate-then-clone baselines in terms of timbre fidelity and synthesis quality, achieving comparable performance with that cloned from a clean solo instrument.
title: Point-and-Play: Instrument Timbre Cloning from Music Mixtures

summary: Music source separation (MSS) has been conventionally addressed by discriminative methods. Recently, flow matching has emerged as a strong generative paradigm for modeling complex data distributions, with successful applications across diverse domains. These advances motivate us to systematically investigate flow matching for MSS in a four-source (Vocals, Bass, Drums, Other) setting in full-band stereo. Specifically, we investigate prediction targets, flow paths, single-source versus multi-source modeling, and mixture consistency constraints. Beyond the signal-level metrics commonly used for MSS, such as signal-to-distortion ratio, we further evaluate MSS methods using embedding-based metrics, as well as a listening test, providing a comprehensive benchmark. On MUSDB18-HQ, our proposed model exhibits competitive performance in both objective and subjective tests, highlighting the potential of flow matching for generative MSS. Demo: https://ik4sumii.github.io/FLOMSS/
title: FLOMSS: Generative Music Source Separation by Flow Matching

summary: Audio source separation models must preserve fine spectral structure while keeping the cost of the separator tractable. Band-split architectures reduce this cost by manually partitioning the spectrum into predefined frequency bands and encoding each band as a token, but the same boundaries are used for every mixture. Because informative spectral structure varies with source content, fixed boundaries can merge discriminative components or spend tokens where little resolution is needed. We introduce Dynamic Band Splitting (DBS), an end-to-end framework that adapts boundary locations and band widths to each mixture under a fixed band-token budget. DBS predicts content-conditioned boundary scores within frequency blocks, selects a prescribed number of boundaries using hard Top-$K$, and applies content-dependent pooling to obtain compact band tokens. After separation, it smooths and expands these tokens to the original STFT grid, refines them along frequency, and decodes complex masks with a frequency-shared head. DBS improved separation over the corresponding static models on DnR v2, MUSDB18-HQ, and EchoSet, with DBS-BSRNN achieving relative gain of 29.0% in average SI-SDR on DnR v2. These results and boundary analyses on DnR v2 show that content-adaptive frequency partitioning benefits multiple separator backbones under a fixed band-token budget. Code and audio demos are available at https://cslikai.cn/Dynamic-Band-Splitting
title: Learning Where to Split: Dynamic Band Splitting for Audio Source Separation

summary: Speaker verification (SV) systems now achieve very low error rates on standard public protocols, but those results do not fully describe deployment generalization. VoxCeleb-style evaluations remain useful anchors for English in-the-wild media speech. Scenario-specific evaluations and challenges are also valuable. However, neither setting directly shows whether the same system remains reliable across diverse deployment scenarios. We introduce OpenSVBench, a public benchmark for cross-scenario SV evaluation. Its fixed public core contains 26 trial sets organized into 11 scenario groups, with 9.15M verification trials, frozen target/non-target keys, and metadata for scenario-wise reporting. Around this core, the online leaderboard acts as a diagnostic evaluation interface rather than only a ranked list. It accepts score packages from new systems, evaluates them with frozen keys and common scoring, and reports trial-set breakdowns, scenario-group metrics, macro EER/minDCF, model-wise profiles, and scenario-wise comparisons. We evaluate 18 public checkpoints spanning x-vector, ECAPA-TDNN, CAMPPlus, ResNet and ERes variants, ReDimNet2, SAM-ResNet, and pretrained Transformer speaker recipes. The results show clear cross-scenario gaps: systems with similar macro EER can have different scenario profiles, strong performance in one scenario does not guarantee strong performance in another, and same-scenario trial sets can still expose source and protocol gaps.
title: OpenSVBench: Diagnosing Speaker Verification Generalization Across Deployment Scenarios

summary: Speech anonymization is evaluated with automatic speaker verification attackers whose performance depends on the attribute distribution of both their training and evaluation data, which may bias privacy estimates for some speaker groups. To alleviate this issue, we introduce VoxAnon, a dataset built from VoxCeleb1 and 2 with training and evaluation splits balanced across gender, age, accent, and pitch. We extract and cross-check attributes using two complementary methods, balance trial lists per subgroup, and draw test/enrollment utterances from distinct video sources in order to limit linguistic and session bias. Comparing VoxAnon with unbalanced training and test data across four attackers and three anonymizers, we show that attribute imbalance changes which subgroups appear hardest to re-identify, in directions that depend on the attribute. In the balanced setting, residual disparities persist, mostly tied to accent and pitch, and depend on the anonymizer/attacker pair. Code and trial lists are publicly available.
title: VoxAnon: A balanced dataset for a fair evaluation of speech anonymization

We extract and cross-check attributes using two complementary methods, balance trial lists per subgroup, and draw test/enrollment utterances from distinct video sources in order to limit linguistic and session bias. Comparing VoxAnon with unbalanced training and test data across four attackers and three anonymizers, we show that attribute imbalance changes which subgroups appear hardest to re-identify, in directions that depend on the attribute. In the balanced setting, residual disparities persist, mostly tied to accent and pitch, and depend on the anonymizer/attacker pair. Code and trial lists are publicly available.
title: VoxAnon: A balanced dataset for a fair evaluation of speech anonymization

summary: This paper describes our systems for the Track 1 time-stamped speaker-attributed ASR task of the SmartGlasses Challenge. To handle overlapping speech, background noise and far-field conditions in two-person conversations, we employ SoulX-Transcriber, a multimodal large language model that takes full-length audio as input and generates structured transcriptions. In addition, we investigate the effect of speech frontend processing, including a rule-based Guided Source Separation method and a data-driven speech separation model, both of which improve performance on the validation set. Considering inference stability, our final submission uses the fine-tuned SoulX-Transcriber system, achieving a tcpCER of 6.22 on the test set.
title: Frontend-Assisted Large Audio-Language Models for SLT2026 SmartGlasses Challenge

summary: Spatial semantic segmentation of sound scenes (S5) jointly performs audio source separation and tagging on a multichannel audio mixture. Therefore, an S5 system can be decomposed into an audio tagging model and a separation model. The baseline S5 system in task~4 of the DCASE 2025 challenge uses M2D and ResUNet models for tagging and separation, respectively. These are large in overall size and therefore not appropriate for use in embedded devices. The main aim of this paper is to assess the performance loss in an S5 system when using lightweight tagging and separation models instead. To this end, we first compare the tagging performance of lightweight audio tagging models, namely PANNs and DyMNs, in terms of label prediction accuracy against the baseline M2D model. Secondly, we assess separation performance in terms of the scale-invariant signal-to-distortion ratio of the baseline ResUNet separator relative to that of a convolutional-based separator using SuDoRMRF. Finally, we combine the tagging and separation models across various configurations and assess the overall performance of the S5 system using the class-aware signal-to-distortion ratio.
title: Lightweight Systems for Spatial Semantic Segmentation of Sound Scenes
