summary: Speech-pretrained models have shown promise in animal bioacoustics, but the factors governing their cross-species transfer remain poorly understood. We evaluate 15 frozen encoders spanning monolingual and multilingual speech, speaker verification, animal bioacoustics, and general audio on caller identification across four species and call-type classification across three. Differences between the strongest speech- and animal-pretrained representations range from $-0.027$ to $+0.119$ UAR; speech is significantly better in three of seven settings ($p<0.01$) and not significantly different in the remaining four. Controlled comparisons show no systematic advantage from increased language coverage or animal-domain pretraining, while frozen speaker-verification embeddings transfer poorly. The results also show that transfer is strongly layer-dependent: raw-waveform models peak early, whereas patch-spectrogram models peak deeper.
title: Neural Representations, Natural Connections: What Transfers From Human Speech Foundation Models to Animal Vocalizations?

summary: C. J Tully. Independent Research https://orcid.org/0009-0007-5661-7332 chloetully5@gmail.com   18 th October 2026                   Most of what you call your life arrives half a second late. Something happens. A sound, a face, a tightness in the chest. Before you have chosen anything, a voice — yours, apparently — has already named it, judged it, and filed it under a chapter called me. You do not notice the filing. You notice the file. And so you spend your days inside a commentary about a world you have not, strictly speaking, met. This is not a moral failure. It is a timing error. Awareness is not a mood you work up and not a belief you adopt. It is what is already underway before the sentence starts. The breath you are taking does not consult your biography. The light on the wall does not ask what you meant to become. For a fraction of a second there is contact without a commentator. Then the commentator returns, a little late, a little proud, and explains what just occurred as if the explanation were the event. People talk about waking up as if it were a prize for the patient and the pure. It is closer to catching a clerical mistake. You have been treating the report as the room. The report is useful. It gets you across streets, through grief, into love, out of traffic. It is also not the thing it reports on. The word water has never once made a hand wet. Watch the exact moment a thought claims you. There is a sensation, then a grab. The grab feels like identity. It is older than that, and thinner. It is a habit of ownership so practiced it forgot it was optional. You do not have to defeat it. You only have to notice that noticing is already happening, and that the one who seems to be doing the noticing cannot be found as an object inside what is noticed. Sit with that past the point of comfort. Comfort is how the narration gets rehired. If the “you” who plans, defends, remembers, and suffers is a pattern appearing in awareness, then who has been afraid all this time? Not a cosmic answer. A local one. Look. Fear is weather. The sky it crosses was not manufactured by the storm. Nothing theatrical follows from this. You will still want things. You will still lose them. You will still answer the message and miss the person. The only change is a small, stubborn order of operations: experience first, story second. And the recognition, quiet enough to miss if you perform it, that you were never inside the story. You were the place it was being told. That place does not improve. It does not arrive. It does not need you to become someone else in order to be what it already is. The only work, if it can even be called work, is to stop leaving a half-second early — to remain, once, with what is here before you agree with your own explanation of it. Stay. The explanation can wait. It always could.
title: Most of what you call your life arrives half a second late.

summary: Code and data to reproduce all analyses and the figure in Sellers et al. (2026) “Failure of a tropical upwelling rapidly collapsed Panama’s anchoveta fishery and its exports”. Includes Python scripts for the bay-wide composite upwelling index, the observer set records, the unified 1956 to 2025 landings series, the main figure, and every statistic reported in the paper and its Supporting Information. Data include weekly sonde casts from the three deep central stations of the Bay of Panama, reef temperature loggers in the Gulf of Panama running since 1995, the Copernicus Marine Service biogeochemical reanalysis of net primary production (1994 to 2026), anchoveta and thread herring landings spliced from the digitised national stock assessment (1956 to 2014) and the ARAP landings register (2015 to 2025), 3,077 onboard observer purse-seine set records (2017 to 2025), 645 dockside proximate assays of landed anchoveta (2016 to 2025), and fish oil and fishmeal export tabulations from INEC customs statistics (1997 to 2025). Version 2.0 accompanies the revised manuscript and corrects three errors in version 1.0 (the units of the 1956 to 2005 landings, a wrongly masked grid cell in the production analysis, and a duplicated logger record), as listed in README.md. Data are released under CC BY 4.0 and code under the MIT Licence.
title: Code and data for: Failure of a tropical upwelling rapidly collapsed Panama's anchoveta fishery and its exports

summary: The Empty Occupant: Answerability, Testimony, and the Limits of Machine-Mediated Authority examines a problem of institutional AI: automated decisions can scale faster than institutions' capacity to justify, reconsider, correct, or repair them. Identifying a responsible institution does not establish that its decisions were warrantedly adopted or that resulting obligations can be discharged. Across philosophy of language, social epistemology, social ontology, normative theory, AI governance, and administrative law , the monograph develops a substrate-neutral Discursive Ontology connecting three questions: who bears an institutional commitment, what warrants its adoption, and whether answerability can be sustained at scale. It distinguishes commitment ownership, warranted adoption, adequate discharge, causal contribution, and legal liability. Five contributions follow: Discursive Ontology and Answerability. Defines commitment-bearing through four jointly necessary relations within reciprocal normative standing: attribution continuity, challenge-responsive reconsideration, repair competence, and standing-consequence . It distinguishes Actual, Residual, Prospective, and Empty Occupancy . Empty Occupancy requires presentation as an independent bearer and affirmative evidence that the relevant standing is absent , not a mere machine interface. The axiom is that missing bearership is not defective ownership : a principal may remain responsible for commitments its interface cannot independently bear. Testimony Without a Testifier. Separates hearer-side epistemic uptake from speaker-side commitment ownership . Machine outputs can inform without establishing an answerable speaker. On assurance-based accounts, they can exercise testimonial force without constituting testimony . Reliability, fluency, and conversational memory alone confer no authority to retract a commitment. Normative Sponsorship. Specifies five conditions for warranted institutional adoption: epistemic access, authority, review bandwidth, independent rejection, and repair power . Its contestation-grain opacity threshold requires reconstructing relevant grounds where a challenge must take effect—at input, case, rule, shared-premise, or architecture—without complete transparency. It distinguishes technical opacity from organizational capture , where reasons are knowable but cannot bind, and considers model succession and agentic chains. Deontic Debt and Institutional Insolvency. Derives consequence-sensitive reconsideration from the defeasibility of presumptive authority. Deontic Debt comprises matured obligations deficiently serviced, not simply pending work. Institutional Insolvency arises when no credible service plan meets relevant obligations and protections for a specified claim mix, issuance scale, lawful architecture, and horizon. Its consequence is targeted loss of presumptive authority , not automatic legal invalidity or release from ownership and repair duties. Institutional Stewardship. Connects permissible automated use to warranted sponsorship, protective review, binding reconsideration, and effective repair. Restoration requires legacy discharge, demonstrable future capacity, and scaled resumption. Public-record analyses examine Australia's Robodebt scheme, Moffatt v. Air Canada , A.M.C. v. Smith (TennCare), the Post Office Horizon scandal, the Dutch childcare-benefits affair, and a press-based DPD generative-interface episode. Neither Air Canada nor DPD establishes determinate Empty Occupancy. An explicitly fictional, stipulated Meridian–Aster appeals-agent comparator yields a determinate verdict: Aster lacks independent standing while its insurer, Meridian, remains the Actual institutional bearer. This is not empirical evidence and settles neither sponsorship nor serviceability. A stipulated positive comparator illustrates review and repair. Objections address synthetic agency, status conferral, intentionality, human–machine parit
title: The Empty Occupant: Answerability, Testimony, and the Limits of Machine-Mediated Authority

summary: We develop a rigorous finite-dimensional mathematical framework connecting the renormalization group, gradient flows, Lyapunov stability, and noncooperative game theory. The central object is a renormalization-group flow written in gradient form, dg_i/dt = β_i(g) = - ∑_j G_ij(g) ∂Γ/∂g_j(g),          (1) where g = (g_1, …, g_n) belongs to an open domain M ⊂ ℝⁿ, Γ is a C² function, and G(g) is a symmetric positive-definite matrix. We associate to this flow a common-payoff game whose payoff is U(g) = - Γ(g).                   (2) We prove, with complete arguments, that ordinary Nash equilibria always imply renormalization-group fixed points, but the converse is false. We then identify the exact condition under which a fixed point becomes a genuine stable equilibrium of the game: a nondegenerate renormalization-group fixed point is asymptotically stable if and only if the Hessian of Γ is positive definite, if and only if it is a strict local minimum of Γ, if and only if it is a strict strong Nash equilibrium of U = -Γ. The distinction between ordinary Nash equilibrium and strong Nash equilibrium is essential. Ordinary Nash equilibria allow only unilateral deviations, while strong Nash equilibria exclude all small joint deviations. We provide explicit counterexamples showing that fixed points need not be Nash equilibria, that ordinary Nash equilibria need not be stable, and that invertibility of G alone does not imply finiteness of equilibria. We also prove global existence results under compactness and finiteness results under Morse nondegeneracy. The paper is self-contained at the level of multivariable calculus, linear algebra, ordinary differential equations, and basic Lyapunov stability theory. The framework is intentionally conditional: it does not claim that the gradient-flow representation has been proven in four-dimensional QCD or in any specific quantum field theory. Those issues are placed in a final section of open problems.
title: Gradient-Flow Renormalization Group as a Common-Potential Game: A Rigorous Equivalence Between Asymptotically Stable Fixed Points and Strict Strong Nash Equilibria

summary: We develop a rigorous reduction inside the Connes–Consani–Moscovici programme for the Riemann hypothesis. The main unconditional result is the following symmetry principle: for the truncated Weil quadratic form QW_λ^N, simplicity of the lowest eigenvalue ε_N implies evenness of the corresponding ground state ξ, provided the natural reflection symmetry γV_n = V_{-n} and the normalization ℓ_N(ξ) = 1 are imposed. This converts two structural requirements of the programme into one spectral requirement. We then prove a precise spectral approximation criterion. If the finite-dimensional form QW_λ^N approximates the prolate wave operator PW_λ in a form-strong sense sufficient to preserve the first isolated simple eigenvalue, then ε_N is simple for all large N. Combining this criterion with the symmetry principle gives evenness of the ground state. Finally, we prove a windowed determinant criterion for the Riemann hypothesis. If the regularized determinants attached to the Connes–Consani–Moscovici finite-rank perturbations have only real zeros and converge locally uniformly, on an exhausting family of windows, to nonzero multiples of the Riemann Ξ-function, then every zero of Ξ is real, and therefore the Riemann hypothesis follows. The paper separates cleanly the proved logical reductions from the analytic objectives required for their unconditional verification. Those objectives are collected in a final section of open problems, giving a foundational reference for the remaining work in the programme. We emphasize that this paper does not claim an unconditional proof of the Riemann hypothesis; rather, it provides a precise structural reduction and isolates the remaining analytic challenges.
title: Evenness from Simplicity in the Truncated Weil Quadratic Form and Conditional Spectral Criteria for the Riemann Hypothesis

summary: Code, trained weights and campaign results for the paper "Morphological diffusion by ball births: generative models of binary images with exact Betti increments" by M. Zéraï, submitted to the Journal of Mathematical Imaging and Vision. The model generates binary images by births of maximal balls. Its forward process is a random granulometry, and its reverse process learns a birth map. morpho_repro.tar.gz contains the implementation (model, sampler, exact Euler increments, measurement protocol), the averaged (EMA) weights of all trained models on the three datasets (GRF, BBBC039 nuclei masks, MNIST), the campaign reports and logs, and the GRF data. README.md gives the hyperparameters, the source of each table and the reproduction commands. figs_print.tar.gz contains the figure boards of the paper with their statistics. The BBBC039 masks and MNIST are public and are downloaded by prepare_data.sh. Note: the two archives are gzip-compressed tar files, deposited as morpho_repro.tar and figs_print.tar (README.md names them morpho_repro.tar.gz and figs_print.tar.gz). Extract them with: tar xzf morpho_repro.tar
title: Morphological diffusion by ball births: code, trained weights and campaign results

summary: Region means and contrasts with a full error budget, correlated shift errors, error bars for shot noise, a faster fit_map , two tutorials, and three fixes. Added region_mean(coefficients, dw1, dw2, sigma1, sigma2, mask, *, shift_correlation=None, ref_sigma=None) and region_contrast(coefficients, dw1, dw2, sigma1, sigma2, mask_a, mask_b, *, shift_correlation=None) , returning a RegionEstimate : the mean strain and density of a map region, or region A minus region B, with the error split into shift noise (averages down over pixels), calibration (from a two-mode CalibrationResult ; does not average down) and reference frequencies ( ref_sigma ; does not average down, and cancels exactly in a contrast). region_mean also tests whether the pixels agree within their error bars (chi-square with 2 (N - 1) degrees of freedom, the same in shift space and in (strain, density) space) and reports the pixel spread. Validated against the mean and per-pixel covariances of SeparationModel.invert , separation_with_calibration , finite differences of a re-solve, and seeded Monte Carlo over 400 trials that repeat the calibration, the map noise and the reference error (spread within 12 % of the reported error bars). Propagation as in JCGM 100:2008 (GUM), 5.2.2, Eq. (13). SeparationModel.invert(..., shift_correlation=None) : the correlation of the two shift errors (from a joint fit) enters the error bars through the full 2 x 2 shift covariance. Zero gives the old result bit for bit. On 400 repeats of two overlapping E' + A'1 peaks the density error bar without the correlation is 27 % above the actual spread; with it, it matches (tutorial 2). separation_with_calibration passes it through. MapFitResult.shift_correlation : the correlation of the two shift errors per pixel (the joint fit's value, 0 for separate window fits, NaN where masked). noise="varying" in fit_lorentzian , fit_two_modes and fit_map : error bars from the heteroskedasticity-consistent ("sandwich") covariance of H. White, Econometrica 48, 817 (1980), for spectra whose noise level changes along the axis, as shot noise does. Fitted values are unchanged. On 600 seeded Poisson spectra the center scatter is 1.7 times the default error bar and within 10 % of the new one; checked also against an independent finite-difference sandwich (relative 1e-5). summary: MULTI-AGENT ROUTING OF NEUROVASCULAR MICROROBOT SWARMS AT THE LIMIT This research monograph develops a falsifiable, non-clinical framework for routing heterogeneous microrobotic teams through branching neurovascular vessel phantoms. It asks whether decentralized task assignment, flow-aware navigation, independently tracked agent identity, and verifiable recovery can improve qualified sensing or inert-sample collection without increasing collision, occlusion, flow disturbance, thermal burden, sample confusion, or residual material risk. Organized around low-Reynolds-number hydrodynamics, multi-agent coordination, and independently enforced physical safety boundaries, the volume contains 30 mathematical derivation plates, 82 full research chapters with five separately paginated sections each, 200 detailed Research Gates, and 33 provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos. A DOI evidence ledger distinguishes established component physics and published demonstrations from the original system-level hypotheses proposed here. Strong passive-transport, single-agent, and information-matched centralized alternatives remain valid competitors throughout. Research failures, abandoned models, experimental uncertainty, and successor reconstruction are treated as scientific outputs, not editorial defects. The monograph provides a research architecture and prospective tests, not results from experiments performed for this publication. It does not assert demonstrated autonomous navigation in human cerebral vessels, clinical safety, therapeutic efficacy, or authorization for human intervention.

summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Twenty-three entries are documented, nine of them confirmed defects in the source literature: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7, a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients, a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset, and a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten. Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from. The package computes the direct and veiling components along a horizontal underwater path, converts spectra to CIE XYZ, sRGB, or the response of an arbitrary camera or set of photoreceptors, gives the Jerlov type that typically applies in each 10 m layer down to 200 m and carries the downwelling irradiance down through those layers, integrates photosynthetically available radiation (PAR), or the photon flux over any other band or weighted by any spectral sensitivity, with depth, gives the spectrum at any depth and the effective Kd between two, and finds the depth at which PAR falls to 1 percent, ranks the Jerlov types by their distance from a measured Kd spectrum, carries Jerlov's measured profiles of quanta irradiance (350-700 nm) by water type and checks the depth profile against them, carries Tyler's (1958) measured radiance distribution in Lake Pend Oreille, carries the Paulson & Simpson (1977) shortwave penetration parameters used by ocean circulation models, converts a backscattering sensor's single-angle reading into the backscattering coefficient, and carries Petzold's (1972) volume scattering functions for eight measured ocean waters.
title: jerlov: inherent optical properties of the Jerlov optical water types, with provenance

summary: Coding agents can now interpret a specification, implement it, write and execute tests, repair failures, and declare the result ready for release. When the same agentic system produces both the software and the evidence of its correctness, a passing test suite no longer constitutes independent evidence. Visible tests become an optimization target, and code, tests, and oracles may share a single misinterpretation of the specification. This paper argues that agent-produced software requires an assurance plane that is structurally independent of the build plane. We first characterize four gaps along the chain from stakeholder intent to production, namely the requirement, conformance, evaluation, and model gaps, and identify which of them verification can close. We then propose a framework that separates building from verifying, introduces a Verification Contract stating what must be demonstrated before release, and organizes verification in two phases: a specification-first phase designed without access to the implementation, and an implementation-aware phase that strengthens the evidence through mutation analysis, property-based testing, and fuzzing. The resulting evidence is consolidated into an assurance report that makes residual uncertainty explicit and leaves the release decision to a human. We evaluate the framework in a pre-registered study on three stateful services, two of them written by third-party models, and an EvalPlus pilot, comparing self-validation with independent verification under context-level and model-level independence. The builder's programs were correct, but its own tests missed subtle interactions: a verifier in a fresh context detected more of the 46 seeded faults than the builder's tests (Holm-corrected p = 0.006), and surfaced the ambiguities of the specification, at the price of rare false oracles. A verifier from another provider did not add detection. The framework and the study provide a basis for governing the release of software produced by agents.
title: Who Verifies the Builder? Toward Independent Assurance for Agent-Produced Software

summary: Code, archived production results and figure scripts that reproduce the numbers and figures of two companion papers on a small flat universe, a cubic three-torus that begins at a Casimir turning point: A. Zhang, Gauge Field Fluctuations Protect the Higgs Vacuum When a Small Universe Begins (2026), a Letter; A. Zhang, A Casimir turning point as the beginning of a small flat universe (2026). The companion technical report, A. Zhang, Casimir Cosmology: Derivations and Numerical Validation, version 1.0 (2026), is deposited as a separate record, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23434140; a copy is included in docs/technical_report/. Contents. Four chains of result directories: casimir/ (Standard Model Casimir weight, gauge and Higgs zero-mode energy, shape Hessian), higgs/ (finite-volume criterion for the Higgs zero mode: Standard Model couplings at the turning-point scale, one-loop finite-volume matching, two-dimensional zero-mode model with cross terms, hazard integral, critical top-quark masses and error budget, real-time ξ_H condition, robustness, universality, two-branch analysis), shape/ (emptiness gate, real-moment theorem, shape fossil, nonlinear survival, Moyal and Wheeler–DeWitt checks, primordial spectra) and cmb/ (temperature and polarization covariance of a three-torus, Fisher information and exact Kullback–Leibler divergences, fossil ensemble, joint inflaton–shape state). Every result directory has a quick and a full mode and compares fresh output with the archived production values under stated tolerances; python run_all.py --quick reproduces the quick checks and all figures. validation/ archives the independent reimplementations of the main results, with their specifications, code and outputs, and compares them with the main calculation. numbers/ is the single source of the numbers quoted in the papers and in the report. cmb/02_ensemble/data/ contains the ℓ ≤ 80 CAMB transfer table. Verification. On a fresh copy of this release (Python 3.12, Windows 11), python run_all.py --quick passes in all 25 verification runs (241 of 242 checks passed, 1 optional check skipped: the compiled SMDR refit), and the 51 shared numbers of the papers and the report (numbers/) agree with the archived outputs. Details and known limitations are given in RELEASE_NOTES.md. Integrity. MANIFEST.json and SHA256SUMS.txt list the size and SHA-256 of every file; python tools/sha256sums.py check verifies a copy. This record archives release v1.0.0 of https://github.com/Ailun-Zhang/casimir-cosmology. Licenses. Code: MIT. Data and text: CC BY 4.0. The SMDR 1.3 tarball (shipped unmodified) and the four files derived from or linked against it: GPL-2.0-or-later (see README.md, section License).
title: Code and data for: A Casimir turning point as the beginning of a small flat universe

summary: This is the replication package of the paper Required to Test or Inspired to Test? A Survey of the Socio-Technical Conditions of Software Testing . The paper reports a survey of 52 software developers on how organizational, technical and social conditions relate to their motivation to test and to how extensively they test. It validates the survey instrument and tests eight hypotheses that we published before data collection. We changed the title and reworded the abstract. The research questions, hypotheses and survey questions are unchanged. The paper discusses where the study deviates from this report. The reef–ocean-oxygen–land coupling documented in the End-Permian record demonstrates that marine biosphere collapse propagates to terrestrial extinction through the shared oxygen and biogeochemical infrastructure of the coupled Earth system; contemporary marine indicators are therefore leading indicators of terrestrial as well as marine risk. The five largest mass-extinction events of the Phanerozoic share a consistent causal chain: rapid carbon injection to the ocean-atmosphere system, followed by warming, ocean deoxygenation, acidification, and preferential loss of marine calcifiers, with multi-million-year recovery for reef ecosystems. Every element of that chain is presently active and gaining speed. The current anthropogenic perturbation is capable of driving a combination and magnitude of ocean geochemical changes unparalleled in the geological record reviewed by Hönisch et al. (2012), which covers approximately the past 300 million years. The reef–ocean-oxygen–land coupling documented in the End-Permian record demonstrates that marine biosphere collapse propagates to terrestrial extinction through the shared oxygen and biogeochemical infrastructure of the coupled Earth system; contemporary marine indicators are therefore leading indicators of terrestrial as well as marine risk. Approach. This three-part synthesis compiles peer-reviewed reconstructions of the Big Five causal chain, measures each element against the contemporary Earth system using the most recent authoritative data (Friedlingstein et al. 2026; Wu et al. 2021; Zeebe et al. 2016; Hönisch et al. 2012; Schmidtko et al. 2017; Eddy et al. 2021; Spady et al. 2026), specifies the physically necessary intervention portfolio, and characterizes the near-term feedback, resource, and civilizational risk environment those interventions must succeed in. Part I establishes the paleoclimate analog. Part II specifies the intervention portfolio. Part III maps the contemporary Earth system the Part II portfolio must succeed in — which climate feedbacks are already engaged and how they cascade, which physical resources are hitting hard limits inside the same two-to-three-decade window, and how those pressures translate into food, water, migration, health, economic, and governance strain — and closes with the North American Climate Pain Scale (NAPS), a 1–10 diagnostic instrument that anchors climate severity to concrete events so policymakers and the public can locate today's conditions and the trajectory ahead. Atmospheric CO₂ (422.8 ppm, 2024 global annual mean; Friedlingstein et al. 2026) has exceeded the reconstructed latest-Permian baseline of 426 (+133 / −96) ppm (Wu et al. 2021, Nature Communications). The rate of contemporary carbon release is at least an order of magnitude above the sustained maximum Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum rate (Zeebe, Ridgwell and Zachos 2016, Nature Geoscience). Ocean acidification is proceeding at roughly ten times the PETM rate (Hönisch et al. 2012, Science). The global ocean has lost 4.8 ± 2.1 petamoles of dissolved oxygen since 1960 (Schmidtko, Stramma and Visbeck 2017, Nature). summary: Climate change affects human well-being through interacting physical, ecological, infrastructural, and socioeconomic processes rather than through a single exposure or disease pathway. Major assessments identify observed harms to health, food and water security, livelihoods, settlements, and ecosystems, alongside increasing risks with additional warming (IPCC, 2022a). This narrative review develops a cross-sector framework from a source inventory of 154 human-impact pathways in 14 domains, supported by major assessments, selected peer-reviewed studies, and institutional datasets. Literature selection used targeted web-index searches and source verification through 2 October 2026; the review does not estimate pooled effects or claim exhaustive systematic coverage. The synthesis distinguishes direct injury and illness, ecosystem-mediated harms, failures of essential services, financial transmission, and losses of social and cultural continuity. Representative quantitative findings illustrate substantial existing burdens, but attribution studies, ecological associations, exposure models, displacement records, and conditional forecasts measure different quantities and cannot be combined into a universal five-year trajectory (Vicedo-Cabrera et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2026; Clement et al., 2021). Compound hazards and service interdependencies can increase losses beyond the directly affected sector, while repeated shocks can reduce the capacity to recover or adapt (Zscheischler et al., 2018; IPCC, 2023). A reporting framework is proposed that records the outcome, population, baseline, geography, time horizon, emissions and development assumptions, adaptation, and uncertainty for each indicator. The central contribution is an integrated interpretation and measurement architecture, not a new forecast of global mortality, migration, or societal collapse. Effective assessment should preserve evidence of serious and interacting harms without converting uncertain thresholds or heterogeneous studies into unsupported calendar-specific predictions.
title: Climate change impacts humans: A cross-sector narrative review of impact pathways, cascading risks, and accountable quantification

summary: Reconstructing Earth's deep-time paleoclimate record provides a critical framework for evaluating modern anthropogenic climate forcing. Here, we synthesize proxy records from the "Big Five" mass extinction events—Late Ordovician (LOME), Late Devonian, Permian-Triassic (PTME), Triassic-Jurassic (TJME), and Cretaceous-Paleogene (K-Pg)—and evaluate their proxy signals against modern biogeochemical trends. While cumulative carbon emissions during deep-time hyperthermals were larger in absolute magnitude, current annual carbon injection rates ( ∼ 10 G t C / y e a r ) and global warming velocities ( ∼ 0.2° C / d e c a d e ) exceed reconstructed pre-extinction baselines by factors of 10x to 100x. We catalog 17 positive climate feedback loops, 16 of which are currently active, and apply an Earth System Feedback Framework to demonstrate that integrating biogeochemical and cryospheric tipping dynamics elevates standard Equilibrium Climate Sensitivity ( E C S ≈ 3.0° C ) to an Earth System Sensitivity gain factor of G E S S ≈ 4.76 ( E S S ≈ 4.0–5.0° C for doubled C O 2 ). Synthesizing this feedback framework with Earth system tipping point literature (e.g., Armstrong McKay et al., 2022; Steffen et al., 2018; Kemp et al., 2022), we use this feedback gain function to model the boundary and evaluate the risk horizon for reaching a "Point of Human Agency Loss"—defined as the biogeochemical threshold where autonomous natural feedback emissions ( ≥ 10.0 G t C O 2 e / y e a r ) match or exceed maximum technological human mitigation and carbon removal capacity. We establish that crossing the 1.5° C to 2.0° C global warming horizon (projected mid-century) shifts the Earth system into a self-sustaining feedback regime. Driven by coupled biophysical stress vectors (niche thermal limits, crop yield collapses, and hydrological contraction; Xu et al., 2020) and the non-linear carrying-capacity decay function K ( T ) , human support capacity is projected to contract non-linearly from baseline Holocene levels ( ∼ 8.5–9.0 b i l l i o n ) to an equilibrium ceiling of ∼ 1.3–1.5 b i l l i o n at a stabilized state ( +3.3–3.5° C ). Finally, we perform a Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) across 16 proposed climate interventions, evaluating scale, cost, geopolitical friction, termination shock, and moral hazard risk. We conclude that while physical variables (temperature, ocean pH) may be geochemically reversible over centuries via solar radiation management and permanent carbon removal, biospheric destruction, species extinction, and sea-level commitment exhibit severe hysteresis (path-dependence where a system fails to return to its initial state even if forcing is removed), making damage containment rather than ecosystem restoration the primary operational objective.
title: Climate forcing, positive feedbacks, and planetary tipping points: A synthesis of deep-time proxies, earth system sensitivity, and interventional feasibility

summary: This reproducibility archive accompanies Marco Mantovanelli's A Multi-Arch Perturbed Hofstadter Q-Recursion: Gaussian Profiles and Exact Frequency Laws. It contains the manuscript PDF, complete LaTeX source, six vector figures, independent verification programs, figure-generation code, numerical reports, and sampled figure data. The paper studies Q(n) = Q(n - Q(n-1)) + Q(n - Q(n-2)) - (-1)^n for n >= 8, with the seven prescribed initial values (1, 1, 3, 3, 3, 3, 5). A causal binary-word construction proves global existence and an exact factorization into three signed excursions. Their uniformly convergent Gaussian profiles explain three limiting sign transitions per standard dyadic block and a sharp normalized error envelope of approximately 0.067088003576. The paper also proves exact finite transition locations, an ordered frequency factorization, a shifted 2-adic valuation law on pure dyadic value blocks, and a summatory asymptotic with an explicit continuous periodic term. The archived verification compares all 33,554,432 directly computed terms with an independent word reconstruction, checks complete frequency blocks through level 21, and verifies the exact summatory identity at every even cutoff from 8 through 33,554,432. Separate programs audit the word maps, finite transitions, and exact two-head identities. These computations supplement the general proofs in the manuscript. The original perturbation, OEIS A394051, is discussed for comparison.
title: A Multi-Arch Perturbed Hofstadter Q-Recursion: Gaussian Profiles and Exact Frequency Laws (Reproducibility Archive)

summary: This archive contains supplementary code, data, finite certificates, and reproduction instructions for “Merge Trees of Length-Filtered Lattice Knot Spaces” by Makoto Ozawa (arXiv:2605.25322). This release accompanies the 41-page revision prepared in October 2026 and preserves all files from the two supplementary archives published in the previous Zenodo version. The computations concern embedded polygons in the simple cubic lattice under standard BFACF moves. Polygons are identified under translations, proper cubic rotations, cyclic changes of starting point, and reversal of traversal; spatial reflections are retained. The archive includes the original implementations, seed files, search summaries, and explicit merge-path certificates, together with the complete minimal-layer material for the figure-eight knot and the knot 6_3. For the figure-eight knot, four minimal-layer components at length 30 merge into one component at cap 32. For 6_3, twelve minimal-layer components at length 40 merge into two mirror-related branches at cap 42 and one branch at cap 44. These statements concern the branches originating in the minimal layers, rather than an enumeration of every component at higher caps. The new trefoil supplement certifies six nonminimal components born at length 26 for a fixed chirality. Five first meet the minimal layer at cap 28, whereas a 20-state component first meets it at cap 30. The archive supplies closed component lists, capped-component separation certificates, explicit connecting paths, verification programs, and audit logs. The individual component and exact merge-height certificates do not assume exhaustion of the length-26 population; exhaustiveness at that level remains conditional on the reported literature population. The trefoil material also includes the actual BFACF path used in Figure 2: 47 configurations connected by 46 moves, with maximum length 30. All coordinates, the complete sequence of configurations, figure-generation code, and independent transition checks are provided. Additional checks verify coordinate spans of the specified trefoil components and singleton capped components for supplied 48-edge representatives of 8_3 and 8_7, including an improper spatial symmetry of the 8_3 representative. The release includes the corresponding manuscript source and figures, current documentation, checksums, provenance records, and a verification runner. Historical manuscripts are retained separately in the legacy directory; the current manuscript source is arxiv_revision/main.tex. The documentation distinguishes certified finite results from conditional completeness statements and open questions concerning eventual connectivity, Gordian configurations, and unbounded strong local-minimum birth levels. Requirements: Python 3 for the verification scripts and a C++17 compiler for the large capped-component audits. Regenerating the trefoil figures additionally requires NumPy and Matplotlib. Detailed commands and the scope of each verification are given in the included README files.
title: Supplementary code and data for "Merge Trees of Length-Filtered Lattice Knot Spaces"

summary: rnaseq-flow offline Singularity container bundle (v1.7.0) A complete set of Singularity/Apptainer container images for running the rnaseq-flow bulk RNA-seq pipeline on systems with no internet access — Trusted Research Environments, secure enclaves, and air-gapped HPC. Built for pipeline release 1.7.0. By default rnaseq-flow provisions several containers on the fly with Nextflow Wave, which contacts an external service at run time. That is not possible in an air-gapped setting. This bundle pre-materialises every image the pipeline can use, so a run resolves all 26 containers from local disk and makes no outbound connection. Contents 26 Singularity images (~7 GB). Twenty are pass-through copies of the upstream Bioconda/BioContainers images: STAR, HISAT2, Salmon, kallisto, fastp, FastQC, MultiQC, RSeQC, subread/featureCounts, samtools, deepTools, rMATS, STAR-Fusion, tximport, edgeR, IsoformSwitchAnalyzeR, genomepy and Python. Seven are built from the pipeline's Conda specifications: DESeq2 with apeglm and pheatmap, edgeR with tximport, DEXSeq with tximport, fgsea, gprofiler2, msigdbr, and the Quarto reporting environment. nf-prov — plugin for part of rendering provenance reports for pipeline runs tre.config — a Nextflow profile that disables Wave and pins the seven Conda-built processes to the image names in this bundle. README.txt — usage summary. Usage tar -xf rnaseq-flow-1.7.0-singularity.tar export NXF_SINGULARITY_CACHEDIR=$PWD/singularity-1.7.0 nextflow run main.nf -c $NXF_SINGULARITY_CACHEDIR/tre.config -profile tre,<your-executor-profile> --input samplesheet.csv --aligner star ... Verify the download with: sha256sum -c rnaseq-flow-1.7.0-singularity.tar.sha256 Notes The tre profile requires this bundle. The seven Conda-built images are named locally to it and resolve nowhere online, so the profile is not usable on its own. Licensing. Each image carries the licences of its own upstream software. This record redistributes them unmodified for offline use and does not relicense them. Source: https://github.com/nicholas-owen/rnaseq-flow
title: rnaseq-flow offline Singularity container bundle (v1.7.0)

summary: Replication files for “Bans versus Controlled Access: Reserve Substitution and Issuer Buybacks under Financial Sanctions”. The A7A5 archive covers the TRON base contract TLeVfrdym8RoJreJ23dAGyfJDygRtiWKBZ from 7–27 August 2025 UTC. Data were retrieved on 17 October 2026 UTC. It includes 5,244 unique events from 37 daily response pages, additional event-class and receipt checks, frozen source responses and request provenance, event-level records, daily and weekly aggregates, supply accounting, data definitions, and analysis and verification scripts. Coverage is specific to the queried contract and provider. Gross transfers do not measure trading volume, beneficial ownership, reserve flows, or issuer buyback expenditure. The pilot is descriptive and does not identify a causal sanctions effect. The model archive contains Python scripts and supplied outputs for hypothetical numerical examples of route substitution, constrained issuer purchases, monitoring-dependent depth, surplus access and fallback. Parameters are not calibrated to A7A5. Both archives use Python 3.9 or later and its standard library; their README files give offline reproduction commands. Access: metadata are public; files are restricted and available on request to the corresponding author, hyoungkang@hanyang.ac.kr. The accompanying RIGHTS_AND_SOURCES.md distinguishes author-created materials from third-party responses. Rights in original materials are reserved; no blanket open license is granted for the mixed archive. The associated manuscript is unpublished.
title: A7A5 pilot data and model replication files for Bans versus Controlled Access

summary: Version 1.6 adds four preregistered analyses of LEGA-C star-forming discs at z ~ 0.8 and of SPARC: KCAL, a calibration of the gas pressure coefficient against stellar JAM masses; PIPE-6, a0 at R_e and 2R_e from ionized gas; PIPE-7, a local SPARC control; and PIPE-8, JAM-gas offsets and a0 at both radii. It also adds two analyses that were designed but not run (PIPE-5, GAP). Combined reading: in the same galaxies the gas a0 rises outward (+0.30 dex on 40), the JAM a0 does not (−0.08, no pre-stated reading), and the JAM-gas mass offset falls outward (−0.16). With measured mass models local discs show no rise; with the LEGA-C stellar recipe the 53 massive discs show none, but all 138 rise by +0.14. Preregistrations and code were drafted with Claude (Anthropic) and audited by fresh Claude sessions; locks are self-recorded SHA-256 manifests with UTC times. summary: This report establishes an exact conditional mathematical correspondence between a specified two-component phase model and the sine-Gordon equation appearing in a classical string-theory reduction. Developed within the Harmonic Physics Research Programme, the model uses interacting phase components labelled expansion and contraction in the proposed physical interpretation. For a continuum action with a cosine interaction, constant coefficients and equal component propagation speeds, an invertible change of variables separates the dynamics into an exact nonlinear sine-Gordon equation for the normalized relative phase and a free wave equation for the common phase. The interaction potential can also be expressed through the squared magnitude of the difference between two complex phase components. The derivation retains the full nonlinearity, extending the correspondence beyond the small-angle approximation. Direct numerical evolution of the original component fields provides a reproducible check at finite relative-phase amplitude. The reported breather benchmark reaches a peak relative-phase excursion of approximately 2.574 radians, with a maximum sampled error of approximately 6.3 × 10⁻⁹ radians over two oscillation periods. Component amplitudes remain fixed. Interaction-removal and unequal-speed controls document the failure to recover the same target when the specified conditions are changed. The string-theory connection is examined through the Pohlmeyer reduction of classical strings on R_t × S². A separate conventional kink embedding is checked against the local geometric constraints and string equations of motion. The evolved phase breather is not reconstructed as a string. The established result is a conditional correspondence between reduced classical equations; a full physical or quantum equivalence between the proposed phase model and string theory remains unestablished. Version 1.0 includes the standalone report and an accompanying reproducibility archive containing mathematical derivations, executable Python scripts, numerical settings, sampled synthetic data, control results, figures, source provenance, checksum manifests and reproduction instructions. A documented replay of the retained calculation and an AI-assisted computational audit support inspection and reuse of the reported results. summary: This paper offers a candidate descriptive model based on the author’s retrospective account of internal agent-like experience during a past period of social isolation, emotional distress and perceived high cognitive load. It is a non-clinical reconstruction, not a technique, treatment or recommendation. No contemporaneous physiological, behavioral or neuroimaging measurements were recorded. The Opposition–Load–Coupling vocabulary organizes reported phases of self-talk, opposition, felt load, perceived coupling, autonomy, boundary degradation and disengagement. These are reported experiences and interpretive constructs, not demonstrated causal mechanisms. Claimed benefits and harms are unmeasured first-person reports. The Shared Value Anchor is an untested candidate predictor, not an established stabilizer or necessary condition. The case does not establish whether value conflict preceded initial boundary degradation or distinguish the proposal from a simpler load-based account. The model is situated alongside dialogical-self, Internal Family Systems, predictive-processing, imaginary-companion, writer-agency and tulpa literature. Any incremental contribution lies in the proposed coupling vocabulary and separately testable value-anchor hypothesis, not in discovering internal multiplicity or proving a new mechanism. Safety: do not intentionally induce or replicate the conditions described. This is the author’s own past experience, published at the author’s direction; no formal ethics approval or exemption is claimed. Version 4 incorporates author-adopted revisions following advisory and changed-text checks, including prior-involved AI reviewers. Those checks are not independent peer review, clinical validation or evidence of effectiveness.

summary: Four-dimensional beam-matrix reconstruction from quadrupole scans is the standard way to mea- sure cross-plane coupling and the intrinsic emittances that a decoupling section can recover. We show that a scan of a single thin quadrupole, normal or skew and placed anywhere in a linear lattice, determines at most nine of the ten beam-matrix parameters for any number of settings, because each measured second moment is quadratic in the quadrupole strength. The unmeasured direction lies in the x–y cross block and has a closed form in terms of the transfer matrices; for a quadrupole followed by a drift of length L its nonzero entries are Wxpy = Wpxy = 1 and Wpxpy = −2/L. Both projected emittances are therefore measured, but the beam matrices consistent with the data form a line segment along which the smaller intrinsic emittance ranges from zero to slightly above its true value, so a single-knob scan gives only an upper bound on it. A thick quadrupole restores the miss- ing direction only weakly, its singular value scaling approximately as the sixth power of the magnet length. Scanning two independently powered quadrupoles of any type makes the reconstruction well posed without additional hardware.
title: Single-knob quadrupole scans do not determine the intrinsic emittances

summary: Description This dataset accompanies a comparative evolutionary-genomics study of ancestral cytosine substitution patterns across human, chimpanzee, bonobo and gorilla lineages. Using hg38-centered UCSC multiz primate alignments and a seven-species phylogenetic framework, we reconstructed ancestral nucleotide states and quantified cytosine substitutions across all 22 human autosomes. The analysis examined CG, CHG and CHH sequence contexts, 256 strand-canonicalized ancestral 5-mer motifs, and lineage-specific substitution patterns. The deposited files include: Chromosome-level ancestral-site datasets at a minimum ancestral-state posterior probability of 0.95. Chromosome-specific 5-mer substitution summaries and quality-control records. Genome-wide cytosine substitution frequencies and context-enrichment ratios. Chromosome-bootstrap uncertainty estimates and cross-lineage motif comparisons. Statistical analyses of lineage-specific motif deviations, including simultaneous confidence intervals. Leave-one-autosome-out predictive comparisons of ancestral 3-mer and 5-mer sequence context. Frozen methodology documentation, validation records, checksums and the fixed seven-species phylogenetic tree. The dataset supports independent examination and downstream reanalysis of the reported numerical findings. Data provenance: UCSC Genome Browser hg38-centered 30-primate multiz alignments, restricted to seven primate species. Computational methods: IQ-TREE 2.3.6 ancestral-state reconstruction under GTR+F+G4, followed by custom Python-based sequence-context and statistical analyses. Limitations: The archive contains processed ancestral-site data and numerical outputs, not the original complete multiple-sequence alignments. It does not contain ancestral DNA methylation measurements, direct estimates of net CpG gain or loss, or calibrated mutation rates. Associated code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23425960 Archive organization: This dataset is distributed across two Zenodo records. This record contains Part 1 of 2. Part 2 is available at https://zenodo.org/records/23442145 . Both parts are required to reconstruct the complete archive. Download all files from both records and follow the instructions in RECONSTRUCTION.txt to assemble and verify the dataset.
title: Ancestral Cytosine Sequence-Context Substitution Data Across Four Hominid Lineages: A 22-Autosome Comparative Analysis. Part 1

summary: The rapid expansion of the gig economy, facilitated by digital talent platforms, has fundamentally reconfigured the nature of work, employment relationships, and organizational structures. This paradigm shift from stable, long-term employment to a fluid workforce of contractors, freelancers, and project-based talent presents profound challenges to conventional leadership theories and practices. Traditional models, predicated on hierarchical authority, stable organizational boundaries, and enduring psychological contracts, are proving increasingly inadequate for orchestrating a workforce characterized by autonomy, transience, and distributed networks. This paper conducts a critical review of existing leadership literature—including transformational, adaptive, and emerging platform leadership theories—assessing their applicability and limitations in the gig context. Synthesizing insights from organizational behavior, strategic management, and technology studies, we propose a novel integrated framework: the Fluid Leadership Ecosystem (FLE) Model. The FLE model conceptualizes leadership not as a function of individual authority but as the cultivation of a dynamic ecosystem across three core dimensions: Relational Architecture, Algorithmic Stewardship, and Capability Cultivation. We argue that effective leadership in this new era requires designing trust-enabling infrastructures, ensuring human-centric governance of management algorithms, and fostering portable skill development for a transient workforce. This paper introduces novel theoretical perspectives, including temporal leadership dynamics, polycontextual leadership challenges, and the concept of reverse leadership flows from workers to platforms. By presenting a comprehensive model supported by data visualizations and identifying avenues for empirical validation, this research offers a forward-looking agenda for both scholars and practitioners navigating the complexities of leadership in the 21st-century workforce.
title: The Gig Economy and Talent Platforms: New Models of Leadership for Managing a Fluid Workforce

summary: LONGITUDINAL DEVICE MIGRATION AND MEANING CONTINUITY AT THE LIMIT Device Replacement × Model Bridging × Control Semantics STARLI RESEARCH WORKS | INSTITUTE XXIV | FLAGSHIP 24 Feng Cheng-en 33 × Starli Research Works This research monograph investigates a deceptively difficult question in long-term brain–computer interfaces: when sensors, acquisition electronics, firmware, electrode geometry, or decoding models change, what would justify the claim that a user's task-grounded control meaning has been preserved? Numerical signal alignment alone cannot establish continuity of intention. Two systems may encode different signals while supporting the same functional command, or produce nearly identical latent representations while mapping to incompatible actions. The volume formulates meaning continuity as a conditional, falsifiable engineering and scientific hypothesis. It connects device-specific observation models, neural recording instability, task and action ontologies, paired old/new sensing periods, latent manifold bridging, longitudinal recalibration, calibrated abstention, functional validation, and an accessible right to reject the proposed migration. Its central commitment is that no amount of predictive accuracy can compensate for invalid authorization, an unverified physical reference, or loss of independent control. The research atlas comprises thirty connected mathematical derivations, eighty-two research chapters, and 410 independently paginated chapter sections that examine observables, inverse explanations, discriminating experiments, uncertainty and noncompensable safeguards, and independent requalification. Two hundred detailed Research Gates propose future falsification and handoff programs, while thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos preserve revisable candidate approaches rather than immutable conclusions. A claim-scoped DOI evidence ledger connects the study to published work on neural recording drift, decoder adaptation, manifold alignment, longitudinal neural interfaces, speech BCIs, user preferences, and neurotechnology ethics. The book is designed for both human researchers and future AI research systems. Its formulas, chapter cross-links, DOI anchors, competing models, negative-result requirements, and successor-focused research cards provide structured entry points for independent reconstruction and informed disagreement. The visual presentation combines ivory pages, navy and teal typography, and large gold mathematical plates, while mathematical expressions are also recorded in searchable source notation and a separate Excel reference index. This is a prospective, nonclinical research architecture. It does not report new patient experiments, demonstrate safe autonomous human neurovascular microrobots, establish a universal device-migration system, or claim continuity of private thoughts, consciousness, or personal identity. Scientific benefit remains conditional on explicit task definitions, qualified device evidence, legitimate permissions, external validation, and the successor's freedom to reject a failed bridge. Research question: What should remain invariant when an interface changes, and who has the authority to say that its meaning has changed?

summary: Version 2.0 is a substantive revision of version 1.0 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19174862). It supersedes the earlier procedural interpretation and its exclusion of competing explanations. The revised title is Structural Organization and Interpretive Limits of the Phaistos Disc. Reproduced descriptive findings are retained; failed model comparisons and photographic uncertainties are reported explicitly. The earlier version remains available through the record version history. We examine whether reproducible structural observations on the Phaistos Disc support a procedural interpretation. A pinned numerical transcription contains 242 main-sign positions, including one unreadable position, 45 readable sign types, 61 divider-defined groups and 18 supplementary stroke annotations. Source review reconciles counting and numbering conventions while retaining unresolved photographic uncertainty. The 02-to-12 side contrast persists after exact-family collapse. Adding side to a fixed position-only pairing predictor improves held-family loss by 0.082738 nats, but its exact conditional tail of 0.075 fails the frozen support rule. A positional mixture fails to outperform a bigram baseline. A separate directional test of the proposed 07-to-27 recovery relationship fails, with a one-sided permutation tail of 0.884. Supplementary-stroke comparisons have insufficient controlled overlap for the specified exact test. The work documents organization and constrains specific interpretations without establishing procedural functions or phonetic values. Corpus, code, protocols, full results and uncertainty ledgers accompany the paper.
title: Structural Organization and Interpretive Limits of the Phaistos Disc

summary: DARE TO DRAW YOUR SWORD AGAINST DESTINY is a long-form philosophical poem exploring the courage of individuals who dare to confront fate, even when victory is uncertain and the path ahead remains unknown. At its heart lies a simple yet powerful conviction: heroism is not defined solely by triumph, but by the willingness to stand against overwhelming circumstances without surrendering one’s dignity, conscience, or hope. Through poetic reflections on solitude, struggle, resilience, freedom, and the human spirit, this work portrays the act of drawing one’s sword against destiny as a symbol of existential courage rather than violence. The poem celebrates not only those who overcome adversity, but also those who continue forward despite failure, uncertainty, and the absence of recognition. Beyond its heroic imagery, the work embraces a deeper philosophy: true strength is not merely the power to resist, but also the capacity to protect, to remain compassionate, and to preserve warmth in a world that can often be unforgiving. Created within the imaginative framework of the White Rainbow Era, this literary work reflects the principle of Strength-Grounded Warmth—a vision of kindness supported by courage, boundaries, responsibility, and inner conviction. Ultimately, DARE TO DRAW YOUR SWORD AGAINST DESTINY offers a tribute to every ordinary person who has ever faced an extraordinary struggle. Its central message is timeless: To dare to challenge destiny is already an act of heroism. Victory may belong to circumstance, but courage belongs to the one who dares.
title: ⚔️ English Title DARE TO DRAW YOUR SWORD AGAINST DESTINY

summary: Large language models often penalize multilingual users through hidden 'tokenizer taxes' caused by subword fragmentation. Geographic proper nouns offer a controlled stress case for this distributional asymmetry, as they are standardized, cross-linguistically available entities whose orthographic forms frequently mismatch tokenizer training distributions. We introduce the Cross-Linguistic Orthographic Uniqueness Score (CLOUS), a character-level metric based on Shannon surprisal that quantifies the orthographic rarity of localized country names. We evaluate CLOUS on a controlled corpus of 249 ISO-registered country names; generalization to other geographic entity types remains future work. We evaluate CLOUS against tokenization fertility for six production tokenizers spanning three algorithm families across eleven languages and seven script families. Using Spearman rank correlation with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, CLOUS shows significant associative strength with fertility in 61 of 65 valid language-tokenizer combinations. As a screening tool for high-fragmentation entities, CLOUS achieves ROC-AUC = 0.850 and F1 = 0.740, correctly identifying approximately three-quarters of the highest-fragmentation entities from orthographic properties alone. We further show that CLOUS correlates with fertility more strongly than length-based baselines across all evaluated scripts, and outperforms a character bigram surprisal model in 69.2% of tested combinations, particularly for logographic, syllabic, and Latin scripts. Conversely, the bigram baseline proves superior for morphophonologically complex scripts like Arabic and Devanagari, indicating that tokenizer fragmentation is driven by local orthographic context in some scripts and absolute character rarity in others. Script family appears to be the primary driver of CLOUS-fertility correlation strength, with effect sizes ranging from modest for Latin-script languages ) to large for non-Latin scripts (   up to 0.686 for Japanese). These findings suggest that CLOUS may be useful as a lightweight pre-tokenization diagnostic for multilingual NLP pipelines.
title: Estimating Cross-Lingual Tokenization Fragmentation Risk: A Frequency-Based Uniqueness Score for Geographic Entities

summary: The Voynich Manuscript exhibits strong statistical regularities, but the distinction between recoverable grammar and recoverable lexical meaning remains unresolved. This study asks how far a progressively frozen, cross-validated analysis can reconstruct the manuscript’s internal word-building system without assigning meanings from illustrations, candidate languages, or post-hoc English paraphrase. Using canonical transcription, protected holdout partitions, alternate-transcription replication, exact host substitutions, and adversarial stopping rules, the analysis recovers a cumulative left-edge morphology, a transferable inventory of 39 surface CORE-0 stem/bodies, reproducible host-by-right-state coupling, a stable K/T referential contrast, and a directed network among powered lexical cores. The 39-core inventory predicts protected-frame combinatorics and content-blind contextual fingerprints out of sample, while attempts to decompose these bodies into a deeper transferable root layer fail. Nine recurring hosts show strongly replicated coupling to EY/EEY/EDY right-edge states, supporting a distributed morphological paradigm rather than independent left- and right-side systems. A 28-node directed CORE network also replicates across canonical calibration, untouched Holdout, and alternate-transcription tests, yielding neutral outbound- and inbound-biased stem classes without requiring part-of-speech or semantic assignments. On the project’s fully constrained 1,609-line benchmark, 12,299 of 12,495 positions are role-naturalizable (98.4314%), leaving 196 opaque positions. This percentage is explicitly a conditional benchmark-maturity statistic, not a measure of literal plaintext recovery or manuscript-wide translation accuracy. Repeated attempts to cross from structural organization to ordinary lexical meaning—including deeper-root induction, topic clustering, functional-neighborhood anchoring, local lexical syntax, illustration matching, source-language fitting, and prospective semantic transfer—fail the project’s promotion criteria. The resulting contribution is therefore a structural decipherment rather than a lexical one: a reproducible grammatical and morphological architecture together with an empirically identified lexical-identifiability ceiling. The work extends, but is distinct from, the earlier controlled-translation release at DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22049207.
title: Structural Decipherment Without Lexical Recovery: A Cross-Validated Morphological Analysis of the Voynich Manuscript

summary: Dataset supporting the article "Who Benefits from Immersion? Prior 3D Experience, User Experience, and Human-Centered Personalization in the Metaverse" (submitted to the International Journal of Human–Computer Interaction). Design. Mixed factorial 3 × 2 × 2 experiment with 519 participants. Between-subjects factors: experimental profile (virtual team leadership, digital marketing, innovation and entrepreneurship) and condition (traditional format vs. immersive multiuser metaverse environment). Within-subjects factor: measurement time (pre-test, post-test). Data were collected in the first semester of 2026 during undergraduate classes at a Brazilian university. Participation was voluntary, with informed consent; no personally identifying information was retained. Contents. One Excel workbook with two sheets: a long-format sheet (1,038 rows = 519 participants × 2 measurement times) and a wide-format sheet (519 rows, pre-test and post-test variables side by side). Variables include participant and cell identifiers, demographic and technological-background items, single items and composite scores for the metaverse-experience constructs (presence, experience fluidity/seamlessness, interoperability, real-time concurrency, economic flow), the technology-adoption constructs (intention to participate, perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, perceived value), baseline enjoyment, and procedural indicators. Item labels are in Portuguese; seven-point Likert scales. Participant identifiers are anonymous codes assigned by the researchers. Access. Files are restricted because participants consented to the use of their responses for academic and scientific purposes without individual identification. Access is granted for research purposes upon reasonable request to the corresponding author (luis.hernan@usp.br).
title: Who Benefits from Immersion? Experimental dataset on immersive versus traditional task formats in organizational metaverse environments (N = 519)

summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Twenty-three entries are documented, nine of them confirmed defects in the source literature: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7, a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients, a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset, and a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten. Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from. The package computes the direct and veiling components along a horizontal underwater path, converts spectra to CIE XYZ, sRGB, or the response of an arbitrary camera or set of photoreceptors, gives the Jerlov type that typically applies in each 10 m layer down to 200 m and carries the downwelling irradiance down through those layers, integrates photosynthetically available radiation (PAR), or the photon flux over any other band or weighted by any spectral sensitivity, with depth, gives the spectrum at any depth and the effective Kd between two, and finds the depth at which PAR falls to 1 percent, ranks the Jerlov types by their distance from a measured Kd spectrum, carries Jerlov's measured profiles of quanta irradiance (350-700 nm) by water type and checks the depth profile against them, carries Tyler's (1958) measured radiance distribution in Lake Pend Oreille, carries the Paulson & Simpson (1977) shortwave penetration parameters used by ocean circulation models, converts a backscattering sensor's single-angle reading into the backscattering coefficient, and carries Petzold's (1972) volume scattering functions for eight measured ocean waters.
title: jerlov: inherent optical properties of the Jerlov optical water types, with provenance

summary: A harness wraps one or more generators (language models, other neural models, programs or people) with a symbolic layer: a rule set and, optionally, a knowledge store. A checker evaluates each candidate output against the rules and returns a verdict and the violated rules. A release gate lets the output, or part of it, leave only when it passes or under an exception policy, fixed in advance or chosen per request. That is the minimal core. Optional modules, used alone or in any combination, extend it. Rules may filter inputs, decoding, finished outputs, agent actions before execution, and outputs already delivered. A failing output may be repaired by a minimal symbolic change, or revised under a budget the generator cannot alter, with the passing part released under caveats. A passing output may carry a receipt tied to the state it was checked against, so that a later change re-checks affected outputs and supersedes a receipt only when its verdict changes (or, optionally, when the facts it records change). The rule set may improve from evidence, each change held inactive until it passes a gate that can refuse unapproved weakening and require independent approval. Further modules separate claims from outcomes, count correlated sources once, re-extract rendered prose, replay decisions, accept statements by cost, add human review, and turn the harness's verdicts, repairs and revisions into training signals. Outputs may also be read into typed records before checking, with size caps and a per-rule estimate of evaluation work, or a step counter, so that each check made by a rule whose work can be estimated or counted is bounded in advance, and a request may bring rules of its own, written by the generator or another source and admitted only when they cannot relax the rules in force. Knowledge and policy changes can then be made in rules instead of model weights, and any fine-tuning that remains needs less manual labelling.
title: Rule-Gated Generation: A Harness That Filters, Repairs, Certifies and Re-Checks Machine-Generated Output and Improves Its Own Rules Under a Gate

summary: Machine-readable evidence and analysis code for a PRISMA-2020 systematic review of fairness in histopathology AI. Contents. (i) The dual-coded, adjudicated extraction table for the 88-study analytical corpus (61 from the main search, 17 from the demographic-term update, 2 retrieved in October 2026, 2 suggested in peer review, 1 candidate resolved on full text and 5 from a re-screen of the keyword-filtered records; 89 records, one conference abstract linked to its journal paper; the earlier 62- and 79-study tables are kept alongside), with the pre-pass snapshots and the script that applies the October 2026 revisions, with the raw multi-coder outputs and inter-coder agreement statistics; (ii) the screening, de-duplication and post-hoc eligibility-audit logs; (iii) adjudicated QUADAS-2 risk-of-bias judgements for all 88 studies, with per-coder judgements for the original 62; (iv) the full consensus-endorsement coding pipeline — screened review pools, the pre-specified random sample (n=30, seed 20260913), the coding specification, two independent coder passes, disagreements and their adjudication, and tallies with Wilson 95% confidence intervals; (v) the 39-dataset demographic-metadata audit; and (vi) a claim-by-claim statistics register mapping every reported number to its source rows, together with the code that produces each value. Full texts of the reviewed papers are not included, for copyright reasons. Code is licensed MIT; data tables are licensed CC BY 4.0. A SHA-256 manifest ( MANIFEST.sha256 ) covers every file in the package. This package is a working-tree snapshot of the manuscript as of 18 October 2026 (61 pp main + 45 pp supplementary). Manuscript v0.6.6 (18 October 2026). Same manuscript text as v0.6.5; this version adds data/context_fulltexts/, the full texts of eleven context-only works cited in the manuscript (final STARD-AI, CLAIM 2020 and 2024, TRIPOD+AI, PROBAST+AI, PRISMA 2020, QUADAS-2, Yang 2025, Bhattacharyya 2025, the EU AI Act and the 2021 GMLP principles) with a per-file licence list; this record's CC BY 4.0 licence covers the depositor's own materials only, and each of those texts keeps its rights holder's terms (three are publisher-copyrighted, one is non-commercial, one licence was not verified). v0.6.5 content, carried forward: Fourth deep-review response (every comment except the human audit, which has not been run); no coded value, count, grade or headline statistic changed. Table 12 caption and Table 10 footnote arithmetic corrected; PRISMA items 8, 13f, 20d and 23c completed; the Methods now separates the adapted QUADAS-2 appraisal from the full-text search for self-reported reporting-guideline adherence; the D6 attention metric is piecewise-normalized on [-1, 1] with an explicit dispersion formula; the final STARD-AI statement, CLAIM 2024, TRIPOD+AI, PROBAST+AI, PRISMA 2020, QUADAS-2, the EU AI Act and the 2021 GMLP principles were read in full as context (full texts are not deposited); ten references carry full author lists and one wrong co-author list was corrected; the 62 re-screen records without an abstract were reassessed (none added). v0.6.4 content, carried forward: One wording fix on top of v0.6.3 (the Confounding exemplars in the taxonomy figure, Results and Appendix S2 no longer cite a study that is coded institutional/selection rather than confounding); no coded value, count, grade or headline statistic changed. v0.6.3 content, carried forward: provenance correction, a record of a second LLM re-read, and a full-manuscript consistency sweep; no coded value, grade or headline statistic changed. This version also replaces v0.6.1 (the v0.6.1 supplement PDF printed an unresolved figure reference). The analytical corpus is 88 studies (89 records, 86 evaluate a model). Headlines: any fairness metric 25/86 (29.1%), external validation 47/88 (53.4%), overall risk of bias 7 low, 60 unclear, 21 high; 113 mitigation rows; feature-level harmonization is the only Strong family. data/coding_

summary: Who supplies, controls and sustains the services needed to inspect and continue AI-assisted research? This article approaches that question through institutional economics and an evolutionary analogy grounded in market competition. It compares targeted evidence with maintained support against fuller research histories with curated access and support. Three activities organize the comparison: scrutiny of a specified claim, reprocessing retained material under a new question, and continuation of unfinished inquiry. A worked access-review example identifies the rights, expertise, labour and resources required, including conditions under which targeted provision is preferable. Market competition supplies the foundational analogy for evolutionary pressure. Repeated decisions about submissions, paid services, funding and volunteer labour can change which research capabilities remain available and which practices spread. Because competing venues can share infrastructure, institutions and their supporting facilities may follow different paths. The article distinguishes internal revision, transmission and differential support, and separates institutional persistence from scientific validity. JOSS and Rainfall Rescue illustrate particular activities and relationships without establishing the comparative benefits of fuller AI histories. The analysis also addresses selective recording, behaviour under scrutiny, unequal burdens and self-selection. Its contribution connects institutional design to the continuing work and support needed to make research records usable.
title: AI Research and the Evolution of Scholarly Institutions
