summary: Data and analytical software for thermally activated Fe-SMA fibre-reinforced concrete This repository accompanies the article “Analytical modelling of thermally activated iron-based shape memory alloy fibre concrete: Finite transfer and capacity compatibility”. It provides the numerical source data, analytical implementation, calibration inputs, and results used to prepare the final article. The work examines finite fibre–matrix transfer, thermally activated composite response, cohesive-law identification, and the compatibility of reported strengths with uncertain fibre orientation and tensile capacity. The deposit contains one final analysis snapshot. It includes the reference formulation and the baselines, thermal alternatives, and cohesive-law candidates examined in the article. These are parts of the reported scientific assessment, rather than separate manuscript versions. Superseded model results, development archives, manuscript drafts, and unrelated source files are excluded. Contents • data/ contains numerical representations of published response curves, reported group statistics, study metadata, fixed constituent and pullout calibrations, optimizer initialization values, and published experimental/finite-element comparison curves. Curve identifiers preserve the link to the source study and figure. These are processed publication-based data, rather than original instrument records. • model/ contains the executable analysis scripts. They fit the concrete and composite controls, evaluate reference responses and competing baselines, compare response curves on matched displacement grids, assess orientation and conditional envelopes, test capacity compatibility, verify the independent finite-transfer solver, and fit/test the nested cohesive laws. model/screen_capacity.py provides a command-line conditional strength screen. • model/fesma/ contains the reusable mechanics: the Fe-SMA backbone and bond-slip law, nonuniform pullout and work-quadrature solvers, concrete/cohesive section response, activation and two-ended bridging diagnostics, capacity-budget relations, analytical envelopes and inverse compatibility relations. Every script and module is described individually in docs/FILE_GUIDE.md, including its inputs and outputs. • results/ contains the final reference results, source calibration/diagnostic outputs, orientation transfer matrices, conditional envelopes and containment checks, inverse compatibility calculations, numerical verification records, and cohesive-law fitting/exclusion results. The candidate fit files and specimen-exclusion folds document the model comparisons reported in the article. • figures/ contains the final analytical/numerical TikZ figure sources and the exact numerical series plotted in them. The figure index links these files to the article numbering. Source experimental photographs are excluded. The supplied figure data preserve the published snapshot; numerical reruns write to results/. • docs/ contains the full file guide, source bibliography, data dictionary, equation-to-code crosswalk, figure/plot-series indices, screening instructions and reproduction-check record. FILE_INDEX.csv provides a searchable inventory of every deposited file and its purpose. Individual analysis scripts • model/fit_concrete.py — Fits 20 source-coordinate concrete compression envelopes and evaluates matrix thermal-retention candidates. • model/reproduce_source_diagnostics.py — Recalculates the source-specific thermal and matched-rate baselines, finite recovery sensitivity, and six two-ended bridging scenarios used in Figures 6, 8 and 9. • model/fit_reference.py — Refits the two PD matrix controls and nine fibre-control groups; derives PF matrix inputs, calibrates the DT activation index, and computes reference strengths and sensitivity profiles. • model/check_reference.py — Checks section refinement, force balance and capac

summary: This repository provides the official reproduction software, numerical simulation datasets, and empirical input fixtures for the manuscript: Song, X., Xu, H., & Bai, Y. (2026). Width Oscillations Regulate Event-Driven Bank Collapse and Point-Bar Growth in Transitional Meanders. Journal of Geophysical Research: Earth Surface. ( Under Review ) ABSTRACT Alluvial meanders dynamically adjust their planform and channel geometry, yet classical meander theory assumes a spatially uniform, constant channel width and continuous bank retreat, failing to capture episodic bank collapse and non-uniform width adjustments in transitional meandering rivers. Situated along the geomorphic continuum between single-thread and wandering streams, transitional meanders exhibit pronounced spatial width variations that break cross-sectional symmetry. Here, we develop a physically closed, reduced-complexity morphodynamic framework coupling a three-parameter asymptotic expansion of the three-dimensional Reynolds-averaged flow equations, continuous basal toe scour with transient pore-water suction, threshold-governed cantilever limit equilibrium, and a mass-conserving sediment partition driving inner point-bar progradation. The formulation demonstrates that the spatial phase relationship between channel width oscillations and centerline curvature steers the spatial displacement of outer-bank shear stress hotspots: channel constriction upstream of the bend apex amplifies cutbank shear stress, whereas channel expansion decelerates flow and promotes point-bar accretion. Discrete slump-block deposits provide self-adaptive hydraulic shielding that stabilizes the toe and regulates decadal channel relaxation. Hindcasting the 40-year morphodynamic evolution of the transitional Powder River, Montana, across 34 monumented cross sections reproduces post-flood channel widening and subsequent multi-decadal recovery narrowing across 228 discrete collapse events, while in the limit of uniform width the model recovers classical constant-width meander theory with first-order convergence along the meandering Juruá River. Global parameter sweeps quantitatively encompass observed erosion-to-accretion balance ratios across 84 worldwide natural rivers, providing a multiscale morphodynamic framework that links event-scale geotechnical failure to multi-decadal width evolution in alluvial channels. ARCHIVE CONTENTS - src/: Python source code implementing the three-parameter asymptotic hydrodynamic solver, local generalized Orr-Sommerfeld and Squire spectral eigenvalue stability diagnostics, two-stage geotechnical bank failure engine with slump-block hydraulic shielding, and Exner point-bar morphodynamic progradation coupler. - data/: Processed empirical input fixtures, including the 40-year Powder River cross-sectional monitoring dataset (powder_river.json) and the Juruá-A remote sensing centerline profile (Jurua-A_mask1_link_sBCMn_flat.npz). - results/simulations/: Pre-computed numerical simulation output arrays (.npz) enabling instant reproduction of Figures 2–9 without re-running intensive multi-hour sweeps. - figures/: Standalone publication figure plotting scripts (plot_fig1.py through plot_fig9.py) and AGU-style formatting utilities (figure_utils.py). - run_all_reproductions.py: Master execution script that automatically reproduces all nine publication figures in vector PDF format in under two minutes. HOW TO REPRODUCE ALL FIGURES 1. Unzip zenodo_release.zip and navigate into the archive root directory. 2. Ensure the required Python environment is activated:    - Python 3.13    - NumPy 2.3.2    - SciPy 1.17.1    - Matplotlib 3.10.8 3. Run the master reproduction script:    python run_all_reproductions.py 4. All nine publication figures will be generated and verified in figures/output/. ( Under Review ) ABSTRACT Alluvial meanders dynamically adjust their planform and channel geometry, yet classical meander theory assumes a spatially uniform, constant channel width and continuous bank retreat, failing to capture episodic bank collapse and non-uniform width adjustments in transitional meandering rivers. Situated along the geomorphic continuum between single-thread and wandering streams, transitional meanders exhibit pronounced spatial width variations that break cross-sectional symmetry. Here, we develop a physically closed, reduced-complexity morphodynamic framework coupling a three-parameter asymptotic expansion of the three-dimensional Reynolds-averaged flow equations, continuous basal toe scour with transient pore-water suction, threshold-governed cantilever limit equilibrium, and a mass-conserving sediment partition driving inner point-bar progradation. The formulation demonstrates that the spatial phase relationship between channel width oscillations and centerline curvature steers the spatial displacement of outer-bank shear stress hotspots: channel constriction upstream of the bend apex amplifies cutbank shear stress, whereas channel expansion decelerates flow and promotes point-bar accretion. Discrete slump-block deposits provide self-adaptive hydraulic shielding that stabilizes the toe and regulates decadal channel relaxation. Hindcasting the 40-year morphodynamic evolution of the transitional Powder River, Montana, across 34 monumented cross sections reproduces post-flood channel widening and subsequent multi-decadal recovery narrowing across 228 discrete collapse events, while in the limit of uniform width the model recovers classical constant-width meander theory with first-order convergence along the meandering Juruá River. Global parameter sweeps quantitatively encompass observed erosion-to-accretion balance ratios across 84 worldwide natural rivers, providing a multiscale morphodynamic framework that links event-scale geotechnical failure to multi-decadal width evolution in alluvial channels. ARCHIVE CONTENTS - src/: Python source code implementing the three-parameter asymptotic hydrodynamic solver, local generalized Orr-Sommerfeld and Squire spectral eigenvalue stability diagnostics, two-stage geotechnical bank failure engine with slump-block hydraulic shielding, and Exner point-bar morphodynamic progradation coupler. - data/: Processed empirical input fixtures, including the 40-year Powder River cross-sectional monitoring dataset (powder_river.json) and the Juruá-A remote sensing centerline profile (Jurua-A_mask1_link_sBCMn_flat.npz). - results/simulations/: Pre-computed numerical simulation output arrays (.npz) enabling instant reproduction of Figures 2–9 without re-running intensive multi-hour sweeps. - figures/: Standalone publication figure plotting scripts (plot_fig1.py through plot_fig9.py) and AGU-style formatting utilities (figure_utils.py). - run_all_reproductions.py: Master execution script that automatically reproduces all nine publication figures in vector PDF format in under two minutes. Ensure the required Python environment is activated:    - Python 3.13    - NumPy 2.3.2    - SciPy 1.17.1    - Matplotlib 3.10.8 3. summary: Decentralized multi-robot shape formation in GPS-denied environments is important for search-and-rescue and disaster response. Conventional consensus-based formation controllers can violate safe separation, oscillate, or stall when communication degrades, sensors are noisy, or an agent drops out. This paper proposes a resilient decentralized controller that combines Huber-weighted consensus and Exponential Moving Average (EMA) state estimation with a Dual-Layer Artificial Potential Field (APF) safety barrier. The first layer adds an anti-symmetric lateral deflection to resolve head-on encounters between peers; the second applies a normal-plus-tangential circulation field around static obstacles. The framework is evaluated on five simulated nonholonomic differential-drive robots in Gazebo Harmonic (ROS 2 Jazzy). Three runs are compared: a linear consensus baseline, the same baseline under faults (15% packet loss, 50-150 ms delay, σ = 0.18 m sensor noise, and a mid-run agent blackout), and the proposed controller under the same faults. The fault-free baseline reached the pentagon fastest (0.0156 m final RMS error) but its minimum separation fell to 0.3918 m, with 31 logged violations of the 0.50 m margin. Under faults the baseline reached 0.0546 m with 5 violations (minimum 0.4833 m). The proposed controller recorded no violations, kept a minimum separation of 0.6757 m, and reached 0.0368 m final error, at the cost of slower convergence (about 21 s versus about 12-15 s). Results are from single simulation runs, and the safety barrier is empirical rather than formally guaranteed.
title: Resilient Decentralized Shape Formation of Multi-Robot Swarms Under Adversarial Real-World Faults in High-Complexity Disaster Environments

summary: The thickness errors of a whole monitored run, two fixes, faster scoring, a third tutorial, and the tutorials in the source distribution. Added monitoring_errors(lam_mon_um, recipe_t_um, n_layers, sigma_signal, n_inc=1.0, n_sub=1.52, quantity="T", theta0_rad=0.0, pol="s", n_exit=None, signal_offset=0.0, max_nonlinearity=0.1) -> MonitoringErrors ( fabtwin.monitor ): the thickness errors of a whole level-monitored run, with the errors of each layer carried into the stops of the layers after it ( monitoring_plan treats each layer as if the layers below it were exact). To first order, with A[j, k] = d S_j / d t_k (the exact derivatives of fabtwin.gradients ), dt = G (e + offset) with G = -A^-1 , so cov(dt) = sigma_signal^2 G G^T and mean(dt) = offset G 1 . Fields: the sensitivity and propagation matrices, mean, covariance, standard deviations and correlations (absolute and relative), the per-layer errors of monitoring_plan for comparison, and a nonlinearity measure; .twin() gives a GaussianTwin of the monitored machine (relative thickness errors, zero index errors). Refused: the inputs monitoring_plan refuses, a non-positive sigma_signal , a non-finite offset, and a run in which a layer ends too close to a turning point for the errors it receives ( nonlinearity above max_nonlinearity , the layers named). simulate_monitored_runs(lam_mon_um, recipe_t_um, n_layers, sigma_signal=None, n_runs=None, seed=0, noise=None, ..., signal_offset=0.0) : the same runs simulated layer by layer without any linearization; each stop is found by bisection on stack_rt on the branch of the layer's monitoring curve that contains the recipe thickness, all runs at once. A stop the signal cannot reach on that branch is NaN, with a RuntimeWarning. README example 22 (the errors of a whole monitored run). MANIFEST.in : the source distribution now contains examples/ (and CHANGELOG.md , CITATION.cff , CONTRIBUTING.md ), so the tutorial tests run from an unpacked sdist instead of being skipped. Fixed Band edges on the wavelength grid. notch_weights and bandpass_weights dropped a grid point that lies exactly on a band edge (in decimal) when binary round-off put the computed edge just past it. Before -> after: notch_weights on np.linspace(0.45, 0.70, 51) with center 0.5325, half-width 0.0125, guard 0.02 (README example 11): 5 -> 6 stop-band points (0.545 was missing, because 0.5325 + 0.0125 is 0.5449999999999999 ); on np.linspace(0.40, 0.70, 61) with 0.55, 0.02, 0.01: the upper pass band started at 0.585 -> 0.58, while the lower one already ended at 0.52. A point within 1e-9 of the largest wavelength of an edge now counts as on it. Effect on README example 11: largest stop-band T at 0 degrees 0.042 -> 0.041, smooth margin J 0.0446 -> 0.0447. No other README example or tutorial changes; where no grid point lies within 1e-6 um of an edge the weights are unchanged exactly (200 random grids). Tests: test_v011.py::test_band_edges_on_the_grid_belong_to_their_band , test_band_edges_off_the_grid_are_unchanged . drift_test p-values too small with few runs. A permutation that reproduces the observed split (or swaps two groups of equal size) has the observed statistic exactly, but recomputed from reordered rows it can come out a few units of the last digit smaller, and was then not counted. Before -> after ( n_perm=999 , seed=0 , two groups 6 standard deviations apart, data seeds of the tests): 2 + 2 runs, data seed 1: 0.036 -> 0.315 (with 4 runs no p-value below 1/3 is possible); data seed 10: 0.065 -> 0.315; 3 + 3 runs, data seed 0: 0.082 -> 0.103; 2 + 3 runs, data seed 6: 0.052 -> 0.106; under the null with 3 + 3 runs, the smallest of 60 seeded p-values 0.046 -> 0.087 (the exact minimum is 0.1). A permuted statistic less than 1e-9 times the mean distance between the runs below the observed one now counts as a tie. README example 13 is unchanged. summary: Lifetime histograms and the cavity budget they measure, the readout errors of each spin state at the threshold you use, a refusal for fields too weak to split the qubit, a faster readout loop, and a third worked tutorial. Added fit_lifetime_histogram(counts, bin_edges_s, background, t_start, tau_start) and LifetimeFit ( vacspin.lab , exported at top level): the excited-state lifetime from a time-resolved photon histogram (time-correlated single photon counting), one exponential plus a constant background, by Poisson maximum likelihood (Fisher scoring with a line search), with large-sample error bars and a Pearson goodness of fit. t_start fits only the bins after the excitation pulse and the timing response. It refuses malformed counts or edges, fewer than 10 counts or too few bins, a background that ends at zero, a lifetime that runs outside 1e-3 of the narrowest bin to 1000 times the window, an amplitude that runs to zero, an error bar above a quarter of the lifetime or amplitude, and non-convergence. summary: Profiles across an edge with the covariance between bins, the extra charge per unit length of edge, exact Bayesian error bars without a dense inverse, two unit dependences fixed, and CI-robust tests of the stacked map fit. Added region_profile(coefficients, dw1, dw2, sigma1, sigma2, coordinate, bins, *, mask=None, shift_correlation=None, ref_sigma=None) , returning a RegionProfile : the mean strain and density in bins of a coordinate (for example the distance from an edge), each bin with the error budget of region_mean (shift noise, calibration, reference frequencies, homogeneity check), plus the covariance between all bins ( covariance , covariance_shifts , covariance_calibration , covariance_reference , shape (R, 2, R, 2)). The bins share the lever arms and the reference frequencies, so their errors are correlated: calibration covariance sum_m (x_i^T C_m x_j) k_m k_m^T between bins i and j, reference covariance K^-1 diag(u1^2, u2^2) K^-T for every pair, no shift covariance (different pixels). Propagation as in JCGM 100:2008 (GUM), 5.2.2, Eq. (13), first order in the calibration. RegionProfile.combination(strain_weights, density_weights) (any weighted sum of the bins, with its error parts, as a new LinearEstimate ), RegionProfile.integrated_excess(bulk, quantity="density", widths=None) (sum over the other bins of width times value minus the bulk value: across a straight edge, the excess per unit length of edge; the reference error cancels) and RegionProfile.contrast(i, j) (bin i minus bin j, as region_contrast gives it). Validation: each bin equals the mean of the per-pixel SeparationModel.invert maps (1e-14) and region_mean on that bin (relative 1e-12); the cross-bin calibration covariance equals that from a finite-difference Jacobian of an independent re-solve (relative 1e-6); combinations equal c^T C c (relative 1e-10); the integrated excess equals the sum by hand (1e-13), its shift part a pixel-level linear form (1e-10) and its calibration part finite differences (1e-6); contrast equals region_contrast (1e-12). Over 300 seeded trials that repeat calibration, map noise and reference error, the spread of the excess and of a bin mean is within 15 % of the error bars (measured 3 % and 4 %), and the measured correlation of two bins (0.988) matches the reported one (0.987). README: the profile and its refusals in the package list, a third tutorial, test descriptions, corrections and limits. Fixed bayesian_map_inversion depended on the units of the lever arms. Before: with the density column in cm^-2 (K / [1, 1e13]), the maps of the test problem differed from an independent dense solve by a relative 6.1e-4 (density) and 1.4e-4 (strain), and with K * [1, 1e6] by 8e-13. After: 1.1e-15 and 6.7e-16 (density in cm^-2). When the column norms of K differ by more than 2^10, the problem is solved for density / t with t a power of two (exact rescaling) and scaled back. Smaller ratios (all shipped sets, all README examples) run the unchanged code. Test: test_bayesian_map_does_not_depend_on_the_density_unit . MultiModeModel , ThreeCauseModel and bayesian_map_inversion refused a well-separating lever-arm matrix as "rank < 2" ("rank < 3") when the density was in m^-2 (arms near 1e-17 cm^-1 per m^-2; also for K / [1, 1e15]), and compare_mode_sets returned [] for it instead of three subsets. The rank is now judged on K with unit-length columns ( _has_full_column_rank ), as calibrate_lever_arms does since 0.14.0. After: the results equal those in 1e13 cm^-2, rescaled (measured relative differences below 1e-14); a rank-deficient matrix is still refused in any unit. Test: test_rank_tests_do_not_depend_on_the_units . Documentation and tests: fit_map was documented (module docstring, README) to give "bit for bit" the numbers of the per-pixel loop over fit_two_modes , and nine tests demanded exact equality between the stacked and the single-spectrum fits (and between ThreeCauseModel runs on stacks of diff

summary: Added fit_xy(model, x, y, theta0, sigmas, x_sigmas, max_iter=200, tol=1e-12) : the fit when the settings have error bars too (errors in variables), for any Model whose prediction for a measurement depends only on its own settings. It minimizes the sum of squared reading residuals and squared setting adjustments, each in units of its error bar, over the parameters and the true settings (Levenberg-Marquardt on the joint problem, with the settings eliminated by a Schur complement at each step). x_sigmas is one number, one per measurement, or an (n, d) array; 0 marks an exact setting. Returns a FitResult with the first-order covariance (with the settings eliminated, the inverse of sum a_i a_i^T / (sigma_y,i^2 + sum_k s_ik^2 sigma_x,ik^2) ), chi2 for n - p degrees of freedom, and the fitted true settings in the new field FitResult.x_adjusted . For a straight line it is the line of D. York et al., "Unified equations for the slope, intercept, and standard errors of the best straight line", Am. J. Phys. 72, 367-375 (2004), doi:10.1119/1.1632486. On Pearson's data with York's weights (C. A. Cantrell, Atmos. Chem. Phys. 8, 5477-5487 (2008), Table 1) it gives intercept 5.47991 +/- 0.29497 and slope -0.48053 +/- 0.05799, chi2 = 11.87 for 8 degrees of freedom. The slope and intercept are the values of the "Williamson-York" row of Cantrell's Table 2; the error bars and chi2 agree with York's equations and with the output of the R package bfsl. Refuses a fit without sigmas , x_sigmas of the wrong shape or negative, and a model whose prediction for one measurement depends on the settings of another. inverse_predict(..., full_cov=False) : only the error bars, no covariance between readings, so memory grows with the number of readings and not with its square (10000 readings took 0.49 s). audit_record of a fit_xy result has the key fit_method and report_text prints it; the data digest then also covers x_sigmas . Records of fit are unchanged. Tutorial examples/tutorial_errors_in_both.py and README example 15 (see Tutorials below). Fixed The conformal rank k = ceil((n + 1)(1 - alpha)) (used by conformal_quantile and coverage_exact ) was one too small for some alphas at large n . Any product within 1e-9 (relative) above an integer was taken to be that integer, and for large n that swallows a true fraction. Before: alpha = 0.0001, n = 109998: k = 109988, coverage_exact = 0.99989999909, below the promised 1 - alpha = 0.9999 (alpha = 0.001: first at n = 1001998, coverage 0.998999999). After: k = 109989 and coverage 0.99990909, from exact integer arithmetic. A decimal alpha of up to 8 significant digits, also one computed as 1 - 0.9 , is now read exactly; other alphas (1/3, 0.099999999999) keep the earlier rule. For every alpha and n of the earlier tests the rank is unchanged (test test_conformal_rank_exact_at_large_n , which fails on 0.4.0, and test_conformal_rank_unchanged_where_it_was_right ). The test suite failed when run from the source distribution (sdist), which left out CITATION.cff and examples/ . Before (a clean copy of the 0.5.0 sources without MANIFEST.in , tests run from the unpacked sdist): 1 failed ( test_version_metadata , FileNotFoundError for CITATION.cff ), 107 passed, 3 tutorial tests skipped. After: a new MANIFEST.in adds CHANGELOG.md , CITATION.cff , CONTRIBUTING.md and examples/*.py to the sdist, and all 111 tests pass there. The wheel is unchanged. Changed The test that compares the batched design with the 0.3.0 loops compares the information matrices to 1e-12 of their largest entry instead of with == , and would accept different picks only for a tie within 1e-9 in the log-determinant: batched and single LAPACK calls are not guaranteed to round alike on every processor. The README no longer says "bit for bit" for the batched design . Version 0.5.0 in pyproject.toml , labplan.__version__ and CITATION.cff (released 2026-10-18). summary: Popper’s (1983, 2002) philosophy of science has enjoyed something of a renaissance in the wake of the replication crisis, offering a philosophical basis for the ensuing science reform movement. However, adherence to Popper’s approach may also be at least partly responsible for the sense of “crisis” that has developed following multiple unexpected replication failures. In this article, I contrast Popper’s approach with that of Lakatos (1978) as well as with a related but problematic approach called naïve methodological falsificationism (NMF; Lakatos, 1978). The Popperian approach is powerful because it is based on logical refutations, but its theories are noncausal and, therefore, potentially lacking in scientific value. In contrast, the Lakatosian approach considers causal theories, but it concedes that these theories are not logically refutable. Finally, NMF represents a hybrid approach that subjects Lakatosian causal theories to Popperian logical refutations. However, its tactic of temporarily accepting a ceteris paribus clause during theory testing may be viewed as scientifically inappropriate, epistemically inconsistent, and “completely redundant” (Lakatos, 1978, p. 40). I conclude that the replication “crisis” makes the most sense in the context of the Popperian and NMF approaches because it is only in these two approaches that the failure to replicate a previously corroborated theory represents a logical refutation of that theory. In contrast, such replication failures are less problematic in the Lakatosian approach because they do not logically refute theories. Indeed, in the Lakatosian approach, replication failures can be temporarily ignored or used to motivate theory development.
title: The replication crisis is less of a "crisis" in Lakatos' philosophy of science than it is in Popper's.

summary: Bulk thermoelectric transport, models periodic in fewer directions than their space (ribbons, which crashed before), three bugs fixed in the k-grid folding and the band filling, the topology and geometry loops made many times faster, and a third tutorial. No public function was removed or renamed; results of valid calls are unchanged except where a bug is fixed below (and by floating-point rounding, about 1e-12 relative or less, where the topology sums are now taken as array operations). Added boltzmann_transport(model, mu, T, mesh=None, kpts=None, weights=None, tau=1e-14, spin=2, ...) (new module hamop.boltzmann ): the conductivity tensor, the Seebeck tensor, the electronic thermal conductivity at zero current and the Lorenz ratio in the relaxation-time approximation of the Boltzmann equation, in SI units (G. K. H. Madsen and D. J. Singh, Comput. Phys. Commun. 175, 67 (2006), Eqs. 9 to 18), for one chemical potential or an array of them from one diagonalization. tau is a constant (seconds) or a function of the state energy. Band velocities are the Kubo velocity matrix elements (overlap included); at degenerate k-points the sum runs over the degenerate pairs, as in drude_weight . Refused: finite models, T <= 0 , a relaxation time that is not positive and finite, a mu with no state within 60 kT, a mu at which nothing conducts, and a mesh on which one state carries more than 5 % of the conductivity. Tests: the chain against an adaptive quadrature of its closed-form dispersion (1e-9; measured 1e-13) for constant and energy-dependent tau ; graphene at +/-0.3 eV, 300 K, against the Dirac-cone closed forms of sigma, S, the Lorenz ratio and S for tau ~ |E| (1 %; measured below 2.5e-3); sigma against the Drude weight times tau / (pi hbar) (1e-10); rotation of an anisotropic crystal (1e-9); scaling with a constant tau (1e-12). hamop.model.H_PLANCK = 6.62607015e-34 J s, exact in the SI (CODATA 2018), and HBAR_EVS derived from it and E_CHARGE ; the tests check them against scipy.constants . Periodic models with fewer lattice vectors than Cartesian dimensions (a ribbon, a chain in a plane): cell of shape (p, dim) with p < dim. The k-points stay Cartesian; monkhorst_pack places them in the span of the lattice vectors; cell_volume is the length or area of the cell. New property TightBindingModel.reciprocal_vectors . Tests: a chain at 30 degrees in a plane against linear_chain (DOS, chemical potential, carrier density to 1e-12; Drude weight and Boltzmann conductivity projected by cos^2 and sin^2); the SSH chain in a plane (Zak phase, 1e-12); a square-lattice strip against its closed-form bands and against the same strip in a 2D cell with vacuum (DOS, optics, Boltzmann, 1e-12). MANIFEST.in : the source distribution now contains examples/ , CHANGELOG.md , CITATION.cff and CONTRIBUTING.md , so tests/test_tutorials.py runs from the unpacked sdist (before it was skipped there). Fixed symmetry_fold iterated ops twice; given a generator, the first loop used it up and the spectral check saw no operation, so a non-symmetry was folded silently. Graphene with one bond of -3.2 eV (the others -2.7 eV) and the three-fold rotation, mesh 12, DOS with eta = 0.1 eV at -3, 1 and 2.5 eV: before 0.2636, 0.0492, 0.2212 (full grid 0.2393, 0.0657, 0.2078); now ValueError, as for a list. Test: test_symmetry_fold_checks_operations_given_as_a_generator . symmetry_fold mapped grid indices (idx g) instead of grid points ((idx / mesh) g), which differ when the mesh is uneven, so an operation that moves points off the grid was not detected and the orbits were wrong. Square lattice with second neighbors, mesh (8, 4), its 8 operations, DOS with eta = 0.2 eV at 0.5 and 2 eV: before 0.0422 and 0.1310 (full grid 0.0729 and 0.2574); graphene on (6, 3) at 0.5 eV: before 0.0000 (full grid 0.0737). Now refused; the axis mirrors, which fit the (8, 4) and (6, 3) meshes, reproduce the full grid to 1e-12. For even meshes the result is exactly the same as before. Test: test_symme
title: hamop: bands, DOS, Kubo optical conductivity and NEGF transmission from one tight-binding Hamiltonian

summary: This archive is provided as artifact material for the article "Synthesis and Verification of Register Automata over Data Sequences" for SETTA 2026. Abstract: Data sequences, such as time series, traces, and sensor streams, are words over large or infinite data domains. Their properties often depend on comparisons between values at different positions, which finite automata cannot express directly. We study synthesis and verification for Deterministic Register Automata (DRAs) over ordered data sequences. DRAs combine finite control with registers for remembered data values, providing compact symbolic descriptions of quantitative sequence languages. Our technical core is a local-search synthesis procedure and an exact robustness checker for DRAs. We fix the alphabet theory to ordered rationals $(\Q;<,=)$ with rational guard constants and use non-negative affine accumulator costs. For a fixed number of DRA registers, the checker runs in polynomial time; its dependence on that number is exponential. It reduces robustness to coverability and then to a shortest-path problem. Since the search ranges over $\Q^+$, it produces variable-length witnesses and, for RAA-definable alignment costs such as DTW, explores a counterexample space with no a priori length bound. As an application, we use learned DRAs as interpretable surrogates for queried neural sequence classifiers. A probably approximately correct (PAC) validation loop refines rejected candidates, returns genuine non-robustness witnesses for the classifier when found, and accepts a surrogate only with statistical guarantees for fidelity and local stability. We implement the framework in \textit{RAExc}, enabling the synthesis of interpretable automata and the verification of their robustness. We evaluate the approach on benchmark languages and sequentialized MNIST, demonstrating high accuracy while verifying the robustness of the learned automata.

As an application, we use learned DRAs as interpretable surrogates for queried neural sequence classifiers. A probably approximately correct (PAC) validation loop refines rejected candidates, returns genuine non-robustness witnesses for the classifier when found, and accepts a surrogate only with statistical guarantees for fidelity and local stability. We implement the framework in \textit{RAExc}, enabling the synthesis of interpretable automata and the verification of their robustness. We evaluate the approach on benchmark languages and sequentialized MNIST, demonstrating high accuracy while verifying the robustness of the learned automata.

summary: Image harmonization methods adjust the colour and lighting of an object pasted into a photograph so that it looks native to its new scene, and they are ranked by average error on one benchmark whose test images are real photographs with one object recoloured. One photograph can yield several such test images, and the benchmark promises that no photograph appears in both the training and the test split. We find that 1,399 photographs do, and the composites built on them are a quarter of the test set. Duplicate checks over file names or bytes miss this, because every composite is a different file. On that quarter the three methods we score end to end read two to five times lower error than on the rest, but most of the gap is composition rather than the sharing: the shared composites come almost entirely from one of the benchmark's four source collections, and inside that collection the gap falls to about one and a half times. An official score is therefore an average over two populations, mixed in a proportion the benchmark does not report. We release a test list of 5,581 composites whose construction identities do not appear in training, with four near-duplicate pairs disclosed rather than removed, adoptable without retraining at the price of one rescore per checkpoint. We leave open whether the sharing itself changes what a model learns. Contents of this record. The paper, the supplement, the LaTeX source of both, the record metadata and the licence statement. The identity matcher, the composite-locality and sensitivity checks, the CPU tests, the official iHarmony4 lists and the corrected test list are released under the MIT license at https://github.com/Buljic/only-means-only . What this record does not contain. No dataset, no images, no masks, no model checkpoints and no third-party baseline code or weights; those are described and cited by the paper and remain under their own terms. This is a preprint. It has not been peer reviewed. Licensed CC BY 4.0.

summary: The dataset, prepared by Patriotisk Selskab for Bikubenfonden and Høbbet A/S, presents spatially distributed soil analysis conducted in 2024. It includes measurements of soil texture (clay content), organic matter (humus content), soil acidity (reaction number, Rt), and nutrient indicators for phosphorus (Pt), potassium (Kt) and magnesium (Mgt). The results are presented through georeferenced sampling locations, field-level maps and thematic maps illustrating spatial variations in soil properties and nutrient levels. The dataset provides baseline information on soil conditions across the investigated areas and can support assessments of soil fertility, vegetation development, habitat restoration and future land management.
title: Soil Analyses of Svanninge Bjerge and Høbbet – Soil Properties and Nutrient Distribution (2024)

summary: Metascience uses a scientific approach to understand and improve science. Critical metascience takes a step back to question metascience’s common assumptions, methods, problems, and solutions. In this article, I aim to raise the profile of critical metascience and offer a rationale for viewing it as a distinct area of multidisciplinary inquiry. I define critical metascience, explain why it is important, and address some potential concerns about it. I also consider some emerging themes in the area and evaluate its potential relationships with metascience. I conclude that there needs to be greater recognition of critical metascience and greater interaction between metascience and critical metascience in order to improve metascience’s objectivity and approach.
title: What is critical metascience and why is it important?

summary: Loss and phase jitter told apart from squeezing pairs at several pump levels, resonances split by backscattering, a wrong error bar of the transmission fit fixed, a faster photonic-molecule model, two test tolerances tied to their floating-point limits, and a third tutorial. Fixed fit_resonance_transmission(..., branch=...) gave wrong error bars for kappa_ex_hz and kappa_0_hz . The derivative of the escape efficiency with respect to the dip depth D, which is -1 / (4 sqrt(1 - D)) on the over-coupled branch and +1 / (4 sqrt(1 - D)) on the under-coupled one, had the opposite sign on both, which flipped the term that carries the (strong, negative) correlation of the linewidth and the depth. Over-coupled ring ( kappa = 100 MHz , eta = 0.8 , 121 points over +/- 300 MHz, 1 % noise): kappa_0_hz_sigma 0.325 MHz -> 0.171 MHz (Monte Carlo scatter of 400 scans: 0.166 MHz), kappa_ex_hz_sigma 0.768 MHz -> 0.946 MHz (scatter 0.900 MHz). summary: This release contains the Python code, synthetic numerical data, figure-generation scripts, verification routines and supporting documentation accompanying "Tempered fractional hypercomplex fuzzy neural networks: μ-pseudo almost automorphic solutions and global exponential attraction." The package includes quaternion and octonion examples, structured real-component controls, compensated-gain comparisons and a manufactured periodic whole-line benchmark. Reproduction instructions, dependency versions and numerical limitations are documented in the README. The computations provide numerical verification of the stated models. No external measured dataset or application-calibrated performance evaluation is included. Code is released under the MIT License; the numerical data and figures are released under CC-BY-4.0. The package includes quaternion and octonion examples, structured real-component controls, compensated-gain comparisons and a manufactured periodic whole-line benchmark. Reproduction instructions, dependency versions and numerical limitations are documented in the README. The computations provide numerical verification of the stated models. No external measured dataset or application-calibrated performance evaluation is included. Code is released under the MIT License; the numerical data and figures are released under CC-BY-4.0. See LICENSE and NOTICE-licenses.md in the archive.

summary: SELF-CALIBRATING NANO-NEURAL INTERFACES AND REFERENCE LINEAGE AT THE LIMIT Built-In References × Drift Attribution × Independent Functional Requalification STARLI / Institute XXIII / Research Flagship 17 PUBLICATION DESCRIPTION When a long-running neural interface changes, is the cause the sensor, the surrounding tissue, or the decoder? An adaptive algorithm can restore predictive accuracy while obscuring the physical origin of its own correction. This book proposes a rigorous, falsifiable architecture for self-calibrating nano-neural interfaces that must retain the scientific history of every reference and every update. Its central axiom is that self-calibration does not imply self-certification: measurement claims, permission to change, electrode safety and functional benefit demand independent evidence. The first coupling is the existence of physically traceable internal references that can be challenged against electrically and temporally independent standards. The second is a source-aware drift-diagnostic process that distinguishes electronics gain, electrode-tissue transfer, tissue-like surrogate changes, changing source signals and model/feature drift, explicitly recording instances of nonidentifiability. The third is external functional requalification, which can reject an apparently successful update after hidden-domain testing, material or reference replacement, loss of selectivity, missing raw observations, or inability to reproduce the frozen predecessor. This research monograph is divided into seven causal layers and 82 chapters. Five major subsections of each chapter are assigned independent pages, yielding 410 separately paginated technical essays. Thirty gold mathematical derivations are linked from chapter-opening equations to discriminating experiments. The mathematics includes augmented state-space observability, nonlinear observation functions, source-separation Jacobians, Kalman innovations, impedance spectroscopy, covariance propagation, change-point statistics, conformal coverage, selective risk, hard-veto constrained update eligibility, reference-bridge covariance, exact rollback and cross-laboratory requalification. A displayed formula is a candidate analytical instrument with stated dimensions and assumptions, not a discovered biological law. Two hundred detailed Research Gates are preserved at the rear: 82 interrogate source identifiability, another 82 challenge independent physical and evidential hard vetoes, and 36 require third-party reconstruction of a frozen reference history. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos propose revisable architectures, beginning with the Neural Interface Calibration Passport. The Passport ties an interface's physical identity to the raw analog and digitized record, calibrated unit chain, hardware reference ancestors, model and feature checksums, reasons for changing any reference, failed updates, revoked permissions, blinded requalification and rollback. These are proposed evidence structures, not commercially validated devices. The DOI bibliography contains 18 unique external research records covering chronic intracortical signal instability, low-dimensional BCI stabilization, decoder adaptation, long-term electrode-tissue behavior, complex impedance metrology, electrochemical reference limits, neural interface materials and conformal uncertainty under covariate shift. Selected publisher and PubMed pages were consulted for source metadata. Their findings cannot establish efficacy of the new self-calibration architecture; source-specific claims and independent replication would be necessary.

summary: Overview This repository contains the two processed datasets analyzed in "Influence of land cover and shade on the thermal environments of schoolyards in Los Angeles" by Levinson et al. (in preparation). The data come from the LAUSD Cool Schoolyards experiment, a field study of how schoolyard surfaces affect surface temperature, air temperature, radiant heat, and outdoor thermal comfort at Los Angeles Unified School District (LAUSD) elementary schools. The study compares four surface types: uncoated asphalt pavement, pavement with a high-reflectance coating (coated pavement), turf, and garden. The first file holds mobile measurements taken with an instrumented cart that was moved across each schoolyard. The second holds continuous measurements from three stationary weather stations placed over different surfaces. Study sites and measurement periods Each school is identified in the data by a two-letter code: HE : Harrison Elementary School, City Terrace, Los Angeles, CA BE : Braddock Drive Elementary School and Gifted Magnet, Culver City area, Los Angeles, CA SE : Saticoy Elementary School, North Hollywood, Los Angeles, CA Mobile cart measurements were made at HE on 2025-09-06, at BE on 2025-09-07, and at SE on 2025-09-14. The weather stations were deployed at BE from 2025-09-10 13:00 to 2025-10-10 09:00 and at HE from 2025-10-10 14:00 to 2025-11-02 00:00. File 1: Transect measurements Transect measurement stats at 1 min + coded transects + open-meteo weather + shade + LSH.csv An instrumented cart was moved along a route of numbered locations ("transect points") across each schoolyard. At each point it stopped for about one minute and recorded readings every second. Each row summarizes one stop, giving the mean, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum of every measured variable. The route was traversed repeatedly in forward and reverse directions. The file includes: Identifiers: school, measurement number, transect point, a tag of the form MMM_SS_PP (measurement number, school, point), transect number, and direction. Microclimate: air temperature, relative humidity, and wind speed and direction measured about 1.5 m above the ground. Radiation and surfaces: downward solar irradiance, ground albedo (the fraction of sunlight the ground reflects), ground surface temperature, sky temperature, and mean radiant temperature (MRT, a measure of the total radiant heat a person receives). Readings from 12 radiometers are also included: six measuring sunlight and six measuring longwave (thermal) radiation, facing up, down, forward, back, left, and right. Instrument orientation and position: radiometer tilt, roll, and zenith angles, plus GPS coordinates. Surface properties: surface description and classification of each point, along with measured solar reflectance and thermal emittance. Derived quantities: solar position, local solar hour, the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI, an index of how hot conditions feel to a person) and its heat-stress category, and a shade classification for each stop. In the Classification column, the labels "Warm pavement," "Cool pavement," "Grass," and "Nature area" correspond to uncoated pavement, coated pavement, turf, and garden, respectively. File 2: Weather station time series All-schools, all-stations + differences + open-meteo weather datatable, 2026-07-17.csv This file is a continuous 1-minute time series from three stationary weather stations placed side by side over different surfaces: Station A: coated pavement Station B: uncoated pavement Station C: garden at BE, turf at HE Each station recorded air temperature, relative humidity, dew point, and ground surface temperature, along with battery voltage, solar-panel voltage, and radiation-shield fan speed. Temperatures are given both as raw values (suffix "_raw") and as values corrected through a cross-calibration of the three stations. The file also gives air and ground temperature differences between stations: B−A (uncoated minus coated pav

summary: Fisher information metric tensors for the 41 held-out SONICOM test subjects, as used in “Evaluating Spatial Discriminability Preservation in HRTF Upsampling Using Fisher Information” (D. Bassett). Code and reproduction instructions: https://github.com/domfrbassett/fisher-rao-hrtf-upsampling What the tensors are At each of the 793 directions of the SONICOM grid, the 2×2 tensor g = JᵀΣ⁻¹J describes how well the auditory cues separate that direction from its neighbours. J is the spatial Jacobian of the cues: Barumerli monaural PGE features, ILD and MaxIACCe-transformed ITD, each fitted with real spherical harmonics. Σ holds the cue noise (σ_mon = 1.25 dB, σ_ILD = 1 dB, σ_ITD = 0.569). All fields are low-pass filtered at 16 kHz before the cues are extracted. The tensor is expressed in a local tangent basis u₁ = a × r, u₂ = r × u₁, where a = z, or y when |r_z| > 0.9, and its units are d′² per rad². Contents metric_tensors.zip has one folder per subject, metric_tensors/subject_####/ , containing 25 files per subject (1,025 in total): reference_metric_tensor.mat : the dense measured HRTF. <METHOD>_N###_metric_tensor.mat : one file per reconstruction. There are six methods: SUpDEq_SH , SUpDEq_MCA , SUpDEq_NN_MCA_6dB (SUpDEq-Natural-MCA in the paper), SUpDEq_Bary_MCA_6dB , RANF and FSP_AE . Each is reconstructed from N = 100, 19, 5 and 3 retained directions. The 164 natural-neighbour and barycentric files at N = 5 and 3 have status “ not_applicable ”. The interpolation is undefined for those masks, so these files carry no tensors. Variables in each file: metricTensor : the tensors at SH order 6 [2×2×793]. familyGram : per-cue-family Gram matrices JᵀJ before noise weighting, at SH orders 4, 6 and 8 [2×2×793×3 families×3 orders]. They let you recompute the tensors with other noise values or SH orders. In reconstruction files only: crossFamilyGram : the unsymmetrised cross terms J_refᵀ J_recon, same layout as familyGram . airmByDirection : the pointwise AIRM discrepancy from the reference. Metadata: coordinates (Cartesian and azimuth/elevation in degrees), cue band, noise values (reference files only), status (“ completed ” or “ not_applicable ”) and, for not-applicable files, a message giving the reason. SHA256SUMS.txt lists a checksum for every file. Format and use The files are MATLAB v7.3 (HDF5), so MATLAB, h5py or any HDF5 reader can open them. Note that h5py reverses MATLAB’s axis order. scripts/fisher_lib.py in the repository reads them and recomputes tensors, AIRM and thresholds from the Gram matrices. To rerun the analysis scripts, unzip into results/evaluation/ so the subject folders sit in results/evaluation/metric_tensors/ . Provenance Produced with run_evaluation("tensors") from the repository above. The values are numerically identical to the tensor files behind results/evaluation/full_evaluation_summary.csv ; this run additionally stores the cross terms. The tensors are derived from the SONICOM HRTF Dataset (Engel et al., J. Audio Eng. Soc. 71(5), 2023, doi:10.17743/jaes.2022.0066). The SONICOM HRTFs are released under the MIT licence. This work develops research begun for the author’s B.Sc. dissertation at Birmingham City University.
title: Fisher information metric tensors for 'Evaluating Spatial Discriminability Preservation in HRTF Upsampling Using Fisher Information'

summary: Code, trained networks and data for the paper “Physics-informed neural networks for maximizing quantum Fisher information in time-dependent many-body systems”. The archive Zenodo_deposit.zip is self-contained. It holds the training method (a counter-diabatic control expanded in Pauli strings, with a learned schedule, propagated with a fourth-order commutator-free Magnus integrator), the trained network and configuration of every reported run, Supplementary Data 1 (source data of every figure and table), Supplementary Data 2 (pulse files), and a script that regenerates the figures, tables and reported numbers and checks them against the deposited values. Instructions are in README.md inside the archive. Version 2.0.6 re-exports the figure PDFs of the archive; the code, trained networks and data are those of version 2.0.5. Version 2.0.5 corrects the description of the QFI floor and of the stored candidates in the README so that it matches the code, redraws Supplementary Fig. 1 with a key grouped by kind of control, and adds the panels of the time-resolved QFI to Supplementary Fig. 4; the trained networks and data are those of version 2.0.4. Version 2.0.4 completes the regeneration path of the Supplementary Information: python reproduce.py baselines covers every size computed in the paper (ideal control up to twelve qubits), python reproduce.py symmetry also reports the symmetry fractions and compares the Holm-corrected p-values and partial correlations, python reproduce.py verify --exact repeats the dense validation, python reproduce.py replay retrains a paper run against its stored history, and the three runs of the propagation-cadence calibration are included (983 runs). The README documents the selection rules and step control as implemented. Supplementary Data 1 no longer lists the unreported right-limit probe rows of exact_controls.csv ; the trained networks and all other data are unchanged. Download: the archive is stored in eleven parts. Rejoin them with cat Zenodo_deposit.zip.part-* > Zenodo_deposit.zip (on Windows, copy /b Zenodo_deposit.zip.part-aa + Zenodo_deposit.zip.part-ab + ... Zenodo_deposit.zip , listing the parts in order) and check the result with shasum -a 256 -c Zenodo_deposit.zip.sha256 . License: the code is released under the MIT License, and the data, trained networks, figures and tables under CC BY 4.0. Preprint of the first version of the manuscript: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18506
title: Physics-informed neural networks for maximizing quantum Fisher information in time-dependent many-body systems

summary: QMBL: Open Problems is a record book of the state of the art in quantum many-body simulation for problems with no exact ground-state energy. Scientists and AI systems should use the shared results to build on each other's work more efficiently and advance frontier science. This snapshot holds the launch target list (targets/v1.json, 153 instances frozen from QMBL v0.4.0; 152 are open today, as one has since been solved exactly), the entry format and its checks, and the maintainer's re-measurement flow; the verifier is quantum-many-body-leaderboard/verifier.
title: QMBL: Open Problems

summary: Large audio-language models (LALMs) are fast becoming a general interface to sound, yet how far their broad pretraining carries into specialized domains remains largely open. Vessel monitoring, maritime safety, and ocean sensing all depend on recognizing underwater signals, but to our knowledge LALMs have not been systematically evaluated on them. Annotated recordings are costly to collect, and a faithful synthetic alternative has to bring together many interacting factors: the structure of detection pulses, communication waveforms, and ship-radiated noise, and the sound-speed profile, geometry, and multipath propagation through which each reaches the receiver. We address this by proposing \textbf{UA-Bench}, to our knowledge the first large-scale benchmark for evaluating LALMs on underwater acoustic signal recognition. It comprises 375,051 audio records that couple parameterized sources with modeled propagation, so that every record can be traced to the conditions that produced it. The records span these three signal families, and each carries a three-level label hierarchy (13 leaf classes), a templated multi-turn dialogue, and source and channel metadata. We evaluate on a balanced 2,600-record subset with a gated coarse-to-fine protocol that locates each error at source routing, fine-grained classification, or output format, and add a paired silent-audio control to test whether the waveform is actually used. Nine open LALMs, evaluated without task-specific adaptation, reach only 2.0\%--13.1\% leaf accuracy, against a random reference of 7.7\%. The waveform helps source routing far more than leaf recognition (for one model, +29.5 versus +2.3 points over silence), and just four models gain reliably at the leaf level, by at most 4.7 points. UA-Bench thus gives a reference point for these models, and its released training partition supports follow-up adaptation work.
title: UA-Bench: Benchmarking Large Audio-Language Models on Underwater Acoustic Recognition

summary: Adaptive modulation and coding (AMC) improves the spectral efficiency of underwater acoustic (UWA) links, but its feedback is inevitably stale: sound propagates slowly, and by the time channel state information (CSI) arrives, the fast time-varying multipath channel has moved on. Predictive link adaptation therefore needs more than a point forecast: it needs a distribution over each candidate action's consequences. We propose PRB-WM, a physics-regularized Beta world model for predictive per-subcarrier link adaptation on real time-varying UWA channels. A persistence-anchored stochastic latent-space dynamics model learns how the channel evolves; a counterfactual outcome head evaluates, for every candidate modulation and coding scheme (MCS), a Beta-binomial distribution of bit errors on shared imagined futures; and a chance-constrained receding-horizon model predictive controller maximizes expected spectral efficiency subject to a bounded probability of violating the bit error rate (BER) target. To the best of our knowledge, PRB-WM is the first world model for UWA communications. In closed-loop replay of six measured sea-trial links from the public UWA Channel Library against a 24-method pool spanning the full methodological spectrum, PRB-WM attains a mean goodput 87% above the strongest baseline, ranks first on all six time-varying links at the longest lookahead, and is the only method whose realized frame risk decreases systematically with lookahead, meeting the BER-violation contract where no baseline does. Ablations confirm that rollout sampling dispersion is essential to the chance constraint and that the physics anchor is necessary for trainability.
title: PRB-WM: Physics-Regularized Beta World Models for Predictive Link Adaptation on Real Time-Varying Underwater Acoustic Channels

summary: Companion code for the preprint "Benchmarking Real-Time DETR Detectors for Multibeam Forward-Looking Sonar: DEIMv2, Detector-Specific Test-Time Fusion, and Domain Shift Analysis on UATD" (Preprints 2026, 2026090449, doi:10.20944/preprints202609.0449.v3). Contains the DEIMv2 engine with UATD configs, the TTA/WBF fusion tooling (default --wbf-rule view-dedup; query-level retained as reproduction control), the paired image-level bootstrap CI scripts, the paper's three central results tables as CSV, and unit tests pinning the WBF view-dedup rule and the bootstrap identity property. title: AppajiDheeraj/uwan-grayhole-detection

summary: Code and data of Chapter 3 of the doctoral thesis Mathematical models to describe tumoral behaviors under treatment regimens (Graduate Program in Biometrics, Institute of Biosciences, São Paulo State University, Botucatu, 2026). The deposit covers a three-population ordinary differential equation model of cutaneous melanoma under CAR T-cell therapy with tumor-associated macrophages: its equilibria and local asymptotic stability, the Hopf bifurcation driven by the pro-tumoral action of the macrophages, a variance-based global sensitivity analysis (eFAST), the Bayesian calibration against the immunocompetent B16 data of Jilani et al. (2024), the structural identifiability analysis with StructuralIdentifiability.jl, the profile-likelihood analysis of practical identifiability, the Fisher-information comparison of experimental designs, and the computational scenarios built on the calibrated model. Each folder has a README with its structure, and REPRODUCE.md gives the command that produces each figure and table of the chapter. The MCMC chains are deposited separately because of their size.
title: Melanoma under CAR T-cell therapy with TAM-mediated immunosuppression: model analysis, Bayesian calibration and identifiability (code and data)

summary: Pareto Support Proofs is the computational companion to “Sparse exact certificates for weighted-sum unsupportedness in finite multi-objective optimisation”. This R1 distribution, OPTL-R1-20261017, contains the corrected engine 0.6.2, the preserved standalone checker 0.6.1 and reproduction layer AC3-candidate.1. The new controlled run is AC3_REPAIRED_20261017_01. Historical engine 0.6.1, R1_01 results and their provenance remain separately preserved. The companion provides exact certificate generation, generator-independent checking, JSON schemas, instances, certificates, raw observations, source manifests, figure sources and editable ODG files. Negative certificates are checked by exact arithmetic on recorded feasible decisions. Positive objects distinguish full P1 verification from the explicitly retained trusted-oracle P2 boundary. The retained study contains 225 objects: 190 correctness, 27 scaling and eight timing-case objects. Of these, 213 are fully verified at P1 and 12 positive binary-linear objects remain conditional P2. Separately implemented checks reproduce the 190 classifications and the arithmetic of all 102 negative objects. The 225 mathematical certificate payloads match the historical R1_01 payloads. All 225 historical trace files are preserved byte-for-byte; new provenance identifies the corrected run. The historical R1_01 timing batch has eight cases, 240 measurements and 24 warmups. The corrected shortest-path timing batch has three cases, 90 measurements and nine warmups. They are reported separately, including the supportable three-objective case in which checking has the higher median. The historical runner-hash gap remains disclosed. These records do not constitute formal software verification or independent human review. Source code is licensed under BSD-3-Clause. Data, instances, certificates, results, figures and prose documentation are licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0). The component boundaries and retained historical licences are documented inside the companion. AI-assisted preparation and validation are disclosed in the associated manuscript and supporting documentation; Antonio Clim remains responsible for the content. The four deposited files are ESM_1_Pareto_Support_Proofs_R1.zip, Fig1_Editable_Sources_R1.zip, PUBLIC_RELEASE_CONTEXT.md and SHA256SUMS.txt. They match the four named assets of the corresponding GitHub release. The ESM file is the journal's Online Resource 1; automatic GitHub source-code archives are different files. Repository: https://github.com/antonioclim/pareto-support-proofs GitHub release: https://github.com/antonioclim/pareto-support-proofs/releases/tag/optl-r1-20261017 Historical software version 0.6.1 DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20832039
title: Pareto Support Proofs: repaired R1 controlled-reproduction companion

summary: Version 3 is an organisational change only: the four subsections of the verification section are reordered so that the two Krook levels, the amplitude equation and the Vlasov solver, precede the two with diffusion and drag, the amplitude equation with diffusion and drag and the Vlasov solver with the Fokker–Planck operator. No text, number, figure or table is changed from version 2, and the description below is version 2’s. Version 2 of this paper adds a related-work section placing the work against the analytic quasi-steady theory of Lestz and Duarte (2021), the regime maps of Zhang et al. (2026) and the steady-or-chirping criterion of Duarte et al. (2017, 2018); places the near-marginal comparison against Lestz and Duarte's two validity constraints and withdraws version 1's reading of the 24 percent gap, which is now a candidate explanation and not an established one; relabels the drag ratio of the ITER-like slice as the collisional ratio of Lilley et al. and places the turbulence-corrected ITER ratio, an order of magnitude smaller, between the two steady slices tested; states the comparison with the cold-background regime map at the point where the reduced model fails; narrows three statements of version 1 to what was tested; and adds the experiments version 1 left open, a reverse ramp pair at the first operating point and the edge and a benchmark pair at a second operating point. An erratum corrects a sentence of version 1's Limits section that had the two near-threshold amplitudes reversed: the held level of the full- f solver is 24 percent above the cubic equation's steady state, not the other way round. The paper builds and verifies a two-level reduced model of a fast-ion-driven mode, the Berk–Breizman bump-on-tail problem, as a plant whose purpose is to locate and characterise the regime in which the mode saturates to a steady state, the regime a fusion power plant must stay in. Level 0 is the near-threshold cubic amplitude equation with Krook, diffusive and drag collisions; Level 1 is a full- f one-dimensional Vlasov solver with a Krook operator; Level 2 adds drag and diffusion acting on the departure from the initial distribution. Each level was verified against the literature before its results were used: the amplitude equation reproduces the critical Krook rate 4.4 and the critical diffusion rate 2.05; the Vlasov solver reproduces the linear growth rate and frequency to 0.01 percent, conserves energy to second order, and reproduces the Berk–Breizman saturation law within 4 percent across the steady region and the diffusive saturation formula within 4 to 7 percent away from marginal stability. For the warm distribution used, the external damping on the field is only 87 percent effective as an amplitude damping, so marginal stability lies at a damping of 1.15 times the collisionless drive rather than 1.0; with that correction the full- f solver agrees with the cubic equation on the steady side of the bifurcation near threshold, and saturates 24 percent above it at a finite distance from marginal stability, in the direction and of the size that other simulations have reported against the same theory. The steady region is mapped in the damping–collision plane: with Krook collisions the oscillating region is a tongue at collision rates below 0.3 to 0.4 of the drive, closed above it; with diffusion equal to the drive, with or without drag at 0.7 of diffusion, every damping from 0.1 to 0.9 of the drive is steady, one point still rising at the end of its run; with drag at 1.2 of diffusion no steady point was found, and at the strongest drives the reduced model leaves its validity where a cold-background resonant model saturates steadily. The edge of the steady region along the collision axis lies between diffusion rates of 0.4 and 0.5 of the drive at a damping of 0.5 of the drive, converged on two velocity grids, and within the same bracket at a damping of 0.3, where every steady level is 1.41
title: A reduced bump-on-tail plant for the steady operating region of a fast-ion-driven mode: amplitude equation, full-f Vlasov solver with Fokker-Planck collisions, regime map and a detection benchmark

summary: This document contains supplemental material of the paper " Global Minima of the Thomson Problem in a Disk: A Molecular Dynamics Approach with Fixed Border Charges ", where the Thomson problem in a disk has been studied. Here we report the lowest minima for the configurations with N = 54 , 60 , 61 , 65 , 66 , 82 , 83 , 85 , 88 , 89 , 90 , 91 , 92 , 97 , 99 , 100 , 101 , 102 , 103 , 104 , 105 , 111 , 113 , 117 , 119 , 133 , 137 , 141 , 149 , 150 , 151 , 153 , 155 , 187 , 286 , and 318 confined particles, obtained by the Quenched Molecular Dynamics (QMD) method. The energy of these configurations is lower than that of the configurations reported by Amore and Zarate ([ Phys. Rev. E. 108 , 055302 (2023) ]; see the supplemental material in Ref. [ 10.5281/zenodo.8301044 ]). For systems with N = 92 , 100 , 102 , 113 , and 133 particles, in contrast to the asymmetric Voronoi diagrams obtained by previous optimization algorithms, our solutions exhibit a clear D1 (axial) symmetry of defects. For a system with N = 286 particles, in contrast to the asymmetric Voronoi diagrams obtained by previous optimization algorithms, our solution exhibits a clear C2  (central inversion) symmetry of defects. However, for a system with N = 150  particles, the lower energy configuration results in a reduction in the symmetry of the defects. Voronoi diagrams are displayed for the 26 configurations that exhibit structural or orientational changes in the defect pattern compared to Ref. [ 10.5281/zenodo.8301044 ], whereas for the remaining 10 systems (with N = 61 , 83 , 85 , 89 , 90 , 91 ,  97 , 99 , 119 , and 137 particles) QMD method refines the equilibrium coordinates and lowers the energy within the same Voronoi topology.
title: Global Minima of the Thomson Problem in a Disk: A Molecular Dynamics Approach with Fixed Border Charges. Supplemental Material

summary: Subclonal reconstruction results produced with CliPP 1.4 for three datasets: 5,424 tumors from TCGA, 2,008 whole-genome tumors from PCAWG, and CliPPSim4k, a cohort of 4,000 simulated tumors with known ground truth. Also deposited are 13,960 TCGA driver mutations annotated with clonality, and the cancer type and tumor purity of every sample in the two real cohorts. These are the files served for download by CliPP-on-Web (https://bioinformatics.mdanderson.org/apps/CliPP/), the web interface to CliPP (https://github.com/wwylab/CliPP). The deposit accompanies manuscript submission and is the stable version as of 16 October 2026. Yujie Jiang and Matthew D. Montierth contributed equally to this work. Wenyi Wang is the corresponding author. README.md describes each archive's layout and the columns of every file.
title: Scalable subclonal reconstruction of cancer cells in DNA sequencing data using a penalized likelihood model

summary: We study the fine phase-space spectral asymptotics of a model class of infinite-order pseudodifferential operators whose symbols grow like exp(c|ξ|^2), c > 0. The leading Weyl law for such operators is known, but the complete logarithmic structure of the heat trace, the singularity structure of the associated zeta function, and the correct notion of a renormalized determinant require a more delicate analysis. We prove that, in dimension four, the reduced heat trace admits the complete asymptotic expansion τ(t) = A L^2 + B L log L + C L + D (log L)^2 + E log L + F + O(1/L), where L = log(1/t), and all coefficients A, B, C, D, E, F are computed explicitly. Consequently, the model zeta function has the structure ζ(s) = α_2 s^(-2) + α_1 (log s)/s + β_1 s^(-1) + γ_2 (log s)^2 + γ_1 log s + ζ_0 + O(s log s) as s → 0^+, with all displayed coefficients determined explicitly. Because the remainder generally produces terms of the form s log s in the renormalized zeta function, the classical derivative ζ'_ren(0) is not automatically finite. We therefore introduce a finite-part renormalized determinant, defined through the constant term in the derivative expansion, and prove its existence under the full asymptotic hierarchy of the heat trace. We also show that in odd dimensions the zeta function possesses algebraic branch points rather than poles, and we explain why the classical zeta determinant construction must be modified. Finally, we recover the growth exponent α from the counting function in the model a(ξ) ∼ exp(c|ξ|^α), and we compare the results with the theories of Pilipović–Prangoski–Vindas, Gilkey–Grubb, Kontsevich–Vishik, and Nicola–Rodino.
title: Fine Structure of Spectral Asymptotics for Infinite-Order Pseudodifferential Operators with Second-Order Exponential Growth

summary: Background. Antireflux fundoplication failure — recurrent reflux, dysphagia, gas-bloat syndrome, secondary to a herniated, slipped, too-tight, disrupted, or twisted valve — remains common, and its endoscopic diagnosis lacks a common, standardized reporting language. Aim. To narratively review existing endoscopic instruments for postoperative antireflux valve assessment, the evidence on their interobserver reliability, and to position an original instrument — the Endoscopic Fundoplication Score (SEF) — within this landscape. Methods. Narrative review, with a targeted search in PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar (last search: 24 September 2026) using the terms “fundoplication,” “endoscopic grading,” “gastroesophageal valve,” “Hill classification,” “antireflux surgery outcome,” “interobserver reliability,” “wrap integrity,” and “hiatal hernia recurrence,” covering literature published between 1996 and 2026 in English or with an English abstract, supplemented by reference-list screening of identified articles. Results. Three major endoscopic instruments were identified — the Hill classification (1996), the Jobe system (2004), and the American Foregut Society (AFS) nomenclature (2025) — alongside a descriptive, non-scored taxonomy of failure types (herniated, slipped, tight, disrupted, twisted). The interobserver reliability studies [1,2] identified in this review for the postoperative setting report low agreement, and a retrospective comparison of endoscopy reports [3] documented major discrepancies between external endoscopists and operating surgeons. The AFS classification of esophagogastric junction integrity achieved substantial agreement on static images (κ=0.65) but only fair agreement under dynamic conditions (κ=0.371), and the postoperative AFS nomenclature has not yet been tested for interobserver reliability. The SEF score, an 11-item composite instrument (0–16 points) applied to a cohort of 178 patients, correlated in preliminary single-centre data with the Hill classification, Los Angeles (LA) esophagitis grade, and the Visick patient-satisfaction score (own data, manuscript submitted for publication), offering a numeric, quantifiable alternative to existing categorical systems. The SEF threshold of ≤10 points, defined in the same cohort, is exploratory. Conclusions. The field of postoperative endoscopic antireflux valve assessment remains fragmented, without an interobserver-reliable consensus standard. The SEF score partially addresses this gap through a numeric structure, with experience-based weights and an exploratory threshold, but requires formal interobserver reliability testing and multicenter validation against the surgical gold standard.
title: ENDOSCOPIC EVALUATION OF THE ANTIREFLUX VALVE AFTER FUNDOPLICATION: SYNTHESIS OF THE EVIDENCE AND PROPOSAL OF A FUNCTIONAL ENDOSCOPIC SCORE

summary: Background. Antireflux fundoplication failure — recurrent reflux, dysphagia, gas-bloat syndrome, secondary to a herniated, slipped, too-tight, disrupted, or twisted valve — remains common, and its endoscopic diagnosis lacks a common, standardized reporting language. Aim. To narratively review existing endoscopic instruments for postoperative antireflux valve assessment, the evidence on their interobserver reliability, and to position an original instrument — the Endoscopic Fundoplication Score (SEF) — within this landscape. Methods. Narrative review, with a targeted search in PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar (last search: 24 September 2026) using the terms “fundoplication,” “endoscopic grading,” “gastroesophageal valve,” “Hill classification,” “antireflux surgery outcome,” “interobserver reliability,” “wrap integrity,” and “hiatal hernia recurrence,” covering literature published between 1996 and 2026 in English or with an English abstract, supplemented by reference-list screening of identified articles. Results. Three major endoscopic instruments were identified — the Hill classification (1996), the Jobe system (2004), and the American Foregut Society (AFS) nomenclature (2025) — alongside a descriptive, non-scored taxonomy of failure types (herniated, slipped, tight, disrupted, twisted). The interobserver reliability studies [1,2] identified in this review for the postoperative setting report low agreement, and a retrospective comparison of endoscopy reports [3] documented major discrepancies between external endoscopists and operating surgeons. The AFS classification of esophagogastric junction integrity achieved substantial agreement on static images (κ=0.65) but only fair agreement under dynamic conditions (κ=0.371), and the postoperative AFS nomenclature has not yet been tested for interobserver reliability. The SEF score, an 11-item composite instrument (0–16 points) applied to a cohort of 178 patients, correlated in preliminary single-centre data with the Hill classification, Los Angeles (LA) esophagitis grade, and the Visick patient-satisfaction score (own data, manuscript submitted for publication), offering a numeric, quantifiable alternative to existing categorical systems. The SEF threshold of ≤10 points, defined in the same cohort, is exploratory. Conclusions. The field of postoperative endoscopic antireflux valve assessment remains fragmented, without an interobserver-reliable consensus standard. The SEF score partially addresses this gap through a numeric structure, with experience-based weights and an exploratory threshold, but requires formal interobserver reliability testing and multicenter validation against the surgical gold standard.
