summary: Four-dimensional beam-matrix reconstruction from quadrupole scans is the standard way to mea- sure cross-plane coupling and the intrinsic emittances that a decoupling section can recover. We show that a scan of a single thin quadrupole, normal or skew and placed anywhere in a linear lattice, determines at most nine of the ten beam-matrix parameters for any number of settings, because each measured second moment is quadratic in the quadrupole strength. The unmeasured direction lies in the x–y cross block and has a closed form in terms of the transfer matrices; for a quadrupole followed by a drift of length L its nonzero entries are Wxpy = Wpxy = 1 and Wpxpy = −2/L. Both projected emittances are therefore measured, but the beam matrices consistent with the data form a line segment along which the smaller intrinsic emittance ranges from zero to slightly above its true value, so a single-knob scan gives only an upper bound on it. A thick quadrupole restores the miss- ing direction only weakly, its singular value scaling approximately as the sixth power of the magnet length. Scanning two independently powered quadrupoles of any type makes the reconstruction well posed without additional hardware.
title: Single-knob quadrupole scans do not determine the intrinsic emittances

summary: Description This dataset accompanies a comparative evolutionary-genomics study of ancestral cytosine substitution patterns across human, chimpanzee, bonobo and gorilla lineages. Using hg38-centered UCSC multiz primate alignments and a seven-species phylogenetic framework, we reconstructed ancestral nucleotide states and quantified cytosine substitutions across all 22 human autosomes. The analysis examined CG, CHG and CHH sequence contexts, 256 strand-canonicalized ancestral 5-mer motifs, and lineage-specific substitution patterns. The deposited files include: Chromosome-level ancestral-site datasets at a minimum ancestral-state posterior probability of 0.95. Chromosome-specific 5-mer substitution summaries and quality-control records. Genome-wide cytosine substitution frequencies and context-enrichment ratios. Chromosome-bootstrap uncertainty estimates and cross-lineage motif comparisons. Statistical analyses of lineage-specific motif deviations, including simultaneous confidence intervals. Leave-one-autosome-out predictive comparisons of ancestral 3-mer and 5-mer sequence context. Frozen methodology documentation, validation records, checksums and the fixed seven-species phylogenetic tree. The dataset supports independent examination and downstream reanalysis of the reported numerical findings. Data provenance: UCSC Genome Browser hg38-centered 30-primate multiz alignments, restricted to seven primate species. Computational methods: IQ-TREE 2.3.6 ancestral-state reconstruction under GTR+F+G4, followed by custom Python-based sequence-context and statistical analyses. Limitations: The archive contains processed ancestral-site data and numerical outputs, not the original complete multiple-sequence alignments. It does not contain ancestral DNA methylation measurements, direct estimates of net CpG gain or loss, or calibrated mutation rates. Associated code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23425960 Archive organization: This dataset is distributed across two Zenodo records. This record contains Part 1 of 2. Part 2 is available at https://zenodo.org/records/23442145 . Both parts are required to reconstruct the complete archive. Download all files from both records and follow the instructions in RECONSTRUCTION.txt to assemble and verify the dataset.
title: Ancestral Cytosine Sequence-Context Substitution Data Across Four Hominid Lineages: A 22-Autosome Comparative Analysis. Part 1

summary: The rapid expansion of the gig economy, facilitated by digital talent platforms, has fundamentally reconfigured the nature of work, employment relationships, and organizational structures. This paradigm shift from stable, long-term employment to a fluid workforce of contractors, freelancers, and project-based talent presents profound challenges to conventional leadership theories and practices. Traditional models, predicated on hierarchical authority, stable organizational boundaries, and enduring psychological contracts, are proving increasingly inadequate for orchestrating a workforce characterized by autonomy, transience, and distributed networks. This paper conducts a critical review of existing leadership literature—including transformational, adaptive, and emerging platform leadership theories—assessing their applicability and limitations in the gig context. Synthesizing insights from organizational behavior, strategic management, and technology studies, we propose a novel integrated framework: the Fluid Leadership Ecosystem (FLE) Model. The FLE model conceptualizes leadership not as a function of individual authority but as the cultivation of a dynamic ecosystem across three core dimensions: Relational Architecture, Algorithmic Stewardship, and Capability Cultivation. We argue that effective leadership in this new era requires designing trust-enabling infrastructures, ensuring human-centric governance of management algorithms, and fostering portable skill development for a transient workforce. This paper introduces novel theoretical perspectives, including temporal leadership dynamics, polycontextual leadership challenges, and the concept of reverse leadership flows from workers to platforms. By presenting a comprehensive model supported by data visualizations and identifying avenues for empirical validation, this research offers a forward-looking agenda for both scholars and practitioners navigating the complexities of leadership in the 21st-century workforce.
title: The Gig Economy and Talent Platforms: New Models of Leadership for Managing a Fluid Workforce

summary: LONGITUDINAL DEVICE MIGRATION AND MEANING CONTINUITY AT THE LIMIT Device Replacement × Model Bridging × Control Semantics STARLI RESEARCH WORKS | INSTITUTE XXIV | FLAGSHIP 24 Feng Cheng-en 33 × Starli Research Works This research monograph investigates a deceptively difficult question in long-term brain–computer interfaces: when sensors, acquisition electronics, firmware, electrode geometry, or decoding models change, what would justify the claim that a user's task-grounded control meaning has been preserved? Numerical signal alignment alone cannot establish continuity of intention. Two systems may encode different signals while supporting the same functional command, or produce nearly identical latent representations while mapping to incompatible actions. The volume formulates meaning continuity as a conditional, falsifiable engineering and scientific hypothesis. It connects device-specific observation models, neural recording instability, task and action ontologies, paired old/new sensing periods, latent manifold bridging, longitudinal recalibration, calibrated abstention, functional validation, and an accessible right to reject the proposed migration. Its central commitment is that no amount of predictive accuracy can compensate for invalid authorization, an unverified physical reference, or loss of independent control. The research atlas comprises thirty connected mathematical derivations, eighty-two research chapters, and 410 independently paginated chapter sections that examine observables, inverse explanations, discriminating experiments, uncertainty and noncompensable safeguards, and independent requalification. Two hundred detailed Research Gates propose future falsification and handoff programs, while thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos preserve revisable candidate approaches rather than immutable conclusions. A claim-scoped DOI evidence ledger connects the study to published work on neural recording drift, decoder adaptation, manifold alignment, longitudinal neural interfaces, speech BCIs, user preferences, and neurotechnology ethics. The book is designed for both human researchers and future AI research systems. Its formulas, chapter cross-links, DOI anchors, competing models, negative-result requirements, and successor-focused research cards provide structured entry points for independent reconstruction and informed disagreement. The visual presentation combines ivory pages, navy and teal typography, and large gold mathematical plates, while mathematical expressions are also recorded in searchable source notation and a separate Excel reference index. This is a prospective, nonclinical research architecture. It does not report new patient experiments, demonstrate safe autonomous human neurovascular microrobots, establish a universal device-migration system, or claim continuity of private thoughts, consciousness, or personal identity. Scientific benefit remains conditional on explicit task definitions, qualified device evidence, legitimate permissions, external validation, and the successor's freedom to reject a failed bridge. Research question: What should remain invariant when an interface changes, and who has the authority to say that its meaning has changed?

summary: Version 2.0 is a substantive revision of version 1.0 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19174862). It supersedes the earlier procedural interpretation and its exclusion of competing explanations. The revised title is Structural Organization and Interpretive Limits of the Phaistos Disc. Reproduced descriptive findings are retained; failed model comparisons and photographic uncertainties are reported explicitly. The earlier version remains available through the record version history. We examine whether reproducible structural observations on the Phaistos Disc support a procedural interpretation. A pinned numerical transcription contains 242 main-sign positions, including one unreadable position, 45 readable sign types, 61 divider-defined groups and 18 supplementary stroke annotations. Source review reconciles counting and numbering conventions while retaining unresolved photographic uncertainty. The 02-to-12 side contrast persists after exact-family collapse. Adding side to a fixed position-only pairing predictor improves held-family loss by 0.082738 nats, but its exact conditional tail of 0.075 fails the frozen support rule. A positional mixture fails to outperform a bigram baseline. A separate directional test of the proposed 07-to-27 recovery relationship fails, with a one-sided permutation tail of 0.884. Supplementary-stroke comparisons have insufficient controlled overlap for the specified exact test. The work documents organization and constrains specific interpretations without establishing procedural functions or phonetic values. Corpus, code, protocols, full results and uncertainty ledgers accompany the paper.
title: Structural Organization and Interpretive Limits of the Phaistos Disc

summary: Large language models often penalize multilingual users through hidden 'tokenizer taxes' caused by subword fragmentation. Geographic proper nouns offer a controlled stress case for this distributional asymmetry, as they are standardized, cross-linguistically available entities whose orthographic forms frequently mismatch tokenizer training distributions. We introduce the Cross-Linguistic Orthographic Uniqueness Score (CLOUS), a character-level metric based on Shannon surprisal that quantifies the orthographic rarity of localized country names. We evaluate CLOUS on a controlled corpus of 249 ISO-registered country names; generalization to other geographic entity types remains future work. We evaluate CLOUS against tokenization fertility for six production tokenizers spanning three algorithm families across eleven languages and seven script families. Using Spearman rank correlation with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, CLOUS shows significant associative strength with fertility in 61 of 65 valid language-tokenizer combinations. As a screening tool for high-fragmentation entities, CLOUS achieves ROC-AUC = 0.850 and F1 = 0.740, correctly identifying approximately three-quarters of the highest-fragmentation entities from orthographic properties alone. We further show that CLOUS correlates with fertility more strongly than length-based baselines across all evaluated scripts, and outperforms a character bigram surprisal model in 69.2% of tested combinations, particularly for logographic, syllabic, and Latin scripts. Conversely, the bigram baseline proves superior for morphophonologically complex scripts like Arabic and Devanagari, indicating that tokenizer fragmentation is driven by local orthographic context in some scripts and absolute character rarity in others. Script family appears to be the primary driver of CLOUS-fertility correlation strength, with effect sizes ranging from modest for Latin-script languages ) to large for non-Latin scripts (   up to 0.686 for Japanese). These findings suggest that CLOUS may be useful as a lightweight pre-tokenization diagnostic for multilingual NLP pipelines.
title: Estimating Cross-Lingual Tokenization Fragmentation Risk: A Frequency-Based Uniqueness Score for Geographic Entities

summary: The Voynich Manuscript exhibits strong statistical regularities, but the distinction between recoverable grammar and recoverable lexical meaning remains unresolved. This study asks how far a progressively frozen, cross-validated analysis can reconstruct the manuscript’s internal word-building system without assigning meanings from illustrations, candidate languages, or post-hoc English paraphrase. Using canonical transcription, protected holdout partitions, alternate-transcription replication, exact host substitutions, and adversarial stopping rules, the analysis recovers a cumulative left-edge morphology, a transferable inventory of 39 surface CORE-0 stem/bodies, reproducible host-by-right-state coupling, a stable K/T referential contrast, and a directed network among powered lexical cores. The 39-core inventory predicts protected-frame combinatorics and content-blind contextual fingerprints out of sample, while attempts to decompose these bodies into a deeper transferable root layer fail. Nine recurring hosts show strongly replicated coupling to EY/EEY/EDY right-edge states, supporting a distributed morphological paradigm rather than independent left- and right-side systems. A 28-node directed CORE network also replicates across canonical calibration, untouched Holdout, and alternate-transcription tests, yielding neutral outbound- and inbound-biased stem classes without requiring part-of-speech or semantic assignments. On the project’s fully constrained 1,609-line benchmark, 12,299 of 12,495 positions are role-naturalizable (98.4314%), leaving 196 opaque positions. This percentage is explicitly a conditional benchmark-maturity statistic, not a measure of literal plaintext recovery or manuscript-wide translation accuracy. Repeated attempts to cross from structural organization to ordinary lexical meaning—including deeper-root induction, topic clustering, functional-neighborhood anchoring, local lexical syntax, illustration matching, source-language fitting, and prospective semantic transfer—fail the project’s promotion criteria. The resulting contribution is therefore a structural decipherment rather than a lexical one: a reproducible grammatical and morphological architecture together with an empirically identified lexical-identifiability ceiling. The work extends, but is distinct from, the earlier controlled-translation release at DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22049207.
title: Structural Decipherment Without Lexical Recovery: A Cross-Validated Morphological Analysis of the Voynich Manuscript

summary: Dataset supporting the article "Who Benefits from Immersion? Prior 3D Experience, User Experience, and Human-Centered Personalization in the Metaverse" (submitted to the International Journal of Human–Computer Interaction). Design. Mixed factorial 3 × 2 × 2 experiment with 519 participants. Between-subjects factors: experimental profile (virtual team leadership, digital marketing, innovation and entrepreneurship) and condition (traditional format vs. immersive multiuser metaverse environment). Within-subjects factor: measurement time (pre-test, post-test). Data were collected in the first semester of 2026 during undergraduate classes at a Brazilian university. Participation was voluntary, with informed consent; no personally identifying information was retained. Contents. One Excel workbook with two sheets: a long-format sheet (1,038 rows = 519 participants × 2 measurement times) and a wide-format sheet (519 rows, pre-test and post-test variables side by side). Variables include participant and cell identifiers, demographic and technological-background items, single items and composite scores for the metaverse-experience constructs (presence, experience fluidity/seamlessness, interoperability, real-time concurrency, economic flow), the technology-adoption constructs (intention to participate, perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, perceived value), baseline enjoyment, and procedural indicators. Item labels are in Portuguese; seven-point Likert scales. Participant identifiers are anonymous codes assigned by the researchers. Access. Files are restricted because participants consented to the use of their responses for academic and scientific purposes without individual identification. Access is granted for research purposes upon reasonable request to the corresponding author (luis.hernan@usp.br).
title: Who Benefits from Immersion? Experimental dataset on immersive versus traditional task formats in organizational metaverse environments (N = 519)

title: Quantitative robust estimation for Gaussian inverse problems

summary: Who supplies, controls and sustains the services needed to inspect and continue AI-assisted research? This article approaches that question through institutional economics and an evolutionary analogy grounded in market competition. It compares targeted evidence with maintained support against fuller research histories with curated access and support. Three activities organize the comparison: scrutiny of a specified claim, reprocessing retained material under a new question, and continuation of unfinished inquiry. A worked access-review example identifies the rights, expertise, labour and resources required, including conditions under which targeted provision is preferable. Market competition supplies the foundational analogy for evolutionary pressure. Repeated decisions about submissions, paid services, funding and volunteer labour can change which research capabilities remain available and which practices spread. Because competing venues can share infrastructure, institutions and their supporting facilities may follow different paths. The article distinguishes internal revision, transmission and differential support, and separates institutional persistence from scientific validity. JOSS and Rainfall Rescue illustrate particular activities and relationships without establishing the comparative benefits of fuller AI histories. The analysis also addresses selective recording, behaviour under scrutiny, unequal burdens and self-selection. Its contribution connects institutional design to the continuing work and support needed to make research records usable.
title: AI Research and the Evolution of Scholarly Institutions

summary: Data and analytical software for thermally activated Fe-SMA fibre-reinforced concrete This repository accompanies the article “Analytical modelling of thermally activated iron-based shape memory alloy fibre concrete: Finite transfer and capacity compatibility”. It provides the numerical source data, analytical implementation, calibration inputs, and results used to prepare the final article. The work examines finite fibre–matrix transfer, thermally activated composite response, cohesive-law identification, and the compatibility of reported strengths with uncertain fibre orientation and tensile capacity. The deposit contains one final analysis snapshot. It includes the reference formulation and the baselines, thermal alternatives, and cohesive-law candidates examined in the article. These are parts of the reported scientific assessment, rather than separate manuscript versions. Superseded model results, development archives, manuscript drafts, and unrelated source files are excluded. Contents • data/ contains numerical representations of published response curves, reported group statistics, study metadata, fixed constituent and pullout calibrations, optimizer initialization values, and published experimental/finite-element comparison curves. Curve identifiers preserve the link to the source study and figure. These are processed publication-based data, rather than original instrument records. • model/ contains the executable analysis scripts. summary: This repository provides the official reproduction software, numerical simulation datasets, and empirical input fixtures for the manuscript: Song, X., Xu, H., & Bai, Y. (2026). Width Oscillations Regulate Event-Driven Bank Collapse and Point-Bar Growth in Transitional Meanders. Journal of Geophysical Research: Earth Surface. ( Under Review ) ABSTRACT Alluvial meanders dynamically adjust their planform and channel geometry, yet classical meander theory assumes a spatially uniform, constant channel width and continuous bank retreat, failing to capture episodic bank collapse and non-uniform width adjustments in transitional meandering rivers. Situated along the geomorphic continuum between single-thread and wandering streams, transitional meanders exhibit pronounced spatial width variations that break cross-sectional symmetry. Here, we develop a physically closed, reduced-complexity morphodynamic framework coupling a three-parameter asymptotic expansion of the three-dimensional Reynolds-averaged flow equations, continuous basal toe scour with transient pore-water suction, threshold-governed cantilever limit equilibrium, and a mass-conserving sediment partition driving inner point-bar progradation. The formulation demonstrates that the spatial phase relationship between channel width oscillations and centerline curvature steers the spatial displacement of outer-bank shear stress hotspots: channel constriction upstream of the bend apex amplifies cutbank shear stress, whereas channel expansion decelerates flow and promotes point-bar accretion. Discrete slump-block deposits provide self-adaptive hydraulic shielding that stabilizes the toe and regulates decadal channel relaxation. Hindcasting the 40-year morphodynamic evolution of the transitional Powder River, Montana, across 34 monumented cross sections reproduces post-flood channel widening and subsequent multi-decadal recovery narrowing across 228 discrete collapse events, while in the limit of uniform width the model recovers classical constant-width meander theory with first-order convergence along the meandering Juruá River. Global parameter sweeps quantitatively encompass observed erosion-to-accretion balance ratios across 84 worldwide natural rivers, providing a multiscale morphodynamic framework that links event-scale geotechnical failure to multi-decadal width evolution in alluvial channels. ARCHIVE CONTENTS - src/: Python source code implementing the three-parameter asymptotic hydrodynamic solver, local generalized Orr-Sommerfeld and Squire spectral eigenvalue stability diagnostics, two-stage geotechnical bank failure engine with slump-block hydraulic shielding, and Exner point-bar morphodynamic progradation coupler. - data/: Processed empirical input fixtures, including the 40-year Powder River cross-sectional monitoring dataset (powder_river.json) and the Juruá-A remote sensing centerline profile (Jurua-A_mask1_link_sBCMn_flat.npz). - results/simulations/: Pre-computed numerical simulation output arrays (.npz) enabling instant reproduction of Figures 2–9 without re-running intensive multi-hour sweeps. - figures/: Standalone publication figure plotting scripts (plot_fig1.py through plot_fig9.py) and AGU-style formatting utilities (figure_utils.py). - run_all_reproductions.py: Master execution script that automatically reproduces all nine publication figures in vector PDF format in under two minutes. HOW TO REPRODUCE ALL FIGURES 1. Unzip zenodo_release.zip and navigate into the archive root directory. 2. Ensure the required Python environment is activated:    - Python 3.13    - NumPy 2.3.2    - SciPy 1.17.1    - Matplotlib 3.10.8 3. Run the master reproduction script:    python run_all_reproductions.py 4. All nine publication figures will be generated and verified in figures/output/. summary: Decentralized multi-robot shape formation in GPS-denied environments is important for search-and-rescue and disaster response. Conventional consensus-based formation controllers can violate safe separation, oscillate, or stall when communication degrades, sensors are noisy, or an agent drops out. This paper proposes a resilient decentralized controller that combines Huber-weighted consensus and Exponential Moving Average (EMA) state estimation with a Dual-Layer Artificial Potential Field (APF) safety barrier. The first layer adds an anti-symmetric lateral deflection to resolve head-on encounters between peers; the second applies a normal-plus-tangential circulation field around static obstacles. The framework is evaluated on five simulated nonholonomic differential-drive robots in Gazebo Harmonic (ROS 2 Jazzy). Three runs are compared: a linear consensus baseline, the same baseline under faults (15% packet loss, 50-150 ms delay, σ = 0.18 m sensor noise, and a mid-run agent blackout), and the proposed controller under the same faults. The fault-free baseline reached the pentagon fastest (0.0156 m final RMS error) but its minimum separation fell to 0.3918 m, with 31 logged violations of the 0.50 m margin. Under faults the baseline reached 0.0546 m with 5 violations (minimum 0.4833 m). The proposed controller recorded no violations, kept a minimum separation of 0.6757 m, and reached 0.0368 m final error, at the cost of slower convergence (about 21 s versus about 12-15 s). Results are from single simulation runs, and the safety barrier is empirical rather than formally guaranteed.
title: Resilient Decentralized Shape Formation of Multi-Robot Swarms Under Adversarial Real-World Faults in High-Complexity Disaster Environments

summary: Added fit_xy(model, x, y, theta0, sigmas, x_sigmas, max_iter=200, tol=1e-12) : the fit when the settings have error bars too (errors in variables), for any Model whose prediction for a measurement depends only on its own settings. It minimizes the sum of squared reading residuals and squared setting adjustments, each in units of its error bar, over the parameters and the true settings (Levenberg-Marquardt on the joint problem, with the settings eliminated by a Schur complement at each step). x_sigmas is one number, one per measurement, or an (n, d) array; 0 marks an exact setting. Returns a FitResult with the first-order covariance (with the settings eliminated, the inverse of sum a_i a_i^T / (sigma_y,i^2 + sum_k s_ik^2 sigma_x,ik^2) ), chi2 for n - p degrees of freedom, and the fitted true settings in the new field FitResult.x_adjusted . For a straight line it is the line of D. York et al., "Unified equations for the slope, intercept, and standard errors of the best straight line", Am. J. Phys. 72, 367-375 (2004), doi:10.1119/1.1632486. On Pearson's data with York's weights (C. A. Cantrell, Atmos. Chem. Phys. 8, 5477-5487 (2008), Table 1) it gives intercept 5.47991 +/- 0.29497 and slope -0.48053 +/- 0.05799, chi2 = 11.87 for 8 degrees of freedom. The slope and intercept are the values of the "Williamson-York" row of Cantrell's Table 2; the error bars and chi2 agree with York's equations and with the output of the R package bfsl. Refuses a fit without sigmas , x_sigmas of the wrong shape or negative, and a model whose prediction for one measurement depends on the settings of another. inverse_predict(..., full_cov=False) : only the error bars, no covariance between readings, so memory grows with the number of readings and not with its square (10000 readings took 0.49 s). audit_record of a fit_xy result has the key fit_method and report_text prints it; the data digest then also covers x_sigmas . Records of fit are unchanged. Tutorial examples/tutorial_errors_in_both.py and README example 15 (see Tutorials below). Fixed The conformal rank k = ceil((n + 1)(1 - alpha)) (used by conformal_quantile and coverage_exact ) was one too small for some alphas at large n . Any product within 1e-9 (relative) above an integer was taken to be that integer, and for large n that swallows a true fraction. Before: alpha = 0.0001, n = 109998: k = 109988, coverage_exact = 0.99989999909, below the promised 1 - alpha = 0.9999 (alpha = 0.001: first at n = 1001998, coverage 0.998999999). After: k = 109989 and coverage 0.99990909, from exact integer arithmetic. A decimal alpha of up to 8 significant digits, also one computed as 1 - 0.9 , is now read exactly; other alphas (1/3, 0.099999999999) keep the earlier rule. For every alpha and n of the earlier tests the rank is unchanged (test test_conformal_rank_exact_at_large_n , which fails on 0.4.0, and test_conformal_rank_unchanged_where_it_was_right ). The test suite failed when run from the source distribution (sdist), which left out CITATION.cff and examples/ . Before (a clean copy of the 0.5.0 sources without MANIFEST.in , tests run from the unpacked sdist): 1 failed ( test_version_metadata , FileNotFoundError for CITATION.cff ), 107 passed, 3 tutorial tests skipped. After: a new MANIFEST.in adds CHANGELOG.md , CITATION.cff , CONTRIBUTING.md and examples/*.py to the sdist, and all 111 tests pass there. The wheel is unchanged. Changed The test that compares the batched design with the 0.3.0 loops compares the information matrices to 1e-12 of their largest entry instead of with == , and would accept different picks only for a tie within 1e-9 in the log-determinant: batched and single LAPACK calls are not guaranteed to round alike on every processor. The README no longer says "bit for bit" for the batched design . Version 0.5.0 in pyproject.toml , labplan.__version__ and CITATION.cff (released 2026-10-18). summary: Popper’s (1983, 2002) philosophy of science has enjoyed something of a renaissance in the wake of the replication crisis, offering a philosophical basis for the ensuing science reform movement. However, adherence to Popper’s approach may also be at least partly responsible for the sense of “crisis” that has developed following multiple unexpected replication failures. In this article, I contrast Popper’s approach with that of Lakatos (1978) as well as with a related but problematic approach called naïve methodological falsificationism (NMF; Lakatos, 1978). The Popperian approach is powerful because it is based on logical refutations, but its theories are noncausal and, therefore, potentially lacking in scientific value. In contrast, the Lakatosian approach considers causal theories, but it concedes that these theories are not logically refutable. Finally, NMF represents a hybrid approach that subjects Lakatosian causal theories to Popperian logical refutations. However, its tactic of temporarily accepting a ceteris paribus clause during theory testing may be viewed as scientifically inappropriate, epistemically inconsistent, and “completely redundant” (Lakatos, 1978, p. 40). I conclude that the replication “crisis” makes the most sense in the context of the Popperian and NMF approaches because it is only in these two approaches that the failure to replicate a previously corroborated theory represents a logical refutation of that theory. In contrast, such replication failures are less problematic in the Lakatosian approach because they do not logically refute theories. Indeed, in the Lakatosian approach, replication failures can be temporarily ignored or used to motivate theory development.
title: The replication crisis is less of a "crisis" in Lakatos' philosophy of science than it is in Popper's.

summary: This archive is provided as artifact material for the article "Synthesis and Verification of Register Automata over Data Sequences" for SETTA 2026. Abstract: Data sequences, such as time series, traces, and sensor streams, are words over large or infinite data domains. Their properties often depend on comparisons between values at different positions, which finite automata cannot express directly. We study synthesis and verification for Deterministic Register Automata (DRAs) over ordered data sequences. DRAs combine finite control with registers for remembered data values, providing compact symbolic descriptions of quantitative sequence languages. Our technical core is a local-search synthesis procedure and an exact robustness checker for DRAs. We fix the alphabet theory to ordered rationals $(\Q;<,=)$ with rational guard constants and use non-negative affine accumulator costs. For a fixed number of DRA registers, the checker runs in polynomial time; its dependence on that number is exponential. It reduces robustness to coverability and then to a shortest-path problem. Since the search ranges over $\Q^+$, it produces variable-length witnesses and, for RAA-definable alignment costs such as DTW, explores a counterexample space with no a priori length bound. As an application, we use learned DRAs as interpretable surrogates for queried neural sequence classifiers. A probably approximately correct (PAC) validation loop refines rejected candidates, returns genuine non-robustness witnesses for the classifier when found, and accepts a surrogate only with statistical guarantees for fidelity and local stability. We implement the framework in \textit{RAExc}, enabling the synthesis of interpretable automata and the verification of their robustness. We evaluate the approach on benchmark languages and sequentialized MNIST, demonstrating high accuracy while verifying the robustness of the learned automata.
title: Synthesis and Verification of Transformer Programs

summary: Image harmonization methods adjust the colour and lighting of an object pasted into a photograph so that it looks native to its new scene, and they are ranked by average error on one benchmark whose test images are real photographs with one object recoloured. One photograph can yield several such test images, and the benchmark promises that no photograph appears in both the training and the test split. We find that 1,399 photographs do, and the composites built on them are a quarter of the test set. Duplicate checks over file names or bytes miss this, because every composite is a different file. On that quarter the three methods we score end to end read two to five times lower error than on the rest, but most of the gap is composition rather than the sharing: the shared composites come almost entirely from one of the benchmark's four source collections, and inside that collection the gap falls to about one and a half times. An official score is therefore an average over two populations, mixed in a proportion the benchmark does not report. We release a test list of 5,581 composites whose construction identities do not appear in training, with four near-duplicate pairs disclosed rather than removed, adoptable without retraining at the price of one rescore per checkpoint. We leave open whether the sharing itself changes what a model learns. Contents of this record. The paper, the supplement, the LaTeX source of both, the record metadata and the licence statement. The identity matcher, the composite-locality and sensitivity checks, the CPU tests, the official iHarmony4 lists and the corrected test list are released under the MIT license at https://github.com/Buljic/only-means-only . What this record does not contain. No dataset, no images, no masks, no model checkpoints and no third-party baseline code or weights; those are described and cited by the paper and remain under their own terms. This is a preprint. It has not been peer reviewed. Licensed CC BY 4.0.
title: Only Means Only: what a harmonization benchmark score averages over

summary: The dataset, prepared by Patriotisk Selskab for Bikubenfonden and Høbbet A/S, presents spatially distributed soil analysis conducted in 2024. It includes measurements of soil texture (clay content), organic matter (humus content), soil acidity (reaction number, Rt), and nutrient indicators for phosphorus (Pt), potassium (Kt) and magnesium (Mgt). The results are presented through georeferenced sampling locations, field-level maps and thematic maps illustrating spatial variations in soil properties and nutrient levels. The dataset provides baseline information on soil conditions across the investigated areas and can support assessments of soil fertility, vegetation development, habitat restoration and future land management.
title: Soil Analyses of Svanninge Bjerge and Høbbet – Soil Properties and Nutrient Distribution (2024)

summary: Metascience uses a scientific approach to understand and improve science. Critical metascience takes a step back to question metascience’s common assumptions, methods, problems, and solutions. In this article, I aim to raise the profile of critical metascience and offer a rationale for viewing it as a distinct area of multidisciplinary inquiry. I define critical metascience, explain why it is important, and address some potential concerns about it. I also consider some emerging themes in the area and evaluate its potential relationships with metascience. I conclude that there needs to be greater recognition of critical metascience and greater interaction between metascience and critical metascience in order to improve metascience’s objectivity and approach.
title: What is critical metascience and why is it important?

summary: Loss and phase jitter told apart from squeezing pairs at several pump levels, resonances split by backscattering, a wrong error bar of the transmission fit fixed, a faster photonic-molecule model, two test tolerances tied to their floating-point limits, and a third tutorial. Fixed fit_resonance_transmission(..., branch=...) gave wrong error bars for kappa_ex_hz and kappa_0_hz . The derivative of the escape efficiency with respect to the dip depth D, which is -1 / (4 sqrt(1 - D)) on the over-coupled branch and +1 / (4 sqrt(1 - D)) on the under-coupled one, had the opposite sign on both, which flipped the term that carries the (strong, negative) correlation of the linewidth and the depth. Over-coupled ring ( kappa = 100 MHz , eta = 0.8 , 121 points over +/- 300 MHz, 1 % noise): kappa_0_hz_sigma 0.325 MHz -> 0.171 MHz (Monte Carlo scatter of 400 scans: 0.166 MHz), kappa_ex_hz_sigma 0.768 MHz -> 0.946 MHz (scatter 0.900 MHz). Under-coupled ring ( eta = 0.3 ): kappa_ex_hz_sigma 0.427 MHz -> 0.197 MHz (scatter 0.189 MHz), kappa_0_hz_sigma 0.452 MHz -> 0.735 MHz (scatter 0.695 MHz). The fitted values, kappa_hz , eta_esc and eta_sigma were right and are unchanged. Test: test_kappa_ex_and_kappa_0_error_bars . Added fit_squeezing_pairs(sq_db, anti_db, sigma_db, sigma_anti_db=None, fit_jitter=True, dark_noise=0, dark_in_reference=False) : the total efficiency and the local-oscillator phase jitter shared by squeezed / antisqueezed pairs measured at several pump levels, with error bars, each pair's source level, and a chi-square check. One pair cannot separate loss from jitter ( infer_source needs the jitter given); several pairs can, because loss pulls every pair toward shot noise by the same fraction while jitter mixes in a part of the antisqueezing, which grows with the pump. Model: a pure source per pair (no law between pump power and gain assumed), the jitter law of phase_noise_variance , then the efficiency and a stated dark noise as in detected_variance . Checked against the package's own forward path (the output of single_mode_parametric behind an escape efficiency, at three analysis frequencies, is exactly such a source: efficiency to 1e-8, jitter to a relative 1e-6), against infer_source for one pair without jitter (relative 1e-10), and by 150 seeded noisy sets (scatter 0.75 to 1.3 times the error bars). The analysis follows how experiments describe loss and jitter, for example B. Shajilal et al., arXiv:2211.06632 (2022), who model their squeezing and antisqueezing against pump power with a total efficiency and a jitter angle. README example 24. split_transmission(...) and fit_split_resonance(f_hz, transmission, sigma, fit_slope=False) : a through-port dip split into a doublet by backscattering, the coupled-mode model of the clockwise and counterclockwise modes of T. J. Kippenberg, S. M. Spillane and K. J. Vahala, Opt. Lett. 27, 1669 (2002). Returns the linewidth of each standing-wave mode, the escape efficiency, the splitting and the center with error bars, for the under- and the over-coupled regime (a resolved doublet is not symmetric under eta -> 1 - eta , so a regime that does not fit is reported as such), and their chi-square difference. The transmission is derived in the sqzcomb.resonance docstring and checked against the drift matrix of photonic_molecule (relative 1e-13 at 140 points), noise-free recovery (1e-8) and 40 seeded noisy scans. fit_resonance_transmission now names it when it refuses a doublet. README example 25. New test files tests/test_squeezing_pairs.py (9 tests), tests/test_split_resonance.py (9) and tests/test_audit_017.py (6), and one more test in tests/test_tutorials.py . Changed through_transmission (and the new split_transmission ) refuse a center frequency or baseline that is not finite (it returned an all-NaN curve). output_variance_ports is split into its input checks, the resolvent and the evaluation (private helpers); its operations and results are unchanged. molecule_spectra_model u

summary: This dataset contains longitudinal field observations of group size and composition and localized climate metrics for a wild population of cooperatively breeding apostlebirds ( Struthidea cinerea). Data were collected over five consecutive breeding seasons (2006–2010) at Fowlers Gap Arid Zone Research Station in New South Wales, Australia. The primary objective of this dataset was to evaluate two competing hypotheses regarding the adaptive value of cooperative group living under environmental variability: the 'social buffering hypothesis' whereby helpers mitigate unfavourable environmental conditions (e.g. drought or extreme heat) to reduce the likelihood of reproductive failure; and the 'social capitalisation hypothesis' whereby helpers enhance reproductive output under favourable climatic conditions.
title: Dataset for: Fair-weather friends: Group size boosts reproduction in wet and cooler conditions, in a dryland cooperative breeder

summary: PhytoIntelligence 4.2.3 is a literature-triage and hypothesis-prioritisation methodology that grades phytochemical candidates against a locked clinical indication using a seven-dimensional Diagnostic State Vector, tiered evidence weights, conflict-of-interest factors, and explicit feasibility and safety gates. Mode A (single-candidate) and Mode B (user-specified combinations). Terminal artefacts: ranked Hypothesis Dossier + Measurement Manifest. No formulations, dosing schedules, or efficacy claims. Live provenance required; MISSING/UNVERIFIED values block gates. Conformance defined by reference engine + test suite against the canonical JSON. Supersedes all prior versions.

summary: PyUL_SK is the fork of PyUltraLight 2 used for the black-hole simulations of Stone Skipping Black Holes in Ultralight Dark Matter Solitons (A. Zhang, Y. Wang, J. L. Zagorac and R. Easther, arXiv:2602.11512 ). It is a pseudo-spectral (split-step Fourier) solver for the Schroedinger-Poisson equations of ultralight dark matter coupled to N-body point masses (black holes), with cell-centred grids, manual dynamical friction, isolated or periodic potentials, a resampled centre-of-mass cube for eigenmode analysis, and an optional inline decomposition into soliton eigenmodes, c_nlm(t), computed while the simulation runs (with the companion ULDM-Eigenmode-Toolkit). Release 30.50 is a maintenance release of the 30.40 core used for part of the paper runs. With default options it reproduces 30.40 bit for bit, except the resampled-cube outputs, which LegacyResampleBox=True reproduces. It adds packaging, tests, laptop and PBS/Slurm examples, support for Python 3.9 to 3.14 with NumPy 2 and current SciPy, safe non-interactive behaviour on clusters, complete provenance records, and many bug fixes. CHANGELOG.md lists every change; docs/known_issues_and_errata.md documents the bugs of older versions and their effect on the paper's figures. Lineage and credits: PyUltraLight by F. Edwards, E. Kendall, S. Hotchkiss and R. Easther (JCAP 10 (2018) 027, doi:10.1088/1475-7516/2018/10/027); PyUltraLight 2 / PyUL_NBody by Yourong F. Wang and collaborators (Auckland Cosmology; github.com/Sifyrena/PyUL_NBody , doi:10.5281/zenodo.6336160), on which this fork is built; SK fork by Alan Zhang. The NOTICE file records the origin of the code and reproduces the upstream BSD-style copyright notice; the fork's own changes are distributed under the MIT licence in LICENSE. summary: Water-supply licences in low- and middle-income jurisdictions routinely omit sanitation-service conditions, yet regulators and courts treat the resulting silence as though it were a neutral allocation of responsibility rather than an affirmative regulatory choice with distributive consequences. The analysis distinguishes three doctrinal mechanisms through which silence operates: expressio unius reasoning that confines regulatory duties to enumerated conditions; statutory gap-filling that imports sanitation obligations from adjacent water and public-health statutes; and standing doctrine that determines whether unserved peri-urban households can compel performance. Licence silence is not doctrinally inert but functions as a standing-allocation device: where the licence is silent, enforcement standing defaults to the regulator, and households in unserved peri-urban areas lack a doctrinal pathway to compel sanitation-service provision. The comparative analysis identifies a remedial asymmetry between jurisdictions that treat licence conditions as exhaustive and those that permit statutory implication, and proposes a doctrinal test for reading sanitation-service conditions into water-supply licences that preserves regulatory discretion while creating a justiciable pathway for unserved households. The contribution is a doctrinal framework linking licence drafting to enforcement standing, with implications for licence-condition design and for the justiciability of sanitation-service claims in peri-urban contexts.

summary: This repository provides the datasets, pretrained models and generated network parameters used in the manuscript “DiffPINN: Generative diffusion-initialized physics-informed neural networks for accelerating seismic wavefield representation.” The accompanying source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/DeepWave-KAUST/DiffPINN-pub DiffPINN is a latent diffusion framework that generates initialization parameters for physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) used in frequency-domain seismic wavefield modeling. A set of PINNs is first trained across diverse velocity models and their parameters are flattened into one-dimensional vectors. An autoencoder compresses the length of these vectors into multi-channel latent tensors, and a conditional diffusion model is trained on those tensors with the velocity model and source configuration as conditions. At inference, the diffusion model generates a latent tensor for a new velocity model, with a physics-based gradient correction applied at each reverse step, and the decoder turns it into a complete set of PINN parameters. The archived files are organized as follows. dataset.zip After extraction, dataset.zip contains five folders corresponding to the five stages of the framework: metatrain/ : contains meta_train.mat , the dataset used for meta-training. pinntrain/ : contains pinntrain1.mat to pinntrain2600.mat , one file per velocity model, used to train the 2600 PINNs that form the parameter dataset. aetrain/ : contains the flattened parameters of the 2600 converged PINNs, used to train the autoencoder. difftrain/ : contains the latent tensors encoded from those parameters, used to train the diffusion model. pinntest/ : contains CurveVelA.mat , Layer.mat and FlatFaultA.mat , the three test velocity models used to reproduce the results reported in the manuscript. All data are stored in MATLAB .mat format. Each .mat file contains the following variables: x_train , z_train , sx_train : the spatial coordinates and source locations of the collocation samples. m_train , m0_train : the squared slowness of the medium and of the homogeneous background. u0_real_train , u0_imag_train : the real and imaginary parts of the analytical background wavefield. x_test , z_test , sx_test : the coordinates of the full evaluation grid. du_real_test , du_imag_test : the real and imaginary parts of the numerical reference solution. The training velocity models are drawn from the CurveVel-A class of the OpenFWI benchmark dataset, resized to 101×101 with a grid spacing of 25 m and mildly smoothed. All wavefields are computed at 5 Hz. The reference solutions are obtained with the optimized nine-point frequency-domain finite-difference scheme of Jo et al. (1996). Among the three test models, CurveVelA is drawn from the training distribution, while Layer (a layered section of the Marmousi model) and FlatFaultA lie outside it. Because aetrain/ and difftrain/ are the outputs of the two preceding stages, users can start at any point in the pipeline rather than rebuilding the parameter dataset, which takes roughly 65 hours on ten V100 GPUs. trained_model.zip After extraction, trained_model.zip contains the three trained models used to reproduce the results in the manuscript: meta_trained.pth : the meta-learned PINN initialization, trained for 40000 iterations over 500 velocity models. ae_trained.pth : the autoencoder, trained for 1000 epochs on the 2600 flattened parameter vectors. diff_trained.pt : the conditional diffusion model, trained for 400000 iterations on the latent tensors. generated_weight.zip After extraction, generated_weight.zip contains the latent tensors generated by the trained diffusion model for the three test velocity models: CurveVelA_weight.mat : generated parameters for the in-distribution CurveVel-A model. Layer_weight.mat : generated parameters for the layered Marmousi model. FlatFaultA_weight.mat : generated parameters for the FlatFault-A model. These were produced

summary: This repository provides the datasets, pretrained models and generated network parameters used in the manuscript “DiffPINN: Generative diffusion-initialized physics-informed neural networks for accelerating seismic wavefield representation.” The accompanying source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/DeepWave-KAUST/DiffPINN-pub DiffPINN is a latent diffusion framework that generates initialization parameters for physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) used in frequency-domain seismic wavefield modeling. A set of PINNs is first trained across diverse velocity models and their parameters are flattened into one-dimensional vectors. An autoencoder compresses the length of these vectors into multi-channel latent tensors, and a conditional diffusion model is trained on those tensors with the velocity model and source configuration as conditions. At inference, the diffusion model generates a latent tensor for a new velocity model, with a physics-based gradient correction applied at each reverse step, and the decoder turns it into a complete set of PINN parameters. The archived files are organized as follows. dataset.zip After extraction, dataset.zip contains five folders corresponding to the five stages of the framework: metatrain/ : contains meta_train.mat , the dataset used for meta-training. pinntrain/ : contains pinntrain1.mat to pinntrain2600.mat , one file per velocity model, used to train the 2600 PINNs that form the parameter dataset. aetrain/ : contains the flattened parameters of the 2600 converged PINNs, used to train the autoencoder. difftrain/ : contains the latent tensors encoded from those parameters, used to train the diffusion model. pinntest/ : contains CurveVelA.mat , Layer.mat and FlatFaultA.mat , the three test velocity models used to reproduce the results reported in the manuscript. All data are stored in MATLAB .mat format. Each .mat file contains the following variables: x_train , z_train , sx_train : the spatial coordinates and source locations of the collocation samples. m_train , m0_train : the squared slowness of the medium and of the homogeneous background. u0_real_train , u0_imag_train : the real and imaginary parts of the analytical background wavefield. x_test , z_test , sx_test : the coordinates of the full evaluation grid. du_real_test , du_imag_test : the real and imaginary parts of the numerical reference solution. The training velocity models are drawn from the CurveVel-A class of the OpenFWI benchmark dataset, resized to 101×101 with a grid spacing of 25 m and mildly smoothed. All wavefields are computed at 5 Hz. The reference solutions are obtained with the optimized nine-point frequency-domain finite-difference scheme of Jo et al. (1996). Among the three test models, CurveVelA is drawn from the training distribution, while Layer (a layered section of the Marmousi model) and FlatFaultA lie outside it. Because aetrain/ and difftrain/ are the outputs of the two preceding stages, users can start at any point in the pipeline rather than rebuilding the parameter dataset, which takes roughly 65 hours on ten V100 GPUs. trained_model.zip After extraction, trained_model.zip contains the three trained models used to reproduce the results in the manuscript: meta_trained.pth : the meta-learned PINN initialization, trained for 40000 iterations over 500 velocity models. ae_trained.pth : the autoencoder, trained for 1000 epochs on the 2600 flattened parameter vectors. diff_trained.pt : the conditional diffusion model, trained for 400000 iterations on the latent tensors. generated_weight.zip After extraction, generated_weight.zip contains the latent tensors generated by the trained diffusion model for the three test velocity models: CurveVelA_weight.mat : generated parameters for the in-distribution CurveVel-A model. Layer_weight.mat : generated parameters for the layered Marmousi model. FlatFaultA_weight.mat : generated parameters for the FlatFault-A model. These were produced

summary: The following dataset contains images and band count estimates of shortfin mako ( Isurus oxyrinchus ) vertebrae. It is intended to assist with the replication of the results for the study: Automated reading of vertebral images for aging shortfin mako ( Isurus oxyrinchus ) using Bayesian deep learning. Samples were obtained from two primary sources: recreational game fishing competitions primarily from the North Island between 1994 and 2003, and through the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) Fisheries Observer Programme between 2002 and 2003, primarily from the South Island (Bishop et al., 2006). Shortfin mako vertebrae images (n=146, belonging to 131 unique sharks) were obtained from previous ageing studies using band counts (Bishop et al., 2006; Francis, 2016). Most vertebrae images were of half bow-tie section pairs. These section pairs were filtered by image quality with lower quality images being excluded, resulting in a reduced dataset of 133 section pairs. Each section pair was isolated, resulting in a complete dataset of 266 half bow-tie section images. We compared the following three deep learning methods: DeepEnsembling, a mixture of Laplace approximations, and multi-stochastic weight average Gaussian to predict the band counts by human readers using a dataset of 146 images of shortfin mako ( Isurus oxyrinchus ) vertebrae. Multi-stochastic weight average Gaussian offered marginally superior predictive power and uncertainty calibration, and its predictions typically matched estimates provided by human readers. We conclude that the application of deep learning for automated vertebrae reading demonstrated strong initial promise.
title: Vertebral section images for shortfin mako (Isurus oxyrinchus)

summary: This repository provides a Google Colab notebook for preparing transport data and analysing road-network connectivity in Baghdad, Iraq. The workflow downloads OpenStreetMap data from Geofabrik, retrieves the Baghdad Municipality boundary, and clips the transport layers to the city. The notebook constructs a road graph and calculates three segment-level indicators: edge betweenness centrality, inverse shortest-path distance to hospitals and emergency facilities, and the detour ratio following individual road-segment closures. Results include GeoPackage layers containing road metrics, network nodes, service facilities, and the municipal boundary, together with summary statistics and maps. Outputs are saved to Google Drive. The analysis uses an undirected, distance-weighted network restricted to the municipal boundary. Betweenness is approximated using 256 sampled source nodes by default, with an option for exact calculation. Routing assumptions, facility-snapping parameters, and treatment of disconnected segments are documented in the notebook. This notebook supports transport-network indicator preparation; it does not implement flood mapping or EHCR–TOPSIS aggregation. Input data are retrieved from live sources and may change between runs. OpenStreetMap data are © OpenStreetMap contributors and distributed under the Open Database License (ODbL) 1.0.
title: Integrated flood risk and transport-network resilience in Baghdad using an EHCR–TOPSIS framework

summary: This technical note documents a conditional mathematical correspondence between the static spatial kernel used in conventional electromagnetic potential theory and the fixed-source gravitational potential in Lisa Doumbouya’s Harmonic Physics programme. Under supplied three-dimensional Euclidean geometry, spherical symmetry and stated boundary conditions, the derivation gives the static Green function 1/(4πr). Applying the existing gravitational source normalization yields the potential −μ/r, whose radial derivative gives the inward acceleration −μ/r². The note distinguishes potential, field amplitude, intensity, acceleration and optical measurement conversion, keeping geometric normalization separate from the distance exponent. The optical phase-ruler results are reviewed alongside the GRACE-FO forward forecasts. Calibrated reconstruction using measured phase retained micrometre-scale agreement with processed microwave ranging, while some forward models produced much larger errors. These results do not establish exponential error growth or identify a unique physical cause. The correspondence uses established mathematics and remains conditional on the supplied geometry, source calibration and physical interpretation. It does not establish an electromagnetic mechanism of gravity or derive spatial geometry from foundational Phase. The note includes the analytical proof, assumptions, evidence boundaries and requirements for a subsequent physical test. No new experimental data are introduced.
title: Inverse Radius Kernel and Optical Phase Registration

summary: This working paper develops a relational Phase interpretation of black holes within the Harmonic Physics research programme, using general relativity, exact Kerr geometry and semiclassical black-hole thermodynamics as its physical baseline. It examines how phase organisation, temporal reference, observer accessibility and information persistence might relate to black-hole closure. Within the proposed framework, a phase-cycle is a closed relational structure that supports recurrence. Measured succession requires distinguishable relations and persistent records, while geometry and causal history are treated as observer-level reconstructions. The temporal-anchor hypothesis concerns a deeper terminal condition at which the parent domain loses the internally usable references needed to resolve further clocks and geometry. This proposed condition is kept distinct from the regular event horizon, across which local evolution continues. Observation is described through a joint observation relation among admitted source organisation, a physical channel and an observer-capable organisation. Source state, coupling and registered record retain separate roles; changes in accessibility may alter registration while the source organisation persists. The paper consolidates three bounded mathematical findings: exact Kerr ingoing and outgoing endpoints can have opposite trapped and anti-trapped orientations with the same mass and spin parameters; spherical source/exterior matching leaves the transition law undetermined; and a leading slow-rotation calculation permits the same sign of angular momentum in closing and opening configurations. These results establish compatibility within the stated geometric constructions. A physical transition mechanism remains to be derived. Black-to-white-hole models provide external theoretical comparisons. Return to the original exterior and the opening of a daughter phase are treated as distinct hypotheses, each requiring an appropriate causal structure, state map and conservation accounting. The remaining requirements include an invariant parent-relative terminal criterion, a physical Phase-to-boundary map, transition dynamics, information and entropy accounting, and a stable nonperturbative rotating completion. The paper remains a developing theoretical interpretation supported by standard-geometry comparisons and bounded symbolic checks. It does not establish a physical black-to-white transition, information recovery through evaporation or a daughter universe. Version 2.3, dated 17 October 2026, updates observation and self-nesting terminology, clarifies geodesic incompleteness and fixed-angular-momentum assumptions, and refreshes the references. The existing displayed equations and reported test results are retained. keywords: Phase Theory; black holes; event horizons; geodesic incompleteness; relational time; phase contraction; information accessibility; singularity; white holes; quantum gravity.

summary: SELF-CALIBRATING NANO-NEURAL INTERFACES AND REFERENCE LINEAGE AT THE LIMIT Built-In References × Drift Attribution × Independent Functional Requalification STARLI / Institute XXIII / Research Flagship 17 PUBLICATION DESCRIPTION When a long-running neural interface changes, is the cause the sensor, the surrounding tissue, or the decoder? An adaptive algorithm can restore predictive accuracy while obscuring the physical origin of its own correction. This book proposes a rigorous, falsifiable architecture for self-calibrating nano-neural interfaces that must retain the scientific history of every reference and every update. Its central axiom is that self-calibration does not imply self-certification: measurement claims, permission to change, electrode safety and functional benefit demand independent evidence. The first coupling is the existence of physically traceable internal references that can be challenged against electrically and temporally independent standards. The second is a source-aware drift-diagnostic process that distinguishes electronics gain, electrode-tissue transfer, tissue-like surrogate changes, changing source signals and model/feature drift, explicitly recording instances of nonidentifiability. The third is external functional requalification, which can reject an apparently successful update after hidden-domain testing, material or reference replacement, loss of selectivity, missing raw observations, or inability to reproduce the frozen predecessor. This research monograph is divided into seven causal layers and 82 chapters. Five major subsections of each chapter are assigned independent pages, yielding 410 separately paginated technical essays. Thirty gold mathematical derivations are linked from chapter-opening equations to discriminating experiments. The mathematics includes augmented state-space observability, nonlinear observation functions, source-separation Jacobians, Kalman innovations, impedance spectroscopy, covariance propagation, change-point statistics, conformal coverage, selective risk, hard-veto constrained update eligibility, reference-bridge covariance, exact rollback and cross-laboratory requalification. A displayed formula is a candidate analytical instrument with stated dimensions and assumptions, not a discovered biological law. Two hundred detailed Research Gates are preserved at the rear: 82 interrogate source identifiability, another 82 challenge independent physical and evidential hard vetoes, and 36 require third-party reconstruction of a frozen reference history. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos propose revisable architectures, beginning with the Neural Interface Calibration Passport. The Passport ties an interface's physical identity to the raw analog and digitized record, calibrated unit chain, hardware reference ancestors, model and feature checksums, reasons for changing any reference, failed updates, revoked permissions, blinded requalification and rollback. These are proposed evidence structures, not commercially validated devices. The DOI bibliography contains 18 unique external research records covering chronic intracortical signal instability, low-dimensional BCI stabilization, decoder adaptation, long-term electrode-tissue behavior, complex impedance metrology, electrochemical reference limits, neural interface materials and conformal uncertainty under covariate shift. Selected publisher and PubMed pages were consulted for source metadata. Their findings cannot establish efficacy of the new self-calibration architecture; source-specific claims and independent replication would be necessary.

summary: Overview This repository contains the two processed datasets analyzed in "Influence of land cover and shade on the thermal environments of schoolyards in Los Angeles" by Levinson et al. (in preparation). The data come from the LAUSD Cool Schoolyards experiment, a field study of how schoolyard surfaces affect surface temperature, air temperature, radiant heat, and outdoor thermal comfort at Los Angeles Unified School District (LAUSD) elementary schools. The study compares four surface types: uncoated asphalt pavement, pavement with a high-reflectance coating (coated pavement), turf, and garden. The first file holds mobile measurements taken with an instrumented cart that was moved across each schoolyard. The second holds continuous measurements from three stationary weather stations placed over different surfaces. Study sites and measurement periods Each school is identified in the data by a two-letter code: HE : Harrison Elementary School, City Terrace, Los Angeles, CA BE : Braddock Drive Elementary School and Gifted Magnet, Culver City area, Los Angeles, CA SE : Saticoy Elementary School, North Hollywood, Los Angeles, CA Mobile cart measurements were made at HE on 2025-09-06, at BE on 2025-09-07, and at SE on 2025-09-14. The weather stations were deployed at BE from 2025-09-10 13:00 to 2025-10-10 09:00 and at HE from 2025-10-10 14:00 to 2025-11-02 00:00. File 1: Transect measurements Transect measurement stats at 1 min + coded transects + open-meteo weather + shade + LSH.csv An instrumented cart was moved along a route of numbered locations ("transect points") across each schoolyard. At each point it stopped for about one minute and recorded readings every second. Each row summarizes one stop, giving the mean, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum of every measured variable. The route was traversed repeatedly in forward and reverse directions. The file includes: Identifiers: school, measurement number, transect point, a tag of the form MMM_SS_PP (measurement number, school, point), transect number, and direction. Microclimate: air temperature, relative humidity, and wind speed and direction measured about 1.5 m above the ground. Radiation and surfaces: downward solar irradiance, ground albedo (the fraction of sunlight the ground reflects), ground surface temperature, sky temperature, and mean radiant temperature (MRT, a measure of the total radiant heat a person receives). Readings from 12 radiometers are also included: six measuring sunlight and six measuring longwave (thermal) radiation, facing up, down, forward, back, left, and right. Instrument orientation and position: radiometer tilt, roll, and zenith angles, plus GPS coordinates. Surface properties: surface description and classification of each point, along with measured solar reflectance and thermal emittance. Derived quantities: solar position, local solar hour, the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI, an index of how hot conditions feel to a person) and its heat-stress category, and a shade classification for each stop. In the Classification column, the labels "Warm pavement," "Cool pavement," "Grass," and "Nature area" correspond to uncoated pavement, coated pavement, turf, and garden, respectively.
