summary: The following dataset contains images and band count estimates of shortfin mako ( Isurus oxyrinchus ) vertebrae. It is intended to assist with the replication of the results for the study: Automated reading of vertebral images for aging shortfin mako ( Isurus oxyrinchus ) using Bayesian deep learning. Samples were obtained from two primary sources: recreational game fishing competitions primarily from the North Island between 1994 and 2003, and through the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) Fisheries Observer Programme between 2002 and 2003, primarily from the South Island (Bishop et al., 2006). Shortfin mako vertebrae images (n=146, belonging to 131 unique sharks) were obtained from previous ageing studies using band counts (Bishop et al., 2006; Francis, 2016). Most vertebrae images were of half bow-tie section pairs. These section pairs were filtered by image quality with lower quality images being excluded, resulting in a reduced dataset of 133 section pairs. Each section pair was isolated, resulting in a complete dataset of 266 half bow-tie section images. We compared the following three deep learning methods: DeepEnsembling, a mixture of Laplace approximations, and multi-stochastic weight average Gaussian to predict the band counts by human readers using a dataset of 146 images of shortfin mako ( Isurus oxyrinchus ) vertebrae. Multi-stochastic weight average Gaussian offered marginally superior predictive power and uncertainty calibration, and its predictions typically matched estimates provided by human readers. We conclude that the application of deep learning for automated vertebrae reading demonstrated strong initial promise.
title: Vertebral section images for shortfin mako (Isurus oxyrinchus)

summary: This repository provides a Google Colab notebook for preparing transport data and analysing road-network connectivity in Baghdad, Iraq. The workflow downloads OpenStreetMap data from Geofabrik, retrieves the Baghdad Municipality boundary, and clips the transport layers to the city. The notebook constructs a road graph and calculates three segment-level indicators: edge betweenness centrality, inverse shortest-path distance to hospitals and emergency facilities, and the detour ratio following individual road-segment closures. Results include GeoPackage layers containing road metrics, network nodes, service facilities, and the municipal boundary, together with summary statistics and maps. Outputs are saved to Google Drive. The analysis uses an undirected, distance-weighted network restricted to the municipal boundary. Betweenness is approximated using 256 sampled source nodes by default, with an option for exact calculation. Routing assumptions, facility-snapping parameters, and treatment of disconnected segments are documented in the notebook. This notebook supports transport-network indicator preparation; it does not implement flood mapping or EHCR–TOPSIS aggregation. Input data are retrieved from live sources and may change between runs. OpenStreetMap data are © OpenStreetMap contributors and distributed under the Open Database License (ODbL) 1.0.
title: Integrated flood risk and transport-network resilience in Baghdad using an EHCR–TOPSIS framework

summary: CasADi is a symbolic framework for numeric optimization implementing automatic differentiation in forward and reverse modes on sparse matrix-valued computational graphs. It supports self-contained C-code generation and interfaces state-of-the-art codes such as SUNDIALS, IPOPT etc. It can be used from C++, Python, Matlab/Octave, Julia or Javascript
title: CasADi - A software framework for nonlinear optimization and optimal control

summary: This dataset tests whether public density-functional-theory (DFT) databases can guide composition selection for metastable magnet phases. It compares energy above the convex hull and computed Fe moments from Materials Project, AFLOW, JARVIS-DFT, NOMAD (Alexandria PBE calculations), OQMD and GNoME (628 entries, snapshot 2026-10-13) with 38 published observations of phases formed in Sm–Fe and Sm–Fe–M alloys (M = Co, Ti, V, Zr, Nb, Cu, Si, Ga, Al, Mo; none found for Cr, Mn, Hf) after rapid solidification or mechanical milling, 30 of which are scored. Because no database contains the disordered TbCu7 structure, a stability proxy is built from each database's ordered parents (CaCu5, 2:17, 3:29, ThMn12); the proxy and per-family best entries are given in stability_proxy_table.csv . Main finding: Materials Project, OQMD and Alexandria place no Sm–Fe compound on the convex hull, so their energies for equilibrium Sm2Fe17, metastable TbCu7 SmFe9 and SmFe12 (not formed by melt spinning) differ by less than 5 meV/atom. JARVIS-DFT ranks them correctly but places TbCu7 SmFe9 at 89 meV/atom. AFLOW and GNoME contain no comparable entries. The package contains raw database snapshots with provenance (SHA-256), the curated observation table with DOIs, numbered pipeline scripts (Python), a QA report, four figures and documentation (codebook, limitations, verification checklist). Code: MIT. Data and documents: CC BY 4.0. AI assistance: data retrieval scripts, curation drafting and analysis code were prepared with an AI assistant (Claude, Anthropic); the author verified the numbers and decisions before release.
title: TbCu7 Stability Screen: validation of public DFT databases against observed metastable phases in Sm–Fe–M alloys (stability proxy table)

summary: mm-ADL-Home is a cross-environment millimeter-wave radar point-cloud dataset for human activity recognition in furnished residential environments. The dataset was collected in four indoor environments comprising three simulated bachelor-unit layouts and one real bachelor unit, using the same activity taxonomy and radar configuration as the mm-ADL dataset (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22405011).  Each participant–environment recording is preserved as a continuous point-cloud stream and includes: (1) point_cloud.csv , containing radar point-cloud observations; (2) frame_labels.csv , containing frame-level activity annotations; (3) timestamps.csv , providing the temporal correspondence between radar and annotation frames; and (4) location_annotations.csv , containing the intervals used to register the radar sensor and landmark furniture in the radar coordinate system. The activity taxonomy covers locomotion, sitting and lying transitions, stationary sitting and lying, simulated falls, and floor-to-standing recovery. Location annotations identify sittable furniture, lieable furniture, kitchen locations, entry locations, and the radar sensor origin. These annotations support the reconstruction of room-level spatial context and furniture landmarks on the horizontal radar coordinate plane. The dataset contains complete recordings without a prescribed windowing or segmentation scheme, allowing users to implement their own preprocessing, temporal segmentation, domain adaptation, and evaluation protocols. Synchronized RGB recordings used during annotation are not included in the public release. Participant identifiers are pseudonymous.

summary: The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 allows a child aged sixteen or seventeen who is alleged to have committed a heinous offence to be tried as an adult after a "preliminary assessment" by the Juvenile Justice Board. This paper argues that the transfer mechanism is less a principled answer to serious adolescent offending than a legislative compromise whose costs fall on the procedural guarantees the Act otherwise extends to children. It reads section 15 against the Supreme Court's decisions in Shilpa Mittal and Barun Chandra Thakur, the age-determination case law, and the developmental research on adolescent culpability, and it engages the retributive and victim-centred case for transfer on its own terms. Accountability and rehabilitation, the paper contends, are not two poles to be traded off at a single age threshold. Both depend on institutional capacity that the system has never been resourced to supply: functioning Boards, trained probation staff, individual care plans that are actually followed, and aftercare that reaches young people beyond eighteen. Reform should narrow and proceduralise transfer, introduce statutory diversion, decouple offence classification from the general penal code, and treat implementation failure as a rights violation rather than an administrative shortfall.
title: Reforming Juvenile Justice in India: Balancing Child Rights, Accountability, and Rehabilitation

summary: Sixteen commits since v1.0.0 (2026-07-05). The pipeline was run end to end for the first time on the current Claude Science product in this window — ComputationalReviewSSTdisease — and most of what follows comes from defects that run exposed. Runtime Runs with nothing to install: the coordinator saves skills/*.md as artifacts at session start and hands sub-agents the skill files they need (new "Runtime: Claude Science" section in the orchestrator). LITREVIEW and DATAML are roles delegated to default sub-agents, not profiles. Legacy delegate_to / operon.* / pipeline.* calls updated to host.* (#5). All 20 skills carry name / description frontmatter. Fixes found by running the pipeline Authorship widget published empty. The Phase 14 instruction said :authors: ../authors.yml ; the plugin resolves that path relative to the document directory, and 00_frontmatter.md and authors.yml both live in content/ . Corrected to ./authors.yml , with the silent-failure mode documented (#5). Evidence Database page published empty from a complete evidence set, with a green build. Four independent faults: the plugin never followed the v29 evidence_section_NN.json rename, looped sections 02..13 , read argument_groups.*.supporting_findings cite-key strings as finding records, and swallowed every read failure in catch { continue } . It now discovers the section files present, accepts all three historical naming conventions, prefers ev.findings , and throws rather than publishing empty (#6). Build failed on an un-instantiated evidence directory. A directory with no JSON at all is now treated as a template awaiting a run and renders a placeholder; JSON present but matching no package name stays fatal (#8). comprev-scoping.md 's description frontmatter was truncated mid-sentence (#5). Version management The pipeline generation number lived in a filename and in ~20 loose strings, while the only release tag described itself as "Expert Review Pipeline v29". The generation now lives solely in skills/manifest.json , which also records the sha256 and byte count of every skill file; the release version lives solely in git tags and is written into no file (#7). scripts/build_skill_manifest.py generates and verifies the manifest — standard library only — and a Skill manifest workflow runs --check on every push and pull request. It fails on a skill edited without a manifest regeneration, a version-bearing skill filename, a frontmatter name that disagrees with its filename, a description quoting the wrong generation, or a README naming a generation the manifest does not. Session setup writes provenance/pipeline_version.json into each review (generation, template commit, template tag, manifest hash, per-skill artifact ids). Phase 1's review_request.md header, Methods M.8 and pipeline_metrics.json read the version from that file instead of carrying a typed-in number. Renamed skills/comprev-orchestrator-v29.md → skills/comprev-orchestrator.md . Update saved prompts that name the old path. Nothing depends on this repository programmatically, and reviews already produced carry their own copy of skills/ , so they are unaffected.
title: AllenNeuralDynamics/ComputationalReviewTemplate: v1.1.0

summary: Lecture 1 formulated the recommendation problem in abstract terms: a set of users U , a set of items I , and a preference function r(u,i) that must be estimated for the pairs that have not been observed. Every algorithm studied in this course, however, operates on concrete data rather than on abstractions. The quality of a recommender system is therefore bounded by the quality, the structure, and the representation of the data from which it learns. In practice, improving the data frequently brings larger gains than changing the algorithm. A sophisticated model trained on noisy, biased, or poorly prepared data produces poor recommendations, a principle often summarized as garbage in, garbage out . This lecture therefore addresses three questions: è Which data does a recommender system collect, and what do these data really mean? è How can these data be organized and represented so that algorithms can process them? è How must the data be prepared and partitioned before a model is built and assessed? After studying this lecture, the reader should be able to: · Identify the sources and categories of data used in a recommender system; · Characterize explicit and implicit feedback, including their strengths and weaknesses; · Construct a user–item matrix and interpret its sparsity; · Represent users and items as vectors built from interactions and descriptive features; · Apply the main preprocessing operations to ratings and implicit signals; · Split a dataset correctly and avoid information leakage. The path followed by the data throughout this lecture is: Data sources → Feedback signals → User–item matrix → Vector representations → Preprocessing → Data splitting

summary: Anonymized replication materials for the manuscript "Clustered Convergence: Spatial Dynamics and Multiscale Correlates of Digital Creative Firm Entry in Urban China" (under review). The archive contains: (1) city-year panels for 285 Chinese prefecture-level cities, 2012-2022, with the dependent-variable family and covariates and a codebook; (2) de-identified firm-level identification outputs for 5,837,010 registration records (no firm names or identifiers); (3) the catalogue identification rule v0.6p1 with its frozen specification, SHA256 sums and a 55-case test suite; (4) the blind human review of 1,000 firms and diagnostics; (5) all analysis scripts with run order and software versions; (6) result workbooks, supplementary tables and figures. Raw registration files, yearbook workbooks and the base map are licensed and are not redistributed; see LICENSE_NOTE.md. Author information will be added after peer review.

summary: Section 166(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires directors to act with 'due and reasonable care, skill and diligence' and to exercise 'independent judgment'. The provision was drafted for human decision-makers and is silent on what that duty demands when a board relies on an algorithmic system whose reasoning it cannot inspect. This article argues that the gap is practical, not theoretical. Indian courts have not fixed a consistent standard of care, the protections available to directors under sections 463 and 149(12) operate only after a dispute arises, and the regulatory material now addressing AI in Indian finance, from SEBI's 2025 consultation paper to the RBI's FREE-AI report and 2026 draft model-risk guidance and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, binds entities rather than defining the individual director's duty of care. Drawing on Delaware's process-based oversight cases and on the distinction between substance and process in corporate governance scholarship, the article proposes a five-part Board AI Oversight Standard (identify, understand, challenge, monitor and document). It recommends two routes to give the Standard legal force: an amendment to Regulation 21 and Schedule II of the SEBI Listing Regulations, and a rebuttable presumption of due care under section 166(3) for boards that follow it. The proposal gives firms an ex ante and auditable benchmark for defending board decisions, and gives courts a workable test.
title: Who Is Minding the Algorithm? Section 166(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 and a Process Standard for AI-Assisted Board Decisions

title: Who Is Minding the Algorithm? Section 166(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 and a Process Standard for AI-Assisted Board Decisions

summary: Section 166(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires directors to act with 'due and reasonable care, skill and diligence' and to exercise 'independent judgment'. The provision was drafted for human decision-makers and is silent on what that duty demands when a board relies on an algorithmic system whose reasoning it cannot inspect. This article argues that the gap is practical, not theoretical. Indian courts have not fixed a consistent standard of care, the protections available to directors under sections 463 and 149(12) operate only after a dispute arises, and the regulatory material now addressing AI in Indian finance, from SEBI's 2025 consultation paper to the RBI's FREE-AI report and 2026 draft model-risk guidance and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, binds entities rather than defining the individual director's duty of care. Drawing on Delaware's process-based oversight cases and on the distinction between substance and process in corporate governance scholarship, the article proposes a five-part Board AI Oversight Standard (identify, understand, challenge, monitor and document). It recommends two routes to give the Standard legal force: an amendment to Regulation 21 and Schedule II of the SEBI Listing Regulations, and a rebuttable presumption of due care under section 166(3) for boards that follow it. The proposal gives firms an ex ante and auditable benchmark for defending board decisions, and gives courts a workable test.

Negative outcomes are intentionally preserved as routes for later human and AI research successors.

summary: Research compendium for the article "Climate warming is projected to reduce and redistribute Aedes albopictus abundance, away from Po Valley hotspots towards Alpine margins" (M. C. Darılmaz, Science of the Total Environment; manuscript STOTEN-D-26-01129R1). The study predicts weekly ovitrap egg counts of the Asian tiger mosquito at 149 monitoring stations in Italy, Albania, Switzerland and France (VectAbundance, 2010–2022). The framework has four layers: a mechanistic life-history model (dynamAedes 2.2.9); gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost) and random forests with climate, remote-sensing, land-use, demographic and population-genetic predictors; an ablation of the population-genetic layer; and projections under 48 CMIP6 combinations (four General Circulation Models, three Shared Socioeconomic Pathways, four periods to 2100). The archive contains: - 48 Python, 8 R and 1 Google Earth Engine scripts, with PIPELINE.md giving the order in which they run; - the processed station-level data and the final modelling tables (42,118 station–week records), with the station-to-fold assignment used by every cross-validated analysis; - the trained XGBoost and Random Forest models with their cross-validation predictions, feature importance and SHAP values; - the outputs of the ablation and sensitivity analyses: mechanistic and genetic ablations, genetic structure versus geographic position, fold-count sensitivity, fold-level inference, feature correlation and VIF, spatio-temporal and leave-one-year-out cross-validation, remote-sensing gap-filling, baseline period, calibration and validation detail, treatment of the year predictor, inputs that carry the projected change, and the fill of weeks without mechanistic output; - the inputs and outputs of the 48-scenario projection, per climate model, as ensemble and at station level. Main results reproduced by the archive: cross-validated R² of the full model 0.534 ± 0.093 (XGBoost; pooled 0.539) and 0.544 ± 0.081 (Random Forest). Projected change in mean active-season abundance over the 12 SSP–period combinations: −4 to −27 % at Hot lowland stations (−6 to −44 % in the Po Valley) and +10 to +106 % at Cool upland and Alpine margin stations. Raw inputs that are publicly available from their primary archives (ERA5-Land, WorldClim 2.1 and its CMIP6 projections, satellite imagery, GHS-POP, the population-genetic source data and GenBank sequences) are not redistributed; README.md lists the sources and how the scripts locate them. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

summary: This dataset contains longitudinal field observations of group size and composition and localized climate metrics for a wild population of cooperatively breeding apostlebirds ( Struthidea cinerea). Data were collected over five consecutive breeding seasons (2006–2010) at Fowlers Gap Arid Zone Research Station in New South Wales, Australia. The primary objective of this dataset was to evaluate two competing hypotheses regarding the adaptive value of cooperative group living under environmental variability: the 'social buffering hypothesis' whereby helpers mitigate unfavourable environmental conditions (e.g. drought or extreme heat) to reduce the likelihood of reproductive failure; and the 'social capitalisation hypothesis' whereby helpers enhance reproductive output under favourable climatic conditions.
title: Dataset for: Fair-weather friends: Group size boosts reproduction in wet and cooler conditions, in a dryland cooperative breeder

summary: PhytoIntelligence 4.2.3 is a literature-triage and hypothesis-prioritisation methodology that grades phytochemical candidates against a locked clinical indication using a seven-dimensional Diagnostic State Vector, tiered evidence weights, conflict-of-interest factors, and explicit feasibility and safety gates. Mode A (single-candidate) and Mode B (user-specified combinations). Terminal artefacts: ranked Hypothesis Dossier + Measurement Manifest. No formulations, dosing schedules, or efficacy claims. Live provenance required; MISSING/UNVERIFIED values block gates. Conformance defined by reference engine + test suite against the canonical JSON. Supersedes all prior versions.
title: PhytoIntelligence 4.2.3 Framework Release + 10 Output Examples

summary: This dataset tests whether public density-functional-theory (DFT) databases can guide composition selection for metastable magnet phases. It compares energy above the convex hull and computed Fe moments from Materials Project, AFLOW, JARVIS-DFT, NOMAD (Alexandria PBE calculations), OQMD and GNoME (628 entries, snapshot 2026-10-13) with 38 published observations of phases formed in Sm–Fe and Sm–Fe–M alloys (M = Co, Ti, V, Zr, Nb, Cu, Si, Ga, Al, Mo; none found for Cr, Mn, Hf) after rapid solidification or mechanical milling, 30 of which are scored. Because no database contains the disordered TbCu7 structure, a stability proxy is built from each database's ordered parents (CaCu5, 2:17, 3:29, ThMn12); the proxy and per-family best entries are given in stability_proxy_table.csv . Main finding: Materials Project, OQMD and Alexandria place no Sm–Fe compound on the convex hull, so their energies for equilibrium Sm2Fe17, metastable TbCu7 SmFe9 and SmFe12 (not formed by melt spinning) differ by less than 5 meV/atom. JARVIS-DFT ranks them correctly but places TbCu7 SmFe9 at 89 meV/atom. AFLOW and GNoME contain no comparable entries. The package contains raw database snapshots with provenance (SHA-256), the curated observation table with DOIs, numbered pipeline scripts (Python), a QA report, four figures and documentation (codebook, limitations, verification checklist). Code: MIT. Data and documents: CC BY 4.0. AI assistance: data retrieval scripts, curation drafting and analysis code were prepared with an AI assistant (Claude, Anthropic); the author verified the numbers and decisions before release.
title: TbCu7 Stability Screen: validation of public DFT databases against observed metastable phases in Sm–Fe–M alloys (stability proxy table)

summary: Anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate. A bounded audit of one published five-variable 2-SAT transformer separates semantic ranking, fixed-threshold fidelity, numerical effective-state geometry, agreement with the native answer, and Boolean clause-edit sufficiency. A fresh balanced bank of 4096 formulas supplies additional same-checkpoint evidence; it is not independently trained-model replication. The public package documents exact replay scope and exclusions. Some historical image-dependent checks cannot be reproduced from the public files. Native replay requires separately retrieved, hash-pinned upstream source dependencies that are not redistributed here. Short independent-training feasibility attempts did not meet the predeclared competence threshold and supply no confirmatory representation evidence. Internal AI-assisted review and producer replay are not external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. CC0 applies only to original research prose, diagrams and data. Original executable code is MIT-licensed; retained third-party components retain their own terms. Consult LICENSES.md and the dependency provenance for component-level boundaries.
title: Assignment-Aligned Effective States in a 2-SAT Transformer

The archive contains: - 48 Python, 8 R and 1 Google Earth Engine scripts, with PIPELINE.md giving the order in which they run; - the processed station-level data and the final modelling tables (42,118 station–week records), with the station-to-fold assignment used by every cross-validated analysis; - the trained XGBoost and Random Forest models with their cross-validation predictions, feature importance and SHAP values; - the outputs of the ablation and sensitivity analyses: mechanistic and genetic ablations, genetic structure versus geographic position, fold-count sensitivity, fold-level inference, feature correlation and VIF, spatio-temporal and leave-one-year-out cross-validation, remote-sensing gap-filling, baseline period, calibration and validation detail, treatment of the year predictor, inputs that carry the projected change, and the fill of weeks without mechanistic output; - the inputs and outputs of the 48-scenario projection, per climate model, as ensemble and at station level. Main results reproduced by the archive: cross-validated R² of the full model 0.534 ± 0.093 (XGBoost; pooled 0.539) and 0.544 ± 0.081 (Random Forest). Projected change in mean active-season abundance over the 12 SSP–period combinations: −4 to −27 % at Hot lowland stations (−6 to −44 % in the Po Valley) and +10 to +106 % at Cool upland and Alpine margin stations. Raw inputs that are publicly available from their primary archives (ERA5-Land, WorldClim 2.1 and its CMIP6 projections, satellite imagery, GHS-POP, the population-genetic source data and GenBank sequences) are not redistributed; README.md lists the sources and how the scripts locate them. summary: Notes cover the changes since 0.5.0. pip install metabeta==0.6.0 Tutorials Three notebooks in demos/ replace intro.ipynb and priors.ipynb . Each runs on a CPU runtime in Colab. 01-quickstart : lme4's sleepstudy end to end, next to lme4's estimates. 02-families : Bernoulli ( cbpp ) and Poisson ( Salamanders ) fits, posterior predictive checks, and random-walk moves next to a NUTS reference. 03-priors : prior specification, prior sensitivity in one call, and model comparison by Bayes factors. New reports posteriorDraws(result) : posterior draws of the global parameters on the data's scale, as a DataFrame named as in posteriorSummary (#31). groupDraws(result) : each group's coefficients per draw, the fixed effect plus the group's deviation (#33). posteriorPredictive(result) : the observed responses and one replicate per posterior draw, in the data's units (#33). bayesFactor(result, reference) : the Bayes factor of one model over another, per prior, with its Kass–Raftery grade; both results come from sample(evidence=True) (#33). sample n_samples defaults to 1,000 draws (#19). seed= makes a call reproducible and leaves the caller's random stream untouched (#32). posteriorPredictive and plotPPD take seed= too (#26, #33). Every summary ends with a fit metric: R² (Gaussian), AUC (Bernoulli) or deviance (Poisson) (#29). loo=True adds PSIS-LOO to the summary; it replaces diagnostics=True (#29). random_walk=True runs silently and warns only below an IMH effective sample size (ESS) of 10 (#29). Warnings state the failure, its consequence and numbered remedies, and point at the user's call (#18, #29). The first call after loading costs about as much as a warm one; warmup() runs that pass explicitly (#19). Formulas, scales and names Formulas follow lme4: y ~ 1 + (1 | g) fits an intercept-only model, preprocessing reads only the columns the formula names, and column names keep their case (#15). The order of fixed terms no longer changes the fit; names are mapped back in every output (#16). Summaries default to x_scale='original' . Random-effect SDs, correlations and per-group effects are on the data's scale like the fixed effects, and so are the prior lines (#17). rfxSummary labels each group correctly (#17). Api.from_pretrained('gaussian') is an alias of 'normal' , in any case (#30). Reports pick a dataset row by prior_id , a prior's name or its index (#32). Errors Unsupported formula syntax raises NotImplementedError with a workaround: || , nested or crossed grouping factors, interactions ( : , * ) and function calls such as log() or factor() (#18). Data outside every submodel's range raises one ValueError that names the limits; a family mismatch names the checkpoint to load (#18). A named predictor dropped as collinear or near-constant raises an error that names it (#18). Formulas the pretrained models cannot fit raise an error that names the fix: a random intercept without a fixed one, or the reverse, and a random slope that is not a fixed term (#16). GPU from_pretrained(..., device='cuda') works on GPUs whose torch build lacks a cholesky_solve kernel, such as Colab's T4 with torch 2.11 for CUDA 13 (#26). plotParameters and sample(loo=True) work on a CUDA device (#26). Packaging Python 3.13 support, with dependency floors at Colab's preinstalled versions (#20). The code is licensed under Apache-2.0, previously CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (#21). CITATION.cff drives GitHub's citation button (#21). Deprecated, removed in 0.7 Each alias still works and raises a FutureWarning (#29, #32). sample(diagnostics=True) : use loo=True . batch_index= in posteriorSummary and rfxSummary , and index= in plotParameters : use prior_id= . indices= in plotPPD : use prior_ids= .

summary: This article proposes a theoretical framework for transporting large physical masses at the speed of light C by analyzing the behavior of photons through advanced single-photon imaging techniques. By examining the temporal and spatial distribution of photons captured via Single-Photon Avalanche Diode (SPAD) cameras, we establish a correlation between the visual reconstruction of an object and its potential physical translation across space-time. We argue that light possesses an inherent volumetric, cell-like structure capable of carrying mass, provided an engineering mechanism can replicate its fundamental properties: diffraction, momentum, and precise synchronization.
tags: proof of possible travel at light speed
title: Single-photon imaging is evidence of the possibility of mass traveling at the speed of light.

summary: We establish almost infinite log-monotonicity of the Bell numbers, settling a conjecture of Chen, Guo and Wang (2013). The result extends to the Touchard sequence Tn(λ) = Pk S(n, k)λk for every fixed λ > 0. For each integer m ≥ 2, (−1)m∆m log Tn(λ) ∼ (m − 2)!n1−m , uniformly for λ in compact subsets of (0, ∞). We obtain two further terms in inverse powers of W(n/λ) through an arbitrary-order saddle-point expansion and direct estimates for finite differences.

The substantive study asks a deliberately implausible question: is living with a cat associated with untreated dental decay among US adults? It uses public data from NHANES 2005–2006 with survey-weighted modified Poisson regression, prespecified confounders, sensitivity analyses and equivalence testing. The preregistered primary result was inconclusive (prevalence ratio 1.12, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.36). The meta-experiment measures what producing the study took: time, human interventions, agent errors and the share of code and text written by the agent. The accompanying preprint, "Do cats rot your teeth? A by-the-book paper written by an AI agent, and what it means for scientific communication", shows how four of the 45 preregistered estimates could support a positive paper without breaking the registration, and argues that verification, not writing, is now the bottleneck of scientific communication. Version 1 (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23435708) is the frozen preregistration, deposited before any exposure–outcome association was computed and later registered on OSF (doi:10.17605/OSF.IO/RVH7J). Its files remain available in version 1. summary: We develop a counterfactual semantics based on reopening partial information states. Evaluation first removes enough stated content to leave the antecedent’s attributes unresolved, retaining what the chosen scope protects, then asserts the antecedent and considers the surviving consistent refinements. Would and might quantify over the admissible alternatives; a weighted extension supplies graded evaluations. The principal result concerns finite models with fully supported residues. When a conjunctive antecedent reopens each constituent attribute, adding a supported conjunct can remove the grounds of another conclusion. A four-attribute countermodel therefore violates Cautious Monotony, excluding any smooth preferential representation that preserves the evaluable verdicts. We also establish a sufficient nesting condition for Cut and exhibit its failure without that condition. The conjunctive reopening rule is an explicit interpretive commitment; its suitability for ordinary-language counterfactuals remains an empirical question. The account uses declared dependencies, scope restrictions, and priorities, while the quantitative extension assumes a weight kernel. Comparisons with belief revision, premise semantics, update semantics, and causal intervention identify the consequences of reopening an attribute rather than merely making its proposed value consistent with retained information.

summary: Replication package for the article Unequal Rewards and the Direction of Scientific Work: Evidence from U.S. Public Universities . It contains the code, the estimation data and the documentation needed to reproduce every table, figure and number reported in the article and its online appendix. Study The article links administrative payroll records of tenure-line faculty at 93 U.S. public universities (fiscal years 2004–2026) to their publication records in OpenAlex. For each department it estimates a department-specific pay equation and measures the pay dispersion that the department’s formal ladder (rank, contract basis, seniority) does not explain. This residualized Gini is related to five dimensions of members’ research: productivity, citations, novelty, conventionality and disruption. The analytic sample has 124,056 department-person records, covering 105,050 faculty members in 4,839 departments. Contents README.md : overview, layout, coding of identifiers, environment. HANDOFF_FOR_AI_AGENTS.md : the pipeline end to end (inputs, outputs, run order, checkpoints), with a map from each table, figure and number of the paper to the script and file that produce it. Written for an AI agent or a human reader.  DATA_DICTIONARY.md : every column of every data file in 3_analysis/ . 1_data_collection/ : code that acquired and parsed the public salary disclosures, plus the department backfill, Wayback supplement (code only). 2_data_cleaning_and_linking/ : code that assembled the salary panel, standardized names, ranks and departments, linked faculty to OpenAlex authors, and computed the work-level measures (code only). 3_analysis/ : the pseudonymised estimation frames and the analysis code (first stage, panel and matching, tables, figures, appendix analyses), with the shipped outputs. run_all.sh and notebooks_step_by_step/ : the full analysis as one shell script, and the same pipeline as one Jupyter notebook per script in run order (outputs saved). Reproducing the results Install the pinned environment (Python 3.12.7 and the exact versions in requirements.txt , x86-64 Linux), then run run_all.sh or the notebooks in order. The analysis in 3_analysis/ runs end to end from the shipped frames and needs no API key; a full run takes about 15 minutes on a multi-core machine (the first-stage bootstrap runs 12 parallel processes of about 3.5 GB each; set S19_WORKERS lower on a smaller machine). run_all.sh records each step in run_status.tsv and writes a SHA-256 manifest of the outputs ( run_manifest.tsv ). Folders 1 and 2 document how the data were produced; they require the raw source caches, an OpenAlex snapshot and SciSciNet, and are not re-runnable from this package. Data and privacy The salary records are public disclosures, but they name individuals. In this replication package, universities, departments and people are replaced by codes (for example  AZ University A , AZ University A Employee 00042 ). The mapping is held by the author and is not distributed. The frames retain exact salary, fiscal year, rank, career age, state and inferred gender and race, so the data are pseudonymised. Please do not attempt to re-identify individuals. License CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Please cite the article when using this package.
